title: A 20 years' experience on granulosa cell tumour
author: Martin PJM
text: Retrospective multi-institution review from Chennai, India (records 1993/1995-2015) of 126 patients with ovarian granulosa cell tumour, mostly adult type; 34 relapsed patients are tabulated individually. Only two JGCT patients appear in the relapse table: a 14-year-old with stage Ia, 10 cm JGCT treated with fertility-sparing surgery who progressed at 7 months (pelvis), received EP and died at 7 months; and a 21-year-old with stage IIIc JGCT, fertility-sparing surgery, relapse in the pelvis, 2 cycles of chemotherapy, then lost to follow-up. Of the 126 patients, 3% were aged under 10 and 3% aged 10-19 years; precocious puberty was reported in 2% of the series. Whole-series findings (mainly adult GCT): 84-85 had complete staging, 41 incomplete surgery, 7-10 fertility-sparing surgery; patients with complete surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy did not relapse; of 34 relapsed patients, 19 survived; relapse was more frequent with tumour >9-10 cm, spill and advanced stage. Authors' discussion states juvenile type occurs in younger patients with increased recurrence risk and poorer prognosis, cites FOXL2 mutation in 97% of adult and 10% of juvenile type, and says adjuvant chemotherapy yields complete, long-lasting response in children with stage Ic JGCT with a high mitotic index (>20/HPF); these are literature statements, not results of this series. Authors conclude chemotherapy has a compelling role in advanced, inoperable and metastatic cases, with tumour spill or rupture, certain variants such as JGCT, and tumours >10 cm (abstract says >9 cm).  Largely an adult-type GCT series; contributes 2 individually described relapsed JGCT cases (one fatal at 7 months) and literature statements. JGCT numbers in the whole series are not reported.

title: Premature Thelarche and Precocious Puberty in a Three-Year-Old Girl with Granulosa Cell Tumor
author: Ghanbari Z
text: A 3-year-old girl presented to the pediatric clinic of the Children's Hospital (Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Iran) in July 2011 with breast enlargement (premature thelarche), abdominal swelling and pain, and no significant past medical history. Pelvic ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic solid mass; abdominopelvic MRI with and without contrast showed a left adnexal enhancing mass with multiple cystic components pushing bowel loops to the right with tumor adhesion to anterior bowel loops. Microscopic features of the resected mass were reported as characteristic of juvenile granulosa cell tumor (figure legend: with hyaline globules); no hormone levels, immunohistochemistry, stage, surgical procedure details or follow-up are reported. The author concludes precocious puberty may be the most common presentation of GCT in children and that ovarian tumors must be considered among its causes; the discussion also states stage I disease is treated by unilateral oophorectomy without adjuvant chemotherapy and that prognosis depends on stage, with better prognosis in premenarchal girls than adults.  Brief case report of a 3-year-old with JGCT presenting as precocious puberty; very limited clinical detail (no hormones, stage, treatment or outcome).

title: Ascites as a Sole Presentation of Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor
author: Dhaiban M
text: 2-year-old girl (consanguineous parents; two earlier siblings died at 3 months and 2 years of unknown causes) with 2 months of urinary retention and gradual abdominal distention; no signs of precocious puberty. Ultrasound: 11.5 x 6.7 cm mixed solid-cystic pelvic mass with gross ascites; CT: heterogeneous solid-cystic mass (11 x 8.1 x 7.5 cm) arising from the left adnexa without calcification, ascites, no lymphadenopathy. AFP and beta-hCG normal. Left salpingo-oophorectomy with 1 L ascites drained; ascitic fluid cytology negative for malignant cells; tumor 1.3 kg, capsule intact; staged FIGO IA; bone scan and chest radiograph normal. Histology: diffuse sheets and macrofollicular pattern, polygonal cells, atypical nuclei without grooves, mitoses more than 10/10 HPF, focal luteinization, consistent with JGCT; IHC positive for inhibin and CD99, negative for EMA, CD117 and AFP. Outcome: well at 3 months; no adjuvant chemotherapy given; long-term follow-up planned because of late recurrence risk. Authors claim this is the first reported JGCT stage IA with massive ascites and tumor-cell-negative ascitic fluid; they note ascites occurs in about 10% of JGCT, usually with advanced stage or rupture, and cite another case (age 13, stage IC) with massive ascites. Authors state (citing literature) that JGCT is about 5% of granulosa cell tumors, stage IA is treated by unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy alone, 5-year survival is up to 90% for stage IA, and late recurrence requires lifelong follow-up.  Case of pediatric JGCT presenting with massive ascites and urinary retention rather than precocious puberty, stage IA, with IHC.

title: Juvenile granulosa tumor of the ovary: Report of two cases
author: Lahfaoui M
text: Two girls, 8 and 11 years, presenting with abdominopelvic pain and a rapidly enlarging abdominal mass (about 25 x 20 cm and 30 x 20 cm on examination) without signs of hormonal hypersecretion. Case 1: ultrasound and CT showed a multicompartment cystic mass; AFP and beta-hCG normal; surgery found a 25 x 20 cm left ovarian tumor with serous effusion; ovariectomy with normal margins; immunostaining confirmed juvenile granulosa cell tumor; multidisciplinary decision for no chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Case 2: CT showed a 32 x 21 cm semi-solid cystic right laterouterine mass; laparoscopic right cystectomy first, histology showed tumor within margins but a partial resection, so she was re-operated with right adnexectomy, peritoneal biopsies and endometrial curettage; final stage pT1a with no residual tumor, normal endometrium and negative peritoneal biopsies. Histology of case 2: predominantly cystic tumor of partially luteinized proliferating granulosa cells with variable thecal cell proliferation; high vimentin positivity reported. Both patients received adnexectomy without chemotherapy and follow-up (clinical, radiological, and AMH/inhibin in case 2) was uneventful; follow-up duration is not stated. The authors cite 5% of ovarian tumors in children and adolescents, 97% unilateral with mean size 12.5 cm, and 92% 5-year survival, with poor prognostic factors large size, ascites and capsular rupture.  Two pediatric JGCT cases, both large (25-32 cm) stage I tumors treated by surgery alone, including one restaging after cystectomy.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell ovarian tumors: Report of a case
author: Djelti S
text: Case report from Oran, Algeria: 33-year-old mother of two, labeled juvenile granulosa cell tumor, presenting with paroxysmal left pelvic pain. Ultrasound: heterogeneous left lateral uterine mass 10 cm with solid and fluid components and moderate ascites. CT: well-circumscribed pelvic mass about 80x110 mm enhancing after contrast with fluid areas and calcification, free ascites, no lymphadenopathy. CA 125 62.84 U/ml; biology otherwise unremarkable. Laparotomy: solid-cystic grayish-white tumor of about 8x12 cm with necrotic and hemorrhagic changes and citrine ascites; enucleation cystectomy done first; ascitic fluid cytology negative for malignant cells. Pathology of the specimen suggested granulosa cell tumor (no immunohistochemistry or mitotic counts are given for this patient). A second laparotomy completed surgery with total hysterectomy, bilateral adnexectomy, pelvic lymph node dissection and omentectomy: no residual tumor; three right and four left lymph nodes reactive; staged pT1a pN0 pMx. Authors' discussion (cited statements): JGCT is 5% of granulosa tumors; classically in women under 30 or prepubertal; 92% 5-year survival; poor prognostic factors are large size, ascites and capsular rupture; pseudo-precocious puberty reveals the tumor in 70% of cases; surgery is the treatment, conservative in young women wanting pregnancy with stage Ia. The authors chose radical surgery for this stage Ia patient because of the ascites and capsular rupture.  Low-value single report of a tumor labeled JGCT in a 33-year-old with no IHC or mitotic data, so the juvenile-type classification is unsupported in the text; shows radical completion surgery chosen over fertility sparing for a ruptured stage Ia tumor.

title: Ovarian sex cord stromal tumors: an institutional experience
author: Bhargava S
text: Retrospective histopathology series at SMS Medical College, Jaipur (July 2009 to June 2017): 158 ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors, ages 8 to 82 years, most commonly 30-40 years (22.8%) and 40-50 years (17.7%, text says maximum in 40-50 group). Histologic types: adult granulosa cell tumor 67 (42.4%), juvenile granulosa cell tumor 8 (5.1%), fibroma 31 (19.6%), Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor 24 (15.2%), fibrothecoma 14 (8.9%), sclerosing stromal tumor 7 (4.4%), thecoma 6 (3.8%), sex cord tumor with annular tubules 1. Whole series presentation: abdominal pain and lump 81, menstrual irregularity 49, anorexia and weight loss 14, virilization 12, precocious puberty 2; 152 tumors were unilateral and 6 bilateral (3 granulosa cell tumors, 2 fibromas, 1 SCTAT); 87 solid and 71 solid-cystic; 142 of 158 measured 5-15 cm. No JGCT-specific age, stage, treatment or outcome data are given. The authors note their JGCT percentage exceeds that of Cartault and Schneider and resembles Haroon et al. Authors conclude sex cord-stromal tumors are rare in Indian women and need a high index of suspicion and clinicopathological correlation.  Provides only a JGCT frequency (8/158, 5.1%) among ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors in one Indian institution.

title: Single tertiary care centre experience of ovarian granulosa cell tumour in Chennai, India: a retrospective analysis
author: Deenadayalan T
text: Single-centre retrospective series (Madras Medical College, Chennai, 2011-2015) of 25 ovarian granulosa cell tumors (4% of ovarian cancers in that period): 23 adult-type (92%) and 2 juvenile-type (8%); median age 48 years (range 7-70), median follow-up 48 months. JGCT patient 1: diagnosed at 7 years in 2012 with precocious puberty and mastalgia; fertility-sparing operation then observation; disease free at last follow-up. JGCT patient 2: diagnosed at 19 years with torsion of an ovarian mass and virilisation features; fertility-sparing operation then observation; pelvic and omental metastasis at 13 months; three lines of palliative chemotherapy (EP, docetaxel plus carboplatin, oral cyclophosphamide); died, overall survival 21 months. Whole series: 84% FIGO stage Ia (n=21), Ib 2, Ic 1, IIIa 1; 13 (52%) had complete staging; only two patients received adjuvant chemotherapy (EP); 5 patients (20%) recurred, mean time to relapse 29.6 months (95% CI 12.3-46.8) and one died of disease; estimated mean overall survival 84.8 months (95% CI 74.3-95.4). Tumor size >9.7 cm (ROC cut-off) had more recurrence events (HR 1.058) but the log-rank association was not significant (P=0.839); menopausal status, torsion, stage, age and residual tumor were not significantly associated with recurrence or survival. The authors conclude that patients with JGCT have a poorer prognosis than adult subtype, citing 'we also documented ... the worse prognosis of juvenile subtype', although this rests on 2 patients (1 recurrence and death); they also quote FOXL2 mutation in 97% of adult and 10% of juvenile GCT (D'Angelo 2011) and that JGCT adjuvant chemotherapy is usually recommended for stage IC with mitotic index >20/10 HPF.  Mostly adult granulosa cell tumor series; includes two JGCT cases (one disease free, one fatal relapse at 21 months) and cites background JGCT facts. Weak evidence on JGCT prognosis.

title: Gynandroblastoma: a rare case report of ovarian sex cord tumour
author: Tanouti S
text: 61-year-old postmenopausal woman with an abdominopelvic mass and no virilization; ultrasound showed a latero-uterine mass of 27.8 cm, predominantly cystic with a partial solid component; CT showed a left adnexal heterogeneous cystic mass with a peripheral solid component. AFP 2.53 ng/mL, CEA 2.43 ng/mL, CA19-9 3.19 U/mL and CA125 30 U/mL were within normal range (hCG not measured); hormonal work-up (estrogen, testosterone) was not done. Laparotomy showed no peritoneal implants and negative peritoneal washing; left adnexectomy was done with biopsies; specimen weighed 4500 g with two cystic masses (25 x 20 x 15 cm and 20 x 13 x 6 cm) joined by a firm pale-yellow nodular area. Histology: mixed tumor with Sertoli component (tubules lined by 2-3 cell layers), Leydig cell nests and juvenile granulosa cells; juvenile granulosa cells and Sertoli-Leydig cells were alpha-inhibin positive; diagnosis gynandroblastoma. Completion total hysterectomy, right adnexectomy and omentectomy were benign. Close observation without adjuvant chemotherapy (clinical review every 3 months for 2 years, markers every 6 months, yearly imaging years 2-5); at 2 years inhibin A, inhibin B and AFP negative with no suspicious imaging. Literature cited: a meta-analysis of 22 gynandroblastoma cases reported no recurrence over 6 months to 13 years, with unilateral adnexectomy in 17/22; tumors mostly stage I; the authors call for a registry to define management.  Case of ovarian gynandroblastoma with a juvenile granulosa cell component in a postmenopausal woman; limited JGCT-specific information (histology, inhibin positivity, no recurrence at 2 years).

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour in the third trimester of pregnancy
author: Gaughran J
text: 26-year-old nulliparous woman (BMI 31) in her first pregnancy; enlarged polycystic right ovary (85 cc) was seen at the 20-week scan, but she missed follow-up and re-presented at 37 weeks with a 139 x 107 x 105 mm solid mass with cystic areas, moderate Doppler flow, footling breech and a fetus at the 5th centile. Non-contrast MRI showed a 13 x 7.5 cm complex right adnexal mass with hemorrhage and no restricted diffusion, read as a presumed benign process such as torsion, conflicting with the malignant-appearing ultrasound. Pre-operative markers: inhibin B 3220 pg/ml (reference 0-341), AFP 44.5 kIU/L (0-5.8), LDH 307 U/L (135-214), CA-125 55 kU/L (0-35), CA 15-3 18 kU/L (normal). Caesarean section with right salpingo-oophorectomy, omental and uterine serosa biopsies and washings: 790 g tumor with extensive infarction and hemorrhage; omental and ligament biopsies and washings negative; no capsular breach; viable tumor cells at a uterine serosa adhesion site. Histology: sheets of round-to-oval cells with eosinophilic or clear vacuolated cytoplasm, follicle-like spaces, easily found mitoses; IHC diffuse inhibin, CD56, pancytokeratin and SMA; focal calretinin, S100 and MNF116; PAX8, WT1, GATA3, EMA and CD10 negative. Difficult classification (differential pregnancy luteoma, GCT, Sertoli-Leydig tumor); expert review (McCluggage) favored juvenile granulosa cell tumor because of architecture and intermediate-size follicles; MDT diagnosis stage IA JGCT. Follow-up: inhibin B normal at <9.8 pg/ml and CT without disease at first review; 3-monthly inhibin for the first year and 10-year follow-up planned. Authors discuss diagnostic difficulty in pregnancy, MRI limits, that pregnancy produces disorderly cell arrangement, edema and luteinization not usually seen in non-pregnant JGCT, and note chemotherapy is not usually given in stage IA.  JGCT detected in the third trimester of pregnancy in an adult (26 years), with marked inhibin B elevation and mildly raised AFP; illustrates diagnostic challenge and fertility-preserving surgery.

title: A case of ovarian juvenile granulosa cells tumor with peritoneal and jejunal localisation at Amath Dansokho Regional Hospital, Kedougou, Senegal
author: Wade M
text: Case report from a level-2 rural hospital in Kedougou, Senegal (702 km from Dakar): 18-year-old with abdominal and pelvic pain, nausea and vomiting and a voluminous solid mobile right pelvic mass. Ultrasound: heterogeneous myometrium with multiple hypoechoic subcentimetric nodules and a heterogeneous adnexal mass of 18 cm; CT not performed; tumor markers (inhibin, AFP, hCG, CA125, LDH) were not available. Labs: anemia 7.1 g/dl, thrombocytosis 611,000/mm3, CRP 138.3 mg/l, renal failure (creatinine reported as 35.4 mg/l). Laparotomy: friable 20 cm right ovarian tumor with adhesions to the abdominal wall, a solid obstructive 7 cm jejunal tumor 40 cm from the angle of Treitz with upstream dilatation, lymphadenopathy, no ascites or liver nodules. Right adnexectomy, jejunal resection with anastomosis and omentectomy were performed; occlusion at 10 days led to re-laparotomy showing numerous large celiac lymph nodes obstructing the duodenum and anastomotic suture loosening; anastomosis redone with gastro-enteric anastomosis; cardiac arrest on day 1 after the repeat operation was not recovered (death). Histology: ovarian tumor of small monomorphic cells with abundant basophilic cytoplasm, ovoid vesicular nuclei and rare mitoses; tumor invading the jejunum; diagnosis juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the right ovary extending to jejunum and peritoneum; retrospectively classified FIGO stage IIIC. Authors' conclusion: prognosis is mostly favorable with early diagnosis; delayed diagnosis in the rural context is associated with high risk of pre- and intraoperative peritoneal spread; stage is the key prognostic factor (cited: stage Ia survival 83-98%, median survival 5 years for stages III-IV).  Fatal late-presenting JGCT in a resource-limited setting with jejunal and peritoneal extension; illustrates consequences of diagnostic delay and absence of marker and imaging availability.

title: A rare encounter with juvenile granulosa cell tumor: diagnosis, management, and outcome
author: Gupta S
text: A 19-year-old nulliparous woman had 8 months of lower abdominal pain and bloating with regular menses; a firm 20-week-sized pelvic mass was palpable. CA-125, AFP, LDH, beta-hCG and CA 19.9 were normal; ultrasound showed an 18 x 9 cm multiseptated cyst and MRI a large multiseptated right abdominopelvic mass read as suggestive of mucinous cystadenoma. Intraoperatively a trilobed 15 x 10 x 18 cm adnexal mass had one lobe ruptured; frozen section suggested a borderline surface epithelial tumor; staging was FIGO IC1 intraoperatively. Final histopathology: JGCT with omental micrometastasis, pT3aN0; IHC positive for inhibin, PR, calretinin, WT1; negative for p63, CK7, CK20, synaptophysin, chromogranin, ER. Tumor board recommended adjuvant paclitaxel and carboplatin; four cycles were completed and the patient was in remission at one year under three-monthly surveillance. Authors conclude for early recognition, comprehensive surgical staging and adjuvant therapy and long-term follow-up; discussion (literature-based) says chemotherapy is reserved for advanced/recurrent cases and late recurrence beyond 4 years has been reported.  Young-adult (19 y) JGCT with omental micrometastasis treated with fertility-sparing surgery and carboplatin/paclitaxel.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor: A Case Report
author: Vijayamohanan L
text: 19-year-old woman with hirsutism, clitoromegaly and oligomenorrhea (cycles every 45-60 days) and a palpable pelvic-origin abdominal mass. CT and MRI: cystic left ovarian mass, thick-walled and multiloculated, with minimal ascites. Estradiol 400 pg/mL (reference 63.9-356.7), FSH 0.40 and LH 2.00 mIU/mL (below reference ranges); AFP, hCG, CEA, CA 19-9 and inhibin B within normal limits. Unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy specimen: 22 x 15 x 6 cm ovarian mass (tube 8.5 cm), solid grey-white cut surface with small mucinous cysts. Histology: follicles with eosinophilic material between sheets of round to polyhedral cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and occasional grooves, luteinized cells, thecomatous/fibromatous stroma, mitotic index 3 per HPF, marked necrosis and hemorrhage; focal areas resembling poorly differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor. Reticulin stain showed a paucity of reticulin in thecomatous foci (granulosa nature) with reticulin surrounding tumor cell nests; IHC positive for vimentin, CD99, CD56 and cytokeratin AE1/AE3 (inhibin result not stated). Diagnosis: JGCT; omentum free of tumor. Authors' conclusions: JGCT is uncommon, accurate histopathologic diagnosis is key, and fertility-sparing surgery is appropriate; their discussion notes this patient's age and androgenic presentation differ from the typical prepubertal estrogenic presentation.  Case of a 19-year-old with an androgenic presentation and large JGCT with focal Sertoli-Leydig-like areas; relevant to differential diagnosis and the use of reticulin stain.

title: Juvenille granulosa cell tumor of the ovary in 15-year-old patient (Ziarniszczak jajnika u 15-letniej pacjentki wczesniej leczonej z powodu guza mozgu)
author: Jablonska K
text: Case report from the Children's Memorial Health Institute, Warsaw (article in Polish with English abstract): 15-year-old girl with a testosterone-secreting juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the right ovary whose main sign was a lowered voice for about 6 months. Pre-operative labs: testosterone 2.920 and 3.410 ng/ml (reference <0.950), androstenedione 410 ng/dl (90-300), 17-OHP 2.79 ng/ml (0.11-1.14), DHEAS 1648 ng/ml (normal range), estradiol 21 pg/ml and gonadotropins normal (LH 14.12, FSH 4.85 mIU/ml); tumor markers negative (beta-hCG 0.16, AFP 1.26, CA 125 10.10 U/ml, HE4 20 pmol/l). Ultrasound: enlarged right ovary 43x30x41 mm, solid-cystic, smooth wall; left ovary not seen. MRI: right ovary entirely replaced by a well-demarcated solid-cystic tumor with septa and mural nodules enhancing after contrast, about 39x31x43 mm, no fat, no lymphadenopathy; left ovary 14x6x12 mm. Laparoscopy found left ovarian hypoplasia; karyotype 46,XX and FISH excluded Y chromosome material. Tumor enucleated to preserve fertility. Histology: 4x2.5x2.5 cm cystic beige-brown tumor with a hyperemic capsule area; cystic and solid fields, edema, many luteinized cells; tumor tissue in the coagulation line; 6 mitoses per 10 HPF; Ki-67 up to 30%; inhibin alpha positive, CK7 negative, Melan-A focally positive, EMA negative; stage at least T1a Nx Mx (FIGO I). Because of tumor cells at the coagulation line and the tumor's character, a second laparoscopy removed the remaining right ovary and tube (no tumor cells; pelvic fluid negative; left ovarian cyst biopsy normal), followed by 3 cycles of PVB. After surgery testosterone fell to 0.464 ng/ml, androstenedione to 99 ng/dl, and urinary steroid profile normalized; estradiol remained normal. Authors' discussion: androgen secretion is more often reported in adult-type GCT; they cite Young et al. (125 JGCT: precocious puberty 82%, irregular or absent menses 15%, 2 with Ollier disease and 2 with Maffucci syndrome) and note that late recurrence can occur even in stage I JGCT, so long follow-up is needed. They conclude that an optimal treatment strategy for JGCT is needed to avoid unnecessary procedures and preserve quality of life and fertility.  Case of androgen-secreting JGCT in an adolescent with prior brain tumor chemo-radiotherapy; shows fertility-sparing enucleation followed by completion surgery and PVB because of positive margin.

title: Survival benefit of lymphadenectomy in patients with early-stage juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary: a single center retrospective cohort study
author: Li Z
text: Single-center (West China Second Hospital) retrospective cohort, March 2013 to February 2022: 16 early-stage JGCT patients met criteria, one excluded (stage III by omental micrometastasis), 15 analysed: 8 with lymphadenectomy, 7 without. Mean age 17.0 +/- 9.08 years (range 3-31); the non-lymphadenectomy group was much younger (9.33 vs 22.11 years, P=0.003); 5/15 (33.3%) pre-pubertal; mean tumor diameter 14.23 +/- 10.37 cm (range 4-35); rupture in 10/15 (66.7%); CA-125 >=35 IU/mL in 6/15. No lymph node metastasis was found in any of the 8 patients who had lymphadenectomy. Median follow-up 31.87 months (range 2-85): 3/15 (20.0%) relapsed (2 no-lymphadenectomy, 1 lymphadenectomy); 3-year DFS 80.0% and OS 93.3%; lymphadenectomy status not associated with DFS (P=0.40). Relapses at median 12 months (range 6-20) in the abdomen/pelvis (2) and sigmoid colon (1), all treated with surgery plus chemotherapy; one patient died of disease (age 18, USO, TC x3 adjuvant, relapse at 6 months); CA-125 at relapse 89.7, 77.5 and 171.9 IU/mL. Adjuvant chemotherapy in 8/15 (BEP 4, BVP 1, TC 3), seven with more than three cycles; no DFS difference between chemotherapy and none. Authors conclude fertility-sparing surgery is the treatment of choice and prognosis good, and that lymphadenectomy showed no survival benefit in early-stage JGCT in their limited data; larger multicenter studies are needed. Authors note 20 JGCT diagnosed at their hospital over 9 years, with peritoneal metastases in 5.  Directly addresses whether lymphadenectomy adds benefit in early-stage ovarian JGCT; small retrospective cohort with confounded groups (age).

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor and High Blood Ca-125 Levels in Children with Pseudo-Meigs Syndrome
author: Ciftci I
text: A 2-year-old girl presented with one month of breast enlargement (Tanner III), abdominal distension and a 15 cm mobile mass, with ascites and right pleural effusion (pseudo-Meigs syndrome). CA-125 was 366 U/mL (normal 0-35) and estradiol 602.5 pg/mL (normal 6.0-27). Ultrasound/MRI showed a 12 x 7.5 cm (US) to 13 x 10 x 8 cm (MRI) cystic-solid mass with peripheral enhancement and necrosis, thought to arise from the left ovary. At surgery a 15 cm capsulated left ovarian tumor adherent to the left uterine cornu and omentum was removed with the cornu and tube; pathology size 17 x 16 x 15 cm; solid islets and follicle-like structures, no nuclear grooves, notable mitoses, occasional theca cells. At 1 month CA-125 fell to 12 U/mL, estradiol to 30 pg/mL, and the hydrothorax had disappeared; follow-up showed no problems (duration not specified). Authors state this was the youngest reported JGCT with pseudo-Meigs syndrome and that thoracic intervention is unnecessary unless respiratory distress is present.  Toddler JGCT presenting with pseudo-Meigs syndrome, high CA-125 and estradiol that normalized after surgery.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor with massive ascites: A case report and immunohistochemical study of ascites formation
author: Takeuchi K
text: 23-year-old nulliparous woman with two weeks of progressive abdominal distention and no menstrual irregularity; MRI showed a multilocular cystic and solid right ovarian mass with large ascites. Preoperative CA-125 244 U/ml (normal <35), estradiol 2760 pg/ml, FSH and LH both <0.10 U/ml; AFP <0.7 ng/ml, CEA 2.0, CA19-9 0.6 and testosterone 0.76 ng/ml were normal. At laparotomy the dark reddish encapsulated right ovarian tumor was edematous and fragile and ruptured during the procedure; no peritoneal implants; about 5 L of transudate ascites were drained and ascitic cytology was negative; tumor resection with right salpingo-oophorectomy and partial omentectomy was done (stage I). Histology: granulosa cells around microfollicles with hyperchromatic nuclei, frequent mitoses, no Call-Exner bodies; strong calretinin and alpha-inhibin positivity supported JGCT. VEGF staining was diffuse in tumor cell cytoplasm and partly in endothelial cells, with CD34 microvessel density above 60 vessels per visual field; the authors speculate that VEGF-driven angiogenesis and capillary permeability caused the massive ascites. After surgery the ascites disappeared rapidly, CA-125 and estradiol decreased, LH and FSH increased, and there was no recurrence 12 months postoperatively; no adjuvant therapy is described. VEGF Adult-age JGCT presenting only with massive ascites and very high estradiol; adds VEGF and microvessel immunohistochemistry as a possible mechanism for ascites.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor in a 35-year-old pregnant woman: A rare case report
author: Sharma JD
text: Case report from Guwahati, India: 35-year-old woman at 14 weeks of gestation with sudden left abdominal and lower back pain; ultrasound showed an adnexal mass (reported as '90 cm' in diameter in the text); CA 125, CEA, CA 19.9, AFP, LDH and beta-hCG all normal. Left ovarian tumor resection: 13x12x5 cm tumor with ruptured capsule, solid grayish-white cut surface with focal papillaroid and hemorrhagic areas. Histology: round to oval cells with hyperchromatic vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, irregular nuclear contours, occasional nuclear grooves and numerous mitoses; no Call-Exner bodies. IHC: strong diffuse nuclear WT1, patchy panCK, focal calretinin, CK7 negative; diagnosis JGCT. Recurrence 3 months later treated by left ovariotomy (JGCT on histology); she delivered a healthy baby at term by cesarean section 2 months later with heavy vaginal bleeding; hysterectomy with salpingo-oophorectomy again showed JGCT. She developed ascites a few weeks later; adjuvant chemotherapy was advised and she remains under follow-up (duration not stated). Authors' background and discussion (cited, not original): JGCT is 5% of GCT with average age at diagnosis 13 years and only 3% diagnosed after age 30 (Young: 4 of 125 over 30); about 90% are stage I at diagnosis; advanced stages recur or cause death within 3 years; adjuvant chemotherapy recommended for stage IC or higher or mitotic index above 20/10 HPF; pregnancy tumors can show disorderly arrangement and many luteinized cells. Authors' conclusion: JGCT is uncommon in pregnancy and can be dangerous because it often goes unnoticed.  Single case of aggressive recurrent JGCT diagnosed in pregnancy at age 35 (outside the usual age range), with WT1/calretinin IHC; no stage given and limited follow-up.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary: A rare cause of precocious puberty in a toddler
author: Salih KA
text: Case report from Trivandrum, India: 18-month-old girl with isosexual peripheral precocious puberty (breast enlargement, pubic hair, vaginal bleeding) and a palpable left lower abdominal mass of 8x5 cm. Labs: estradiol 351 pg/mL (<10), LH 0.01 mIU/mL and FSH 0.49 mIU/mL (suppressed), inhibin A 790 pg/mL (<7), hCG and AFP normal. Ultrasound: heterogeneously hyperechoic solid pelvic lesion with cystic areas and internal vascularity, 8x4x7.2 cm, no calcification, mildly bulky uterus with 6 mm endometrium, normal right ovary. Laparotomy: uniformly enlarged left ovary with solid, freely mobile 7x6x4 cm tumor, 10-15 mL serous fluid with negative cytology, no lymph node enlargement; left oophorectomy with staging. Histology: well-encapsulated, predominantly solid with trabeculated cystic areas; macrofollicular, microcystic, cord and pseudopapillary patterns; polygonal cells, pleomorphic vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, no nuclear grooving; 7-9 mitotic figures per hpf; inhibin A positive; FIGO stage IA. After surgery breast size and pubic hair regressed, bleeding stopped and estradiol normalized; free of recurrence at 30 months. Authors' discussion (cited statements): isosexual precocity occurs in 70-80% of prepubertal girls with GCT but GCT causes only 1% of precocity in girls; 5-year survival 90-95% for stage I JGCT and 25-50% for advanced; adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy needed for stage IC and IIIC or high mitotic rate; recurrences mostly in the first 3 years but late recurrence can occur; inhibin/AMH follow-up recommended. Authors' conclusion: JGCT must be included in the differential diagnosis of girls with precocious puberty; timely complete excision normalizes hormones; ovary-preserving operations should be performed when feasible.  Case of an infant (18 months) JGCT with very high inhibin A and precocious pseudopuberty, treated by oophorectomy alone at stage IA with 30-month disease-free follow-up.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell ovarian tumor- a rare presentation
author: Saha E
text: 14-year-old previously healthy girl with regular menses presented with 5 days of acute abdominal pain and gross distension; clinically suspected gut perforation. No palpable lump, mildly anemic. Ultrasound: multilobulated cystic mass about 11.5 x 7 cm in the right ovarian region with moderate peritoneal fluid; plain abdominal X-ray normal. At laparotomy about 3 L of yellowish watery mucous fluid escaped; 12 x 7 cm multilobulated cystic right ovarian mass with a ruptured capsule, no peritoneal seedlings or enlarged nodes; peritoneal fluid cytology negative; staging done and right salpingo-oophorectomy performed (no frozen-section facility). Histopathology confirmed JGCT (immature nuclei, atypia, high mitotic rate); final FIGO stage IC; referred to an oncologist and healthy without recurrence at time of reporting (duration not stated). No tumor markers or immunohistochemistry reported. Discussion cites literature: JGCT about 5% of granulosa cell tumors; 97% of patients under 30; about 90% FIGO stage I at presentation with 5-year survival 90-100%; stage II 55-75% and stage III-IV 22-50%; ascites in about 10% and rupture at presentation in 10%; cisplatin-based multidrug regimens used in advanced or recurrent disease; inhibin for monitoring.  Case of adolescent JGCT presenting as acute abdomen with ruptured capsule and ascites, stage IC, treated by fertility-sparing surgery.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Tumor of the Ovary: Case Report
author: Mazouzi C
text: Case report from Bejaia, Algeria: a 38-year-old woman (four children; mother and aunt with breast cancer) with left-sided abdominopelvic pain and 3 months of amenorrhea; examination showed a firm, regular, painless, mobile abdominopelvic mass. Ultrasound showed a lateral uterine mass with mixed, solid-predominant content; CA125 was 18; MRI showed a solid-cystic mass with multiple fluid compartments and a tissue portion with high signal on b1000 diffusion, homogeneously enhancing, no hemorrhagic component. Laparotomy found a regular, encapsulated solid left ovarian tumor about 10 cm without capsular rupture and two 4 cm uterine fibroids; left adnexectomy and myomectomy were performed. Pathology was reported as 'juvenile granulosa tumor' with diffuse proliferation forming small lacunae/Call-Exner bodies and monomorphic cuboidal cells with grooved nuclei ('coffee bean'), classified pT1Nx, confined to the ovary; the postoperative course was favorable and a reoperation with additional wide excision was decided. The discussion is generic to granulosa cell tumors (95% adult-type, stage I in 78-91%, 5-year survival 95% stage I, late recurrence up to 37 years) and no immunohistochemistry, hormone assays or molecular testing are reported.  Case report titled as JGCT, but the described features and the discussion are adult-type; limited as evidence for JGCT.

title: Adolescent Girl with a Left Adnexal Solid-Cystic Mass-Granulosa Cell Tumor: A Case Report
author: Rundla SR
text: A 15-year-old girl had a year of intermittent lower abdominal pain and a firm, non-tender left lower abdominal mass; no menstrual irregularity or other hormonal symptoms. Ultrasound and CECT showed an 8 x 10 cm heterogeneous solid-cystic left adnexal mass without peritoneal deposits, lymphadenopathy or significant ascites. AFP, beta-hCG, LDH and CA-125 were normal; inhibin B and AMH were not measured. At laparotomy about 50 mL of straw-colored ascitic fluid and an 8 x 10 cm left ovarian mass were found; frozen section suggested juvenile granulosa cell tumor. Left salpingo-oophorectomy with staging procedures was done; final histopathology confirmed JGCT confined to the ovary, FIGO stage IA (follicle-like structures). Recovery was uneventful; regular clinical, imaging and hormonal follow-up was advised. Authors conclude that GCT should be considered in adolescent adnexal masses even without hormonal symptoms or raised markers, and that fertility-sparing surgery gives excellent outcomes in early stage with prolonged follow-up needed.  Adolescent stage IA JGCT presenting without endocrine symptoms and with normal conventional tumor markers.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
author: Danielson D
text: A 3-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with an abdominal mass, symptoms of bowel obstruction, and precocious puberty. Abdominal radiograph raised suspicion of intussusception; ultrasound showed a large complex low anterior abdominal mass (10 x 6.6 x 9.3 cm) abutting the uterine fundus, with an endometrial stripe of about 7 mm. Serum estradiol was 'dramatically elevated' (no value given). CT showed a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous, enhancing mass with cystic and solid components, no calcifications, free abdominal/pelvic fluid, no lymphadenopathy, and prominent subareolar breast tissue. Treatment was laparotomy with tumor resection and unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy; diagnosis was juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary. No histology details, stage or follow-up are given. Discussion (citing Young et al. 1984): of 125 JGCT patients, 78% presented within the first 2 decades; hyperestrogenism (precocious puberty) is typical; most patients are stage I with favorable prognosis, stage II-IV have higher recurrence; the role of chemotherapy/radiation is uncertain; long-term follow-up recommended.  Radiology teaching case of a prepubertal JGCT with imaging features and background statements; no outcome data.

title: Neonatal juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the testis
author: Liu S
text: Newborn boy (39 weeks gestation) with an enlarged right testicle at birth; ultrasound showed a 7 mm mixed solid and cystic mass at the inferior pole of the right testicle (testis 0.8 x 0.7 x 1.3 cm) with internal color Doppler flow; left testis normal; AFP and other tumor markers normal for age. Partial orchiectomy was performed; histology showed a mucinous lesion with cystic regions surrounded by granulosa cells; final diagnosis juvenile granulosa cell tumor; he recovered uneventfully and was discharged on day 8. Discussion (from cited literature): testicular JGCT is benign, about 3% of primary testicular tumors in boys under 12, the most common testicular sex cord-stromal tumor in infancy with fewer than 100 reported cases; about half present in the first days of life and over 90% by 6 months. Cited features: normal AFP for age (excludes yolk sac tumor), inhibin-alpha positivity, no precocious puberty, association with Y-chromosome structural abnormalities, ultrasound showing cystic or partly cystic mass 0.8-5.0 cm; no recurrence or metastasis reported after orchiectomy or testis-sparing enucleation, and enucleation is advocated when AFP is normal.  Neonatal testicular JGCT treated with partial orchiectomy; background statements summarize benign behavior and testis-sparing options.

title: Pseudo-precocious puberty secondary to Juvenile Granulosa cell tumour in a 30-month-old female toddler: A case report
author: Oni TE
text: A 30-month-old Nigerian girl presented with 3 months of vaginal bleeding, breast enlargement, sparse pubic/axillary hair, accelerated height (94 cm, 97th centile) and temper tantrums; Tanner stage 2 breast and pubic hair; a 4 x 6 cm firm lower abdominal mass; bone age was normal; no cafe-au-lait spots. A 2-year history of maternal use of a steroid-containing skin cream (stopped 3 months before symptom onset) initially clouded the work-up. Estradiol was <9.0 pg/ml at presentation, 64.6 pg/ml 6 months later (reference <15), and 26.9 pg/ml 1 month after surgery; FSH and LH stayed low-normal; AFP, CA-125 and beta-hCG were normal. Ultrasound showed a 62.1 x 33.6 x 53.8 mm heterogeneous left lower abdominal mass; pelvic MRI showed a 47.8 x 38.6 x 50.4 mm round heterogeneous mass with multiple cystic foci inseparable from the left ovary. At laparotomy 7 months after presentation: encapsulated 6 x 4 cm left ovary with adherent tube, about 60 ml ascites, normal pelvic and para-aortic nodes; left oophorectomy was done. Peritoneal fluid cytology showed no malignant cells. Histology: solid sheets of tumor cells with small immature follicles containing secretions, round hyperchromatic ungrooved nuclei, occasional Call-Exner bodies, consistent with JGCT; no IHC is reported. Staged FIGO IA. No recurrence of symptoms 17 months after surgery; authors note that follow-up was hampered by financial difficulties, and conclude that rare causes such as JGCT should be considered in prepubertal girls with pseudo-precocious puberty.  Toddler ovarian JGCT with peripheral precocious puberty in Nigeria, stage IA, treated by oophorectomy alone.

title: Pseudoprecocious puberty due to functional cystic juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary in a 5-year-old girl
author: Prabhala S
text: A 5-year-old girl (21.5 kg, 113 cm, 97th percentile) presented with 10 days of scanty-to-moderate vaginal bleeding and bilateral painful breast bud enlargement (Tanner stage 2 breasts, axillary hair Tanner 1, normal external genitalia, no cafe-au-lait spots or bony deformity). Serum estradiol was 39 pg/ml (normal 6-27); CA125 13 U/ml, AFP, beta-hCG, testosterone, FSH, LH and prolactin were normal; wrist X-ray showed bone age of 6 to 7 years; chest X-ray and brain MRI were normal. Ultrasound showed an enlarged uterus and a 36 x 28 mm right ovarian cyst with smaller cysts; pelvic MRI showed a 42 x 31 x 42 mm thin-walled cystic lesion with daughter cysts and no solid component, read as a simple ovarian cyst. Cystectomy and right ovariotomy was performed; aspirated cyst fluid smears showed round hyperchromatic cells without grooving, suggesting JGCT; histology showed cysts lined by 2-10 cell-thick round-to-oval tumor cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, no nuclear grooving, eosinophilic secretions and 6-8 mitoses per 10 HPF. Immunohistochemistry: calretinin 100% positive and EMA negative; inhibin IHC was advised but not done. Diagnosis was JGCT of the right ovary, confirmed only on histopathology; the patient was lost to follow-up. The authors conclude cystic JGCT must be distinguished from functional follicular cysts in pseudoprecocious puberty, that histology and IHC help, and that long-term follow-up is essential given metastatic potential and late recurrence.  Case report of a purely cystic JGCT that mimicked a functional ovarian cyst on imaging in a 5-year-old with isosexual pseudoprecocity; no follow-up outcome.

title: Clinicopathological Evaluation of Ovarian Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor: Is Fertility-Sparing Surgery Safe?
author: Guo L
text: Retrospective single-center series (Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital of Fudan University, China; January 2004 to October 2018) of 8 surgically treated JGCT patients, ages 9 to 32 years; JGCT was 8.7% (8/92) of the center's granulosa cell tumors (AGCT 84/92). Presentation: irregular vaginal bleeding in 6, abdominal mass and pain in 2; 5/8 (62.5%) had a pelvic mass over 10 cm; all unilateral; 7 ruptured tumors; cytology negative in the 5 patients tested. Staging (FIGO 2009): 7 patients stage I (6 IC, 1 IA) had fertility-sparing surgery, median age 17 years (range 9-31); 1 patient with stage IIIC who had completed childbearing had complete surgery. Immunohistochemistry: inhibin A positive in the stage I patients and negative in the stage IIIC patient; calretinin positive in patients 1-3, 6 and 7; CD99 and vimentin positive (patients 1, 2-8 as stated); EMA negative. Mitotic counts available for only 3 patients; one had more than 20 per 10 HPF and no recurrence. Of 4 patients with pelvic lymphadenectomy versus 3 without, no difference in recurrence-free survival was found. 7 of 8 received adjuvant chemotherapy (2-7 courses): bleomycin-etoposide-carboplatin in 4 and bleomycin-vincristine-carboplatin in 3. Median follow-up was 64 months (range 2-117). No recurrence in the fertility-sparing group (overall survival 100%); the stage IIIC patient recurred and died 1 month after initial treatment. Authors' conclusion: fertility-sparing surgery seems safe for stage I JGCT in carefully selected, informed patients treated by gynecologic oncology specialists, with complete surgery considered after childbearing; the small number of cases requires larger or multicenter confirmation.  Small JGCT series (n=8) with outcomes after fertility-sparing surgery in stage I disease and adjuvant chemotherapy in nearly all; supports but cannot prove oncologic safety of fertility sparing.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound and tumors markers in diagnosis of complex ovarian cysts in adolescent, histopathological correlation
author: El saedy EKH
text: Prospective cohort of 300 patients (described as adolescents; mean age 18.9 +/- 1.3 years, 83.3% married) with ovarian cysts at Al-Azhar University Hospital (Assiut); 252 (84%) simple and 48 (16%) complex cysts on ultrasound, mean size 8.42 +/- 2.87 cm. Histopathology of the complex cysts included 27 dermoid cysts, 7 endometriomas, 8 serous cystadenomas, 3 mucinous cystadenomas, 2 immature teratomas and 1 juvenile granulosa cell tumor (2% of the complex cysts). The single JGCT was detected by ultrasound and by tumor markers (reported detection 1/1, 100%); no clinical details, stage, treatment or outcome of this patient are given. Overall ultrasound sensitivity and specificity were 87% and 84% in the text (Table 6: 87% and 79.5%), tumor markers 84% and 80%, combined ultrasound plus markers sensitivity 89.6% and specificity 83.3%. Markers measured included beta-hCG, LDH, CA-125, AFP, inhibin, estrogen and testosterone; the authors conclude that ultrasound is the first-line tool and that adding tumor markers helps exclude malignancy.  Marginal. Diagnostic-accuracy study of ovarian cysts in young women in which one JGCT is counted among 48 complex cysts; no patient-level JGCT data.

title: Hormone Secreting Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Ovary in an Infant Presenting with Massive Ascites and Precocious Pseudopuberty
author: Bhosale M
text: A 3-month-old girl presented with 10 days of abdominal distension, fever, feeding intolerance and vaginal discharge, with tachypnea, breast development (Tanner B2) and protruding vaginal mucosa (isosexual pseudo-precocious puberty). Hemoglobin 9 g%; AFP and beta-hCG normal; CA-125 160 units/ml; LDH 1000 IU/L. CT showed an enhancing solid-cystic mass of 5.2 x 5.7 x 6.3 cm and free abdominal fluid without lymphadenopathy. Laparotomy drained about 900 cc blood-tinged ascitic fluid and found a 7 x 6 x 6.5 cm solid-cystic left ovarian mass with a small capsular rent (preoperative rupture); uterus, right ovary and other organs normal. Left oophorectomy preserving the fallopian tube was performed (to preserve future fertility); one or two episodes of vaginal bleeding occurred 24 h after surgery, explained by authors as hormone withdrawal. Histology: diffuse and macrofollicular growth of round to oval cells with prominent nucleoli; IHC diffuse inhibin and vimentin, focal calretinin positivity. The authors staged the case FIGO IC although ascitic fluid showed no malignant cells. At 1 year the child was asymptomatic, tumor-free and meeting age-appropriate milestones; authors stress long-term follow-up and IHC for diagnosis, and claim this is probably the youngest JGCT with precocious puberty reported. Discussion cites Young et al. (125 ovarian JGCTs): rupture in 13 (11%), ascites in 11 (9%), isosexual pseudoprecocity in 82% of prepubertal patients.  Infant ovarian JGCT with ruptured tumor, massive ascites and precocious pseudopuberty, treated by fertility-sparing surgery alone.

title: Outcome of fertility-preserving surgery for ovarian malignancy in young women
author: Ashraf MA
text: Three-case report (immature teratoma, juvenile cystic granulosa cell tumor, dysgerminoma) of fertility-sparing surgery followed by chemotherapy in young women. JGCT case (Mrs. C, 25 years, married): acute abdominal pain with ascites; ultrasound suggested ruptured ovarian cyst (2009); laparotomy and left ovariotomy; histopathology juvenile cystic granulosa cell tumor; capsule rupture led to upstaging. She received four cycles of BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin), did not conceive for 4 years (husband had oligospermia), conceived on the second clomiphene cycle with antioxidants, delivered by cesarean for fetal distress, and had a second spontaneous pregnancy 2 years later. All three women achieved pregnancy and had normal children; there was no recurrence to date and the authors conclude tumor spill or capsule rupture should not prompt radical surgery in women wishing to preserve fertility. Authors state juvenile GCT is rarer than adult GCT and usually presents as a predominantly solid mass; BEP is the most widely used regimen for germ cell tumors, whose duration has no consensus.  One JGCT patient with ruptured tumor treated with fertility-sparing surgery plus BEP and two later pregnancies; chemotherapy choice follows a germ cell regimen.

title: Investigation of the Cause of Precocious Puberty in an 8-Year-Old Girl Ended up in Juvenile Granulosa and Theca Cell Tumor of the Ovary
author: Ordooei M
text: Case report from Yazd, Iran: 8-year-old girl with isosexual precocious puberty (Tanner III breasts, then vaginal bleeding after about 5 months) and a large left abdomino-pelvic mass. Labs: FSH 0.2 and LH 1.9 IU/l (prepubertal range), estradiol 120.9 pg/ml (reference 6-27), LDH 1040 U/l (up to 580), CA 125 469 U/ml (up to 35), inhibin A 320 pg/ml (<2.2); CA 19-9, CEA, beta-hCG and AFP normal; bone age about 12 years. Imaging: ultrasound showed a lobulated echogenic solid mass of 4 cm in the left abdomen with free fluid; contrast CT showed a 20 x 11 cm multiloculated cystic mass with marked septation, initially suggesting ovarian cystadenoma or mucinous cystadenoma. Laparoscopic resection; histopathology and ascites cytology confirmed juvenile granulosa (and theca) cell tumor with high mitotic activity, wide necrosis, calcification and bizarre nuclei; IHC positive for CD99, BCL2, progesterone receptor and cytokeratin AE1/AE3. BEP chemotherapy was started; after the third course the tumor relapsed with abdominal pain and a huge mass; complete resection (left oophorectomy, appendectomy, bowel and peritoneum), uterus, right ovary and tube preserved; stage equivalent to IIIC; BEP continued. After the second additional BEP course status deteriorated, lung metastases were detected, and the patient died 6 months after diagnosis; estradiol had fallen and breast size regressed with treatment before relapse. Authors' conclusion: because functional cysts are far more common than neoplastic masses in childhood, malignancies may be underdiagnosed, and attention to clinical features with early investigation may allow earlier diagnosis and better prognosis; they cite stage as the most important prognostic factor.  Fatal advanced-stage JGCT presenting as precocious puberty with high inhibin A and CA 125, showing relapse after 3 BEP cycles.

title: Anaesthetic Management of Malignant Granulosa Cell Tumour of Ovary in a Paediatric Patient: A Case Report
author: Dwivedi MB
text: Case report with an anaesthesia focus: 1-year-old girl, 8.5 kg, with 2 months of weight loss, abdominal swelling and pain, bilateral breast enlargement and premature pubic hair; abdominal lump about 8 x 10 cm from epigastrium to pelvis. Contrast CT: heterogeneously enhancing, well-defined abdominopelvic mass from the right adnexa up to the subhepatic region, suggestive of ovarian origin. Complete excision removed a 2900 g mass; histopathology confirmed JGCT (no immunohistochemistry or marker results given); the tumor was assigned FIGO stage I. Intraoperative course was hemodynamically stable with uneventful extubation; the authors emphasize airway, hemodynamic, respiratory and fluid risks of giant ovarian masses (vena cava compression, post-excision hypotension, pulmonary edema). Authors conclude complete surgical resection is the key prognostic factor for localized disease, with patients responding well to surgery alone. No postoperative follow-up or hormone data are reported.  Case of infantile JGCT with precocious puberty features and a very large (2900 g) stage I tumor; the report concerns anaesthetic management, with limited oncologic detail.

title: Testicular and Paratesticular Tumors in Children
author: Dörücü D
text: Narrative review of pediatric testicular and paratesticular tumors; testicular tumors are about 1% of pediatric solid tumors with incidence 0.5-2 per 100,000, peaking before age 3 and after puberty. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor is listed among gonadal stromal tumors (with Leydig and Sertoli cell tumors) and is described as a benign tumor that usually appears in the first year of life with a painless testicular mass. The review states JGCT is associated with Y-chromosome structural anomalies, mosaicism and ambiguous genitalia; histology shows solid and cystic structures surrounded by granulosa-like cells, and inhibin-alpha staining separates it from yolk sac tumor. Treatment of JGCT can be radical inguinal orchiectomy or testis-sparing surgery; the review states recurrence or metastasis is not expected. General management: AFP is the main marker (elevated in about 90% of yolk sac tumors; may be physiologically high under 1 year); testis-sparing surgery with frozen section is increasingly used because most prepubertal tumors are benign; COG staging 1-4 used in prepubertal tumors. Gonadal stromal tumors in this review: Leydig cell tumor is the most common (age 5-10); Sertoli cell tumor is second, benign under 5 years but can be malignant in older children.  General pediatric testicular tumor review with a short JGCT paragraph; JGCT statements are secondary citations without original patient data.

title: Tumor de células de la granulosa juvenil de ovario. Presentación inusual. Reporte de un caso
author: Lara E
text: Spanish-language case report of a 31-year-old woman with 6 months of abdominal enlargement and 10-15 kg weight loss; massive ascites and a large multilobulated pelvic tumor (25 x 20 cm on ultrasound, 24 x 18.5 cm on CT, 30 x 20 cm at surgery); 5 L of ascites. CA-125 389.4 IU/mL; AFP, CEA, CA 19-9 and beta-hCG were normal; no hormonal symptoms were present and preoperative inhibin B could not be measured. Laparotomy with frozen section positive for malignancy led to total hysterectomy, right salpingo-oophorectomy, pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy, omentectomy and peritoneal sampling; the lymphadenectomy was done because malignancy of epithelial origin could not be excluded. Final pathology: sex cord-stromal tumor suggestive of malignant juvenile granulosa cell tumor, vascular invasion present, ovarian surface involvement; ascitic fluid, peritoneal samples and right iliac nodes contained tumor cells; inhibin B positive; staged IIIA2. The patient was referred to medical oncology for adjuvant chemotherapy (regimen not stated); no follow-up data are reported. Authors conclude JGCT should be in the differential for young women with massive ascites and an ovarian tumor, stage at diagnosis is the main prognostic factor, and diagnosis requires histology and immunohistochemistry.  Adult-age (31 years) advanced-stage JGCT (IIIA2) presenting with massive ascites; limited by lack of treatment detail and follow-up.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Testis in a Newborn with Swelling in the Scrotum: A Rare Case and Literature Review
author: Tartar T
text: 12-day-old boy with a 1-week history of painless, mobile 2 x 2 cm left scrotal swelling; no genital anomaly, karyotype 46,XY. Scrotal ultrasound: complicated cystic lesion with 15 x 10 mm septations and occasional vascular flow, contours indistinct from testicular parenchyma; MRI: septated left testicular lesion with 15 x 11 mm cystic area; a 2 mm right epididymal cyst. The lesion was evaluated as teratoma. Markers: hCG <2 mIU/mL; AFP 33.118 ng/mL on day 7 and 2.209 ng/mL on day 25 (as printed); postoperative AFP 450 ng/mL. The authors state AFP has no diagnostic value for teratoma in infants under 6 months. Treated with high scrotal orchiectomy via left inguinal incision (testis 2 x 1.5 cm, three cysts, largest 1 cm); histopathology showed JGCT; no complications in follow-up. Orchiectomy rather than organ-sparing surgery was chosen because tumor could not be macroscopically separated from testicular tissue. Literature review table (16 entries) in the paper: the authors found 24 JGCT cases in English literature; 6 (25%) intra-abdominal, of which 3 bilateral; chromosomal or multiple anomalies (triploidy, chromosome 4 deletion) in 5 of 6 (83%) abdominal cases; 12 scrotal cases, none diagnosed preoperatively, all confused with teratoma, none recurrent and none given medical or oncologic treatment. Authors' conclusions: testicular JGCT is a rare, painless, benign mass particularly in newborns, hard to diagnose preoperatively (usually thought to be teratoma), and inguinal orchiectomy is satisfactory treatment. They state JGCT is the most frequent testicular tumor in infants under 6 months and that sex chromosome disorders and ambiguous genitalia occur in about 20%.  Neonatal testicular JGCT case with imaging, markers and treatment, plus a tabulated literature review of earlier testicular JGCT cases.

title: Subserosal fibroid thought to be recurrent granulosa cell tumor in a pregnant patient
author: Mustafa HJ
text: 30-year-old Jamaican woman presented in 2005 with one year of hirsutism, 3 cm clitoromegaly and acne; total testosterone 365 ng/dl and 17-OH progesterone 253 ng/dl; ACTH stimulation excluded late-onset 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Pelvic ultrasound showed an 11 x 7 x 10 cm adnexal solid mass; endometrial biopsy was benign. She had laparotomy, right salpingo-oophorectomy, lymph node sampling, pelvic washings and partial omentectomy; pathology was androgen-secreting granulosa cell tumor of the ovary, stage IA. Testosterone normalized after surgery. Surveillance with examination, testosterone, inhibin A and B and imaging was normal, but hirsutism and clitoromegaly persisted for years despite medical treatment. In 2014 CT showed a 7 cm adnexal mass (7.3 x 5 x 5.4 cm) and MRI an 8 x 8 x 7 cm (8.9 x 7.1 cm in the figure legend) pelvic mass with cystic changes, separate from the uterus, in a patient who had become pregnant; testosterone and inhibin were normal. The tumor board decided on surgery for suspected recurrence. Laparotomy at 16 weeks of pregnancy found an 8 cm pedunculated subserosal fibroid of the lower uterine segment, excised and confirmed on frozen section and pathology; fetal monitoring showed no complications. Author conclusion: recurrent androgen-secreting JGCT is rare, can be confused with a pedunculated fibroid even on MRI, and laparoscopy before laparotomy should be considered.  Single case labeled juvenile androgen-secreting granulosa cell tumor with persistent virilization after resection and a false-positive suspected recurrence in pregnancy (fibroid).

title: A rare tumor during pregnancy; juvenile granulosa cell tumor (Gebelik sirasinda nadir gorulen bir tumor; juvenil granuloza hucreli tumor)
author: Temizkan O
text: Case of a patient with ovarian JGCT found during late pregnancy: she presented with pain at 38 weeks and ultrasound showed a 17 cm right adnexal mass; cesarean delivery with right salpingo-oophorectomy was done (no frozen section in an emergency). Gross: 17 x 14 x 9 cm smooth solid-cystic mass with yellow soft contents; microscopy: necrosis within fibrovascular stroma, diffuse spindle cells with vacuolated cytoplasm and mild pleomorphic nuclei, atypical mitoses. IHC: EMA, cytokeratin 7, CA125 and calretinin negative; inhibin focally positive; diagnosed as poorly differentiated juvenile-type granulosa cell tumor; staged IA. Because of early stage and incomplete fertility (patient was 17 and parous), surgery was limited to unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy; no adjuvant treatment was given; follow-up used serum inhibin, which did not rise. Three years later (age 20), surveillance ultrasound showed a left ovarian cystic mass and PET/CT showed a hypermetabolic left adnexal focus; she was found to be 5 weeks pregnant with a 5x4 cm simple cyst thought to be a corpus luteum cyst, and after counselling about PET/CT she chose to terminate; one month later transvaginal ultrasound showed a normal left ovary, so this was considered a pregnancy luteoma/false positive, not recurrence. The authors note PET/CT should not be done without excluding pregnancy, and cite from literature that stage I 5-year survival is 75-90%, adjuvant chemotherapy is recommended for stage IC-IV, and recurrence may occur after a mean 4-6 years. The authors claim this is the youngest patient with JGCT diagnosed in pregnancy in the literature.  Ovarian JGCT diagnosed during pregnancy at age 17, with 3-year inhibin-based follow-up and a PET false-positive scenario.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour: a rare clinical entity
author: Reddy KH
text: 17-year-old unmarried girl, menarche at 14, with 3 months of irregular cycles then 6 months of amenorrhea; known hypothyroid; abdominal mass of about 18 weeks size. Serum CA-125, CEA, AFP, beta-hCG and LDH were within normal limits; thyroid function, prolactin and testosterone were normal; inhibin was not measured. Ultrasound: 11.2 x 6.2 cm well-defined predominantly cystic mass with increased vascularity, probably from the left ovary, no solid component; CECT: heterogeneously enhancing left lower abdominal/pelvic mass with mild left hydroureteronephrosis, no free fluid; MRI not done. At laparotomy a 20 x 15 cm left ovarian tumor with intact capsule, no free fluid, negative saline-wash cytology and no omental, hepatic or nodal disease; left salpingo-oophorectomy performed because the tube merged with the capsule; omental and peritoneal biopsies were negative. Histopathology: well-differentiated juvenile granulosa cell tumor with hyaline globules; vimentin positive; inhibin and smooth muscle actin could not be done for lack of reagents; staged IA. No adjuvant chemotherapy given on oncologist's advice; at one year after surgery she was doing well under follow-up. The authors discuss (from the literature) that stage is the best prognostic factor, that surgery is the cornerstone, that BEP or taxane-platinum have been used for advanced or recurrent disease, and that radiotherapy has not been shown to confer survival benefit.  Single teen JGCT case with amenorrhea as presentation, stage IA, fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and no adjuvant treatment.

title: A rare testicular solid mass in children: juvenile granulosa cell tumour of testis
author: Couture J
text: A 3-month-old boy had a hard, mobile, painless right testicular mass enlarged for one month. Ultrasound showed near-complete replacement of the right testis by a 3.7 x 2.2 x 2.5 cm multicystic mass without Doppler vascularization; AFP and beta-hCG were normal for age; karyotype 46,XY. Right radical inguinal orchiectomy was performed; gross specimen was a 4.1 x 2.8 x 2.2 cm testis with a unilocular cystic mass containing pinkish fluid; mitoses were rare. IHC positive for inhibin, vimentin, smooth muscle actin, S-100 and CD99; negative for PLAP and CD117. Authors' review: testicular JGCT mostly occurs in the first 6 months of life (90% under 1 year), fewer than 50 cases reported all with benign course, only two bilateral cases (both intra-abdominal testes), chromosomal anomalies in 20% of reported cases. Authors note the benign behavior suggests a role for testis-sparing surgery, but radical inguinal orchiectomy with surveillance remains usual practice at their centre. Karyotype and metastatic work-up can wait until after pathology. karyotype Infant testicular JGCT case with IHC profile and a literature-based summary of testicular JGCT features.

title: Pubertas Prekoks Perifer Isoseksual akibat Juvenille Granulosa Cell Tumor
author: Santosa PA
text: Indonesian-language case report of a 16-month-old girl with isosexual peripheral precocious puberty: vaginal bleeding from 1 year, breast enlargement from 7 months, sparse pubic hair from 15 months (Tanner M3P2), a palpable immobile pelvic mass. Estradiol 2230 pg/mL with LH under 0.1 and FSH 0.14; AFP 3.63 ng/mL, CEA under 5.3, beta-hCG 0.10 mIU/mL, CA-125 87.8 U/mL, LDH 620 U/L; karyotype 46,XX; chest X-ray showed thymic hyperplasia. Ultrasound showed a solid pelvic mass and thickened endometrium; CT showed a hypodense heterogeneous intraperitoneal mass 11 x 7.4 x 11.3 cm and enlarged uterus; the left ovarian tumor measured 13 x 10 x 6 cm at surgery. Left salpingo-oophorectomy by laparotomy (5 October); H&E suggested sex cord-stromal tumor (granulosa cell versus Sertoli-Leydig), and IHC with CK7, EMA, CD99 and calretinin led to a diagnosis of juvenile granulosa cell tumor (individual stain results are not given). Bleeding stopped 6 days after surgery; estradiol after surgery was 15.26, 24.47 and 5.30 pg/mL on three later dates; no residual tumor on ultrasound at 14 October; uterus still consistent with precocious puberty; secondary sexual characteristics were still monitored monthly; no chemotherapy is reported. The authors state, citing others, that JGCT is mostly confined to the ovary and clinically benign despite malignant-appearing histology, that recurrence is rare and usually within the first year, and that inhibin positivity is definitive.  Classic JGCT presentation in a toddler: estrogen excess with precocious pseudopuberty, large ovarian mass, stage I-type surgery with hormonal normalization.

title: Evaluation of general characteristics of adolescent girls who had ovarian cystectomy (1-year single center experience)
author: Ozguc Comlek F
text: Retrospective single-center series (Selcuk University, Konya, Turkiye; March 2023 to March 2024) of 15 adolescent girls (median age 14.8 +/- 1.15 years) who underwent ovarian cystectomy. Pathology (Table 2): simple cyst 7 (46.7%), paratubal serous cyst 4 (26.7%), endometrioma 2 (13.3%), serous cystadenoma 1 (6.7%), juvenile granulosa cell tumor 1 (6.7%). The paper gives no individual details for the JGCT patient (age, presentation, markers, imaging, stage or treatment are not separately reported); the discussion refers to the tumor and the cystadenoma as the two patients with a solid component on ultrasound. Across the series no hormonal disorders were found: LH, FSH, estradiol, testosterone and tumor markers (AFP, beta-hCG, CEA, CA-125, LDH) were summarized as means; no abnormalities were reported; hirsutism was mild/moderate in 3 with normal ACTH, 17-OHP and DHEA-S. Ultrasound: mean long axis of cyst 75 +/- 55 mm in 13 patients; septate in 4, solid component in 2, otherwise pure cystic. No recurrent cysts were seen in approximately 9 months of postoperative follow-up; the authors emphasize ovary-preserving surgery given the low malignancy rates in this age group, and note that the small sample limits conclusions.  Marginal: gives a single JGCT among 15 surgically treated adolescent ovarian cysts and tumors (6.7%) with no JGCT-specific clinical data. Useful only as an illustration that JGCT can present as an ovarian cyst/mass in a general adolescent surgical series.

title: Successful pregnancy outcome with a large ruptured juvenile granulosa cell tumor: A case report
author: Sonigra K
text: 19-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks with abdominal pain, headaches and reduced fetal movements; ultrasound showed a 15.7 x 15 cm cyst with a solid hypervascular mass and maternal ascites; fetal biophysical profile 4/8. Emergency laparotomy found a massive torsed right ovary with a ruptured mass and edematous, necrosed fallopian tubes (abstract also refers to a left-sided mass on ultrasound). After cesarean delivery of the fetus, right salpingo-oophorectomy with cystectomy was performed; histology confirmed JGCT, FIGO stage IC2. Postoperative chemotherapy: six sessions of cisplatin and paclitaxel; post-chemotherapy MRI showed normal abdominal viscera with minimal free fluid in the posterior cul de sac and a normal left ovary; inhibin B dropped to 3.17 (units not stated). Planned follow-up for 5 years with tumor markers and CT; authors conclude aggressive treatment is necessary for advanced-stage tumors like this one to prevent recurrence or death.  Adult-age JGCT in late pregnancy presenting with torsion and rupture (stage IC2) treated with surgery and platinum-taxane chemotherapy; short follow-up.

title: Testis-sparing surgery for benign and malignant tumors: A critical analysis of the literature.
author: Giannarini G
text: Narrative review (Medline to December 2007; 49 full papers plus one abstract) of testis-sparing surgery; highest evidence level 2c, no randomized trials. In the pediatric series table, one Shukla 2004 series of 3 patients (1 testis-sparing, 2 radical orchidectomy) is footnoted as juvenile granulosa cell tumor on final histology, with no local recurrence at 5-14 years follow-up. The text cites Shukla et al. as reporting the first case of a seven-day-old boy with a testicular juvenile granulosa cell tumor treated with testis-sparing surgery, free of recurrence at 5 years. Pediatric testicular tumors are more often benign than adult ones and rarely have concomitant testicular intratubular germ cell neoplasia; testis-sparing surgery is described as most suitable for prepubertal teratoma, epidermoid cysts and Leydig cell tumors. Authors report many pediatric surgery centers now apply testis-sparing surgery first for elective management when serum tumor markers are normal, but call for prospective multicenter studies.  Secondary (review) source for a single cited case of testicular JGCT in a newborn managed with testis-sparing surgery and no recurrence at 5 years; not an independent patient series.

title: Patterns of spread and recurrence of sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary.
author: Thrall MM
text: Retrospective review of 87 ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor patients (Seattle, 1990-2009): 71 adult granulosa cell tumors, 11 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, 2 mixed, 2 unclassified and 1 juvenile granulosa cell tumor (1%). No individual clinical, staging, treatment or outcome data are given for the single JGCT patient. Of 59 patients with complete or partial staging, 47 had lymph nodes examined (median 14 nodes, range 3-80) and none had nodal involvement. 18 of 79 patients with follow-up had at least one recurrence (median time to recurrence 46.6 months, range 2.6-186); 2 had isolated retroperitoneal recurrence, neither with nodal sampling at primary surgery. Tumor size predicted survival: median survival 177 months for tumors under 10 cm versus 101 months for 10 cm or larger (p=0.006); no recurrences with tumors under 7 cm; multivariate HR about 1.20 per cm. Authors conclude lymph node metastasis is rare in sex cord-stromal tumors and routine lymphadenectomy can be omitted from staging.  Mostly adult granulosa cell tumor series; included only because it contains one JGCT patient (a count), with no JGCT-specific outcomes. Its lymph node findings apply to a predominantly adult population (median age 50).

title: Ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors, pleuropulmonary blastoma and DICER1 mutations: a report from the International Pleuropulmonary Blastoma Registry.
author: Schultz KA
text: Search of the International PPB Registry (325 children with PPB from 296 kindreds) found 9 OSCST in PPB probands or relatives: 5 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, 2 Sertoli cell tumors, 1 juvenile granulosa cell tumor and 1 gynandroblastoma; plus 3 additional OSCST patients (SLCT, jGCT, gynandroblastoma) from families without PPB but with suspected genetic predisposition. Only two jGCT patients are described: case 8, diagnosed at age 2 years, a second-degree relative of a PPB patient, treated by surgery, no evidence of disease at 33 years; and case 11, diagnosed at age 16 years, with nodular thyroid hyperplasia and a lung cyst, sister of a girl with gynandroblastoma (case 12, age 16), treated with surgery and chemotherapy, no evidence of disease at 1.5 years. Germline DNA was available for 8 of 12 patients and 6 of 8 had a DICER1 mutation, including patients with Sertoli-Leydig tumor, juvenile granulosa cell tumor and gynandroblastoma; the jGCT mutation listed is c.3073G>T (p.Glu1025X), identical to one found in a gynandroblastoma (the two sisters). Ages at diagnosis of Sertoli/SLCT tumors in PPB patients (6, 8, 13 years) and relatives (4, 7, 15, 32 years) were younger than sporadic SLCT (mean 25 years, as cited); ovarian tumor ages in family members were 2, 4, 7, 15, 18 and 32 years (median 11). All family members with OSCST were alive without disease at median 20.5 years (range 13-45) after the ovarian diagnosis; numbers were too small to draw prognostic conclusions. Four OSCST patients had nodular thyroid hyperplasia; the authors conclude that ovarian OSCST are a manifestation of the familial PPB/DICER1 syndrome (extending to jGCT and gynandroblastoma), may be the first presentation of DICER1 mutation in a family, and that a lung cyst or PPB-related tumor in an OSCST patient or family should prompt consideration of DICER1 testing. The authors note that juvenile granulosa cell tumors have been described with Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome (citing literature) and that the prevalence of germline DICER1 mutations in OSCST in general cannot be determined from this group. DICER1 Early registry evidence linking jGCT (and gynandroblastoma) to germline DICER1 mutations in familial pleuropulmonary blastoma syndrome, though only two jGCT patients are reported.

title: Granulosa cell tumor in a six-year-old girl presented as precocious puberty.
author: Hashemipour M
text: A 6-year-old girl presented with 4 months of breast enlargement and periumbilical abdominal pain with nausea, followed by vaginal bleeding; she was initially treated with medroxyprogesterone and then an LHRH agonist for presumed precocious puberty. Labs showed peripheral precocious puberty: estradiol 216 pmol/L, FSH <0.5 IU/L, LH <0.4 IU/L, alpha-fetoprotein 2 ng/ml; the LHRH test produced no rise in LH or FSH. Pelvic ultrasound showed a 6.2 x 5 x 4.1 cm hypoechoic solid left adnexal mass with multiple cysts up to 1.2 cm; CT showed a large non-uniform solid mass with necrotic regions. The right ovary and uterus were normal. At laparotomy a 5 x 7 cm left ovarian mass was resected with the left ovary; no pelvic lymphadenopathy; histology was reported as ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumor (no staging reported in the case). At 4-6 months of follow-up the response was good, with regression of breast size and a fall in serum estradiol. The authors state that GCTs are 0.1% of ovarian tumors and 4-5% of GCTs occur in children, isosexual precocity occurs in 70-80% of prepubertal girls with GCT, about 90% of JGCT are stage I, and that unilateral oophorectomy is appropriate for stage I without adjuvant chemotherapy (literature statements cited by the authors). The authors conclude that ovarian tumors must be considered among causes of precocious puberty, and that persistent ovarian cysts with a solid component beyond three months should raise suspicion of JGCT.  Case report of ovarian JGCT presenting as peripheral precocious puberty in a 6-year-old; illustrates presentation and surgical cure.

title: Clinicopathologic characteristics of granulosa cell tumors of the ovary: a multicenter retrospective study.
author: Lee IH
text: Five-hospital Korean retrospective study (1995-2007) of 113 granulosa cell tumors: 102 adult type and 11 juvenile type (9.7%). JGCT patients: mean age 20.0 years (range 8-45), more than half under 20, 5/11 (45.5%) premenarchal; 10 of 11 symptomatic; most common symptom abdominal mass (45.5%), vaginal bleeding in 3 (27.3%). JGCT tumors: mean diameter 12.4 cm (range 5-26), all unilateral (right 7, left 4); preoperative CA-125 was elevated (>35 IU/mL) in 5 of the 10 measured. JGCT surgery: unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with staging 6, unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy 3, hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy 1, cystectomy 1; intraoperative rupture in 3 (27.3%); no capsule invasion; no residual disease; no positive ascites or washings. JGCT stage: stage I in 9 (81.8%) and stage III in 2 (18.2%); 3 patients received adjuvant BEP. JGCT outcome: no recurrences or deaths at mean follow-up 69.8 months (range 20-156); four patients had seven pregnancies, six normal term deliveries and one cornual pregnancy. Adult-type comparison (102 pts): stage I 86, II 11, III 5; recurrence 10 (9.8%); 3 deaths; stage the only factor independently associated with recurrence; 8 of 36 fertility-sparing patients had 9 pregnancies. Authors conclude JGCT prognosis is good in their small group and fertility-sparing surgery is an option for early-stage disease.  Multicenter GCT series with a clearly reported 11-patient JGCT subgroup (presentation, stage, surgery, chemotherapy, outcome, pregnancies); the adult-type findings are context only.

title: Urogenital tumours in childhood.
author: Swinson S
text: Imaging-focused review of paediatric urogenital tumours (renal tumours, rhabdomyosarcoma, ovarian and testicular tumours); JGCT receives two sentences in the ovarian non-germ-cell section. Sex cord stromal tumours are described as approximately 10% of ovarian malignancies in adolescent girls; the two main categories are granulosa theca cell and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours. In the first 2 decades granulosa theca cell tumours tend to be juvenile granulosa cell tumour (JGCT), the most common paediatric sex cord stromal tumour, which often presents early with oestrogen-led precocious puberty. Of 70 patients in the Kiel Pediatric Tumour Registry (sex cord stromal tumours), mean age at diagnosis was 7 years for JGCT and 14 years for Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour (secondary citation). The review's ovarian imaging and staging sections concern germ cell tumours (COG staging for ovarian GCT); it states non-germ-cell ovarian tumours cannot be reliably distinguished from GCTs on imaging. The testicular section covers germ cell, Leydig cell and secondary tumours only; JGCT of the testis is not mentioned.  Minimal: general paediatric urogenital tumour imaging review with a brief JGCT statement (most common paediatric sex cord stromal tumour; oestrogen-driven precocious puberty; Kiel registry mean age 7 years). No JGCT patient data of its own.

title: Recurrent somatic DICER1 mutations in nonepithelial ovarian cancers.
author: Heravi-Moussavi A
text: Whole-transcriptome/exome sequencing of 14 discovery tumors (2 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, 4 juvenile granulosa-cell tumors, 8 yolk-sac primitive germ-cell tumors) found clustered DICER1 RNase IIIb mutations, including four missense changes at D1709; Sanger sequencing then screened 101 additional nonepithelial ovarian tumors and 39 testicular tumors. JGCT-specific result (Table 1): a hot-spot DICER1 mutation was found in 1/14 juvenile granulosa-cell tumors (7%), c.5126A>G encoding p.Asp1709Gly (D1709G). Adult granulosa-cell tumors were 0/15, all with FOXL2 mutation. Overall, DICER1 RNase IIIb hot-spot mutations were found in 30/102 nonepithelial ovarian tumors (29%), predominantly Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, 26/43 (60%); yolk sac tumor 2/15 (13%), mature teratoma 1/8 (12%); dysgerminoma 0/1, mixed germ-cell 0/1, immature teratoma 0/5. Outside the ovarian sex cord-stromal and germ-cell groups: 1/14 nonseminomatous testicular germ-cell tumors (D1709N), 2/5 embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas, and 1/266 epithelial ovarian and endometrial carcinomas (an ovarian carcinosarcoma, E1813G); 33/159 tumors had hot-spot mutations across discovery and validation sets.
