Mutations were restricted to codons for metal-binding residues of the RNase IIIb catalytic centers, were somatic in all 16 cases with germline DNA, were heterozygous, and no RNase IIIa mutations were seen; they were absent from 1000 Genomes, TCGA public data, COSMIC hot spots, over 1000 cancer-sequencing libraries and the 15 FOXL2-mutant adult granulosa-cell tumors. Seven samples carried a hot-spot mutation plus another germline or somatic DICER1 mutation (Table 2: 1 embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, 1 yolk-sac tumor, 5 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors); in six the second allele was predicted null. No JGCT is listed among them. In vitro RNA cleavage assays showed hot-spot mutants (D1709N, D1709E, E1705K) had markedly reduced RNase IIIb activity (22-nt product) but retained RNase IIIa activity (18-nt product); all tumors stained positive for DICER1 by immunohistochemistry. Authors conclude the focal, recurrent pattern and retention of expressed mutant protein argue against a classic two-hit tumor suppressor and suggest an oncogene-like altered DICER1 function; they conclude aberrant miRNA processing from hot-spot mutations is a key oncogenic event in nonepithelial ovarian cancers. DICER1 DICER1 First report of recurrent somatic DICER1 RNase IIIb hot-spot mutations in nonepithelial ovarian tumors; JGCT showed a low rate (1/14) compared with Sertoli-Leydig tumors (60%), distinguishing it from adult GCT (FOXL2, DICER1 0/15).

title: Management of ovarian and testicular sex cord-stromal tumors in children and adolescents.
author: Schultz KA
text: Consensus/review guidance (Children's Oncology Group, MAKEI authors) on pediatric ovarian and testicular sex cord-stromal tumors (SCST): SCST are about 7% of ovarian tumors overall and about 15% of ovarian tumors in children; JGCT is the most common pediatric ovarian SCST, followed by Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors. Ovarian JGCT is seen in young children and may present with precocious puberty; the vast majority are stage I at diagnosis with favorable prognosis; recurrence is rare and generally within 2-3 years (median 2.8 years for stage I ovarian SCST recurrences, mostly abdominopelvic or regional nodes). Adult-type GCT is very rare in children and has late relapse (>10 years). Both GCT types may secrete inhibin; serum inhibin A/B (B more specific), AFP, beta-hCG, CEA, CA-125, LDH and calcium are advised in suspected ovarian tumors; inhibin IHC and calcium help distinguish JGCT from small cell carcinoma of the hypercalcemic type, which can mimic pseudofollicular growth. Associations: JGCT, Sertoli-Leydig tumors and gynandroblastoma occur in families with pleuropulmonary blastoma and DICER1 mutations; enchondromatosis (Ollier) and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are linked to granulosa cell tumors; no association with BRCA1/2. 25% of JGCT in one series had chromosomal imbalance, usually gain of chromosome 12. Prognosis (Schneider et al, cited): 10-year EFS 0.88+/-0.05 for JGCT (n=34) vs 0.67+/-0.19 for Sertoli-Leydig tumors (n=6). Mitoses <20/10 HPF (n=35/35) had 100% 10-year EFS vs 53% for >=20/10 HPF (n=7/13), significant also within stage Ic (100% vs 48%). Marked nuclear pleomorphism (about 15% of stage I JGCT) was not associated with adverse prognosis. Stage Ic subgroups (cited): intraoperative rupture (n=12; 9 had no adjuvant therapy, all survived relapse-free) did better than preoperative rupture or malignant ascites (n=9; EFS 0.44+/-0.17 vs 1.0, log-rank 0.003). Staging by FIGO ovarian carcinoma criteria with detailed description of stage Ic spillage; stage I treated by unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy without hysterectomy or routine lymphadenectomy. Recommended: adjuvant platinum chemotherapy (4 or 6 cycles PEB) for JGCT stage Ic with preoperative rupture/malignant ascites and stages II-IV; consider for stage Ic intraoperative rupture with >=20 mitoses/10 HPF; observation may be considered for intraoperative rupture with low mitotic count. Stage IV is rare with poor prognosis. Follow-up advised: abdominopelvic MRI or ultrasound plus inhibin B, hormonal markers, CA-125 about every 3 months for at least the first 3 years; relapse carries poor prognosis and no regimen for relapse is established. Testicular JGCT: usually presents under 6 months of age, inhibin positive, benign with no evidence of recurrence or metastases; associated with Y-chromosome structural abnormalities or ambiguous genitalia; testis-sparing surgery reasonable if normal AFP for age; no adjuvant therapy for stage I; serial imaging generally not required. Registries cited: Prepubertal Testis Tumor Registry had 43 stromal tumors including 9 JGCT, none metastatic at diagnosis; unpublished MAKEI analysis of 40 testicular SCST found no metastases, all in continuous remission; Harms and Kock described 29 testicular SCST with no relapses. chromosome 12 DICER1 Core pediatric guidance document for ovarian and testicular JGCT covering presentation, markers, IHC, genetic associations, staging, risk-adapted adjuvant therapy and follow-up; most outcome data are cited from the German MAKEI studies.

title: BMP-specific SMADs function as novel repressors of PDGFA and modulate its expression in ovarian granulosa cells and tumors.
author: Tripurani SK
text: Laboratory study (mouse granulosa cells, Smad1/5 double conditional knockout tumors, human COV434 cell line, four archived human JGCT samples from Texas Children's Hospital tissue bank). Not a clinical study. In Smad1/5 dKO mouse tumors and peritoneal metastases, qPCR showed significant upregulation of Pdgfa, Pdgfb and Vegfa, but not Vegfb, versus wild-type granulosa cells; the model develops highly vascularized, hemorrhagic, metastatic tumors resembling human JGCT. Knockdown of SMAD1 and SMAD5 raised PDGFA, but not PDGFB or VEGF, in mouse granulosa cells and in COV434 (a juvenile human granulosa cell tumor-derived line; about 2-fold PDGFA increase); the effect did not depend on BMP receptor signaling (dorsomorphin plus BMP7 did not change Pdgfa). ChIP showed SMAD1/5 binding to the proximal human PDGFA promoter (three-fold enrichment); reporter assays showed SMAD1/5 repress promoter activity and antagonize Sp1 by reducing Sp1 occupancy; mutating the SMAD1/5 site abolished repression. Two-hybrid assays showed no direct SMAD1/5-Sp1 interaction. In four human JGCTs (T1-T4), PDGFA, PDGFRA and PDGFRB transcripts were detected in 75% and PDGFB was not expressed; most tumors expressed BMP receptors, ligands (BMP4, BMP7) and SMAD1/SMAD5 transcripts, though functional status was unknown. The authors propose that PDGFA upregulation after BR-SMAD loss is an early step in JGCT development and suggest PDGF pathway expression could make JGCT or its recurrences a candidate for tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment; this is speculation with no treatment data. PDGFA / PDGFRA / PDGFRB SMAD1/SMAD5 Mechanistic evidence on BMP/SMAD1/5 loss and PDGFA in a mouse model resembling JGCT and in 4 human JGCT specimens; no clinical outcomes.

title: The multifaceted granulosa cell tumours-myths and realities: a review.
author: Kanthan R
text: Five unusual GCT index cases from one Saskatchewan hospital plus a 14-year (1997-2011) pathology review of 37 GCTs (overall prevalence 0.0041%, 37/902,100), used to discuss 'myths and realities' of granulosa cell tumors. Index case 1: a 5-month-old boy with a 2 cm left testicular mass treated by orchiectomy; histology solid with cystic spaces, extensive fibrocollagenous stroma, inhibin positive; the only male GCT, disease-free 20 years later. Index case 2: a 7-day-old girl with a 10 cm multiseptated cystic left ovarian mass with torsion, estradiol 310, prolactin 34.9, TSH 11.05, normal LH, FSH, AFP and beta-hCG; histology was intermediate between adult and juvenile GCT (macrofollicular pattern with small solid insular areas, no theca interna); cured by oophorectomy, well at 18 years. In the 37-case pathology review (36 female, 1 male), female age ranged 7 days to 85 years (mean 52, median 48); only 4 (10.8%) GCTs were of the juvenile type; sites included 17 right ovary, 15 left ovary and one each bowel, abdominal wall and omentum. Review statements (cited literature): about 95% of GCT are adult-type; up to 90% of JGCT occur under 30 years of age, half under 10 years and 10% in infants under 1 year; estradiol-producing cells are present in 70% of JGCT; isosexual precocious pseudopuberty occurs in 80-90% of JGCT patients under 8 years; average tumor size is 12 cm; few Call-Exner bodies; JGCT is considered by many to be relatively benign with survival as high as 97% at 3.5-year follow-up in one study; advanced JGCT can be aggressive with short interval to relapse and responds to platinum combination chemotherapy. Testicular JGCT (cited): sex cord-stromal tumors are 4% of testicular tumors; JGCT is far more common than adult GCT in the testis; about half are diagnosed in the first month and over 95% in the first year of life; 25% have gynaecomastia; usually benign, treated by radical orchiectomy; stage-matched testicular GCT has a better prognosis than ovarian. Rare JGCT presentations cited: paraneoplastic hypercalcemia and Meigs-type pleural effusion with ascites; tumor rupture mimicking ectopic pregnancy in 10-15% of GCT; inhibin sensitivity/specificity in 30 women with GCT (Mom et al): inhibin A 67%/100%, inhibin B 89%/100%. Adult-type GCT dominates the review's data: late recurrence (quarter recur, mean 5-10 years, 10-20% as late as 20-40 years), BEP as standard for advanced/recurrent disease, lifelong follow-up recommended; the authors conclude GCT is an indolent neoplasm of low malignant potential with unpredictable behaviour and late relapses. FOXL2 chromosome Mixed adult and juvenile GCT case series and narrative review. JGCT-specific content: one infantile testicular JGCT case (20-year follow-up), a neonatal ovarian GCT with hybrid histology, a count of 4 juvenile-type tumors among 37, and cited statements on JGCT age, hormones and prognosis; most review content concerns adult-type GCT.

title: GATA-4 and FOG-2 expression in pediatric ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors replicates embryonal gonadal phenotype: results from the TREP project.
author: Virgone C
text: Italian TREP project (registry of very rare pediatric tumors; patients 18 years or younger): 15 girls with ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors: 6 JGCT, 6 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors (SLCT), 1 fibrothecoma, 1 fibroma (bilateral, Gorlin syndrome), 1 sclerosing stromal tumor. COG/POG staging: stage I 12, II 2, IV 1 in the whole series. JGCT patients (ages 31, 7, 40, 73, 97 and 118 months): stage I in 5 and stage II in 1 (case 3, age 40 months); tumor size 3 to 22 cm (case 1 3 cm, case 2 8 cm, case 3 10 cm, case 5 9 cm, case 6 22 cm); mitotic rate <1, >10, >10, 21, 6, >10 per 10 HPF; cysts in 5/6. JGCT outcome: all six in complete remission, with follow-up of 67, 57, 36, 72, 52 and 15 months; only case 6 (stage I, 22 cm) received PEB chemotherapy. No JGCT was clinically malignant despite frequently high mitotic rates. JGCT immunohistochemistry: inhibin and vimentin positive in all evaluable JGCT (inhibin not available in 1), pancytokeratin focally positive in 3/6; FOG-2 strongly expressed in 5/6; GATA-4 negative in 4 of 5 evaluable cases and weakly positive in 1 (the case with 21 mitoses/10 HPF). In the whole series inhibin was positive in 11/15, vimentin 13/15, pancytokeratin 6/15, GATA-4 5/13 and FOG-2 11/15. SLCT expressed FOG-2 in 4/6 and GATA-4 in 3/5; fibroma/thecoma expressed both, sclerosing stromal tumor was FOG-2 negative. Whole-series outcome: 13 in first complete remission, 1 second remission after a metachronous contralateral SLCT, 1 death of disease (a stage II SLCT with retiform pattern and heterologous elements, relapsed pelvis with rhabdomyosarcoma-like component, died at 33 months). PEB was given in 3/15 (stage I, II, IV). Authors conclude pediatric JGCT show a FOG-2/GATA-4 pattern resembling primordial ovarian follicles, that low GATA-4 may relate to the good JGCT outcome, and that FOG-2 may have prognostic value; they stress the very small numbers and that histology and complete excision remain the main prognostic factors. FOG-2 (ZFPM2) GATA-4 Small Italian TREP series of pediatric ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors with a 6-patient JGCT subgroup reporting stage, size, mitoses, chemotherapy, outcome and FOG-2/GATA-4/inhibin immunohistochemistry.

title: N-cadherin Expression in Testicular Germ Cell and Gonadal Stromal Tumors.
author: Heidenberg DJ
text: Immunohistochemical study of N-cadherin in 105 testicular germ cell tumors and 12 gonadal stromal tumors from the Armed Forces Institute of Pathology Testicular Tumor Registry; stromal tumors were 6 Sertoli cell, 4 Leydig cell, 1 Sertoli-Leydig and 1 juvenile granulosa cell tumor. The single testicular juvenile granulosa cell tumor showed mainly weak cytoplasmic N-cadherin positivity (focal, variable intensity); the figure legend describes membranous and cytoplasmic staining. No patient age, clinical or outcome data are given. Nine of the 12 gonadal stromal tumors were positive to a variable extent; Sertoli cell tumors 4/6 positive (weak to moderate membranous), Leydig cell tumors 3/4 weakly positive. Main finding (germ cell tumors): N-cadherin was positive in 82/83 (98.7%) yolk sac tumors, typically strong, and authors propose it as an additional marker for yolk sac tumor, while embryonal carcinoma was largely negative. N-cadherin (CDH2), protein by IHC Minimal: one testicular JGCT with N-cadherin IHC result; no clinical data.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the testis: prenatal diagnosis and prescrotal approach.
author: Bulotta AL
text: A full-term newborn (3200 g) had a multicystic left testicular mass on fetal ultrasound at 36 weeks; postnatal ultrasound showed a 1.57 x 1.33 cm enlarged testis with a well-encapsulated complex cystic mass and increased Doppler flow; contralateral testis normal. Karyotype, blood chemistry and abdominal ultrasound were normal; no ambiguous genitalia or dysmorphism; family history included two cases of Down syndrome. Markers: AFP 6679 IU/mL, hCG 8 mIU/mL, testosterone 1.75 ng/mL, inhibin B 346 pg/mL; the authors note neonatal AFP is physiologically elevated and cite age-based reference ranges, but chose total orchiectomy because of the elevated AFP. Left radical orchiectomy through a prescrotal/sub-inguinal incision; gonad pearly white, spongy yellow with many microcysts and no normal parenchyma; histology JGCT, inhibin and calretinin positive, AFP negative. Ultrasound one month after surgery showed an empty left scrotum and no abdominal masses; the infant is healthy with annual ultrasound and clinical follow-up planned for at least 5 years. The authors state, citing others, that JGCT is 1-5% of prepubertal testicular tumors, benign, hormonally inactive, and that only one prior prenatal diagnosis had been reported; they conclude that radical orchiectomy is sufficient and that follow-up is too short to exclude recurrence although none are reported in the literature.  Rare neonatal testicular JGCT diagnosed prenatally, with markers, histology and orchiectomy-only outcome.

title: Massive ascites as the only sign of ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumor in an adolescent: a case report and a review of the literature.
author: Ashnagar A
text: 13-year-old premenarchal girl with 2 months of progressive painless abdominal distension and massive ascites as the only manifestation; no signs of hormonal excess. Ultrasound: cystic lesion with few septations 70 x 64 mm arising from the left adnexa, right ovary also enlarged with a 36 mm cystic lesion; CT: multilocular thick-walled cystic mass from left ovary with large ascites. beta-hCG, AFP, CEA, CA 19-9 and CA-125 were normal; inhibin was not measured preoperatively but was increased immediately after surgery. Surgery: left salpingo-oophorectomy and bilateral omentectomy; about 10 L of transudate ascites evacuated, ascitic cytology negative. Tumor 9 x 5 x 3.5 cm, multilocular cystic with papillary projections. Histology: JGCT with ovoid and polygonal pale cells, irregular follicles, pseudopapillary projections; IHC positive for calretinin, inhibin and CD99. Chest CT and bone survey unremarkable. Staged FIGO IC (surface projections; negative ascitic cytology). Because of residual tumor on postoperative imaging and inhibin level, 4 cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy were given; patient was in complete remission at 18 months. Menarche began about 10 days after surgery. Authors state that to their knowledge massive ascites as the only clinical manifestation of JGCT had not been reported. They cite platinum-based chemotherapy response rates of 63% to 80% in advanced or recurrent disease and 5-year survival for stage I GCT above 90% (as low as 75% in some reports).  Atypical JGCT presentation (massive ascites without hormonal signs) in an adolescent, with inhibin as a marker and 18-month remission after surgery plus 4 cycles of chemotherapy.

title: MicroRNAs and Recent Insights into Pediatric Ovarian Cancers.
author: Francis JC
text: Review of pediatric ovarian cancers with emphasis on microRNA biology; states that about 40% of ovarian tumors in the young are germ cell tumors and 25% sex cord-stromal tumors, and that 2-8% of pediatric adnexal masses are ultimately cancer. Granulosa cell tumors are the most common sex cord-stromal tumor; juvenile GCT occurs mainly in premenarchal girls and is roughly 5% of GCTs. Coffee-bean nuclei and Call-Exner bodies are typical of adult GCT and only rarely seen in JGCT. Estrogen secretion by GCT can present as premature menarche or isosexual precocious puberty (elevated serum estrogen, no gonadotropin response to GnRH stimulation); contrasexual precocity with virilization is attributed mainly to Sertoli-Leydig tumors. Ollier disease: nine cases of ovarian JGCT reported in individuals with Ollier disease (cited as a number greater than expected by chance); the ovarian tumors are usually unilateral and often on the same side as the most recently resected enchondroma. Estimated Ollier prevalence about 1 per 100,000. The FOXL2 somatic mutation was found in 86/89 adult GCTs but only 1/10 JGCTs and 3/14 thecomas, and none of 49 other sex cord-stromal tumors or 329 unrelated tumors; the authors state that juvenile and adult GCTs may be molecularly distinct despite shared clinical and histologic features. DICER1 germline mutations occur in familial pleuropulmonary blastoma and multinodular goiter; somatic DICER1 mutations are reported in up to 60% of Sertoli-Leydig tumors, a finding not described for JGCT in this review. Mouse models: Smad1/Smad5 conditional knockout in granulosa cells and inhibin-alpha knockout give granulosa cell tumors; PI3K/mTORC1 hyperactivation is common to human and mouse GCT, but everolimus only slowed tumor growth in one mouse model. FOXL2 DICER1 chromosomes Narrative review; JGCT content is limited to epidemiologic context (about 5% of GCTs), Ollier disease association, FOXL2 mutation absent in 9/10 JGCTs and the idea that JGCT and adult GCT are molecularly distinct. No original patient data.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor presenting as isosexual precocious puberty: A case report and review of literature.
author: Haroon NN
text: A 7-year-old girl presented with 18 months of progressive breast development (Tanner IV breast, Tanner III pubic hair), menarche a year earlier, and height 125.2 cm and weight 26 kg above the 75th centile; bone age was 8.5 years at chronological age 7 years 2 months. Serum estradiol was 414 pg/ml (prepubertal <20 pg/ml) with suppressed FSH (<1 IU/L); beta-hCG, CEA and AFP were negative; inhibin was not measured because testing was unavailable at the center. Pelvic ultrasound showed a 6 x 7 x 9 cm heterogeneous solid right adnexal mass with hypoechoic necrotic areas and increased vascularity; elective excision was planned but she presented a week later with ovarian torsion and underwent emergency laparotomy with right salpingo-oophorectomy. The resected tumor was encapsulated, 450 g, 10 x 8 x 5 cm, without capsular breach; histology showed microfollicular and nodular patterns, nuclear grooving, inconspicuous nucleoli and extensive luteinisation; ascitic fluid was negative for malignant cells; final diagnosis was benign feminizing JGCT, FIGO stage IA. After surgery the breast size regressed, bleeding stopped and estradiol normalized; no recurrence at 3.5 years. No chemotherapy was given. In its literature discussion the paper states JGCT is under 5% of childhood ovarian tumors, 5-year survival is 90-95% for FIGO stage I and 25-50% for advanced stages, recurrences occur mostly in the first 3 years, and cisplatin-based adjuvant chemotherapy is needed for stage Ic, IIIc or high mitotic rate (these are the authors' review statements, not data from this patient). The paper cites activating G-alpha-s mutations in 30%, trisomy 12, 14 and monosomy 22 as genetic aberrations, and states FOXL2 expression, age <10 years, precocious pseudopuberty and stage I are associated with good prognosis; no molecular testing was performed in this patient.  Typical estrogen-secreting stage IA ovarian JGCT with isosexual precocious puberty cured by unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy alone.

title: Clinicopathologic review of ovarian masses in Korean premenarchal girls.
author: Ki EY
text: Retrospective review of 65 premenarchal girls operated on for ovarian masses at Seoul St. Mary's Hospital (1990-2012); 14 (21.5%) were malignant; juvenile granulosa cell tumor accounted for 2 (3.1%) of all masses and 14.3% of malignant tumors. JGCT patient 1: age 9, vaginal bleeding, left ovarian cystectomy, FIGO stage Ia, no adjuvant treatment, no evidence of disease; beta-hCG under 2. JGCT patient 2: age 14, abdominal distension, right adnexectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection and partial omentectomy, stage Ia, carboplatin-VP16 adjuvant, no evidence of disease; CA125 258, AFP 21, beta-hCG under 2. The authors report one of the two granulosa cell tumors presented with pseudoprecocity (vaginal bleeding) and the other did not; CA125 was nonspecifically raised in the patient with a granulosa cell tumor. Among all malignant tumors, 3 patients died (2 yolk sac tumors, 1 mixed germ cell tumor); both JGCT patients were disease-free at last follow-up (follow-up length not stated). Authors conclude epithelial and sex cord-stromal tumors are relatively uncommon in children and their clinical behavior is unpredictable.  Small pediatric ovarian-mass series providing two individually described JGCT cases (stage Ia, both disease-free).

title: DICER1 hotspot mutations in non-epithelial gonadal tumours.
author: Witkowski L
text: Sanger sequencing of the DICER1 RNase IIIa and IIIb domains in 154 gonadal tumours (135 female, 19 male) and 43 extra-gonadal germ cell tumours found 14 heterozygous RNase IIIb mutations in 14/197 non-epithelial tumours (7.1%). Juvenile granulosa cell tumour: 0/4 ovarian JGCTs carried a DICER1 hotspot mutation (Table 2a). Sex cord-stromal tumours overall were mutated in 9/28 (32%): Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour (SLCT) 8/15 (53%), unclassified SCST 1/7 (14%), Leydig cell tumour 0/1, SCST with annular tubules 0/1. One SLCT with components of JGCT (16-year-old female) carried c.5429A>T, p.D1810V, a variant not previously reported; the table lists it under SLCT, not JGCT. Gonadal germ cell tumours were mutated in 5/118 (4.2%); 0/43 extra-gonadal GCTs, 0/7 small-cell carcinoma of the ovary hypercalcaemic type and 0/1 ovarian embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma were mutated. In all five patients with matched constitutional DNA, the mutations were somatic; mutations clustered at the RNase IIIb metal-binding sites, with most at D1810 and E1813. Median age of mutation-positive patients was 18 years (range 20 months-54 years) versus 17 years (birth-66 years) for mutation-negative (P=0.72). The authors conclude that DICER1 mutation analysis may aid classification of histologically problematic SCSTs; the study could not test germline DNA in all mutation-positive patients and had small numbers in some subtypes. DICER1 Mixed series of gonadal non-epithelial tumours; the only JGCT-specific datum is 0/4 pure ovarian JGCTs DICER1 hotspot-mutated, plus one SLCT with JGCT components that was mutated. Suggests DICER1 RNase IIIb hotspots are not a feature of JGCT, in contrast to SLCT.

title: Neoplastic causes of abnormal puberty.
author: Wendt S
text: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital review (1975-Oct 2011): 24 of 13,615 children with neoplasms (0.18%; 16 male, 8 female) had precocious puberty (PP) at or within 60 days of presentation; brain tumors 12, adrenocortical carcinoma 5, hepatoblastoma 4, other 3 (including 2 ovarian JGCT and 1 Leydig cell tumor). Two patients had ovarian JGCT (Table I): patient 19, a girl aged 3.5 years (PP noted at 3 years, 6 months before diagnosis) with pubarche and an ovarian mass, endocrine testing done before diagnosis, outcome complete response; patient 17, a girl aged 6.8 years (PP at 5.8 years, 12 months before diagnosis) with central-type PP picture, 'benign' enlarged ovarian follicles and no response to GnRH analog, outcome CR. Patient 17 was treated with a GnRH agonist for presumed idiopathic central PP before the gonadal tumor was found; the lesion was initially interpreted as benign. The authors note secondary central PP induced by persistently high sex hormones can mask the underlying tumor in gonadal neoplasms. Time from PP onset to tumor diagnosis was median 6 months (range 0-48) across all 24; signs of PP were misinterpreted or underappreciated in half of the cohort, and 16 of 24 had PP signs for 3 months or more before the tumor diagnosis. In the authors' pathophysiology grouping, JGCT falls under proliferative process with excessive sex hormone production (estradiol; first decade of life; endocrine abnormalities more frequent in younger patients); 8 of 24 patients were in this group (3 gonadal, 5 adrenocortical carcinoma). The authors recommend that a final diagnosis of idiopathic PP not be made before assessment of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and appropriate tumor markers/imaging of gonads and adrenals, and give a diagnostic algorithm (Fig. 2) including malignancy.  Documents two JGCT patients presenting with precocious puberty in a pediatric cancer center series and illustrates diagnostic delay or misclassification as idiopathic central PP; the rest of the series is non-JGCT.

title: Central precocious puberty and granulosa cell ovarian tumor in an 8-year old female.
author: Calcaterra V
text: Caucasian girl with breast development (B2) and pubic hair (PH2) at 7 years 9 months, evaluated at 8 years 5 months: GnRH-stimulated peak LH 6.4 and FSH 13.4 mU/mL, bone age advanced (SDS 2.1), tumor markers negative, pelvic ultrasound with normal ovaries; diagnosed with central precocious puberty. Four months later, before GnRH-analog treatment, she had vaginal bleeding, a palpable pelvic fullness and increased abdominal girth; basal FSH fell to 0.1, estradiol rose to 65 pg/mL, progesterone to 1.7 ng/mL and CA-125 to 74.3 U/mL. Ultrasound showed a 13 x 8 cm left ovarian lesion and MRI a capsulated mixed mass of 13 x 13.7 x 6 cm; laparotomy with left salpingo-oophorectomy achieved complete resection; histology showed sex-stromal cell proliferation with high mitotic activity and low-grade atypia, diagnosed as juvenile granulosa cell tumor. No chemotherapy or radiotherapy was given; at one month estradiol, progesterone and CA-125 had returned to prior values and ultrasound showed no pelvic mass; at 7 months there was no recurrence; MRI of the hypothalamic-pituitary region showed a pineal cyst. The authors propose that FSH overstimulation or aberrant FSH receptor activation may have contributed to tumor growth (FSHR mutations not investigated) and that CPP and granulosa cell tumors might not be coincidentally associated; this is the authors' hypothesis.  Unusual JGCT arising within months of documented central precocious puberty with normal ovaries on prior ultrasound; hypothesis-generating single case.

title: Clinicopathological spectrum of ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors; 20 years' retrospective study in a developing country.
author: Haroon S
text: Single-center retrospective study (Aga Khan University Hospital, Karachi, 1992-2012) of 480 ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors (SCST); median age 45 years (range 1-92); 24 were juvenile granulosa cell tumors (5%) and 211 (43.9%) adult GCT. JGCT: median age 19 years and mean tumor size 15 cm (Table 3); the authors state JGCT was the most frequent SCST in children and that JGCT were around 10% of all GCT in this series, higher than in other large series. IHC was done in 20 JGCTs and showed negative cytokeratins; across all GCT inhibin was positive in every case tested, calretinin about 90% and CD99 68% of the 163 tested adult/granulosa cases (JGCT split not given). Follow-up of only 11 JGCT cases was available: 2 recurred after 8 and 17 months and one died of disease after 7 months. Authors note JGCT shows greater nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic activity than AGCT, and that cytokeratin negativity helps exclude epithelial malignancy. In comparison, for adult GCT (follow-up available for 86): 5 late recurrences (18-52 months), 4 with metastasis, 2 deaths from AGCT (11 and 18 months); 13 AGCT had spread at presentation. Authors conclude SCSTs are uncommon with good prognosis in the Pakistani population, that IHC is needed to exclude epithelial tumors, and that follow-up data were missing for about half the patients (FOXL2 and SF-1 not available).  Large histopathology series of ovarian SCSTs that contains 24 JGCTs with age, size, surgery type, cytokeratin IHC and limited follow-up (11 patients).

title: Hypercalcemia in a child with juvenile granulosa cell tumor of ovary: Report of an unusual paraneoplastic syndrome and review of the literature.
author: Rod J
text: A 15-year-old girl (menarche at 14) presented with 2 days of abdominal pain, vomiting, fever and a painful right lower quadrant mass; appendicitis was initially suspected. Corrected serum calcium was 14.9 mg/dL (3.70 mmol/L), phosphorus 0.50 mmol/L, intact PTH 10 pg/mL (normal 10-65), CA-125 204 U/mL, CRP 259 mg/L, LDH 348 U/L; AFP and beta-hCG normal; serum inhibin was never checked; PTHrP was not assayed. Ultrasound and CT showed a semisolid right ovarian mass (125 x 105 x 65 mm) with pelvic ascites; bone scan showed no bone metastasis. Hypercalcemia was treated with saline hydration, pamidronate 1 mg/kg and furosemide; right salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy and ascites drainage followed on day 6 and calcium remained normal. Tumor 120 x 90 x 65 mm, intact capsule; histology solid nodular proliferation with pseudofollicles, necrosis, luteinization, 7 mitoses per 10 HPF; positive for alpha-inhibin, calretinin, estrogen and progesterone receptors, CD56, SMA, focal KL1; negative for TTF1, synaptophysin, chromogranin, S100, EMA and CD99; diagnosis JGCT, FIGO IA, excluding small cell and clear cell carcinoma. No chemotherapy was proposed given stage IA; calcium checked every 3-4 months was normal and ultrasound at 24 months showed no recurrence. The authors attribute the hypercalcemia to tumor PTHrP secretion because it did not recur after resection (not measured). The authors report this as the third published JGCT with hypercalcemia (Daubenton, age 11, stage III, died of disease at 4 months after surgery and chemotherapy; Piura, age 25, stage IC, remission at 10 months after chemotherapy) and note FOXL2 expression prognostic data in JGCT are controversial (cited). FOXL2 Documents paraneoplastic hypercalcemia as a rare presentation of JGCT, with a differential diagnosis against small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type, and a note that the patient had stage IA disease.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor with an unusual immunoprofile, presenting as precocious puberty.
author: Dogra S
text: A 4-year-old girl presented with 6 months of vomiting, abdominal distension and intermittent periumbilical pain, with significant breast development, pubic hair and an infraumbilical mass. Hormones indicated peripheral precocious puberty: estradiol 234 pmol/L, LH <0.5 IU/L, FSH <0.5 IU/L, testosterone 0.5 ng/mL, DHEAS 46 ng/mL, 17-hydroxyprogesterone 0.3 ng/mL, AFP 1 ng/mL. Ultrasound and CT showed a large cystic-solid septated lower abdominal mass; the resected left adnexal tumor measured 22 x 20 x 18 cm, tan, multilobulated, variegated with solid and cystic areas. Histology showed a cellular tumor with irregular, variably sized follicles containing eosinophilic fluid, round hyperchromatic nuclei without grooves and no Call-Exner bodies. IHC was strongly positive for calretinin and negative for inhibin, hCG, AFP, cytokeratin and EMA; the diagnosis of JGCT was made despite negative inhibin, which the authors present as an unusual immunoprofile. The authors conclude that inhibin negativity does not exclude granulosa cell tumor and that calretinin is useful in inhibin-negative sex cord-stromal tumors; they note adjuvant treatment may be unnecessary when completely excised at an early stage.  Documents a JGCT with precocious puberty that was inhibin-negative but calretinin-positive, a diagnostic pitfall for immunohistochemistry.

title: Continuous subcutaneous IGF-1 therapy via insulin pump in a patient with Donohue syndrome.
author: Weber DR
text: Girl with molecularly confirmed Donohue syndrome (compound heterozygous INSR frameshift mutations) treated from 19 months with subcutaneous recombinant human IGF-1 and from 30 months with continuous rhIGF-1 via insulin pump; HbA1c fell from 9.8% to 8.8% on pump therapy and weight gain rose from 175 to 202 g/month. Polycystic ovaries were present since infancy and enlarged with age; cyst marsupialization was done at 21 months. At 35 months she presented with respiratory distress and an enlarged abdomen; ultrasound showed a large cystic abdominal structure with possible ovarian torsion. Bilateral oophorectomy: right ovarian mass 1.2 kg, 16.5 x 12 x 9 cm, consistent with juvenile granulosa cell tumor with desmoplastic non-invasive implants of borderline serous tumor; an adult-type granulosa cell tumor was also seen in the left ovary. Postoperative course: prolonged intubation for acute respiratory distress syndrome; parents withdrew care and she died at 36 months. Authors state it was unclear whether the ovarian tumor was related to rhIGF-1 treatment or to the natural course of Donohue syndrome; JGCT had been reported in another infant with Donohue syndrome who never received rhIGF-1 (cited). Authors discuss theoretical concerns that IGF-1 signalling (Akt pathway, proliferation) and high IGF-1 levels are linked to malignancy. INSR Rare association: bilateral granulosa cell tumors (juvenile right, adult-type left) with borderline serous implants in a toddler with Donohue syndrome (INSR loss) on rhIGF-1 therapy. Causality unresolved. No marker, IHC or molecular tumor testing described.

title: DICER1-pleuropulmonary blastoma familial tumor predisposition syndrome: a unique constellation of neoplastic conditions.
author: Schultz KA
text: Case report and pathology review: a girl with germline DICER1 loss-of-function variant developed Type II pleuropulmonary blastoma (age 5), follicular-variant papillary thyroid carcinoma (age 8), peritoneal cysts, nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma and an ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor with heterologous mucinous elements (age 13); alive 2 years after the SLCT. The reviewed text states that ovarian stromal tumors including SLCT, juvenile granulosa cell tumor and gynandroblastoma have been seen in children and young adults with germline DICER1 mutations, and that tumors with both Sertoli-Leydig and juvenile granulosa features have occasionally been seen. SLCT in DICER1 carriers may be cystic and solid, often with heterologous epithelial glands, with an inhibin-positive Sertoli component invariably present in primary tumors; the SLCT in this case carried the germline variant plus a somatic RNase IIIb mutation. Authors recommend appropriate intraoperative staging, including peritoneal fluid sampling, to determine need for adjuvant therapy. Germline DICER1 loss-of-function mutations are reported in nearly 70% of children with PPB; 49/51 PPBs tested had somatic RNase IIIb missense mutations. Authors conclude that PPB, ovarian stromal tumors especially SLCT, and other syndrome tumors, particularly in combination or at an early age, should prompt consideration of germline DICER1 testing. DICER1 No JGCT patient is described; JGCT appears in a pathology statement that it is among the ovarian stromal tumors seen with germline DICER1 mutation, sometimes mixed with Sertoli-Leydig features.

title: Large malignant ovarian tumors during pregnancy: two cases.
author: Xu D
text: Two cases of large ovarian malignancy in pregnancy at Zhejiang University Women's Hospital are reported; only case 2 was a juvenile granulosa cell tumor (case 1 was a grade I borderline mucinous tumor, 45 cm, and is not JGCT). JGCT patient: 24-year-old at 32 weeks of gestation with a 28x25x12 cm multiloculated cystic right ovarian mass with rich blood flow; AFP 266.8 ng/mL, CA-125 466.9 U/L, CEA 0.4 ng/mL. Lower segment cesarean (live girl, 1,800 g, Apgar 10) with right adnexectomy (30x25x15 cm smooth, unruptured tumor; 2,000 mL cyst fluid aspirated), partial omentectomy, pelvic lymph node dissection and peritoneal biopsies; pelvic fluid cytology negative; frozen section suggested JGCT and final pathology confirmed right ovarian JGCT with fallopian tube and 19 lymph nodes negative. Postoperative AFP fell to 39.5 ng/mL and CA-125 to 359.9 U/mL at day 6; she received three cycles of first-line BEP (from 23 Nov 2012, then 25 Dec 2012 and 23 Jan 2013) with leuprolide, which the authors say is recommended by FIGO for cord stromal tumors; stage is not explicitly stated. Follow-up at 2 years showed she remained healthy. The authors state that stage Ia granulosa cell tumors can be treated conservatively in pregnancy, and that BEP, etoposide-cisplatin and cisplatin-vinblastine-bleomycin protocols show no adverse effects on the fetus (their general statements, not data from the cases).  Case series of two large ovarian tumors in pregnancy, one a JGCT with elevated AFP and CA-125 treated with surgery plus BEP; only that case is JGCT.

title: Overview of pediatric testicular tumors in Korea.
author: Chung JM
text: Narrative review of pediatric testicular tumors with Korean registry data (studies of 2004 and 2011); incidence 1.6 (0.5 to 2) per 100,000 boys under 15 and 0.98 per 100,000 children in Korea. Gonadal stromal tumors are stated to be rare in children; Leydig cell tumors and juvenile granulosa cell tumors are described as universally benign in children. JGCT (testicular) occurs almost only in the first year of life, most in the first 6 months; light microscopy resembles ovarian JGCT; chromosomal mosaicism, structural Y-chromosome abnormalities and ambiguous genitalia are common, so chromosomal analysis is advised. The review states JGCT may be treated by orchiectomy or tumor enucleation without metastatic evaluation or adjuvant therapy. In the Korean registries germ cell tumors were 88.7% (1997-2001; yolk sac 41.8%, teratoma 35.7%) and 79.1% (2002-2008; yolk sac 29.4%, teratoma 39.2%); about 75% of prepubertal testicular tumors are benign. Testis-sparing surgery is advocated for benign tumors with normal AFP; RPLND and radiotherapy play very limited roles.  Pediatric testicular tumor review; only a short statement on testicular JGCT, with no JGCT patient counts.

title: Scrotal swelling in the neonate.
author: Basta AM
text: Pictorial review of neonatal scrotal masses and mimics; JGCT is a small part. The authors state JGCTs are very rare but the most common testicular tumors in infants younger than 6 months, and are uniformly benign. JGCTs lack accompanying endocrine abnormalities; a minority of cases are associated with abnormal external genitalia and an abnormal karyotype. Sonography: multiseptated cystic appearance with a hypervascular rim on Doppler; differential includes cystic dysplasia of the testis, teratoma, yolk sac tumor, Sertoli cell tumor and paratesticular sarcoma. Preoperative diagnosis is difficult; a multiseptated cystic and solid mass with negative AFP and beta-hCG is suggestive (AFP is physiologically high in infants under 6 months). Illustrative case (Figure 6): a 3-day-old boy with a left testicular mass seen on day 2 of life; 1.6 x 1.9 x 1.9 cm solid-cystic hypervascular mass replacing most of the testis; beta-hCG < 1 IU/L and AFP 17,260.2 ug/L; radical left orchiectomy on day 6 with JGCT on pathology. Management view: testis-sparing surgery (enucleation or partial orchiectomy with frozen section) is attempted in suspected neonatal neoplasms because benign histology is likely; complete orchiectomy if frozen section is not reassuring; no clear long-term follow-up guidelines, with follow-up advised particularly for tumors with high mitotic figures or poor differentiation.  Radiology pictorial essay that places testicular JGCT in the neonatal scrotal-mass differential with one illustrated case.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell ovarian tumor: clinicopathological evaluation of ten patients.
author: Karalok A
text: Retrospective single-centre (Etlik Zubeyde Hanim hospital, Ankara) series: 10 JGCT among 143 granulosa cell tumors (7%) diagnosed April 1995 to January 2014; median age 21.5 years (range 13-36). Presenting symptoms: bloating in 5, abdominal pain in 4, menometrorrhagia in 1; CA-125 measured in 5, normal in 4, 74 U/mL in the patient with a ruptured cyst; ascites in 4; median tumor diameter 140 mm (60-400); right side 5, left side 5. FIGO 1988 stage IA in 9 and stage IC in 1 (preoperative rupture, negative cytology); all tumors completely resected; 8 had unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, 1 cystectomy, 1 TAH+BSO elsewhere (re-staged). Five patients had pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy (median 54 nodes, range 7-94), none positive; omentectomy in 7 (6 infracolic, 1 partial), appendectomy in 2, no omental tumor. Three patients had adjuvant therapy: BEP x4 (stage IC), VAC x6 (stage IA) and radiotherapy (stage IA); frozen section was diagnostic for JGCT in 2 of 5, sex cord-stromal tumor NOS in 2, lymphoma suspected in 1. No recurrence in median follow-up 58 months (range 3-113). Of 5 patients desiring pregnancy, 4 had 5 term pregnancies after fertility-sparing surgery, including the stage IC patient treated with BEP. Authors conclude surgery is primary management, adjuvant therapy benefit is unclear, and fertility-sparing surgery can be safely suggested in early stage; they suggest lymphadenectomy may be unnecessary in sex cord-stromal tumors and recommend long follow-up with inhibin B.  Small adult-and-adolescent series showing excellent outcomes and preserved fertility after fertility-sparing surgery for stage I JGCT.

title: A Hot-spot of In-frame Duplications Activates the Oncoprotein AKT1 in Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumors.
author: Bessière L
text: Cohort of 16 histologically proven JGCTs in girls under 15 years (collected 1994-2014, Necker-Enfants Malades Paris and Montpellier); 12 FFPE and 4 frozen samples; peritumoral DNA was available for only 8. In-frame tandem duplications of AKT1 exon 3 were found in 10 of 16 JGCTs (more than 60%); the 10 duplications had not been reported before and all but two were different, which the authors attribute to a dynamic mutational process (DNA-polymerase errors). The two duplications tested against peritumoral DNA were somatic. No duplications were found in 10 adult-type GCTs, 15 colorectal carcinomas, 59 NCI cell lines, or in AKT2 exon 3. Full AKT1 sequencing found conserved-residue point mutations in 10 tumors, confirmed somatic in 7 with peritumoral DNA; in total 14 of 16 JGCTs carried putative AKT1 driver alterations. GNAS R201C/H mutations were absent in all 16 and PIK3CA exons 9, 18, 20 had no mutations in the 7 tumors tested. In HeLa cells the duplicated AKT1 proteins localized almost exclusively under the plasma membrane (with filopodia-like processes), were strongly phosphorylated at S473 compared with wild-type and E17K, and were hyperactive and serum-independent in a FOXO3a luciferase reporter; the Q79K-W80R double mutant (and each mutation alone) was also hyperactive. Phospho-AKT immunostaining confirmed phosphorylated AKT1 in a tumor section (T5) bearing a duplication. The authors conclude that somatic AKT1 mutations are a major driver event in JGCT, that the duplications could facilitate molecular diagnosis, and that PI3K-AKT-mTOR inhibitors in clinical trials open targeted-therapy perspectives; functional work was in HeLa cells, not patient-derived cells. AKT1 AKT1 GNAS (Galphas) PIK3CA Identifies recurrent activating AKT1 pleckstrin-homology-domain duplications in about 60% of pediatric JGCTs, one of the main known somatic drivers and a candidate therapeutic target.

title: Ovarian tumors related to intronic mutations in DICER1: a report from the international ovarian and testicular stromal tumor registry.
author: Schultz KA
text: Two young women with ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (SLCT) carried the same novel germline DICER1 intronic variant c.5096-12G>A; no patient in the report had a juvenile granulosa cell tumor. Patient 1: undifferentiated ovarian sarcoma at age 10 (inhibin negative; lacked JGCT features; treated with vincristine, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide), then FIGO IIA SLCT in the other ovary 4 years later (6 cycles cisplatin, etoposide, bleomycin); alive and well 15 years after the first and 12 years after the second diagnosis. Patient 2: adolescent with SLCT plus lung cyst and thyroid nodule; alive and well more than 1 year after diagnosis. Each ovarian tumor carried the germline variant plus a tumor-specific somatic RNase IIIb mutation (two-hit pattern); TP53 mutated only in the sarcoma. Preliminary OTST Registry data cited: 20 individuals with ovarian SLCT tested positive for germline DICER1 mutations, 5 with splice-site base substitutions (these 2 plus 3 canonical splice-site); earlier registry data cited germline DICER1 mutations in 48% of SLCT. Authors state that DICER1 mutations remain a risk for metachronous ovarian tumors beyond the usual 2-5 year surveillance window and recommend surveillance imaging (usually ultrasound) and genetic counseling. Authors conclude germline DICER1 mutations should be suspected in patients with SLCT, and also in patients with juvenile granulosa cell tumor, gynandroblastoma or any ovarian stromal tumor or sarcoma with a personal or family history of nodular thyroid disease or other DICER1 conditions; somatic tumor testing is the most sensitive way to detect DICER1 mutations. DICER1 DICER1 JGCT appears only as an authors' statement that germline DICER1 testing should be considered in JGCT and other ovarian stromal tumors with DICER1-related personal or family history; no JGCT patient or JGCT sequencing result is reported.

title: [Juvenile granulosa tumor of the ovary: report of a case].
author: Azahouani A
text: An 8-year-old girl without history had about 15 days of moderate paroxysmal pelvic pain, increasing abdominal volume and weight loss; examination found a hard, ill-defined, painless abdominopelvic mass of about 25 x 20 cm with collateral venous circulation and no signs of hypersecretion. Ultrasound showed a very large cystic multiseptated abdominopelvic mass occupying almost the whole abdomen with small intraperitoneal effusion, no deep lymph nodes and no liver involvement; CT showed a multiseptated cystic left supravesical mass. Alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG were normal; inhibin and estradiol are not reported for the patient. Surgery found a 25 x 20 cm tumor of the left ovary with serohemorrhagic effusion; pathology with immunostaining supported juvenile granulosa cell tumor (strong vimentin positivity); FIGO stage is not stated. Left adnexectomy was performed; a multidisciplinary meeting decided that neither chemotherapy nor radiotherapy was necessary; periodic clinical and radiological follow-up was unremarkable. The authors state in the discussion (citing literature) that JGCT is about 5% of ovarian tumors in children and adolescents, 80% occur under 20 years and 50% under 10 years, unilateral in 97% with average size 12.5 cm, 5-year survival is 92%, adjuvant chemotherapy is reserved for recurrence, and poor prognostic factors are large size, ascites and capsular rupture.  Case of a very large non-secreting JGCT in a school-age child managed by unilateral adnexectomy alone.

title: A survey of DICER1 hotspot mutations in ovarian and testicular sex cord-stromal tumors.
author: Conlon N
text: Sanger sequencing of DICER1 exons 24 and 25 in 32 ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, 8 Sertoli cell tumors, 5 gynandroblastomas, 1 sex cord tumor with annular tubules, 1 ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor NOS, 15 testicular sex cord-stromal tumors and 10 female genital tract tumors with rhabdomyosarcomatous differentiation. No juvenile granulosa cell tumors were included. DICER1 hotspot mutations in 20/32 (63%) ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, 16/20 (80%) of which were p.E1705K; frequencies were 6/10 (60%) in poorly differentiated, 14/20 (70%) in intermediately differentiated, and 0/2 in well-differentiated tumors; 9/14 (64%) with heterologous or retiform elements versus 11/18 (61%) without. Gynandroblastomas 2/5 (40%) and ovarian Sertoli cell tumors 5/8 (63%) carried DICER1 hotspot mutations, all p.E1705K; the sex cord tumor with annular tubules (0/1) and sex cord-stromal tumor NOS (0/1) were wild-type. Two DICER1 wild-type gynandroblastomas carried FOXL2 p.C134W in both granulosa-like and Sertoli-Leydig-like components, suggesting gynandroblastoma encompasses two genetic groups (FOXL2-mutant granulosa-like or DICER1-mutant Sertoli-Leydig-like); FOXL2 and DICER1 mutations appeared mutually exclusive. No DICER1 hotspot mutations in 15 testicular sex cord-stromal tumors (8 classical Sertoli cell tumors, 3 large cell calcifying variants, 4 NOS); combined with the earlier report, 20 testicular tumors tested were all wild-type, so the authors suggest ovarian and testicular sex cord-stromal tumor pathogenesis differ. DICER1 hotspot mutations were found in 2/10 female genital tract rhabdomyosarcomatous tumors (an adult cervical rhabdomyosarcoma metastasis p.D1709N and the rhabdomyosarcoma component of a uterine carcinosarcoma p.E1813Q); 0/2 pediatric cervical embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas. Authors note in the introduction that adult granulosa cell tumors usually harbor somatic FOXL2 mutations and that germline DICER1 mutations cause the DICER1 syndrome; they re-analyzed TCGA endometrial data (6/248, 2.4% with DICER1 hotspot residue mutations). DICER1 FOXL2 Contributes only context for JGCT: no JGCTs were tested, but the study shows DICER1 hotspot mutations cluster in Sertoli-lineage tumors and not in testicular sex cord-stromal tumors, and that FOXL2 C134W marks granulosa-like gynandroblastoma components.

title: Cytoreductive surgery (CRS) and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) in pediatric ovarian tumors: a novel treatment approach.
author: Hayes-Jordan A
text: Single-institution trial series of CRS plus HIPEC in 8 girls with ovarian primary tumors and multifocal peritoneal disease (from 101 pediatric CRS/HIPEC operations): 3 yolk sac/germ cell tumors, 1 Sertoli-Leydig, 1 PNET, 1 choriocarcinoma, 1 JGCT and 1 mucinous adenocarcinoma. HIPEC used closed technique with cisplatin 100 mg/m2 for 90 minutes at 41 C after complete (CCR 0) or near-complete (CCR 1, residual <2.5 cm) cytoreduction; all patients had prior surgery and chemotherapy, one had abdominal radiation; patients with extra-abdominal disease were excluded. The JGCT patient (patient 3, age 18) had a tumor that had recurred repeatedly over 8 years after BEP, unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, cisplatin/taxane, surgery, high-dose abdominal radiation and stem cell transplant; PCI 15, CCR 1 resection (peritonectomy, jejunal and right colon resection); she developed an enterocutaneous fistula and died of disease at 12 months. Whole cohort: overall survival 64% and relapse-free survival 62%; 3 of 8 (37%) recurred and died (JGCT, Sertoli-Leydig/sarcomatoid, yolk sac), the other 5 are disease free 13 to 74 months after HIPEC (text states 2 to 6 years). No perioperative deaths; complications were 2 wound infections, 1 urinary tract infection and 1 enterocutaneous fistula (in the JGCT patient); 6 of 8 (75%) had no complications. The authors note that heavily pretreated patients offered HIPEC at the 3rd or 4th relapse did worse and all died, and conclude CRS plus HIPEC is safe and may be effective in pediatric-type ovarian tumors, but that the sample is too small for definitive conclusions.  Describes one heavily pretreated recurrent JGCT patient treated with CRS and HIPEC (died at 12 months); evidence for HIPEC in JGCT is therefore a single unsuccessful case within a mixed series.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour of the ovary presenting with hyperprolactinaemic amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea.
author: Iqbal A
text: 16-year-old woman (menarche at 14) with 9 months of secondary amenorrhea and 2 months of bilateral galactorrhea; no headache or visual symptoms. Labs: prolactin 7081 mIU/l (negative macroprolactin screen), LH and FSH <0.1 U/l, estradiol 7442 pmol/l, beta-hCG undetectable, testosterone 2.0 nmol/l (borderline), SHBG >200 nmol/l, IGF1 low 129 ug/l, inhibin B 2735 ng/l (ref <341), inhibin A 79.7 ng/l, CA125 20 U/ml and AFP 1.21 ug/l normal. Imaging: pituitary MRI showed an enlarged anterior pituitary without micro- or macroadenoma; abdominal MRI showed a 4.8 cm right ovarian mass with no metastatic disease. Right salpingo-oophorectomy; histology JGCT FIGO stage IA with mostly luteinised cells and scattered irregular follicular spaces; prolactin immunohistochemistry negative. Estrogen and prolactin normalized after surgery; the patient conceived 6 months post-surgery and had a healthy child; estradiol 821 pmol/l and prolactin 327 mIU/l at 2 years. Authors postulate hyperprolactinemia resulted from estrogenic stimulation of pituitary lactotrophs (state analogous to pregnancy) rather than tumor prolactin secretion, and claim this is the first report of such a mechanism in JGCT; they cite 5-year survival 90-95% in stage I and 25-50% in advanced stage.  Documents an uncommon endocrine presentation of JGCT (estrogen-driven hyperprolactinemia mimicking prolactinoma) with fertility preserved after unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumour of the Ovary with Unilocular Pure Cystic Presentation: A Case Report and Review of Literature.
author: Anandpara KM
text: 18-year-old unmarried girl with abdominal pain and distension for 2 months and facial hair for 1 year; no precocious puberty on retrospective evaluation. Ultrasound showed a large anechoic cystic lesion with posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal echoes or septations; CT showed a large unilocular fluid-density lesion (reported as 85x110x125 cm AP x TR x CC, as printed) without enhancing soft tissue or septae; left ovary not seen separately. Imaging diagnosis was a benign large left ovarian cyst. Estradiol was elevated at 450 pg/mL (reference 15-350); CA-125 and beta-hCG were normal. Left ovarian cystectomy found a cyst wall with a few intervening solid areas; histology showed round to oval cells with moderately pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, scanty cytoplasm, irregular nuclear margins, some grooves, and Call-Exner bodies, diagnosed as granulosa cell tumor (juvenile type per title and discussion). The authors propose that a malignant ovarian lesion be included in the differential diagnosis of a unilocular, purely cystic ovarian lesion even when no malignant imaging criteria are present. Discussion (literature-based statements by authors): juvenile form is about 5% of granulosa cell tumors, survival up to 97% cited, and about 70% of GCTs secrete estrogen; morphology and imaging cannot reliably separate adult from juvenile types.  Unusual purely cystic unilocular JGCT in an 18-year-old, older than typical, with elevated estradiol and virilization features.

title: Insights into granulosa cell tumors using spontaneous or genetically engineered mouse models.
author: Kim SY
text: Review of spontaneous and genetically engineered mouse models of granulosa cell tumor (GCT); it contains no patient cohort data. Background stated by the review: GCT is about 5% of ovarian tumors; 43% of patients recur and 80% of those die of disease (cited); JGCT occurs from infancy through puberty and has malignant potential; JGCT cells are round, non-grooved, luteinized with hyperchromatic nuclei and follicle-like spaces. Molecular statements: the FOXL2 mutation seen in 95% of adult GCT has not been found in JGCT, and loss of FOXL2 expression was observed in aggressive JGCT; activating GNAS R201C/R201H mutations were found in JGCT patients; in-frame AKT1 pleckstrin-homology-domain duplications were found in more than 60% of JGCT patients. SWR/Bm mice are the spontaneous JGCT model: about 1% of inbred females develop malignant JGCT at about 8 weeks, tumors secrete high inhibin and estrogen, metastasize on serial transplantation, and are modified by Gct loci (Gct1 on chromosome 4 essential, responsive to DHEA). Smad1/Smad5 double conditional knockout in granulosa cells (Amhr2-cre) gives 100% GCT penetrance with a phenotype resembling human JGCT, 80% peritoneal/lymphatic metastasis by 8 months and very high inhibin-alpha and AMH; Smad1/5/4 triple knockout delays tumors and prevents metastasis, implicating TGF-beta/SMAD signaling in JGCT. Bmpr1a/1b double knockout mice have similar tumors (up to 40% at 8 and up to 90% at 16 months). Other models (Inha-null, SV40 T-antigen, LH-beta, Wnt/beta-catenin, ER-beta, Foxo1/3/Pten, oocyte PIK3CA) are discussed mostly as adult-type or unclassifiable GCT; Foxo1/3 knockouts are proposed as an adult GCT model. The authors conclude models need reassessing against human histopathology, pathways and recurrence. AKT1 GNAS (G alpha s) FOXL2 Preclinical review; relevant for JGCT molecular genetics (AKT1, GNAS, FOXL2 absence) and for the SWR and Smad1/5 mouse models of JGCT.

title: Constitutive Activation of PI3K in Oocyte Induces Ovarian Granulosa Cell Tumors.
author: Kim SY
text: Mouse study (not human patients): constitutively active PI3K (PIK3CA*) in primordial oocytes (Gdf9-iCre) produced bilateral ovarian granulosa cell tumors with 100% penetrance at postnatal day 65 (n>=35); mice became cachectic and were euthanized by day 85. The authors judged the mouse tumors to resemble JGCT rather than adult GCT: cord-like architecture was similar to human AGCT, but few nuclear grooves or Call-Exner bodies and follicle-like cysts resembled JGCT, and FOXL2 was not mutated. Tumor cells expressed FOXL2 and inhibin alpha, overexpressed inhibin betaA, SMAD3 and GATA4, had high p-AKT, and the mice had high serum AMH, activin A, estradiol, testosterone and inhibin A with low FSH. Tumor cells did not express the mutant PI3K transgene (PCR) and tumor grafts grew independently of oocytes, but interaction with mutant oocytes at primordial/primary follicle stage was essential (co-grafted normal ovaries stayed tumor-free; Zp3-Cre activation at secondary follicle stage caused no tumors). Tumor growth correlated with the activin A to inhibin A ratio (R2 = 0.784 with Ki67 index); cultured tumor cells secreted 40 times more activin A than normal granulosa cells and proliferated in response to activin A (25 ng/ml), suggesting an activin A-SMAD3 autocrine growth circuit. FOXO1 and PTEN were retained in the tumors, so loss of these suppressors was not the cause in this model. The authors suggest, as speculation, that AKT1 mutations in human JGCT may contribute to such an activin A autocrine circuit and that GNAS R201 mutations may sensitize granulosa cells to activin A. PIK3CA (constitutively active transgene in oocytes, mouse) AKT1 FOXL2 GNAS Preclinical mouse model of granulosa cell tumor with JGCT-like features driven by PI3K-AKT pathway activation; provides mechanistic context for AKT1 and GNAS findings in human JGCT. No JGCT patients.

title: Childhood ovarian neoplasms in Ibadan, South-western Nigeria.
author: Ajani MA
text: Single-institution retrospective review (University College Hospital, Ibadan, 1991-June 2013) of 24 ovarian neoplasms in children under 15 years, 2.8% of all ovarian tumors seen. 14 (58.3%) were benign and 10 (41.7%) malignant; germ cell tumors made up 16 of 20 primary tumors; 4 secondary tumors were all Burkitt lymphoma. Sex cord-stromal tumors were 4 of 20 primary tumors (16.7% of all childhood ovarian neoplasms); the authors state juvenile granulosa cell tumor was the most common of these. The Discussion states yolk sac tumor and juvenile granulosa cell tumor were equally the most common primary malignant childhood tumors; the number of JGCT cases, ages, treatment and outcomes are not given in the text. No surface epithelial tumors and no malignant ovarian tumor under 5 years were seen.  Epidemiology only: JGCT is reported as the leading sex cord-stromal tumor and tied for most common primary malignant ovarian tumor in a small Nigerian pediatric series; no JGCT-level data.

title: Malignancy in disorders of sex development.
author: Kathrins M
text: Narrative review of gonadal tumor risk in disorders of sex development (DSD; 1 in 4,500-5,000 live births); DSD patients are at increased risk of testicular carcinoma in situ and germ cell tumors, and the introduction names juvenile granulosa cell tumors (JGCTs) among other tumors of concern. The only JGCT-specific statement: JGCT, a sex cord-stromal tumor, has been noted in rare cases of sex-chromosomal mosaicism and ambiguous genitalia in the neonatal period; the review states that these tumors are benign and hormonally inactive so testis-sparing surgery should be curative (cited to a single source; the review gives no case numbers). Main review conclusions concern other tumors: Y-chromosomal material and gonadal position are risk factors; 46,XX congenital adrenal hyperplasia without Y material is not at higher risk; gonadoblastoma risk in dysgenetic DSD 4.7-25% and overall tumor risk 15-33%; partial AIS with untreated undescended testes up to 50%. Markers discussed for DSD tumors beyond hCG and AFP are OCT3/4, TSPY, stem cell factor and WT1; no JGCT marker data are given.  Marginal: one sentence on neonatal (testicular) JGCT in sex-chromosomal mosaicism with ambiguous genitalia and testis-sparing surgery; the rest is about germ cell tumors in DSD.

title: An Unusual Case of Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Ovary.
author: Rusterholz KR
text: A 19-year-old nulligravid woman presented with right abdominal pain, a lower abdominal mass, hirsutism with male-pattern pubic hair and menstrual irregularity since age 14; no hormone levels were obtained. CT showed a multilobulated, septated, predominantly low-attenuation abdominopelvic mass of about 27 x 22 x 15 cm with moderate ascites and non-enlarged periaortic nodes; ultrasound showed a complex cystic-solid mass. Laparotomy found a 27 x 21 x 15 cm right ovarian cystic and solid mass with some ruptured cysts; right salpingo-oophorectomy and staging (nodes, omentum, ascites negative) were performed; specimen 3482 g, 60% solid, 40% cystic with hemorrhage and necrosis. Histology showed frequent mitoses, some nuclear anaplasia, luteinized irregular follicles and no Call-Exner bodies; inhibin positive and focally AE1/AE3 positive; diagnosis JGCT, FIGO IC. No further treatment was given initially; CT at 3 months showed two new liver lesions (3.4 and 4 cm) and splenic hilum soft tissue masses (metastases). Despite numerous cycles of varying chemotherapy regimens she progressed, with new right adnexal collections and persistently elevated inhibin, less than 1 year after diagnosis. The authors present the case as an aggressive stage IC JGCT and cite that relapses of juvenile tumors tend to be rapid and aggressive, that relapse occurred in 2 of 4 stage IC patients receiving chemotherapy in one cited series, and that cisplatin-based multidrug regimens have been suggested for advanced or recurrent disease.  Example of a large stage IC JGCT in a young adult that metastasized within 3 months despite negative surgical staging, illustrating aggressive behavior of ruptured stage I disease.

title: Rare virilizing granulosa cell tumor in an adolescent.
author: Bus D
text: 14-year-old girl (menarche at 10) with 18 months of secondary amenorrhea followed by virilization: Ferriman-Gallwey score 20, deepened voice, delayed thelarche and clitoromegaly of 5 cm; a 4 cm mass was palpable in the right ovarian area. Total testosterone was 8.84 nmol/l (normal 0.17-2.81); DHEAS, FSH, LH, estradiol, progesterone, TSH, prolactin, AFP, CA-125 and CA 15-3 were normal. Ultrasound showed a heterogeneous right ovarian mass; MRI showed a 36x42x45 mm solid right ovarian lesion with minor hepatosplenomegaly and ascites. Laparoscopy found a 5x4 cm right ovarian tumour with abnormal vascularisation and a normal uterus, left ovary and tubes; right oophorectomy was done with bagging of the specimen. Histology: 5.5x4x3 cm yellow-tan lobulated tumour with solid and cystic areas, lobules, nests and perivascular palisades of cells with scant cytoplasm, ovoid nuclei and grooving; no lymphovascular invasion and intact serosa. IHC positive for inhibin, Melan-A, WT1, calretinin and CD99; negative for EMA, CD117, PLAP, AFP and CD30; diagnosis juvenile-type granulosa cell tumour. Testosterone normalised after surgery and menses returned; follow-up reported at 4 months (testosterone <0.17 nmol/l). The authors state that about 95% of granulosa cell tumours are adult type and 5% juvenile, that hyperestrogenism occurs in 97-98% and hyperandrogenism in 2-3% of cases, and that long-term follow-up is advised because late recurrences are reported.  Case report of a rare androgen-secreting JGCT in an adolescent, with IHC profile and rapid testosterone normalisation after oophorectomy; the epidemiologic statements are cited from other papers.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor associated with Ollier disease.
author: Sampagar AA
text: 2.5-year-old girl presented with precocious puberty (Tanner stage 2) and a hard mass in the right hypochondrium. MRI showed a well-defined right ovarian mass of 10 x 5 x 11 cm with cystic and necrotic areas. MRI also showed multiple small lobulated T2-hyperintense foci in the right femoral neck, trochanters and right iliac blade, initially reported as metastases; radiographs showed expansile lytic lesions with cortical thinning. Bone scan showed no osteoblastic metastasis and bone biopsy showed cartilaginous elements, reported as enchondromas, giving a final diagnosis of Ollier disease with JGCT. Histology: macrofollicles lined by 2-3 layers of granulosa cells with Call-Exner bodies; tumor cells expressed inhibin, calretinin, melan-A (focal) and cytokeratin. Peritoneal aspirate was positive for malignant cells while omental biopsy was not involved; stage was given as 1C3 'as per new FIGO staging'. Treatment was surgical removal followed by chemotherapy per germ cell tumor protocol; breast size and pubic hair regressed a few weeks after surgery. Parents were counseled about chondrosarcoma risk and regular follow-up. The authors state Ollier disease carries an estimated 30%-50% chondrosarcoma risk and argue the association indicates generalized mesodermal dysplasia, so Ollier patients should be screened for mesodermal neoplasms. The authors note maternal ovulation-inducing drug use for 2 years before this conception and propose that estrogen-containing compounds are an etiological factor for granulosa cell tumors.  Case report of JGCT co-occurring with Ollier disease; illustrates that enchondromas can mimic skeletal metastases on staging imaging.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Testicle - Report of a Neonatal Case with Positive Alpha-fetoprotein Immunohistochemical Staining.
author: Dundas M
text: Term male neonate (39 weeks, birth weight 3550 g) with an enlarged smooth firm translucent left testis; ultrasound showed a 2.7 x 1.7 x 2.7 cm multicystic mass with internal flow replacing the testis; no genital ambiguity, anatomic abnormalities or sex chromosome aneuploidy. Serum LDH 885 IU/L (normal 160-450), beta-hCG 48.58 IU/L (normal <=50), AFP 113,200 ng/ml (no reference range given). Left radical inguinal orchiectomy on day 2 of life; 2.5 x 2.0 x 1.0 cm gray-white multicystic mass with basophilic/mucicarminophilic fluid; tumor limited to testis/epididymis without spermatic cord extension. IHC positive for inhibin, calretinin, CD99, SF-4 (as written), FOXL2 and AFP; negative for CD30, CD117, D2-40, PanCK, PLAP, glypican-3, OCT3/4. AFP tumor positivity was unexplained, though clinical, gross and other IHC features fit JGCT. No recurrence; at 7 months inhibin A 1 pg/ml, beta-hCG <1, AFP 41.9 ng/ml; markers followed every 3 months. Authors suggest electron microscopy and GATA6/CSF1R staining may help exclude yolk sac tumor and recommend adding them routinely. From literature cited: Prepubertal Testis Tumor Registry had 395 tumors (244 yolk sac, 43 stromal, 11 JGCT); a 70-case study (Kao) reported AFP uniformly negative apart from one focal case, making this the second AFP-positive JGCT report per the authors.  Highlights a diagnostic pitfall (AFP positivity mimicking yolk sac tumor) in neonatal testicular JGCT.

title: Granulosa cell tumor of the testis in a newborn.
author: Claros OR
text: A term (40 weeks, 3040 g) newborn boy had an enlarged right testis at the first post-delivery examination; ultrasound showed a heterogeneous solid mass without retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP was 97,819 ng/mL (considered within the normal range for gestational age and birth weight) and total hCG was 31.4 mIU/mL (reference <5), the mild hCG elevation being interpreted by the authors as a false positive. Right inguinal orchiectomy at 21 hours of age: a 3.0 x 2.0 x 1.5 cm solid, light-brown, sharply defined tumor replacing most of the testicular parenchyma with focal follicle-like cysts; epididymis and rete testis displaced but not involved; no necrosis, no invasion of tunica albuginea, nerves or vessels; margins free. Histology showed lobulated solid areas of large cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and visible nucleoli, with frequent mitoses and apoptoses; IHC: diffuse vimentin, focal calretinin and inhibin positive; negative for beta-hCG, AFP and cytokeratins, which excluded yolk sac tumor (the main differential). Follow-up at 4 years showed a healthy child with no testicular or scrotal complaints; no adjuvant therapy was given. Literature statements cited by the authors: JGCT is 1.2% of prepubertal testis tumors and the most common testicular neoplasm in the first 6 months of life; 48 cases had been compiled up to 2002; Y-chromosome abnormalities in about 20% of cases; clinical features are an asymptomatic mass without endocrine signs; orchiectomy is the treatment of choice and testis-sparing enucleation is possible after frozen section. The authors regard testicular JGCT as universally benign with an excellent prognosis and consider AFP and hCG useless as tumor markers for it.  Case report of congenital testicular JGCT with IHC profile, marker values and 4-year follow-up after orchiectomy alone.

title: Granulosa Cell Tumors: Novel Predictors of Recurrence in Early-stage Patients.
author: Sakr S
text: Single-institution retrospective cohort of 125 ovarian granulosa cell tumor (GCT) patients diagnosed 1975-2014; median follow-up 120 months (range 1-465); recurrence in 12/125 (9.6%). Histologic type: 113/125 (90%) adult and 12 (10%) juvenile GCT (JGCT); JGCT recurred in 2/12 (17%) versus 10/113 (9%) adult (Table 2: 2/12 recurrences were juvenile, p=0.32; tumor subtype was not significant for recurrence). The two recurrent JGCT cases (Tables 7 and 8): a 25-year-old (cystic, 16 cm, no rupture, mitotic rate 3/10 HPF, moderate pleomorphism; USO with staging, stage II, BEP; recurrence at 24 months, alive) and a 22-year-old (solid/cystic, 34 cm, mitotic rate 12, mild pleomorphism; USO, stage IIIC, BEP; recurrence at 26 months, died). Both had high CD56; SMAD3 high in the first and low in the second. Prognostic factors in the whole cohort: stage III-IV vs I-II (shorter disease-free interval 77.2 vs 432.4 months), mitotic rate 4 or more per 10 HPF, severe nuclear pleomorphism, chemotherapy in addition to surgery, and high HER2, CD56 and SMAD3 expression; on Cox regression only SMAD3 and treatment type remained independent for disease-free interval. In stage I disease, adjuvant chemotherapy (HR 10.26 per Table 6; abstract states HR 10.2) and high SMAD3 (HR 8.9, 95% CI 2.34-34.5 when treatment excluded) predicted recurrence; authors say CD56 and SMAD3 IHC need validation on a larger scale. IHC was run on tissue microarrays of 88 primary tumors (calretinin, inhibin, HER2, CD56, SMAD3, GATA4, VEGF); results are not reported separately for JGCT. Authors cite from other work that FOXL2 C134W occurs in 90-97% of GCTs and that stage I long-term disease-free survival is about 84-95%.  A mostly adult GCT cohort; JGCT is 12 patients, with only the recurrence counts and two case descriptions specific to JGCT.

title: Selecting treatment method for ovarian masses in children - 24 years of experience.
author: Luczak J
text: Wroclaw (Poland) pediatric surgery series of 214 girls operated 1991-2014 for ovarian lesions: 127 non-neoplastic, 65 benign tumors, 22 malignant (10.28%). Malignant lesions: dysgerminoma 7, juvenile granulosa cell tumor 4, immature teratoma 4, Burkitt lymphoma 2, and single cases of malignant mesenchymoma, embryonal carcinoma, serous papillary carcinoma, androblastoma and Sertoli cell tumor. JGCT-specific age, stage, treatment, marker values and outcome are not reported; the 4 JGCT are included in malignant-group figures only. In the malignant group, 17/22 (77.3%) lesions were large (10 cm or more) versus 32.8% of non-malignant; solid or mixed structure in all malignant tumors; markers positive in 14/20 (70%). Positive tumor markers, large size and age under 14 years independently distinguished malignant from non-malignant lesions; no malignancy occurred in 54 patients with purely cystic structure and negative markers. Authors report nearly 80% of malignant cases presented with palpable mass, suggesting delayed diagnosis, and propose a gonad-sparing management algorithm.  Provides a frequency count of JGCT (4 of 22 malignant ovarian tumors) in a large pediatric surgical series; no JGCT-level clinical or outcome data.

title: DICER1-related Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor and gynandroblastoma: Clinical and genetic findings from the International Ovarian and Testicular Stromal Tumor Registry.
author: Schultz KAP
text: International Ovarian and Testicular Stromal Tumor (OTST) Registry report on the first 107 enrolled individuals (December 2011 to March 2016) with ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors: 49 SLCT, 25 JGCT, 5 gynandroblastoma, 10 adult granulosa cell tumors and others; pathology centrally reviewed in 98/107 (local and central diagnoses agreed in 80/98, 82%). JGCT (n=25): median age at presentation 9 years (range 1 month to 28 years); 40% Caucasian; most had hormonal symptoms; median time from diagnosis 15 months (0-415); status NED 21 (84%), in recurrence treatment 1 (4%), deceased 3 (12%). JGCT staging and outcome (Table 4): stage IA 7, IB 1, IC 4, IC2 4, above IC 3, unknown 6; 5 received adjuvant chemotherapy and 20 surgery only; 5 relapses and 3 deaths overall; stage IA/IB patients (8) all treated with surgery alone and free of disease at median 9 months (1-77). Of 11 JGCT patients with stage IC or greater, 3 (27%) died of disease at median 17 months (10-44); by the table, IC: 2 NED, 2 relapse, 1 death of 4; IC2: 4 of 4 NED (2 chemotherapy); above IC: 1 NED, 2 relapse, 2 deaths of 3. Intraoperatively ruptured JGCT was generally treated with surgery alone (14 of 24, 58.3%); the most common chemotherapy was cisplatin-etoposide-bleomycin (JGCT=4); one JGCT patient received carboplatin-etoposide-bleomycin. Germline DICER1 testing was negative in all 19 JGCT tested and tumor sequencing found no DICER1 mutation in the 2 JGCT sequenced; no DICER1 mutation was found in any centrally reviewed non-SLCT/GAB sex cord-stromal type. Two patients with DICER1 mutations diagnosed locally as JGCT were reclassified as gynandroblastoma on central review, which the authors cite as showing DICER1 tumor testing can help in difficult-to-classify cases. By contrast, 97% (36/37) of sequenced SLCTs and 4/4 gynandroblastomas had DICER1 RNase IIIb hotspot mutations, about half with predisposing germline or mosaic mutations; authors recommend central pathology review and DICER1 testing for SLCT/GAB, and consideration in other sex cord-stromal tumors if history suggests DICER1 predisposition. DICER1 DICER1 Registry-derived JGCT cohort (n=25) with stage-specific outcomes and DICER1 results showing JGCT is not DICER1-related, in contrast to SLCT/GAB. Short follow-up limits survival inference.

title: The molecular mechanism of ovarian granulosa cell tumors.
author: Li J
text: Narrative review of molecular mechanisms of ovarian granulosa cell tumor (GCT), which it describes as 2-5% of ovarian cancers; about 95% are adult (AGCT) and the rest juvenile (JGCT); the review says JGCT occurs only in people younger than 30 years (the review's wording attributes hypoestrogenism and abdominal mass to JGCT, although GCT is estrogen-secreting). Most of the review concerns AGCT: FOXL2 402C>G (C134W) in more than 97% of AGCT; the review adds that FOXL2 expression was reported to be downregulated in aggressive JGCT. JGCT-specific molecular statements: conditional deletion of SMAD1 and SMAD5 in mouse granulosa cells causes metastatic GCT that phenocopies human JGCT, and the TGF-beta/SMAD2/3 pathway is active in JGCT, where TGF-beta may promote tumor growth by inhibiting apoptosis (cited work). Other pathways covered, mostly from cell lines (KGN) and mouse models rather than JGCT: PI3K/AKT-FOXO-PTEN, Notch, activin/inhibin, BMP, AMH, GATA4 and VEGF; the review notes the relationship between these pathways and human GCT is often unclear. Review conclusion: 5-year survival is up to 90%, recurrence is the main cause of death, surgery remains the most important treatment, and hormonal, anti-VEGF and pathway-targeted strategies remain at an early, adjunctive stage. FOXL2 SMAD1/SMAD5 TGF-beta/SMAD2/3 pathway Molecular review dominated by AGCT; contains only a few JGCT-specific statements (FOXL2 downregulation in aggressive JGCT, SMAD1/5 knockout mouse phenocopy, active TGF-beta/SMAD2/3 pathway). No patient data.

title: [Granulosa cell ovarian tumor: precocious puberty in infant less than 1 year of age. Case report].
author: Lacourt P
text: 10-month-old girl with 4 months of breast development and 2 months of pubic hair, apocrine odor and whitish vaginal discharge; Tanner III breasts, abundant pubic hair and a palpable abdominal mass (peripheral precocious puberty). Estradiol 457 pg/mL (reference <12), LH <0.5, FSH 0.66 mIU/mL (suppressed gonadotropins), LDH 2,690 mIU/mL (reference 210-420), hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL; AFP 10.7, beta-hCG 2.3, CEA 1.0 normal. Ultrasound showed a large solid-cystic abdominopelvic mass; CT showed a heterogeneous 15 x 13 x 12 cm mass with mass effect, uterus 7 cm with endometrial thickening, adnexa not identified.
