Ten days after the first visit a left salpingo-oophorectomy removed an 800 g mass with necrosis and hemorrhage; histology showed large and medium cells with granular cytoplasm and follicles of different sizes in an edematous stroma, compatible with juvenile granulosa cell tumor. Pubertal signs and ultrasound abnormalities regressed; CT 2 months postoperatively was normal; inhibin B was 50 pg/mL initially (reference <44) then 17 and 10.8; AMH 1.24, 1.23 and 1.26 ng/mL (reference 0.5-4.7); estradiol fell to 15, 7, 6 and <5 pg/mL. At 2 years transient thelarche with normal GnRH test and bone age was judged non-specific transient thelarche (right ovary volume 2.6 cc); no relapse in almost 4 years of follow-up. The authors recommend follow-up with inhibin B or AMH every 6 months for 2 years then annually, and state that stage I tumors are curative with surgery (5-year survival 90-100%, cited).  Infant JGCT presenting with peripheral precocious puberty, with serial inhibin B, AMH and estradiol follow-up after surgery alone.

title: Endogenous c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) activity marks the boundary between normal and malignant granulosa cells.
author: Bildik G
text: Translational laboratory study of granulosa cell tumor (GCT) of the ovary; patient material was 4 fresh tumors (2 adult-type, 2 juvenile-type, confirmed by two gynecologic pathologists) plus the GCT lines COV434 and KGN; non-neoplastic comparators were HGrC1, SIGC and luteinized granulosa cells from 10 IVF patients. Endogenous JNK kinase activity was significantly higher in both adult- and juvenile-type GCT samples and in COV434 and KGN than in non-neoplastic granulosa cells (HGrC1, HLGC, SIGC), including mitotically active non-malignant lines. Ex vivo treatment of fresh adult and juvenile GCT samples with JNK inhibitors for 24 h significantly decreased in vitro growth and estradiol and AMH production and increased cell death. In COV434, JNK inhibition (SP600125, AS601245, or siRNA) gave dose-dependent growth reduction, apoptosis, lower estradiol and AMH, fewer phospho-histone H3-positive cells (2% and 3% vs 17% in controls, p<0.01), reduced EdU uptake (6% and 9% vs 47%), and G2/M accumulation. In a COV434 subcutaneous xenograft in SCID mice (n=4 per group), single-dose JNK inhibitors (10 mg/kg i.p.) or intratumoral JNK siRNA halted growth over the following week and lowered serum AMH. Background statements by the authors: JGCT is about 5% of GCT, lacks the FOXL2 C134W mutation found in 97% of adult-type GCT, affects pre-pubertal girls and young women (mean onset around 8 years), has reduced FOXL2 expression; AKT1 tandem duplications were reported in 16 JGCTs and activating Gas codon 201 mutations in 30% of a JGCT cohort (cited from other studies). Authors' conclusion: targeting the JNK pathway may offer therapeutic benefit in GCT, for which no curative therapy exists beyond surgery; further investigation is warranted. JNK pathway (c-Jun phosphorylation) Preclinical evidence of elevated JNK activity and JNK-inhibitor sensitivity that includes two juvenile-type tumor samples; most experiments use adult-type-derived cell lines, so JGCT-specific inference rests on n=2.

title: A rare case report of ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumor with massive ascites as the first sign, and review of literature: Case report and review of literature.
author: Ma L
text: A 19-year-old woman presented with a week of painless progressive abdominal distention and shifting dullness; ascites was exudative with cytology negative for malignancy; serum and ascitic CA125 were markedly raised while AFP, CEA, CA19-9, CA15-3 and beta-hCG were normal and sex hormones were unremarkable. Ultrasound and CT showed massive ascites, a 50 x 40 mm well-marginated left adnexal lesion read as teratoma, and an enlarged right ovary with a 50 x 50 mm solid-cystic lesion; no lymphadenopathy or infiltration. At laparoscopic exploration about 1200 mL clear ascites was drained, the right tumor had a ruptured capsule with irregular cauliflower surface, and the omentum and peritoneum had several corn-like nodules; a left oophorectomy and right salpingo-oophorectomy with omental and peritoneal biopsies were performed. Frozen section suggested sex cord-stromal tumor; histology showed nodules of ovoid and polygonal pale eosinophilic or clear cells and irregular follicles with pseudopapillary projections; immunohistochemistry positive for inhibin-alpha, CD99, vimentin and calretinin, negative for AE1/AE3, EMA, SMA, Melan-A and CD10; Ki-67 >5%. The authors classified the case as FIGO stage IC on the basis of malignant ascites only; she received 6 courses of nedaplatin and liposomal paclitaxel and at 6 months CA-125 was normal, ascites resolved and no recurrence was seen. The authors conclude that advanced-stage JGCT with massive ascites should be considered in young girls, CA125 and estradiol with imaging may alert to JGCT, but diagnosis depends on histology and immunohistochemistry; the discussion cites platinum-based chemotherapy response rates of 63% to 80% and states no evidence supports radiation or hormonal therapy.  JGCT presenting with massive ascites and raised CA125 without endocrine symptoms in a 19-year-old; treated with platinum-taxane adjuvant therapy; only 6 months of follow-up.

title: A review on pregnancy complicated by ovarian epithelial and non-epithelial malignant tumors: Diagnostic and therapeutic perspectives.
author: Boussios S
text: Literature review (PubMed, 1986-2016, English) of 262 cases of gestational ovarian cancer from 45 reports; 193 were non-epithelial ovarian cancer, of which 145 germ cell tumors and 48 sex cord-stromal tumors. Of the 48 sex cord-stromal tumors, juvenile granulosa cell tumor was the most common subtype with 15 patients (Table 3: 7.7% of 193), followed by Sertoli-Leydig tumor in 5 and other types in 28. Authors state that juvenile granulosa cell tumors could be adequately treated with adnexectomy, with similar surgical management as in non-pregnant women (citing one reference). For sex cord-stromal tumors as a group: obstetric outcome normal in 37/48, IUGR 4/48, fetal death 3/48, abortion 1/48, ventriculomegaly 1/48; neonatal outcome healthy 43/44, one neonatal death; chemotherapy needed in 8 patients (16.6%). A cited series of 46 pregnant patients with sex cord-stromal tumors (mostly USO or node removal in 2nd/3rd trimesters) reported 69.4% fetal preservation, serious adverse events in 40% concentrated in higher stage and older patients. General review conclusions: surgery best in the second trimester; carboplatin-paclitaxel standard for epithelial ovarian cancer in pregnancy; BEP considered reasonable for non-epithelial cancer with alternatives (PVB, cisplatin plus paclitaxel) discussed.  Pregnancy-associated ovarian cancer review; JGCT contributes 15 pooled case-report patients and a brief statement on adnexectomy; no separate maternal or tumor outcomes.

title: Ovarian Gynandroblastoma with a Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor Component in a Postmenopausal Woman: A Case Report and Literature Review.
author: Jang NR
text: 71-year-old postmenopausal woman (G6P4, menopause at 53) with acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain; CT and ultrasound showed a large multiloculated cystic mass of about 13 cm in the right ovary; no endocrine symptoms; CA 19-9 19.48 U/mL and CA125 7.45 U/mL were normal. Preoperative diagnosis was torsion of the right ovarian tumor; total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy were performed. Gross: 13.0 x 7.5 x 6.5 cm multilocular cyst with serosanguinous fluid and a 3.7 x 1.8 cm solid yellowish mass; uterus, tubes and left ovary unremarkable. Histology: tumor was 40% juvenile granulosa cell tumor (nodular growth, follicles with mucin-like basophilic secretions, round to oval nuclei with open chromatin, no striking atypia, no Call-Exner bodies) and 60% well-differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, diagnosed as gynandroblastoma. Both components were positive for calretinin and inhibin and negative for EMA. The tumor was stage I without extra-ovarian involvement; no recurrence during 2 years of follow-up. Authors report this as the first gynandroblastoma with a JGCT component in an elderly patient; they cite 6 of 28 reported gynandroblastomas in English literature having a JGCT component, all in premenopausal women aged 15 to 39 years. Literature statements by the authors: about 97% of JGCTs occur in the first three decades; about 30% of JGCTs reported to harbor the gsp oncogene and 60% an AKT1 mutation; somatic DICER1 hot-spot mutations in about 60% of Sertoli-Leydig tumors; FOXL2 C134W is typical of adult GCT. No molecular testing was done on this case.  Rare gynandroblastoma with JGCT component in a 71-year-old, illustrating JGCT-like histology well outside the usual age range; not a pure JGCT.

title: Multimodal molecular analysis of an atypical small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type.
author: David MP
text: A 12-year-old girl (mild von Willebrand disease) with a ruptured 22 cm left ovarian tumor was initially diagnosed with juvenile granulosa cell tumor at an outside hospital and treated with debulking and four cycles of etoposide, ifosfamide and cisplatin. A pelvic recurrence appeared 9 months later; CA-125 89 U/mL, while inhibin, AFP, hCG and calcium were normal. The recurrence showed sheets and nests of mitotically active small blue cells with cysts and focal mucinous differentiation; EMA, mucicarmine, WT1, CD56 positive; inhibin and calretinin patchy; strong p53; ER equivocal; PR and Melan A negative. Differential considered JGCT, mixed sex cord stromal tumor with heterologous elements, and SCCOHT; the diagnosis was revised to small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT) after NGS found SMARCA4 p.Arg381Ter (germline) and an in-frame TP53 deletion, with 46,XX karyotype and CN-LOH on SNP array. The authors report this as the first SCCOHT with patchy inhibin positivity, a pitfall because inhibin is considered a way to separate JGCT (positive) from SCCOHT (negative); they note EMA positivity has also been described in some JGCT and normocalcemia does not exclude SCCOHT. Authors recommend SMARCA4 sequencing or BRG1 IHC for high-grade small round blue cell tumors of the ovary, and germline testing when SMARCA4 mutation is found; the family declined genetic counseling follow-up. Outcome: after additional chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplant the patient died 5 months after the revised diagnosis from transplant complications. SMARCA4 TP53 Documents a diagnostic pitfall: an ovarian tumor in a 12-year-old first diagnosed as JGCT was SCCOHT with patchy inhibin staining; the case is not a JGCT, but informs JGCT differential and the value of SMARCA4/BRG1 testing.

title: Rapidly growing juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary arising in adult: a case report and review of the literature.
author: Inada Y
text: A 38-year-old Japanese woman presented with abdominal distension and frequent urination; a laparoscopic myomectomy about one year earlier had shown macroscopically normal ovaries, suggesting rapid tumor growth. Estradiol was 214.5 pg/mL (normal 70-160), FSH <0.1 mIU/mL and LH 2.0 mIU/mL (suppressed by feedback), testosterone normal, CA-125 39.2 U/mL (slightly elevated); no menstrual irregularity. MRI showed a 10 x 10 x 12 cm multiloculated cystic right ovarian mass with fluid-fluid levels, intracystic hemorrhage, strongly enhancing septa with high diffusion signal, small ascites, a normal-size uterus without endometrial thickening and an atrophic left ovary (1.7 cm). Frozen section could not exclude malignancy (nuclear atypia; differential yolk sac tumor, malignant mucinous tumor, AGCT) and lacked coffee-bean nuclei and Call-Exner bodies; hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, partial omentectomy and appendectomy were done. Final pathology: 13 cm multiloculated cystic tumor with hemorrhage, macrofollicles, brisk focal mitoses (average 10 per 10 HPF), MIB-1 index about 30%; positive for vimentin, calretinin, CD99 and alpha-inhibin; diagnosis JGCT, FIGO IA, no further treatment. The authors conclude that JGCT can occur in adults, that intraoperative diagnosis may be difficult, that MRI helps, and that the tumor appeared to grow rapidly, possibly related to nuclear atypia and high mitotic rate; the atrophic contralateral ovary may be a clue to hormonal activity. The authors cite a similar adult JGCT in a 43-year-old woman, and cite JGCT as accounting for under 5% of GCTs, mean age about 13 years, 97% before age 30 in one series.  Documents a histologically diagnosed JGCT in an adult (38 years), a diagnostic pitfall versus adult GCT, with possible rapid growth and a high mitotic index.

title: Case series: Five pediatric germ cell/sex cord stroma tumors.
author: Glasser JG
text: Series of five unrelated pediatric tumors from one surgeon's practice (two ovarian, one gastric teratoma, one mesenteric teratoma, one metastatic choriocarcinoma); only case 2 is a JGCT, summarized as stage II JGCT of the right ovary with tumor spillage and Ollier's syndrome. Case 2: a 13-year-old pubertal girl presented with abdominal distension, discomfort and isosexual precocious puberty; the tumor was 33 x 15.5 x 33 cm and adherent to surrounding structures with omental neovascularity; dissection tore the capsule with torrential hemorrhage that was controlled at the ovarian pedicle. She was followed with tumor markers and imaging and the tumor never recurred; no chemotherapy is reported. The author takes this as consistent with the observation that syndromic patients, even with rupture, have an excellent prognosis. The text calls case 2 a 'juvenile germ cell tumor' in one heading although the series table and glossary state JGCT (juvenile granulosa cell tumor); no histology details, IHC or marker values are given for this case. The author's background statements (not data): JGCT incidence peaks in childhood, tumors grow large but have moderate to low virulence; complete resection gives overall survival 95% in children under 10 years even if the tumor ruptures; JGCT arise from uncommitted mesenchymal stem cells beneath the urogenital ridge; inhibin B and AMH are useful markers; cisplatin, etoposide and bleomycin are used for advanced disease (unresectable, recurrent, high mitotic activity or nuclear atypia, or ascites). Table 7 lists syndromes associated with sex cord stromal tumors: Peutz-Jeghers, Maffucci and Ollier's disease are associated with JGCT; the author states syndromic sex cord stroma tumors usually occur in the first decade and are benign.  Narrative case series where one of five cases is a JGCT in a girl with Ollier's disease; useful for the Ollier/Maffucci association and rupture outcome, but with sparse pathology and follow-up.

title: Ovarian lesions among pediatric patients: A tertiary center experience (1997-2016).
author: Alsuhaibani M
text: Retrospective single-center review (King Abdulaziz Medical City, Riyadh, 1997-2016) of 14 girls aged 14 or younger who had surgical removal of ovarian lesions; mean age 5.7 +/- 5.1 years. Histopathology (Table 3): simple ovarian cyst 7 (50%), mature cystic teratoma 3 (21.4%), paraovarian cyst 1, hemorrhagic cyst 1, juvenile granulosa cell tumor 1 (7.1%), mixed germ cell tumor 1 (7.1%). The single JGCT patient was the only one in the series with endocrine disturbance and precocious puberty; no further individual details (age, stage, surgery, outcome) are reported for her. The only death in the series was a girl with a mixed germ cell tumor, not the JGCT patient; the authors list JGCT and mixed germ cell tumor as the two malignant lesions. Authors conclude most pediatric ovarian lesions were benign; the small single-center sample limits generalization.  Series of 14 surgically treated pediatric ovarian lesions; contains exactly one JGCT with precocious puberty and no further JGCT detail. Useful only as a frequency data point.

title: RUNX3 Promotes the Tumorigenic Phenotype in KGN, a Human Granulosa Cell Tumor-Derived Cell Line.
author: Chen H
text: Laboratory study of RUNX proteins in GCT cell lines (KGN, labelled adult GCT; COV434, labelled juvenile GCT; immortalized granulosa SVOG) and human GCT tissue. RUNX3 was undetectable in KGN and SVOG but highly expressed in COV434; RUNX2 was absent in COV434. Re-expressing RUNX3 in KGN increased growth, soft-agar colonies and motility (+59%), raised cyclin D2 mRNA 2.7-fold, lowered p27Kip1 protein by 58%, and 4 of 6 injections of KGN/RUNX3 (0 of 6 vector) formed small tumors in NSG mice. A dominant-negative RUNX3 reduced proliferation of COV434 cells. Human tissue: five JGCT samples (Baylor College of Medicine), three normal ovaries, six AGCT (Baylor) and 11 AGCT (Alberta). RUNX2 was detected in all JGCT samples, whereas RUNX3 protein was not detected in any JGCT sample; RUNX1-3 mRNA by qRT-PCR varied. The authors conclude RUNX3 may play an oncogenic role in a subset of GCT, but note that RUNX3 expression may not be common in human GCT, and that JGCT conclusions are limited. The authors state COV434 may be misidentified and possibly a small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT) line, so its use as a JGCT model is uncertain; its RUNX2/RUNX3 pattern did not resemble the primary JGCT samples. Background statements: AGCT is about 95% of GCT; the FOXL2 C134W (402C>G) mutation is in 97% of AGCT but not in JGCT (cited). RUNX3 Basic-science paper; only 5 primary JGCT tissues (RUNX protein/mRNA expression) and the disputed COV434 line. Mainly relevant to cautions about COV434 as a JGCT model.

title: MR imaging in discriminating between benign and malignant paediatric ovarian masses: a systematic review.
author: van Nimwegen LWE
text: PRISMA systematic review (PubMed and EMBASE, 2008-2018) of MR imaging to separate benign from malignant ovarian masses: 3015 records, 34 studies included (16 paediatric, 18 adult). Of the 16 paediatric studies, 3 were cohort studies (Emil 2017 n=18; Marro 2016 n=32; Lin 2017 n=74 germ cell tumours) and 13 were case reports; paediatric studies were mostly Oxford evidence level 4. Mean age was 10.8 years in paediatric and 46.9 years in adult studies. Three included paediatric case reports were juvenile granulosa cell tumours: Ghanbari 2013 (age 3 years; multiple cystic components; tumour adhesion to anterior bowel loops), Bedir 2014 (age 10; 76 x 87 x 75 mm; multiple cystic and solid components) and Calcaterra 2013 (age 8; 13 x 13 x 7.6 cm). No DWI, DCE or diagnostic-performance data were reported for these cases. Across studies, MRI sensitivity and specificity for malignancy ranged 84.8-100% and 20.0-98.4%; DWI plus conventional MRI reached sensitivity 93.3-100% and specificity 85-96.8% in adult series; the authors suggest an ADC cut-off of 1.1 x 10-3 mm2/s. The authors state that MRI descriptions in paediatric studies were insufficient, no purely paediatric cohort with DWI/DCE data existed, and prospective age-specific studies are needed. The authors note that benign masses such as thecomas or sclerosing stromal tumours can be hypervascular on DCE, so time-intensity curve type alone may not separate benign from malignant.  Imaging review of paediatric ovarian masses; JGCT appears only as 3 single-patient case reports (basic MRI descriptions, no quantitative or performance data). Shows the thin evidence base for MRI features of JGCT.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor with Elevated Peripheral Interleukin-6 Level Shows Prolonged Fever and Delayed Puberty.
author: Okuno K
text: A 13-year-old girl had 5 months of low-grade fever (38.6 C on exam), fatigue, a painless lower abdominal mass and Tanner stage 1 breasts and pubic hair; WBC 16,000/uL, platelets 723,000/uL, ESR 140 mm/h, CRP 18.7 mg/dL, SAA 1750 ug/mL, albumin 1.8 g/dL, with microcytic hypochromic anemia. Serum IL-6 was 348 pg/mL (normal <4) and soluble IL-2 receptor 1,465 U/mL (145-519); CA-125 was 6,020 U/mL (<35); AFP, beta-hCG, CA19-9 and CEA were normal; estradiol 14.5 pg/mL, LH <0.1 and FSH 0.33 mIU/mL were prepubertal. CT/MRI showed a 67 x 61 x 74 mm left pelvic tumor, iso-intense on T1 and high intensity on T2, with no metastasis; laparoscopic left salpingo-oophorectomy was done with piecemeal resection. Histology showed sheet-like growth of cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, focal pseudopapillary pattern and follicles with eosinophilic secretion, no nuclear grooves; immunohistochemistry was focally positive for inhibin-alpha, CD56, CD99 and AE1/AE3, negative for calretinin, PAX8, CD10, ER, PR, chromogranin A, synaptophysin, c-kit and D2-40; Ki-67 about 3%. IL-6 immunostaining showed weak cytoplasmic staining in a subset of tumor cells but also in non-neoplastic stroma, so tumor production of IL-6 could not be confirmed; no fresh or frozen tissue was available for gene expression. After surgery fever resolved, IL-6 fell to 1.6 pg/mL by day 10 and inflammatory indices and CA-125 normalized; LH and FSH rose at 1 month (33.19 and 68.49 mIU/mL), first menses came at 2 months, by 6 months estradiol 23.85 pg/mL, LH 3.92, FSH 4.81, and by 1 year Tanner stage 4 breasts and 3 pubic hair; no recurrence at 3 years. The authors speculate that tumor-associated IL-6 caused the prolonged fever and the delayed puberty (via inflammation-mediated GnRH suppression) and propose considering JGCT in prolonged fever.  Unusual non-estrogenic presentation of a pubertal-age ovarian JGCT with systemic inflammation, extreme CA-125 and delayed puberty that reversed after resection.

title: Clinical utility of SMARCA4 testing by immunohistochemistry in rare ovarian tumours.
author: Genestie C
text: French multicenter (Gustave Roussy and Hospices Civils de Lyon) study of SMARCA4 immunohistochemistry in 44 centrally confirmed SCCOHT and 94 rare ovarian tumors that mimic SCCOHT, including 10 juvenile granulosa cell tumors (Methods: 34 adult GCT; Table 1: 37 adult GCT). SMARCA4 loss in SCCOHT 39/44 (88%) vs 6/94 (6%) mimickers; sensitivity 88.6% (abstract 88%; text 89%), specificity 93.6%, PPV 86.7%, NPV 94.6%, accuracy 92.0%; projected community-setting PPV 40% and NPV 99% at 5% SCCOHT prevalence. The six SMARCA4-negative non-SCCOHT tumors were 3 adult granulosa cell tumors (two FOXL2-mutation confirmed), 1 immature teratoma, 1 desmoplastic round cell tumor and 1 PNET; no juvenile GCT is listed among them, so SMARCA4 IHC separated the 10 JGCT from SCCOHT (specificity in sex cord tumors 94%, 49/52 positive). Diagnostic pitfall: of 36 SCCOHT reviewed as second opinion, 16 (44%; abstract says 43%) had a different initial local diagnosis; the main misdiagnosis was juvenile granulosa cell tumor (6/16, 38%). SMARCA4 IHC would have corrected 14/16 (88%) of the misdiagnosed SCCOHT; two with retained SMARCA4 would not have been helped. Authors recommend SMARCA4 IHC for any non-epithelial ovarian tumor in a young woman where doubt exists, while central expert review remains required. SMARCA4 (BRG1) protein by IHC Important for differential diagnosis: JGCT is the most frequent misdiagnosis of SCCOHT in this series (6/16), and SMARCA4 IHC (retained in JGCT) helps separate them. JGCT numbers (n=10) are the comparator group.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Testis: Prenatal Diagnosis and Management.
author: Vatta F
text: Left testicular multilocular cystic mass (2 x 2 cm) seen on fetal ultrasound at 38 weeks (not seen on earlier routine scans), suspected JGCT; painless enlarged left scrotal mass at birth in a healthy newborn. Postnatal ultrasound excluded torsion and showed multicystic mass without normal parenchyma; AFP and beta-hCG normal for age, karyotype normal, abdominal ultrasound normal. Inguinal approach with left funiculo-orchiectomy because organ-sparing excision was not possible; specimen 2 x 1.5 cm well-circumscribed white mass with thin-walled cysts; tumor did not extend into spermatic cord, epididymis or tunica vaginalis; small rim of residual testis only. Histology: follicle-like structures with basophilic mucicarmine-positive fluid, scant pale cytoplasm, no nuclear grooves, low mitotic activity; IHC positive for alpha-inhibin, CD99, calretinin, focal cytokeratin; negative for FLAP, AFP, CD30, vimentin, beta-hCG; Ki67 1%. Seven-year follow-up uneventful; authors cite this as only the third case suspected prenatally (earlier cases at 36 and 38 weeks) and that testicular JGCT has had a benign outcome in all reported cases; they conclude inguinal orchiectomy is the safest oncological approach when the tumor replaces the testis, although testis-sparing and trans-scrotal surgery have been reported. From literature in the paper: JGCT is the most common testicular neoplasm in first 6 months of life and accounts for 1.2% of prepubertal testis tumors in the Prepubertal Testis Tumor Registry.  Documents prenatal ultrasound detection of testicular JGCT with benign long-term outcome after orchiectomy.

title: Natural history of Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome: Patient survey and review of clinical literature.
author: El Abiad JM
text: Study combined a literature review of 287 publications (160 Ollier disease [OD] and 199 Maffucci syndrome [MS] patients; PubMed search 28 August 2017) with a Facebook-distributed patient survey (May 2017 to May 2018; 126 OD and 36 MS respondents from 27 countries). JGCT is mentioned as a gonadal tumor associated with OD and MS. The paper cites a prior literature review (Pansuriya et al.) with 7 JGCT cases in OD and 6 in MS, and a 2017 report (Burgetova et al.) describing 10 JGCT cases in OD patients. In the literature review the gonadal malignancy rate was 13/160 (8.1%) in OD versus 7/199 (3.5%) in MS (p=.059; OR 2.426, 95% CI 0.944-6.232); gonad tumors are not broken down by histology in the paper, so JGCT-specific counts are not reported by the authors themselves. In the survey, gonadal cancer was reported by 0/126 OD versus 2/36 (5.6%) MS respondents (p=.008); the authors note the survey OD cohort was young (median 17.6 years) and may underestimate cancer prevalence. Overall malignancy prevalence in the literature review was 53.1% in OD and 48.7% in MS (survey 25.4% OD, 36.1% MS); chondrosarcoma about 30.6% OD and 31.7% MS; brain malignancy 16.3% OD vs 4.5% MS (OR 4.1); vascular malignancy 8.5% in MS. Median age at malignancy diagnosis was 25 years (OD) and 30 years (MS) in the review. The authors propose surveillance guidelines for OD and MS (whole-body MRI at diagnosis, clinical exams every 6-12 months in children and 12-24 months in adults, whole-body MRI offered from 25 years in OD and 30 years in MS and repeated every other year); these target chondrosarcoma, brain tumors and other malignancies and do not include JGCT-specific screening. Authors' stated limitations: no radiograph or histology review, dependence on case-report validity and self-reported survey data, unequal OD/MS survey sizes, and different cohort ages. IDH1/IDH2 JGCT is named only as one of the gonadal tumors associated with Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome; the paper gives gonadal-cancer rates in OD/MS and cites earlier JGCT case counts, but has no JGCT-specific patient data of its own.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor with an Unusual Clinical Course: A Late-onset and Late Recurrent Case.
author: San TH
text: 40-year-old woman (G4P3) with a right ovarian tumor removed 5 years earlier (at age 35, originally diagnosed as serous cystadenoma, with torsion artifact) presented with secondary amenorrhea, appetite and weight loss; CA125 283 U/mL and estradiol 360 pg/mL pre-op, falling to 9.0 U/mL and <10 pg/mL 2 months post-op. Imaging: 10.3 x 10.4 x 9.3 cm multicystic left ovarian mass with free fluid; surgery found the left ovarian mass plus an 8.0 cm pouch of Douglas mass and 2 small omental nodules. Histology: multicystic with follicular and solid proliferation, irregular follicles with eosinophilic material, monomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei without grooves, pseudopapillary pattern, frequent mitoses (24/10 HPF), focal steroid cells; omental and POD lesions identical. IHC positive for inhibin A, calretinin, CD56 and FOXL2; negative for WT1, p53, chromogranin A, synaptophysin, TTF-1 and OCT3/4. FOXL2 402C>G mutation absent, supporting JGCT over adult GCT. Review of the original right ovarian tumor showed similar features (cystic, pseudopapillary, mitoses 12/10 HPF) and was reinterpreted as JGCT, so the later tumor was termed a late recurrence (more than 5 years). Course was aggressive: further recurrences at 6 months despite anastrozole, patient declined chemotherapy and died 20 months after the operation. Authors say this is the first comprehensive report of JGCT with late recurrence (>5 years), cite that almost all JGCT recurrences occur within 2 years and only 3% of JGCT present after age 30, and advise long-term surveillance; no Ollier or Maffucci features were found. FOXL2 Documents a late (more than 5 years) JGCT recurrence in a woman first diagnosed at 35, FOXL2 wild-type, with fatal course.

title: Gynecological cancer among adolescents and young adults (AYA).
author: Triarico S
text: Narrative review of gynecological tumors in adolescents and young adults (AYA, age 15-39 per NCI/ENCCA) with a proposed multidisciplinary model of care covering fertility, ovarian failure, contraception and psychosocial effects; it reports no new patient data. The review states JGCT accounts for about 70% of ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors in patients younger than 20 years. Approximately 80% of prepubertal girls with JGCT present with isosexual precocious puberty related to estrogen secretion; rarely the tumor produces androgen with virilizing features; in children JGCT is more frequently associated with acute complications such as torsion and rupture. Inhibin is described as a useful serum tumor marker for diagnosis and follow-up. Up to 90% of JGCT are low-stage disease confined to the ovary and are usually curable with conservative surgery; patients with advanced disease or high mitotic activity have a poorer prognosis and should be treated with chemotherapy. Surgery is needed for histological diagnosis, staging and debulking; chemotherapy is indicated for FIGO stage IC or higher, based on cisplatin with ifosfamide and etoposide (PEI) or etoposide and bleomycin (PEB). For fertility, conservative surgery preserving uterus and contralateral ovary is advised for malignant germ cell tumors and selected stage 1 lesions; AMH is suggested as a marker of ovarian reserve; alkylating agents (ifosfamide, cyclophosphamide) carry high gonadotoxicity, platinum agents moderate risk.  General AYA gynecologic oncology review; JGCT is covered in two paragraphs (epidemiology, presentation, marker, staging-based treatment) plus generic oncofertility guidance relevant to JGCT survivors.

title: Arginine Depletion Therapy with ADI-PEG20 Limits Tumor Growth in Argininosuccinate Synthase-Deficient Ovarian Cancer, Including Small-Cell Carcinoma of the Ovary, Hypercalcemic Type.
author: Ji JX
text: Preclinical proteomics, IHC and xenograft study of rare ovarian cancers; main focus is ASS1 deficiency and arginine-depleting ADI-PEG20 in SCCOHT and clear cell/endometrioid carcinoma, not JGCT. ASS1 IHC on tissue microarrays included juvenile granulosa cell tumor: the Methods text lists n=8 JGCT and the results text says n=8, while Table 1 lists 13 JGCT cases with interpretable ASS1. In sex-cord stromal tumors ASS1 expression was moderate in adult and juvenile GCT (median histoscore 180 for aGCT, n=35; 210 for JGCT). JGCT histoscore distribution (Table 1, n=13): 300 in 2 (15.4%); 200-285 in 5 (38.5%); 100-180 in 3 (23.1%); 10-90 in 0; 0-5 in 3 (23.1%). ASS1 was decreased in Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (n=45, median 40; 60% below 100) and very low in SCCOHT (absent in 12/31, <5% of cells in 9/31); high in HGSC (178/207 with score 300). ADI-PEG20 inhibited growth of ASS1-deficient cell lines and SCCOHT xenografts (COV434 line, PDX-465); no JGCT models or JGCT treatment data were tested. The authors note they had no survival information for GCT and SLCT cases and that further correlation is needed before ADI-PEG20 could be considered for aggressive GCT. ASS1 (protein expression, IHC) Minor: gives ASS1 IHC data for 13 JGCT (moderate expression, median histoscore 210), suggesting a possible but untested ADI-PEG20 rationale. JGCT cases are a small comparator group.

title: Testicular tumours in children: an approach to diagnosis and management with pathologic correlation.
author: Sangüesa C
text: Narrative imaging/management review of pediatric testicular tumours drawing on histologically confirmed cases from the authors' hospital; JGCT is covered in short passages and one illustrative case (Fig. 15), not a series. JGCT is described as the most frequent congenital testicular tumour and the most frequent testicular tumour detectable on prenatal ultrasound; the left testis is most often affected and up to 20% have ambiguous external genitalia. Sex cord-stromal tumours (Sertoli, Leydig, juvenile granulosa cell) account for about 10% of pediatric testicular neoplasms; the 2016 WHO classification lists granulosa cell tumour among the sex cord-stromal tumours. Pathology: reticular appearance with follicle-like structures filled with mucoid material; the illustrated case showed many layers of granulosa cells with oval nuclei and abundant cytoplasm in a multilocular mass. Ultrasound: well-circumscribed, non-invasive multilocular cystic mass with thick septations, or less often a solid mass with intralesional cysts; color Doppler shows hypervascularity of solid components and septations. MRI: hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, with wall and septal enhancement. Illustrative case: 16-day-old boy with a left scrotal mass since birth, multiseptated cystic intratesticular mass with hydrocele on US, treated by radical inguinal orchiectomy. Management statement: JGCT is considered a borderline tumour; radical inguinal orchiectomy is normally performed, though tumour enucleation could be sufficient when healthy testicular tissue is present. Testicular tumours overall are 2-4% of childhood cancers; AFP physiologically high under 12 months must be considered when interpreting markers; percutaneous biopsy is generally avoided because of lymphatic seeding risk.  Source for the testicular JGCT: its congenital presentation, imaging features and surgical approach in the context of all pediatric testicular tumours. No outcome data and no patient series.

title: Molecular Pathways and Targeted Therapies for Malignant Ovarian Germ Cell Tumors and Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors: A Contemporary Review.
author: Maoz A
text: Review of the molecular landscape and targeted therapies of malignant ovarian germ cell tumors and sex cord-stromal tumors (SCST); non-epithelial ovarian tumors are 8-10% of ovarian malignancies and SCST about 2% of ovarian malignancies in the USA. Table 1 lists JGCT alterations: AKT1 duplication/activation (about 60%), GNAS mutations (about 30%), and rare germline IDH1/2 in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome; the text cites about 30% GNAS in a cohort of thirty patients and over 60% AKT1 duplication in a study of 16 patients. FOXL2 C134W is almost ubiquitous in adult GCT (up to 97%) but uncommon in JGCT; the review says GCT subtypes make up over 70% of SCSTs, with JGCT forming the majority of SCSTs in children and adolescents. The review states Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome are associated with increased risk of JGCT, and that SCSTs commonly secrete inhibin, estradiol, testosterone and AMH, causing virilization, menstrual changes or precocious puberty. US SCST stage distribution (all SCSTs, not JGCT-specific): stage I 69%, II 12%, III 14%, IV 5%, with five-year cause-specific survival 98%, 84%, 61% and 41% and 88% overall; chemotherapy for SCST includes BEP, EP and carboplatin-paclitaxel (a randomized phase II trial is comparing carboplatin-paclitaxel with BEP, NCT01042522). Targeted therapy data are mostly for adult GCT (bevacizumab, anastrozole, leuprolide, aromatase inhibitors, CYP17 inhibitors) and none is specific to JGCT; the review notes only 12 interventional trials involving SCSTs on clinicaltrials.gov. The review concludes that molecular characterization should be built into prospective trials in these rare tumors and that targeted candidates have been tested mainly in male germ cell tumors without encouraging results. AKT1 GNAS IDH1/IDH2 FOXL2 Contemporary review whose JGCT content is the molecular profile (AKT1, GNAS, IDH in Ollier/Maffucci, low FOXL2) and the statement that no JGCT-specific targeted therapy data exist. No patient-level JGCT data.

title: Evaluation of the usefulness of laparoscopy in the diagnosis and treatment of adnexal pathologies in the pediatric population.
author: Raźnikiewicz A
text: Retrospective single-center series of 89 patients aged 0-18 years (mean 12.62) who had laparoscopy for suspected adnexal pathology, 2010-2017 (37 emergency, 52 elective). Adnexal cysts were 70.79% (n=63) of postoperative diagnoses and ovarian tumors 28.01% (n=25), of which 23 were benign (20 mature teratomas) and 2 malignant; malignant to benign ratio 2:23 (0.087). The two malignant tumors were a juvenile granulosa cell tumor (13-year-old) and a mixed tumor, mainly sex cord tumor with annular tubules (SCTAT) with separate foci of juvenile granulosa cell tumor (10-year-old). 13-year-old with JGCT: CT showed a cystic structure with small solid component, probably from the right ovary, 85 x 175 x 260 mm reaching the epigastrium; only LDH was raised (200 IU/ml), other tumor markers not elevated. 10-year-old with SCTAT plus JGCT foci: growing abdominal girth, polycyclic cystic lesion filling pelvis and abdomen, CA-125 101.4 IU/ml; the tumor was resected according to an oncological protocol. Series-level outcomes: mean operation time 63.7 min, mean hospital stay 4.34 days, 3 conversions, no intraoperative or perioperative complications; ultrasound sensitivity/specificity was 67.21%/50% for cysts and 26.32%/92.75% for torsion. The authors conclude that pediatric laparoscopy for adnexal pathology appears safe and that ovarian parenchyma-sparing surgery should be used where preoperative diagnosis is not malignant; the 29 cm largest lesion was benign (seromucinous cystadenoma), so size did not indicate malignancy.  Minor. Surgical series of pediatric adnexal pathology in which 2 of 89 patients had a JGCT (one in a mixed SCTAT tumor); only presentation and imaging details are given for them.

title: Ovarian cancer: diagnostic accuracy and tumor types distribution in East Africa compared to North America.
author: Rambau PF
text: Retrospective study of 210 ovarian cancer cases (2002-2017) from three Tanzanian centers and Makerere University, Uganda, re-reviewed with H&E and a 20-antibody IHC panel on tissue microarrays and compared with the Alberta Cancer Registry. Sex cord stromal tumors were 30/210 (14.3%) in East Africa versus 17 (0.92%) in Alberta; among East African SCST, 24 (80.0%) were adult GCT, 4 (13.3%) juvenile GCT, 2 (6.7%) Sertoli-Leydig; no JGCT among the Alberta SCST (adult GCT 12, Sertoli-Leydig 4, other 1). JGCT IHC (Table 2, 4 cases): FOXL2 positive 50%, vimentin diffuse 75%, p16 abnormal 75%, PAX8 positive 25%, ER positive 50%; WT-1, PR, p53 mutant, Napsin A and MSH6/PMS2/ARID1A loss all 0%. Comparator adult GCT (24 cases): FOXL2 66.7%, vimentin 95.8%, WT-1 47.8%, PR 33.3%. Concordance of original vs IHC-integrated diagnosis was 83.3% for SCST (kappa 0.70 for major categories); one case of carcinoma NOS was re-diagnosed as adult GCT after a new H&E stain; one 'neuroblastoma' was reclassified as SCCOHT (BRG1 loss). Stage was available for only four patients and no recurrence or survival data were collected; JGCT age, stage and outcomes are not reported individually. Authors caution that selection bias (younger women with GCT/SCST more likely to reach tertiary care) limits comparison of incidence and tumor-type proportions. FOXL2 Shows JGCT as 4 of 210 East African ovarian cancers and gives IHC marker frequencies for 4 JGCT; no clinical outcomes.

title: Risk factors and treatment outcomes of 239 patients with testicular granulosa cell tumors: a systematic review of published case series data.
author: Grogg J
text: PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42018110112; searches to 5 May 2018): 88 publications, 239 patients with testicular granulosa cell tumor (tGrCT): 166 (69%) juvenile and 73 (31%) adult. Juvenile tGrCT mean age 1.5 years (SD 5); median size 20 mm (IQR 13-38) among 36 with size; adult tGrCT mean age 42 years (SD 19). Juvenile tGrCT presentation (63 with data): testicular enlargement 24 (38%), mass 22 (35%), hormonal changes 9 (14%), abdominal mass 7 (11%), incidental 6 (10%); AFP elevated in 11/63 juvenile cases (17%) versus 1 adult; ipsi- or contralateral cryptorchidism in 18/166 (11%) juvenile. All 166 juvenile tGrCT were benign: no metastatic disease was observed; outcomes among juveniles: 80 no evidence of disease, 1 local recurrence, 3 died (mean follow-up 54 months). Juvenile treatment: 72 orchiectomy, 62 gonadectomy, 15 testis-sparing surgery, 7 laparotomy (intra-abdominal cryptorchid testis), 2 biopsy only. The largest source was Kao 2015 (70 cases: 62 gonadectomy, 6 TSS, 2 biopsy). Adult tGrCT: metastatic disease in 7/73 (10%); risk factors were larger primary (median 70 vs 24 mm, ROC cut-off 46 mm, AUC 0.86), angiolymphatic invasion (57% vs 4%) and gynecomastia (29% vs 3%). Five of 7 metastatic adult cases reached complete remission with resection and/or BEP; one died of disease at 134 months and one had stable disease. Authors conclude juvenile tGrCT is a benign entity, adult tGrCT has metastatic potential, literature supports testis-sparing surgery, germ-cell tumor markers (AFP, HCG, LDH) are not supported for follow-up, and an aggressive curative approach is suggested for metastatic disease.  Testicular JGCT: 166 pooled published cases, all benign; informs surgery (testis-sparing) and prognosis. Ovarian JGCT not covered.

title: Ovarian Gynandroblastoma with a Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor Component in a Postmenopausal Woman.
author: Hwang S
text: 65-year-old woman (15 years postmenopausal) with an abdominal mass; MRI showed a 20 cm multiseptated cystic left ovarian mass without peritoneal seeding, lymphadenopathy or hematogenous metastasis; CA 125 37.1 U/mL, CA 19-9 32.1 U/mL (normal). Treated as presumed ovarian cancer with total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy; gross: smooth glistening surface, yellow-tan solid areas with necrosis, myxoid change and hemorrhage plus multilocular cysts with serosanguinous fluid. Histology: ovarian gynandroblastoma with a juvenile granulosa cell tumor component (nodular growth, follicle-like spaces with eosinophilic/basophilic secretions, no nuclear grooves, up to 8 mitoses per 10 HPF, foci of coagulative necrosis) and a moderately differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor component (cords, solid tubules, nests, Sertoli tubules). IHC: inhibin-alpha positive in both components, Ki-67 about 70% in the JGCT component; negative for EMA, pan-cytokeratin and PAX8. No postoperative therapy; no recurrence at 2 months. Authors state this is the second reported gynandroblastoma with JGCT in a postmenopausal woman and that most gynandroblastomas have adult-type granulosa component and occur in children, adolescents or reproductive-age women.  Shows a JGCT component within a gynandroblastoma in an elderly woman, extending the age range and highlighting the JGCT/Sertoli-Leydig morphologic overlap.

title: Testis Sparing Surgery in Pediatric Testicular Tumors.
author: Kooij CD
text: Systematic review (PRISMA; Cochrane, PubMed, Embase to 15 May 2020) of testis-sparing surgery in pediatric testicular tumors: 20 retrospective studies (all Oxford level 4), 968 patients described, 777 analyzed; no randomized trials. Overall: of 534 benign tumors (444 germ cell tumors, 85 sex cord-stromal tumors [SCSTs], 5 miscellaneous) 331 (61.0%) had TSS; of 243 malignant germ cell tumors only 1 (0.4%, a stage II yolk sac tumor) had TSS. No testicular atrophy occurred; 4 benign germ cell tumors recurred (3 teratomas, 1 epidermoid cyst); no recurrence in SCSTs. JGCT is tabulated within the 85 SCSTs: Bujons 2011 1 JGCT (age 10, TSS, 60 months follow-up, no recurrence); Cecchetto 2010 4 JGCT (median age 0.3 years, range 0.2-1.9; TSS in 1); Valla 2001 1 JGCT (no TSS); Sugita 1999 1 JGCT (age 2.0, no TSS, 12 months follow-up, no recurrence). Serum AFP and hCG were normal where reported and no JGCT recurrence was reported. Text states TSS was performed in 52 patients with SCSTs, including 44 (78.6%) Leydig cell tumors, 6 (37.5%) Sertoli cell tumors and 2 (33.3%) JGCT. Only Cecchetto used a staging system (COG) for SCSTs: 10 stage I cases and 1 stage II Leydig cell tumor; none of the studies described adjuvant treatment. The authors conclude TSS appears safe for prepubertal boys under 12 years with benign germ cell tumors and low-grade SCSTs, propose a surgical algorithm based on ultrasound, age-specific AFP and frozen section, and state no conclusion can be drawn about TSS safety in malignant disease. Limitations stated: no RCTs or meta-analysis possible, varying sample sizes, few patients over 12 years, adjuvant therapy not analyzed, and poor reporting of bias and loss to follow-up.  Systematic review of testis-sparing surgery in pediatric testicular tumors; JGCT is a small subgroup (7 tabulated cases, 2 treated with TSS) within 85 sex cord-stromal tumors.

title: [Juvenile granulosa cell tumor-Testicular tumor of the very young : Report of three cases and contemporary recommendations].
author: Haider M
text: Case A: newborn (38+0 weeks, 3600 g) transferred for grunting and oxygen need had a hard left testis; ultrasound showed multiple intratesticular cysts in the lower pole with hyperperfusion, mimicking older torsion; at emergency inguinal exploration the lower pole was cystic with gelatinous cysts and no visible parenchyma; frozen section showed an epithelial cystic tumor of unclear malignant potential and the lower pole was removed. Case A final histology was juvenile granulosa cell tumor; chromosome analysis showed a normal male karyotype; at 4 months, residual testis with irregular ultrasound texture was removed by scrotal orchiectomy, again JGCT, and the specimen showed mostly fetal A-pale spermatogonia and very few A-dark type; follow-up is almost 11 years without recurrence or metastasis. Case B: infant with hydrocele at birth, change on palpation and suspected malignant testicular tumor at 10 weeks (MRI confirmed, no metastasis), first urological presentation at 12 weeks; the right testis was almost wholly replaced by an inhomogeneous well-perfused mass; AFP 121.4 ng/ml with normal beta-hCG and LDH; orchiectomy was done because tumor could only be separated from sparse residual testis by ultrasound; histology showed multicystic JGCT confirmed by immunohistochemistry and reference pathology. Case C: term newborn (39+2 weeks, 3530 g) with enlarged hard left hemiscrotum and multicystic testicular parenchyma on ultrasound; AFP 48,370 ng/ml, beta-hCG 0.3 U/l, LDH 428 U/l; JGCT was suspected preoperatively and confirmed histologically and by reference pathology after day-5 inguinal enucleation with testis preservation; unremarkable at 4 months. The authors state that testicular JGCT is a benign lesion of neonates and early infancy, that no recurrences or metastases have been described, and that it behaves differently from adult granulosa cell tumor and ovarian JGCT; patients usually show no signs of hormonal activity. Recommendations from the authors: ultrasound is the main diagnostic tool; beta-hCG is irrelevant in childhood; AFP is hard to interpret in the first months because of physiologically high values, and reliable differentiation from yolk sac tumor by AFP is possible only after about 6 months; classical staging imaging is not indicated unless yolk sac tumor is proven; treatment of choice is prompt inguinal exposure with tumor resection and organ preservation, with orchiectomy only when little or no residual parenchyma remains; frozen section is obligatory but immunohistochemistry is needed for final diagnosis; annual follow-up is clinical and sonographic only. Sex chromosome abnormalities in testicular JGCT are reported in the literature only with concomitant external genital abnormalities (marked/penoscrotal hypospadias, ambiguous genitalia, complex malformation syndromes), so the authors state chromosome analysis is no longer indicated for JGCT alone in an otherwise healthy patient. The authors call for systematic registration of pediatric testicular masses with ultrasound correlation in a tumor registry, and note miRNA markers (miR-371~373, miR-302) as promising but not routine.  German-language case series and practical recommendations on testicular JGCT of the newborn; supports organ-sparing surgery and surveillance limited to ultrasound.

title: Partial orchiectomy vs. radical orchiectomy for pediatric testis tumors.
author: Woo LL
text: Narrative review (commissioned article, peer reviewed) of partial versus radical orchiectomy in pediatric testis tumors; contains no patient series of its own for JGCT. States that stromal tumors such as Sertoli cell tumor, Leydig cell tumor and juvenile granulosa cell tumor generally behave in a benign fashion in pre-pubertal patients, whereas pure yolk sac tumor is the most common malignant tumor in pre-pubertal boys. Ultrasound: the review states juvenile granulosa cell tumors may appear as discrete multi-septated hypoechoic cystic lesions reminiscent of 'Swiss-cheese'; calcifications in a lesion help differentiate teratoma from granulosa cell tumors; yolk sac tumors and other malignant lesions tend to be hypervascular and more solid. Partial orchiectomy is described in numerous reports as safe and effective for benign tumors including teratoma, epidermoid cyst, Sertoli cell tumor, Leydig cell tumor and juvenile granulosa cell tumor, performed if intraoperative frozen section shows benign histology and with normal age-adjusted AFP. General recommendations: pre-pubertal patients with normal age-adjusted AFP are candidates for testis-sparing surgery; serum AFP is elevated in 90% of children with yolk sac tumor but is physiologically high in infancy (normal by about 1 year); radical inguinal orchiectomy remains standard for malignant tumors and for most post-pubertal patients. Benign lesions treated with partial orchiectomy showed no atrophy or recurrence after mean follow-up of 5-10 years in cited series; long-term functional data in children are lacking according to the authors.  Review of testis-sparing surgery in children that mentions testicular JGCT only briefly (benign behavior in pre-pubertal boys, characteristic Swiss-cheese ultrasound appearance, eligibility for partial orchiectomy).

title: An Unusual Cause of Secondary Amenorrhea in an Adolescent: Expanding the Differential.
author: Okawa ER
text: Case report: adolescent (15 years 10 months at first visit) with secondary amenorrhea after 4 years of regular cycles; FSH low (<2 then 0.2 IU/L), LH normal (9.1 then 7.0 IU/L), estradiol low (21 pg/mL); pregnancy, DHEA-S, 17-OHP, prolactin, thyroid studies and brain MRI normal; no withdrawal bleeding after medroxyprogesterone. Transabdominal ultrasound: enlarged right ovary 5.0 x 4.6 x 3.6 cm (42.6 mL) with central echogenicity and absent Doppler flow, initially read as a hemorrhagic cyst, persisting at 6 weeks; left ovary normal; endometrium 2.3 mm. Because of the specific FSH suppression, inhibin A and B were measured: inhibin A 49 pg/mL (reference 1.8-17.3) and inhibin B 2220 pg/mL (reference 10-290). Right ovary and fallopian tube were resected; a 4.8 cm tumor with smooth capsule, yellow fleshy partly cystic/hemorrhagic cut surface; pathology: juvenile granulosa-cell tumor with no evidence of local spread. Postoperatively cyclic menses resumed; at 3 months inhibin A was 81 pg/mL (reference <97.5) and inhibin B 34 pg/mL (reference <36), i.e. normal. There was an 11-month gap before return to clinic after the first visit, which the authors note could have delayed diagnosis. Authors' discussion: inhibin-secreting tumors can cause primary or secondary amenorrhea; tumor stage is the most important prognostic factor in girls with JGCT; good prognostic factors cited are low stage, size under 10 cm and absence of rupture. They conclude that atypical hormone patterns, such as isolated FSH suppression with normal LH, should prompt consideration of an inhibin-producing tumor.  Documents an uncommon JGCT presentation (secondary amenorrhea with very high inhibin B and suppressed FSH, no precocious puberty), supporting inhibin measurement as a diagnostic clue and normalization as postoperative confirmation.

title: Re-assigning the histologic identities of COV434 and TOV-112D ovarian cancer cell lines.
author: Karnezis AN
text: COV434 was originally described as a granulosa cell tumour line from a 26-year-old woman; absence of the adult-type FOXL2 mutation and young age had led others to regard it as consistent with juvenile granulosa cell tumor. Re-review of the original COV434 tumour found diffuse sheets of monotonous small cells with occasional pseudofollicles, clusters of larger rhabdoid-appearing cells and high mitotic activity; the histologic differential was JGCT versus SCCOHT. Original COV434 tumour IHC: negative for SMARCA4 and nuclear SMARCA2, inhibin A, FOXL2, CD10, synaptophysin, chromogranin and CD56; positive for SMARCB1/INI1 and diffuse WT1; focal AE1/AE3; p53 wild-type pattern; mismatch repair intact. Exome and Sanger sequencing found a homozygous SMARCA4 splice-site mutation in both the COV434 primary tumour and the cell line; the line is diploid-like with no copy number alterations. COV434 xenografts in NRG mice (n=6) raised serum calcium from 2.42 +/- 0.11 to 2.87 +/- 0.05 mM (P<0.001), analogous to SCCOHT hypercalcemia; re-expression of SMARCA4 strongly suppressed COV434 proliferation. Authors conclude COV434 is a bona fide SCCOHT cell line rather than a granulosa cell tumour line; TOV-112D (original endometrioid carcinoma) is a dedifferentiated carcinoma line, not SCCOHT. The authors state that COV434 had no further clinical information available beyond the original report; the ovarian cell line OVK18 is also discussed as likely a dedifferentiated carcinoma. SMARCA4 FOXL2 Cell-line identity study: COV434, sometimes used as a JGCT/granulosa cell tumor model, is reassigned to SCCOHT, so experiments using it as a JGCT model should be interpreted accordingly.

title: Gender Dysphoria Disrupting the Course of Treatment of a Recurrent Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor in an Adolescent Female: A Case Report.
author: Kwiatkowska A
text: A 17-year-old girl had menarche at 12, irregular menses and hormonal/dermatological problems from age 15 (hypothyroidism, insulin resistance, psoriasis, hirsutism), and underwent laparoscopic enucleation of a left ovarian tumor in 2018, diagnosed as FIGO IA folliculoma. At 9 months, ultrasound and MRI showed a 7 cm left ovarian tumor suggesting recurrence; she was painless with markers in normal range (AFP 3.2 kU/L, CA-125 27.96 U/mL, HE4 36.7 pmol/L, hCG 2 mIU/mL, estradiol 750 pg/mL, FSH 10.7, LH 12.9 mIU/mL) except testosterone 14.96 nmol/L (reference 0.17-2.81) and insulin 19.7 uU/mL. Histology showed granular cells with central nuclear atypia, common mitoses, large eosinophilic cytoplasm, follicular structures and no Call-Exner bodies; IHC positive for alpha-inhibin, CD99 and calretinin. The patient requested hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and disclosed gender dysphoria; parents refused consent; after psychological, psychiatric and endocrine consultations she accepted unilateral removal of the adnexa with staging, confirming a unilateral FIGO IA relapse of JGCT. Testosterone declined to 4.87 nmol/L two days post-operatively; the patient declined adjuvant chemotherapy that had been recommended and scheduled because of recurrent disease; gender dysphoria diagnostics were ongoing and oocyte cryopreservation was being considered. The authors state that most JGCTs secrete estradiol and only several androgen-secreting cases are reported; they suggest the androgen-secreting tumor may have affected gender dysphoria, say the recommended treatment for recurrent JGCT is hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy but fertility-sparing surgery was chosen in this young patient, and suggest postponing any sex-change process 5 years after surgery.  Rare case of recurrent androgen- and insulin-secreting JGCT after enucleation alone in an adolescent, illustrating recurrence after non-radical surgery and ethical/fertility issues in management.

title: DICER1 Syndrome and Cancer Predisposition: From a Rare Pediatric Tumor to Lifetime Risk.
author: Caroleo AM
text: Narrative review of DICER1 syndrome (autosomal dominant, reduced penetrance; DICER1 on 14q32.13); in tumors a germline loss-of-function variant is typically paired with a somatic hotspot variant in the second allele; the review cites a 207-carrier study giving neoplasm risk of 5.3% before age 10 and 31.5% before age 60. In the ovary, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor is the most frequent DICER1-related tumor, and the review states that juvenile granulosa cell tumor, gynandroblastoma and unclassified sex cord-stromal tumors have also been described; most such tumors are stage I. Table 1 of the review (from Foulkes et al.) lists juvenile granulosa cell tumor with an asterisk and age of onset 'undetermined': the association with DICER1 variants 'may not be so strong to warrant testing in the absence of other features suggestive of DICER1 syndrome'. JGCT is not among the major or minor criteria for DICER1 germline testing quoted from Schultz et al. (major criteria include ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor and gynandroblastoma). Surveillance guidance quoted from Schultz et al.: pelvic ultrasound every 6 to 12 months from age 8 years until at least age 40 years for gynecologic tumors in carriers (general DICER1 recommendation, not JGCT-specific). Most patients with germline DICER1 variants live healthy lives; tumor occurs in 19.3% of carriers by age 50, with females at risk of gynecologic neoplasms. DICER1 DICER1 syndrome review; JGCT appears only as a rare, weakly established DICER1-associated ovarian tumor. No JGCT patient counts or outcomes are given.

title: Sex Cord Stromal Tumors in Children and Adolescents: A First Report by The South African Children's Cancer Study Group (1990-2015).
author: Hendricks M
text: Retrospective national multicentre series (9 South African paediatric oncology units, Jan 1990-Dec 2015) of 23 children up to 16 years with biopsy-proven sex cord stromal tumors (SCST): 3 male, 20 female; 13 JGCT (56.5%), 9 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, 1 thecoma. All 13 JGCT were ovarian. From the patient table, the 13 JGCT were stage 1 in 9, stage 3 in 2 and stage 4 in 2; JGCT ages ranged 8 to 162 months; elevated estradiol in 3 JGCT, LDH in 2, AFP in 1; at last report 10 JGCT were alive disease free, 1 was lost to follow-up and 2 (stage 3 and stage 4) died of disease. Across all 23 patients: stage I 14 (60.9%), II 2 (8.7%), III 5 (21.7%), IV 2 (8.7%); upfront resection in 21 (91.3%) with 17 complete resections and 4 incomplete, no surgical morbidity or mortality; no radiotherapy; remission in 21/23 (91.3%). Three patients relapsed and none were salvaged: one stage 2 SLCT, one stage 3 JGCT (primary resection, 6 courses JEb, relapse after chemotherapy, incompletely resectable) and one stage 4 JGCT (good initial response to BEP, recurrence after 6 courses, died before second-line therapy). 5-year OS 82.1% (95% CI 65.5-100%) and 5-year EFS 83.8% (95% CI 68.6-100%) for the whole SCST cohort; no JGCT-specific survival estimate is given. Only underweight-for-age significantly affected OS and EFS (P<0.0001); age, stage, histology, socioeconomic status and chemotherapy type were not predictive; the authors call the nutrition finding tenuous given small numbers. Chemotherapy was not standardized: 12 patients had none; carboplatin-based JEb was used in 6 as an outpatient option because cisplatin was given only as inpatient; 2 of the cisplatin-treated patients had documented hearing loss; GFR and audiology assessment were infrequent and not standardized; DICER1 testing was not available. Authors compare with MAKEI (EFS 87%, OS 88% in 62 non-testicular SCST) and the French TGM-95 study (5-year EFS 85%, OS 94%) and conclude outcomes were similar despite varied treatment; they call for national harmonized protocols and registry reporting of rare tumors.  First African national cohort of paediatric SCST; JGCT is the largest subgroup (13/23), providing stage and outcome data from a resource-limited setting, though survival is reported for the pooled SCST cohort.

title: Precocious Pseudo-puberty in a Two-year-old Girl, Presenting with Bilateral Ovarian Enlargement and Progressing to Unilateral Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumour.
author: Barakizou H
text: Girl aged 2.17 years with 3 months of breast development and rapid growth: height 94 cm (+2.6 SD), Tanner B3P2A1, bone age 5.0 years, one 3 cm cafe-au-lait patch; LH/FSH suppressed (LH basal/peak 0.43/0.18, FSH <0.1/<0.1 mIU/mL) with estradiol 130 pg/mL (prepubertal <20). Ultrasound showed bilaterally enlarged multicystic ovaries (left 76 mL, right 139 mL estimated), pubertal uterus; MAS work-up (calcium, phosphate, IGF-1, cortisol, thyroid, bone scintigraphy) was normal. Tamoxifen 20 mg daily started at 2.3 years; after 7 weeks height increased 4 cm, breast stage B3-4, menorrhagia, bone age 6.5 years, estradiol 184 pg/mL with gonadotrophins still suppressed. Repeat imaging showed a vascular solid-cystic left ovarian tumor (US 10x8x6 cm; MRI 12x10x5 cm) with a normal right ovary (1.83 mL); AFP, hCG and CEA normal, CA-125 slightly raised at 43 IU/mL; inhibin B assay not available. A week later torsion required urgent laparotomy with left oophorectomy and annexectomy: tumor 850 g, capsule intact, negative peritoneal lavage; FIGO stage IA. Histology: nodular tumor with fibrous septae, necrotic foci, abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, rare nuclear grooves and mitoses, reticulin around groups of cells, no follicles, pseudopapillae or Call-Exner bodies; strongly positive for inhibin B; AFP and CD30 negative. Tumor DNA was negative for GNAS hot spots, AKT1 exon 3 hot spot and FOXL2 C134W; after surgery signs regressed immediately, at 5.7 years she was prepubertal with normal ultrasound and at 8.1 years remained prepubertal with mildly elevated basal LH and prepubertal estradiol. Authors call the progression from bilateral ovarian enlargement to unilateral JGCT a novel observation, cannot confirm or exclude McCune-Albright syndrome, and cite AKT1 duplications in 10/16 JGCT and GNAS mutations in 9/30 JGCT from other studies. GNAS AKT1 FOXL2 Molecularly negative (GNAS, AKT1 exon 3, FOXL2) JGCT preceded by bilateral cystic ovarian enlargement; informs the uncertain relationship of JGCT with McCune-Albright signaling.

title: Could MicroRNAs Be Useful Tools to Improve the Diagnosis and Treatment of Rare Gynecological Cancers? A Brief Overview.
author: Di Fiore R
text: Narrative review of microRNA (miRNA) data in rare gynecological cancers (annual incidence <6 per 100,000 women); the review reports no new data. Granulosa cell tumors are described as about 5% of malignant ovarian tumors, with two distinct types, adult-type and juvenile granulosa cell tumor, but the authors state that most data refer to adult-type tumors; the review gives no JGCT-specific patient numbers or outcomes. Testing for the C134W FOXL2 mutation is described as helpful for diagnosing adult-type tumors; it is not presented as a JGCT marker. A comparative study cited by the review of miRNA regulation of FOXL2 in adult- versus juvenile-type granulosa cell tumors showed that reduction of the miR-17 family indirectly increased FOXL2 mRNA expression; through miRNA profiling, juvenile- and adult-derived cell lines were biologically distinct, which the authors say still needs to be addressed in vivo. Cited work by Tu et al. reported that miR-10a promotes granulosa cell tumor development via the PTEN-AKT/Wnt axis and that miR-126 is a tumor suppressor in granulosa cell tumor via EGFL7; granulosa cell tumor type (adult or juvenile) is not specified in the review. Cheng et al. (cited) validated six miRNAs (miR-29c-3p, miR-138-5p, miR-184, miR-204-5p, miR-328-3p, miR-501-3p) as markers for subtype classification in ovarian granulosa cell tumors; low miR-138-5p correlated with early stage and low miR-184 with recurrence in early-stage adult-type tumors. DICER1 RNase IIIb domain mutations are described as common in non-epithelial ovarian tumors, with Sertoli-Leydig tumors highly characteristic of DICER1 syndrome; no JGCT DICER1 data are given. For advanced or recurrent granulosa cell tumor the review states traditional chemotherapy has limited effectiveness and mentions the GOG264 trial (NCT01042522) of carboplatin/paclitaxel versus BEP in sex cord-stromal tumors. miR-17 family / FOXL2 miR-10a miR-126 Low-yield, indirect: a review of rare gynecological cancers in which JGCT appears only within the granulosa cell tumor section, with one cited miRNA/FOXL2 cell-line comparison of juvenile versus adult types. Useful only as a pointer to preclinical miRNA work.

title: Recurrent gynandroblastoma of the ovary with germline DICER1 mutation: A case report and review of the literature.
author: Mercier AM
text: A 24-year-old (G2P2) woman with a history of left ovarian JGCT diagnosed at 15 after laparoscopic cystectomy with intraoperative cyst rupture; she then had left salpingo-oophorectomy, partial bladder resection and excision of abdominal wall peritoneal metastasis for stage IIC JGCT, followed by 4 cycles of bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin. At 24 she presented with worsening hirsutism and irregular menses; inhibin B rose from stable values under 10 to 12 and then 89; CT showed a 5 x 5 cm septated multiloculated right adnexal mass. Surgery found a ruptured cystic right ovarian mass with right common and lower para-aortic lymphadenopathy; pathology showed recurrent gynandroblastoma (intermediately differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor component plus JGCT component with variably sized cysts); inhibin and calretinin positive, reticulin lost in the JGCT-like areas; lymph nodes and omentum were free of tumor. Review of the original 2012 slides showed similar findings, suggesting the first tumor was in fact a gynandroblastoma. Tumor DICER1 testing showed biallelic loss-of-function and RNase IIIb missense mutations; germline testing found DICER1 c.2488G>T (p.E830*) and an NBN variant of unknown significance; both children carry the DICER1 variant. From the literature review: AKT1 mutations are reported in most JGCTs and FOXL2 in adult GCT; seven gynandroblastomas with a JGCT component have been described; the OTST registry median age for DICER1 ovarian tumors is 16.9 years; authors recommend DICER1 germline testing for ovarian SLCT or gynandroblastoma, with consensus screening (pelvic ultrasound every 6-12 months from age 8-10 to 40). DICER1 NBN Shows that an apparent JGCT in a teenager was retrospectively a gynandroblastoma with germline DICER1, supporting DICER1 testing when a JGCT has a Sertoli-Leydig component or recurs.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor diagnosed in 6-month-old infant with precocious puberty.
author: Hansen R
text: 6-month-old girl referred for precocious puberty with breast buds, hyperpigmented areolas, axillary hair, Tanner III pubic hair, vaginal discharge, and acne. Estradiol 668 pg/mL (normal <=25), estrone 36 pg/mL (normal <15), testosterone 90.51 ng/dL (normal 1.2-62.0), LDH 1107.0 U/L (normal 163-452). Ultrasound: heterogeneous cystic and solid adnexal mass 9.0 x 7.5 x 5.5 cm with internal vascularity; post-pubertal uterus and thickened endometrium. MRI: mixed cystic and solid lesion 9.4 x 5.2 x 8.0 cm with enhancing solid component showing restricted diffusion. Intraoperatively the mass arose from the left ovary (although imaging had placed it in the right lower quadrant and left ovary was not visualized); left oophorectomy with staging was done, and peritoneal washings were negative. Histology of the solid component was JGCT; the cystic component was edematous ovarian tissue, which the authors hypothesize reflects estrogen stimulation akin to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome or hyperreactio luteinalis. Literature statements by the authors: JGCT are about 3%-7% of ovarian neoplasms, about 82% of prepubertal patients present with precocious puberty, more than 90% are FIGO stage I at diagnosis, and stage I disease responds well to unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.  Infantile JGCT with marked estrogen excess; documents imaging features and an edematous-ovary hypothesis for the cystic component.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor as the Presenting Feature of McCune-Albright Syndrome.
author: Marks BE
text: 15-year-old girl with secondary oligomenorrhea (irregular periods from age 14 y 4 mo; menarche at 12 y 8 mo), Hashimoto hypothyroidism on levothyroxine; no cafe-au-lait spots. Labs: LH and FSH suppressed (both <0.10 IU/L), estradiol 1074 pg/mL (immunoassay) and 1030 pg/mL by tandem mass spectrometry, inhibin B >4325 pg/mL (ref 50-475), prolactin 56.67 ng/mL, SHBG 175.7 nmol/L, low IGF-I 182.0 ng/mL; hCG, AFP (1.0 ng/mL) and CA125 (14 unit/mL) normal; brain MRI normal. Imaging: pelvic ultrasound 11 x 12 x 8 cm heterogeneous predominantly solid right adnexal mass; MRI and PET/CT showed minimal FDG uptake in the mass but intense multifocal skeletal uptake with expansile lytic lesions (including bilateral proximal femurs, a right femoral neck linear abnormality), characteristic of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, initially concerning for metastases; tibial biopsy equivocal/benign, suggestive of fibrous dysplasia. Surgery: laparotomy with peritoneal fluid suspicious for rupture, right salpingo-oophorectomy; pelvic washings negative, no lymphadenopathy; tumor 14.5 cm encapsulated, solid and cystic with necrosis; coffee-bean nuclei; IHC positive for inhibin, calretinin and SF1, diagnosis JGCT. Tumor and tibial bone both carried GNAS p.R201C while peripheral blood was wild-type at codon 201, consistent with mosaicism; first report of the same GNAS mutation in JGCT and McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS) in one patient. Classified FIGO stage IC2 because of rupture and treated with 4 cycles of bleomycin, cisplatin and etoposide; hormones normalized and she remained in remission 16 months after therapy; prolactin also normalized, attributed to estradiol effect. Authors cite that >60% of JGCTs carry AKT1 duplications and that Kalfa et al. found codon 201 GNAS mutations in 30% of 30 JGCT patients without MAS signs; in a large MAS series (40 of 113 with ovarian sampling) none had JGCT. Authors raise the question of tumor-marker surveillance in MAS with ovarian abnormalities and suggest investigating for the other disorder in patients diagnosed with either JGCT or MAS. GNAS Documents co-occurrence of JGCT and McCune-Albright syndrome driven by the same mosaic GNAS R201C mutation, linking JGCT biology to GNAS and raising surveillance questions.

title: Coincidence of juvenile granulosa cell tumor and serous cystadenoma in a pediatric patient: Case report and literature review.
author: Viet LA
text: 4-year-old girl with 6 weeks of breast enlargement, weight 22 kg and height 116 cm (both 85th-97th centile), a palpable left iliac fossa mass and serum estradiol 133.2 pg/mL. Ultrasound showed a large multilobulated cystic left ovarian mass with septa of varying thickness in a sponge-like pattern, hypovascular walls and fluid-fluid levels; MRI without contrast showed a honeycomb-like multiseptated cystic mass up to about 101 mm with blood-fluid levels (T1 hyperintense hemorrhage), bladder compression and uterine deviation, and about 5 mm of Douglas pouch fluid. Laparotomy: 10 x 5 x 4 cm left ovarian cystic mass with several ruptured cysts; pelvic lymph nodes and ascites negative for malignancy; left salpingo-oophorectomy; staged FIGO IC. Histology: solid nests of cells with narrow cytoplasm and grooved round hyperchromatic nuclei, microcysts with eosinophilic secretions; IHC positive for calretinin, inhibin and Ki-67, consistent with JGCT. Estradiol fell to normal after resection and she received adjuvant chemotherapy (agents not specified) with routine monitoring. One year later a new multilobulated cystic right ovarian mass appeared with normal estradiol (<0.5 pg/mL); after 5 months of follow-up it was resected and was histologically serous cystadenoma (single layer of tall ciliated tubal-type cells), not JGCT recurrence. Authors state that two different tumors in each ovary in a child is extremely rare, that benign thin-walled cystic features on US/MRI helped separate cystadenoma from recurrent GCT, and that chemotherapy is currently recommended only for advanced, recurrent or metastatic disease.  Cautions that a new contralateral cystic ovarian mass after JGCT resection may be a benign tumor rather than recurrence; documents imaging (sponge-like, hemorrhagic) of a childhood JGCT.

title: Cytologic features of sex cord-stromal tumors in women.
author: Edmund LN
text: Memorial Sloan Kettering retrospective review of cytology slides (2009-2020) from females with sex cord-stromal tumors: 30 specimens from 24 patients (25 adult GCT specimens from 19 patients, 2 JGCT from 2 patients, 2 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, 1 steroid cell tumor); age range 7-90 years. JGCT case 1 (patient aged 7 years, FIGO IC2, no evidence of disease at follow-up per Table 2): pelvic washing with loose clusters and single cells, intermediate N:C ratio, moderate to marked nuclear pleomorphism, coarsely granular chromatin, conspicuous nucleoli, bizarre multinucleated cells, atypical mitoses and necrosis; surgical specimen solid diffuse pattern, designated JGCT with anaplastic features; expressed inhibin and FOXL2. JGCT case 1 targeted sequencing found an AKT1 exon 4 insertion (p.R76_C77insLKTERPRPNTFIIR) and a TP53 exon 8 splicing variant. JGCT case 2 (age 65-66 years per tables, FIGO IIIB, first recurrence at 1.3 years): ascitic/peritoneal fluid with similar cytology but only moderate pleomorphism, no bizarre cells, atypical mitoses or necrosis; inhibin and progesterone receptor positive on cell block; no molecular data. Compared with adult GCT, JGCT cytology showed small clusters and single round-oval cells, moderate to marked pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and lacked nuclear grooves and rosettes/microfollicles; 8% of adult GCTs also lacked grooves, so distinguishing the two can be hard in paucicellular specimens. The authors state no immunohistochemical marker distinguishes JGCT from adult GCT; JGCTs often express FOXL2 but lack the canonical FOXL2 p.C134W mutation present in all 7/7 adult GCTs tested; they cite AKT1 duplications in 10 of 16 JGCTs from another study. Authors cite JGCT as 5% of granulosa cell tumors, mean age 13 years, 90% before age 30, and a postoperative 5-year disease-free survival over 90% for stage-confined tumors (background statements, cited from other work). AKT1 TP53 Only two JGCT specimens; useful for cytologic features and for the AKT1 alteration in an anaplastic JGCT. Mostly an adult GCT cytology series.

title: A rare case of Ovarian Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor in an Infant with Isosexual Pseudo Puberty and a Revision of Literature.
author: De Sanctis V
text: A 9-month-old girl presented with vaginal bleeding; breast development and fine genital hair had been noticed 2 months earlier; Tanner stage 2 breasts, no palpable abdominal mass. Estradiol 1,091 pmol/L (reference 0-132), AMH >1714 pmol/L (0.1-38.6), inhibin A 385 pg/mL (<4.7), inhibin B 3805 pg/mL (<111), androstenedione 6.8 nmol/L (high); FSH and LH <0.3 IU/L (suppressed); AFP 6 kIU/L, beta-hCG, DHEAS, testosterone normal. Ultrasound showed a 5.4 x 4.0 x 5.4 cm solid heterogeneous left adnexal mass with enlarged uterus (5.2 x 2.4 x 2.3 cm); MRI confirmed a 5.4 x 4.12 x 5.39 cm enhancing solid lesion with minimal central necrosis; chest CT normal; bone age advanced by 1.8 years. Surgery: left total salpingo-oophorectomy with biopsies of peritoneum, round ligament and omentum; encapsulated yellow solid tumor 6.5 x 4 x 6.5 cm, 75 g, no hemorrhage or necrosis; histology JGCT FIGO IA, calretinin and inhibin A positive. At 1 week and 1 month postoperatively estradiol (62, <55 pmol/L) and AMH (9 pmol/L) were normal; no evidence of recurrence at 12 months; no chemotherapy or radiotherapy needed. Literature update in infants under 12 months (table of 10 cases, mostly case reports): presentations were premature thelarche/adrenarche or signs of puberty, abdominal mass or distension, acute abdomen from rupture, ascites; hormonal data often not reported. The authors cite a 1997 review by Bouffet et al. of 36 JGCT cases under 2 years, 21 under 1 year. The authors, citing other sources, state that stage is the most important prognostic factor (stage IA survival 83-98%, overall 78-92%), recurrences can occur up to 3 years after surgery, inhibin B and AMH are useful monitoring markers, and unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy appears curative.  Well-documented infant JGCT with isosexual pseudo-puberty and a high inhibin/AMH profile that normalized after surgery, plus a short tabulated review of infant JGCT cases.

title: DICER1 tumor predisposition syndrome: an evolving story initiated with the pleuropulmonary blastoma.
author: González IA
text: Pathology-focused review of DICER1 tumor predisposition syndrome (PPB and extrapulmonary tumors); JGCT is mentioned only in the ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor and gynandroblastoma sections. The review states ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors are about 5% of primary ovarian neoplasms and can present in adolescence and young adulthood or earlier, as in juvenile granulosa cell tumor; they may show hormonal signs including hirsutism, virilization, menstrual changes or precocious pseudopuberty, and are also associated with Peutz-Jeghers and Ollier-Maffucci syndromes. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor is the most common ovarian tumor in DICER1 syndrome (International Ovarian and Testicular Stromal Tumor Registry data cited); juvenile granulosa cell tumor, yolk sac tumor, teratoma and mixed germ cell tumors are listed as other ovarian tumors reported with DICER1 mutations but, compared with SLCT, 'may represent coincidences' because increased risk for germ cell tumors in DICER1 carriers is uncertain. Gynandroblastoma (SLCT component with adult or juvenile granulosa cell pattern): one case among 325 ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors from 296 PPB families; in a cohort of 16 gynandroblastomas (age 14-80 years, median 24.5) the granulosa component had juvenile features in 10 (62.5%), three cases had a DICER1 hotspot mutation (all with moderately to poorly differentiated SLCT plus juvenile granulosa component) and none had FOXL2 mutation; 10 of 26 gynandroblastomas tested (38%) had RNase IIIb hotspot mutations. Recommendations quoted: DICER1 testing and genetic counseling when gynandroblastoma, especially with intermediate or poorly differentiated SLCT, is found; pelvic ultrasound every 6 to 12 months until at least age 40 years in carriers (general DICER1 surveillance, not specific to JGCT). No JGCT patient counts, outcomes or DICER1 frequency in JGCT are reported.
