DICER1 FOXL2 DICER1 review with only passing JGCT content: JGCT listed as a possible but uncertain DICER1-associated ovarian tumor; useful mainly for the juvenile granulosa component of gynandroblastoma and the DICER1/FOXL2 findings there.

title: The Role of Omics Approaches to Characterize Molecular Mechanisms of Rare Ovarian Cancers: Recent Advances and Future Perspectives.
author: Subbannayya Y
text: Narrative review of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic (omics) studies in rare ovarian cancers; JGCT appears only briefly, as part of the granulosa cell tumor discussion and in Table 2. The review describes granulosa cell tumors as malignant sex cord-stromal tumors constituting about 5% of ovarian malignancies, of two types (adult and juvenile), and that traditional chemotherapy has limited effect in advanced or recurrent disease; GOG264 (NCT01042522, BEP vs carboplatin-paclitaxel) is cited as ongoing. Table 2 lists juvenile granulosa cell tumor genomic alterations as 'GSP mutation (30%), AKT1', contrasting adult granulosa (FOXL2 402C>G missense, >95%, called pathognomonic) and Sertoli-Leydig (DICER1, 90%, including germline). No primary citation or sample size for the JGCT figure is given in the text. Transcriptomics: the review states that a study performing RNA-Seq of juvenile granulosa cell tumors found genes in cytokine/hormone signaling and cell division-related processes differentially regulated (no numbers given). The authors conclude that omics approaches, especially integrated multi-omics, could help define molecular subtypes, biomarkers and therapies for rare ovarian cancers, and that standardization is needed before clinical use. GSP (GNAS) AKT1 Secondary review of omics in rare ovarian cancers; the JGCT content is limited to a Table 2 entry (GSP mutation 30%, AKT1), one sentence on JGCT RNA-Seq, and general granulosa tumor background.

title: Adult granulosa cell tumor with minor foci of juvenile granulosa cell tumor in postmenopausal woman: A rare case report.
author: Rustamadji P
text: A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman with 6 months of abdominal distension and postmenopausal bleeding had an 18 x 15 x 14 cm solid right ovarian mass at laparotomy (CT 13 x 18 x 19 cm with central necrosis, no ascites or seeding); beta-hCG <1.2 U/mL, AFP 6.51 ng/mL, LDH 185 U/L, CA125 186.3 U/mL. The tumor was predominantly adult-type granulosa cell tumor (diffuse growth, Call-Exner bodies, nuclear grooves, 1-2 mitoses/10 HPF) with minor foci resembling JGCT: well-circumscribed solid areas with many follicle-like cavities of varying size containing thin eosinophilic secretion, small round deeply stained nuclei, no nuclear grooves and no Call-Exner bodies, with luteinization in the minor foci. Two expert gynecopathologists were consulted and agreed with the finding; no immunohistochemistry or molecular testing is reported. The authors state this is the first report of adult GCT with minor foci of JGCT in a postmenopausal woman, and cite prior reports of JGCT with minor adult-type foci (Zhang et al., Young et al.). Authors' histologic criteria for JGCT: diffuse growth with follicle-like structures, absence of Call-Exner bodies, small round nuclei with deep chromatin and no grooves; they note follicle-like structures occur in a small part of adult GCT and 60% of adult GCT may lack Call-Exner bodies. The authors state that age and clinical symptoms cannot discriminate adult from juvenile GCT, imaging cannot either, and an experienced pathologist is needed; they state 3% of JGCTs occur in women over 30 years and that prognosis follow-up of mixed tumors needs more study (only 3 months here).  Postmenopausal tumor that is not a JGCT in the usual sense; shows that juvenile-pattern foci can occur within an adult GCT, relevant to pathologic classification only.

title: Surgical Management of Adnexal Masses in the Pediatric and Adolescent Age Group: Our Experience.
author: Luthra M
text: Retrospective review of 28 girls under 17 years (2000-2020) with adnexal masses treated at tertiary centers in Delhi-NCR by one surgeon; median age 11 years 9 months; histology: functional nonneoplastic lesions 18 (66.7%), benign neoplasms 8 (29.6%), malignant 1 (3.7%). The single malignant lesion was a juvenile granulosa cell tumor (malignant sex cord-stromal tumor), a large solid ovarian mass seen on CT/PET-CT; AFP and beta-hCG were normal in all 19 tested patients, CA-125 raised in the JGCT (also in mucinous cystadenoma and fibroma) and LDH raised in the JGCT. The JGCT patient had laparotomy, salpingo-oophorectomy with peritoneal and lymph node biopsies (liver metastases ruled out); histopathology JGCT pT1NX; she received 3 cycles of adjuvant BEP and serum AFP was monitored; PET-CT at 9 months was normal. Overall survival in the series was 100%; the three patients with ovarian tumors who had laparotomy were followed for 6, 4 and 1 years without complaints. The authors conclude that adnexal masses in children are generally benign, ovary-sparing surgery should be favored, and that with accurate staging, complete resection and chemotherapy for malignant tumors patients showed excellent survival.  Minor. Single JGCT case within a small pediatric adnexal-mass surgical series, with a short description of staging, BEP chemotherapy and follow-up.

title: Oncological Prognosis and Fertility Outcomes of Different Surgical Extents for Malignant Ovarian Sex-Cord Stromal Tumors: A Narrative Review.
author: Li J
text: Narrative review of PubMed literature from January 2011 to December 2021 on surgical extent in malignant ovarian sex-cord stromal tumors (MOSCSTs); the authors identified 12 large retrospective studies and 18 case reports. Most data concern adult granulosa cell tumor (AGCT); JGCT-specific data are sparse. Three JGCT case reports are tabulated: a 5-year-old with isosexual precocious puberty, a 14x10x16 cm abdominopelvic mass, inhibin A 538 ng/L, inhibin B >977 ng/L and NSE 87.2 ug/L (stage I, oophorectomy plus omentectomy; later cystectomy for a contralateral benign mucinous cystadenoma; no recurrence 2 years after the second surgery); a 33-year-old with JGCT and Maffucci syndrome in pregnancy (stage IA, USO); and a 19-year-old with massive ascites (stage IC, USO then 6 cycles of nedaplatin plus paclitaxel liposome, no recurrence at 6 months). The review states that fertility-sparing surgery could be considered for young women with high-stage JGCT: one stage IIIB JGCT patient treated with USO, omentectomy and debulking relapsed 55 months after first surgery, then had second debulking plus carboplatin and paclitaxel and had no relapse in 30 months of follow-up. Management of advanced disease should be decided by a multidisciplinary team. For JGCT with high-risk features (germline PTEN, p53 overexpression), USO with complete staging may have a better prognosis than USO alone, but the cited study had only eight patients; another report found p53 overexpression not associated with outcome. A cited multicenter retrospective study reported a pregnancy rate after fertility-sparing surgery of about 16.7% in AGCT and about 36.4% in JGCT patients. JGCT and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor are described as the most common subtypes of sex-cord stromal tumor diagnosed in pregnancy; the review cites 48 gestational MSCST cases up to 2017 and SCST as 10-20% of ovarian malignancies diagnosed in pregnancy. Isolated case reports and small case series are cited as suggesting that chemotherapy can achieve long-term remission in recurrent JGCT. Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome are stated to be associated with an increased risk of JGCT. General conclusions (all MOSCSTs): USO-only seems feasible in early-stage fertility-desiring patients, cystectomy-only should be avoided; fertility-sparing surgery with staging is described as feasible in advanced stage; lymphadenectomy can be omitted when nodes are not suspicious; endometrial evaluation is advised for patients over 40 or with bleeding; chemotherapy benefit remains controversial (BEP most used; GOG randomized trial of carboplatin-paclitaxel vs BEP cited); long-term follow-up is essential.  Review of surgical extent and fertility outcomes for malignant ovarian sex-cord stromal tumors, predominantly AGCT; JGCT appears in three tabulated case reports and a few cited statements on advanced-stage fertility-sparing surgery, pregnancy rates and chemotherapy.

title: What Should Be the Topics of a Prospective Study on Ovarian Masses in Children?-Results of a Multicenter Retrospective Study and a Scoping Literature Review.
author: Łuczak J
text: Retrospective review of 595 girls aged 0-18 operated on for ovarian lesions at 17 Polish paediatric surgery departments (2012-2017); 44 (7.39%) had malignant tumours. Juvenile granulosa cell tumour was the most common malignant lesion: 10 of the 44 malignant tumours, within 12 stromal tumours (JGCT 10, Sertoli cell tumour 1, serous papillary carcinoma 1 as listed in Table 2). The other malignant tumours were germ cell tumours (22: dysgerminoma 6, immature teratoma 5, yolk sac 4, mixed 7), epithelial (4) and other (6). No malignant tumour occurred in girls younger than 1 year; malignant tumours were not different in age from non-malignant ones (p=0.570); median age of the malignant group 13.1 years. Across all malignant tumours, positive tumour markers (OR 10.3), lesion larger than 6 cm (OR 4.17) and solid mass on ultrasound (OR 5.34) independently distinguished malignant from non-malignant lesions; marker panel included AFP, beta-hCG, CA125 and LDH. Bilateral masses were more frequent in the malignant group (6/44 vs 30/551); ovarian torsion was mostly in non-malignant lesions (3 malignant vs 133 non-malignant). JGCT-specific clinical, treatment and outcome data are not reported; the paper says malignant tumours were treated per oncological guidelines.  Mixed paediatric ovarian-mass series; JGCT-specific content is limited to the count of 10 JGCTs being the most frequent malignant ovarian tumour in this Polish national cohort. Also includes a scoping review of ovarian mass studies of at least 200 children.

title: Transformation of Peripheral Sexual Precocity to Central Sexual Precocity Following Treatment of Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Ovary.
author: Gaikwad PM
text: Case report: 5 year 5 month old girl with 2.5 years of progressive bilateral breast enlargement, intermittent vaginal spotting and growth acceleration; no pubic or axillary hair; hormones initially indicated peripheral precocious puberty. Preoperative labs: LH 0.28 IU/L, FSH 0.81 IU/mL, estradiol 21.10 pg/mL, CA 125 48.31 U/mL (0-35), LDH 310 U/L (140-280); triptorelin stimulation preoperatively gave basal LH 0.01 and 60/180-minute LH 2.2 and 1.7 (not pubertal). Ultrasound: uterine volume 6 mL, uterus 3.6 x 1.2 x 2.6 cm, right adnexal mass 9.46 x 9.2 x 6.4 cm. Laparotomy with tumor resection; histology: large atypical cells in tubulocystic and solid sheet patterns, nuclear atypia, eosinophilic cytoplasm, basophilic mucin secretion and mitoses; IHC positive for inhibin, vimentin, calretinin, CD56 and CD99; diagnosis JGCT; she then received cisplatin, etoposide, bleomycin. At 1.5 years after surgery breast development had progressed (Tanner 3), spotting persisted (every 15-20 days), height 121 cm (+1.81 SD), weight 24 kg, bone age 11 years; pelvic ultrasound showed no mass and CA 125 (15.2 U/mL) and LDH (207 U/L) were normal, excluding recurrence. Postoperative hormones: LH 0.70 IU/L, FSH 3.6 IU/mL, estradiol 11 pg/mL; post-triptorelin LH 5.2 at 60 and 180 minutes with basal 0.01, confirming central precocious puberty; leuprolide depot 11.25 mg every 3 months stopped spotting and regressed breasts. Authors' conclusion: JGCT causing peripheral precocious puberty is known; central precocious puberty after resection is rarer and justifies close follow-up of such patients.  Illustrates a late endocrine sequela of JGCT-related precocious puberty (secondary central puberty after tumor removal and chemotherapy), relevant to long-term follow-up of young JGCT patients.

title: Fertility sparing surgery in sex-cord stromal tumors: oncological and reproductive outcomes.
author: Bergamini A
text: Narrative literature review (PubMed 1994 to July 2021, English) on oncological and reproductive outcomes after fertility-sparing surgery in sex cord stromal tumors: obstetrical outcomes in 255 patients (132 granulosa cell tumors: 98 adult, 26 juvenile, 8 unspecified) and oncological outcomes in 900 patients from 12 publications. Pregnancy after fertility-sparing surgery: 44 of 132 (33%) granulosa cell tumor patients; juvenile 11/26 (42.3%) versus adult 28/98 (28.6%); in articles stating patients tried to conceive the rate was 88.5% (23/26). The authors attribute the JGCT advantage to younger age and lower relapse and chemotherapy rates. JGCT presentation per review: abdominal distension or pain, rarely torsion, hyperestrogenism (pseudo-precocious puberty with thelarche and vaginal bleeding; irregular menses in adolescents), rare virilization; JGCT is ~5% of granulosa cell tumors; most early stage with survival >90% with surgery alone, advanced stage 25-50% 5-year survival. A multicenter study cited (Bergamini 2021, MITO-9) of 17 stage I JGCT: 2 radical, 15 conservative (11 unilateral adnexectomy, 2 cystectomy then adnexectomy, 2 cystectomy alone); no relapses; 6 pregnancies with a 100% live-birth rate in 15 conservatively treated patients. Table 2 lists JGCT series comparing conservative and radical surgery: Wu 2016 (8 JGCT, all conservative, 74 months median follow-up, 75% survival), Zhao 2019 (6 JGCT, 100%), Bergamini 2021 (17 JGCT, 100%). ESGO/SIOPE 2020 recommendations as summarised: unilateral oophorectomy preferred to cystectomy/tumorectomy in stage IA; surgery alone is an option in stage IC1; stage IC2/IC3 and advanced or high-risk (rupture, many mitoses) need adjuvant treatment, standard carboplatin plus paclitaxel for six cycles, BEP for four cycles an option with more toxicity; endometrial thickness to be assessed in asymptomatic patients. Authors conclude that unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with peritoneal staging is the preferred approach for early-stage sex cord stromal tumors; evidence for ultraconservative surgery (cystectomy) in JGCT and for advanced JGCT is limited, and transplantation of cryopreserved ovarian tissue is not recommended.  Review pooling published JGCT fertility-sparing surgery and pregnancy data (26 JGCT with obstetrical data) and summarising ESGO/SIOPE guidance.

title: Sex chromosome DSD individuals with mosaic 45,X0 and aberrant Y chromosomes in 46,XY cells: distinct gender phenotypes and germ cell tumour risks(§).
author: Vogt PH
text: The paper maps Y-chromosome breakpoints in 22 individuals with 45,X/46,XY sex chromosome DSD (11 reared male, 11 female) and studies OCT3/4 and the GBY proteins DDX3Y, TSPY and UTY by IHC in gonadal sections; it is a germ cell tumor risk study, not a JGCT study. One patient (GBY137, reared male, prepubertal, gonadectomized) had a juvenile granulosa cell tumor in the left testis diagnosed after birth; right testis sections were not available. In the GBY137 left testis (1 month postnatal) only single germ cells expressed OCT3/4, but all three GBY candidate proteins (DDX3Y, TSPY, UTY) were expressed, and most germ cells showed a germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) phenotype. Strong AMH staining on the same sections marked immature Sertoli cells, which the authors take to confirm that the JGCT tumor cells originate from immature Sertoli cells (citing Kao et al.); the authors describe JGCT as benign and 1-5% of prepubertal testis tumors (cited). The authors propose that the GBY candidate proteins indicate tumor risk only when OCT3/4 marks pluripotent germ cells, and note GBY137 as a possible exception (low OCT3/4 but strong GBY protein expression with GCNIS). Gender rearing did not depend on the Y breakpoint site or the proportion of 45,X cells; 13 of 22 patients had dicentric Y structures. Y chromosome (dicentric, 45,X/46,XY mosaic) Contains a single testicular JGCT in a 45,X/46,XY DSD infant with IHC (AMH, GBY proteins, OCT3/4) data; supports association of JGCT with sex chromosome DSD and Y-chromosome abnormalities. All other content concerns germ cell tumor risk.

title: Imaging of Pediatric Testicular and Para-Testicular Tumors: A Pictural Review.
author: Hermann AL
text: Narrative imaging review of paediatric testicular and para-testicular tumours based on PubMed papers mainly 2010-2022; it reports that among non-germ-cell prepubertal testicular tumours, Leydig cell tumours (about 5%) are most frequent, followed by juvenile granulosa cell tumours. Testicular juvenile granulosa cell tumour accounts for 1% to 5% of prepubertal testicular tumours (Table 1 gives under 5%) and usually presents in the first year of life, within the first 6 months; a few prenatal diagnoses have been reported. Typical presentation is a painless testicular mass or enlarged testis, with possible hormonal changes including gynecomastia and anomalies of puberty. There is no specific imaging appearance: tumours are classically well circumscribed with median size 1.5 cm, may contain cystic components or be entirely solid; macroscopically yellow-tan. Histology: lobular architecture and follicular differentiation are characteristic; solid and reticular patterns are diagnostic pitfalls; immunohistochemistry helps distinguish from yolk sac tumours, which peak at a later age. The illustrated case (Figure 7) was a 1-month-old boy with a well-circumscribed lobulated mass with a cystic component and calcifications, normal tumour markers, treated with partial orchidectomy by inguinal approach. The review states the juvenile type is a benign entity with low recurrence after testis-sparing surgery, whereas adult testicular granulosa cell tumours have metastatic potential. General management points: testis-sparing surgery with intra-operative frozen section for presumed benign lesions, with tumour size under 2.5 cm generally favourable; radical orchidectomy for malignant tumours.  Imaging-focused review in which testicular JGCT occupies one short subsection; useful for epidemiology (1-5% of prepubertal testicular tumours), age at presentation, benign behaviour after testis-sparing surgery and a single illustrative case.

title: Ovarian cell tumor in a child with neurofibromatosis type 1.
author: Qutub LM
text: 6-year-old girl with clinically diagnosed neurofibromatosis type 1 (more than six cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, affected relatives) presented with 3 weeks of bilateral breast enlargement followed by vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain and distention. Examination: Tanner breast stage 2, no pubic or axillary hair, hard nontender 7 x 7 cm right lower quadrant mass; bone age matched chronological age. CT: well-defined heterogeneous solid right ovarian mass 7.8 x 7.4 x 6.2 cm with uterus stretched superiorly and thickened endometrium. Hormones consistent with pseudo-precocious puberty: LH 0.04 mIU/L, FSH 2.17 IU/L, estradiol 152.72 pmol/L (ref 26-125), inhibin B >1300 pg/mL (ref 0-18); beta-hCG, AFP and CEA normal. Right ovary removed (150 g, 9 x 6.5 x 5 cm, solid multicystic); histology predominantly JGCT type with variable follicles filled with eosinophilic fluid; cytology without malignant cells. No immunohistochemistry reported, no stage or follow-up given. Authors state they found no prior reported case of JGCT associated with NF1 and that isosexual pseudo-precocious puberty from JGCT is not the usual presentation in NF1 (where central precocious puberty is common). NF1 Case of prepubertal JGCT causing pseudo-precocious puberty in a child with NF1; high inhibin B; authors report no earlier JGCT-NF1 case. Association is a single observation.

title: Use of staging for sex cord stromal tumours.
author: Negri S
text: Narrative review of surgical staging of ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors (SCST), mainly granulosa cell and Sertoli-Leydig tumors; SCSTs are 3-7% of ovarian tumors, incidence about 2.1 per million women in Europe. JGCT is described as the most common SCST in children and adolescents, mean age of onset 13 years; adult GCT accounts for up to 95% of GCTs, mean onset 50-55 years. JGCT can manifest with hyperestrogenism and pseudoprecocity, but no studies suggest an association with endometrial pathology (unlike adult GCT, where endometrial hyperplasia occurs in 20-60% and cancer in 1-20%). Lymph node data: in cited series with JGCT (Karalok 10 JGCTs 0/5 positive nodes; Wang 35 JGCTs 0/14; Brown 27 JGCTs, 0/7 in stage I-II and 0/2 in III-IV) no node metastasis was found; lymphadenectomy did not improve disease-free or overall survival and is not recommended by international guidelines for SCST. Cystectomy 'might be well tolerated' in JGCT but a recent review of early-stage JGCT described a 25% recurrence rate with one of four relapsing after 3 months in the same ovary; in that review incomplete surgical staging was significantly associated with disease-free survival and was the only risk factor for recurrence. Laparoscopy seems well tolerated in JGCTs (small series and case reports); surgical staging (peritoneal washing, omentectomy, peritoneal biopsies, no routine lymphadenectomy) should always be performed, and restaging is suggested after incomplete staging. Authors' conclusion: unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is safer than cystectomy for fertility-sparing surgery in adult GCT, and most evidence comes from retrospective studies and case reports.  Review of staging in ovarian SCST with several JGCT-specific statements (nodal metastasis, cystectomy recurrence, laparoscopy, staging). Only secondary data; no original patients.

title: Ollier's disease associated with ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumor and triple X syndrome: A letter to the editor.
author: Shafieyoon S
text: A girl born preterm at 32 weeks with a prenatally detected 47,XXX karyotype (triple X syndrome) was referred at 22 months for left leg deformity and limb-length discrepancy; radiographs showed multiple lower-limb and right upper-limb enchondromas, diagnosing Ollier's disease. At 18 months she developed sudden progressive ascites; ultrasound showed a large solid cystic multilocular mass with heterogeneous echogenicity and internal vascularity, and abdominopelvic CT showed an enhancing heterogeneous mass in the right and central abdomen. Laparotomy and histology showed irregular cells in a myxoid background with basophilic secretions and a high mitotic count; tumor cells expressed cytokeratin, calretinin, Ki-67, inhibin and WT1, and the diagnosis was ovarian JGCT. The letter reports no surgical extent, stage, chemotherapy, hormone levels, molecular testing or follow-up outcome. The authors state this is the first report of triple X syndrome associated with Ollier's disease and JGCT, and conclude that Ollier's disease can increase the risk of various neoplasms, which should be considered in managing these patients.  Single report of ovarian JGCT in an infant with Ollier's disease and 47,XXX; adds to the Ollier's disease-JGCT association but this letter provides no molecular data.

title: Histopathological Spectrum of Ovarian Neoplasms: A Single-Center Study.
author: Batool A
text: Cross-sectional histopathology study of 390 ovarian neoplasms examined November 2020 to October 2021 at the Chughtai Institute of Pathology, Lahore, Pakistan, classified by WHO; ages 10-80 years. Of 390 tumours, 320 (82.05%) were benign, 11 (2.82%) borderline, 57 (14.61%) malignant and 2 (0.52%) metastatic. Surface epithelial tumours were 246 (63.08%), germ cell tumours 115 (29.48%) and sex cord-stromal tumours 27 (6.92%). Among the 27 sex cord-stromal tumours: fibroma 10, adult granulosa cell tumour 7, thecoma 5, juvenile granulosa cell tumour 3 (0.76% of all tumours), Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour 2. Sex cord-stromal tumours had no cases in the 11-20 year age group and peaked at 41-50 years (9 cases); the age of the 3 JGCT cases is not given separately. No clinical follow-up, treatment, marker or outcome data are reported; the authors list lack of follow-up and single-centre design as limitations.  Single-centre histopathology frequency study; its only JGCT content is the count of 3 juvenile granulosa cell tumours among 390 ovarian neoplasms (and 27 sex cord-stromal tumours) in a Pakistani laboratory.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor Mimicking HAIR-AN in a 4-year-old: A Case Report.
author: Kim RC
text: A 4-year-1-month-old girl presented with virilization (Tanner 3 pubic hair, hirsutism, acne) and extensive acanthosis nigricans mimicking HAIR-AN/type A insulin resistance; height 110.4 cm, weight 29 kg, BMI 23.79 kg/m2; bone age 6 years 4 months. Pre-operative labs: total testosterone 205.6 ng/dL (normal <=20), inhibin B 1715 pg/mL (<73.0), inhibin A 43.7 pg/mL (<7-14), AMH 6.75 ng/mL, 17-OH-progesterone 145 ng/dL, insulin 45.2 uIU/mL (2.6-24.9), LDH 363 IU/L; estradiol 11.8 pg/mL normal, FSH and LH suppressed; beta-hCG, AFP and CA-125 normal. Pelvic ultrasound showed a 6.3 x 3.4 x 7.1 cm heterogeneous solid vascular left adnexal mass; CT showed a 4.4 x 4.6 x 4.2 cm solid left ovarian mass without metastasis or lymphadenopathy. Unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy gave stage 1A JGCT; immunohistochemistry (data not shown) was positive for inhibin and negative for pancytokeratin, WT1 and calretinin; histology showed pleomorphic cells. Within 2 weeks of surgery testosterone fell to <1 ng/dL, inhibin B to 25 pg/mL, inhibin A to 1.4 pg/mL and insulin to 2 uIU/mL; at 6 months-1 year testosterone was 4 ng/dL, inhibin B 15.2, insulin 17 uIU/mL; at age 6 years 3 months acne and hirsutism had resolved, acanthosis nigricans regressed substantially, and no residual mass was seen. The authors suggest the androgen excess caused hyperinsulinemia (which improved after tumor removal despite increasing BMI); they note androgen-secreting JGCTs are uncommon (testosterone secretion 2-3% of GCTs), and cite Kalfa et al. reporting absent or low intratumoral aromatase in six hyperandrogenic JGCTs. They considered DICER1 syndrome but the patient did not fit its clinical picture; no genetic testing is reported; family history included distant ovarian cancer at advanced ages.  Rare androgen-secreting prepubertal JGCT with hyperinsulinemia and acanthosis nigricans reversed by tumor resection; inhibin A and B were markedly elevated and normalized after surgery.

title: Imaging of pediatric ovarian tumors: A COG Diagnostic Imaging Committee/SPR Oncology Committee White Paper.
author: Behr GG
text: Consensus imaging recommendations from the COG Diagnostic Imaging Committee and SPR Oncology Committee for pediatric patients with known or suspected primary ovarian malignancy, at diagnosis and during follow-up. Girls with sex cord stromal tumors tend to present with smaller tumors because of hormone production; isosexual precocious puberty is the example given for juvenile granulosa cell tumor. Sex cord stromal and epithelial ovarian tumors are staged with FIGO, whereas ovarian germ cell tumors use the COG surgical staging (2004), so distinguishing tumor types before resection is important. Table 1 lists JGCT as a sex cord stromal tumor with a 'sponge-like' imaging appearance and inhibin as the tumor marker; Sertoli-Leydig tumors are linked to DICER1 mutation. Recommendations: transabdominal US first; MRI abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast for further evaluation (and for cystic lesions >7.5 cm, lesions not fully seen, or with solid components); CT acceptable if MRI not possible; chest CT if malignancy present; pelvic US or MRI surveillance in all girls with a resected ovarian tumor (GRADE C, SOR 1.40). Surveillance statement: adult granulosa cell tumor can recur 10 years after treatment and needs long-term follow-up, though JGCTs 'may be less aggressive'; serum inhibin may be followed for recurrence; adult sex cord stromal data suggest recurrence is unlikely after three years. No formal guidelines exist for post-treatment imaging surveillance in children and none for tumor response assessment specific to pediatric ovarian tumors.  Imaging consensus covering all pediatric ovarian tumors; JGCT-specific content is limited to presentation, marker (inhibin), MRI 'sponge-like' appearance, staging system and surveillance remarks.

title: IDH Mutations Are Potentially the Intrinsic Genetic Link among the Multiple Neoplastic Lesions in Ollier Disease and Maffucci Syndrome: A Clinicopathologic Analysis from a Single Institute in Shanghai, China.
author: Chen C
text: Six patients (3 Ollier disease, 3 Maffucci syndrome) from Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital, 2016-2020; 16 tumors Sanger-sequenced for IDH1/IDH2. One Ollier disease patient (case 1, female, onset 2 years, diagnosed at 4 years) had a right ovarian tumor ipsilateral to the predominant skeletal disease; it was resected with a femoral biopsy and she was alive without recurrence at 31 months. The ovarian tumor was an ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor of primitive ovate to elongated cells with mucinous stromal degeneration, easily found mitoses and no pathologic mitoses; it was positive for alpha-inhibin and negative for desmin, MyoD1, myogenin, SMA, S100, CD34 and BCOR; reticulin surrounded the cells. The authors call it insufficient for a conclusive diagnosis and it is not labeled JGCT. The ovarian tumor carried IDH1 p.R132C, identical to the right upper femur enchondroma of the same patient; IDH2 was wild type. IDH1 mutations were in 8/11 cartilage tumors and 4/4 hemangiomas. The authors write that ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumors are the most commonly reported extraskeletal tumors in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome, and that no previous report had described molecular features of JGCT in these syndromes; they conclude IDH mutations may be a link among the multiple lesions through somatic mosaicism, but that a heterozygous IDH mutation alone is insufficient to cause ovarian tumors or gliomas. IDH1 Documents an IDH1-mutant pediatric ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor in Ollier disease and states the JGCT association; the tumor is not formally diagnosed as JGCT.

title: A 12-Year-Old Girl with Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Ovary, Presenting with Adolescent Hyperprolactinemia, Galactorrhea, and Amenorrhea.
author: Park H
text: 12-year-old obese girl (menarche at 10, no regular menses for 2 years) with intermittent left lower abdominal pain and bilateral galactorrhea; prolactin 70.5 ng/mL (normal 4.8-23.3) with total beta-hCG <0.6; initial working diagnosis was anterior pituitary hyperfunction. Ultrasound showed an incidental large left pelvic mass (heterogeneous, predominantly solid); Doppler showed no torsion. CT: heterogeneously enhancing, partially necrotic cystic-solid mass about 15.0 x 9.0 x 18.8 cm arising from the left adnexa, abutting the uterine fundus without invasion and partially compressing the IVC and common iliac veins. En bloc left salpingo-oophorectomy; resected mass weighed 1425 g, confined to the ovary with intact capsule, no surface tumor or lymphovascular invasion; omental biopsy and peritoneal washings negative. Pathology: JGCT, FIGO stage 1A; immunohistochemistry positive for inhibin and calretinin. No precocious puberty or overt hyperestrogenism. Discharged on hospital day 4 and doing well at 2 weeks; no chemotherapy given. Authors' literature statements: GCT incidence 0.4-1.7 per 100,000 women, JGCT about 5% of GCTs, median JGCT age 8-17 years; stage I 5-year survival 90-95% but GCTs can recur 20-30 years later; tumor rupture in 10%; prognostic factors include stage, size, BMI and failure to resect en bloc. The authors conclude JGCT can present with amenorrhea rather than precocious puberty and should be in the differential for young girls with abdominal pain and hormonal irregularity.  Unusual JGCT presentation with hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea and secondary amenorrhea and a very large (1425 g) stage IA tumor.

title: The Histopathological Patterns of Ovarian Neoplasms in Different Age Groups: A Retrospective Study in a Tertiary Care Center.
author: Farag NH
text: Retrospective single-centre study (King Abdulaziz University Hospital, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, 2016-2020) of 565 ovarian specimens: 357 (63.2%) neoplasms and 208 (36.8%) non-neoplastic; of neoplasms, 64.4% benign, 6.2% borderline, 29.4% malignant. Sex cord/stromal tumors were 32 of 357 neoplasms (9.0%): fibroma 17, fibrothecoma 6, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor 2, juvenile granulosa cell tumor 2 (6.3% of sex cord tumors), adult granulosa cell tumor 5. Both juvenile granulosa cell tumors were classed as malignant and both occurred in the under-20 age group (Table 4: 2 of 105 malignant tumors, 1.9%). Only four malignant tumors occurred under 20 years: two JGCT, one adult granulosa cell tumor and one immature cystic teratoma; no surface epithelial malignancies were seen under 20. The authors note this agrees with previous studies supporting the hypothesis that malignancy is related to older age; the study does not report JGCT stage, treatment or outcome.  Hospital pathology frequency study; JGCT provides only a count (2 cases, both under 20 years, classified malignant) within ovarian neoplasms of all ages. No clinical, molecular or outcome data.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor: 20 years' experience of a Tertiary Center.
author: Hamzaoğlu Canbolat K
text: Retrospective series of 5 JGCT patients (2000-2020, one center, Istanbul) after excluding 3 of 8 with missing records or follow-up; ages 9, 16, 16, 15 and 25; one premenarchal girl (age 9) without precocious puberty signs; none had high estradiol and none were obese (BMI 17.8-24). All had abdominal swelling and a unilateral adnexal mass without signs of metastasis; tumor sizes 14, 11, 24, 30 and 19 cm; CA-125 high in 3 (373, 44 and 135 U/mL as tabulated), serum AMH high (23 ng/mL, normal 0.05-11) in one patient; inhibin and calretinin positive in all. FIGO stage: 3 patients IA, 1 IC1 (intraoperative rupture), 1 IC2 (preoperative rupture with free fluid). All underwent fertility-preserving surgery; 2 patients received adjuvant chemotherapy. Histology: multiloculated cystic tumors with solid areas, no Call-Exner bodies in any, mitoses 7-44 per 10 HPF; one patient had focal striking atypia; pseudopapillary and trabecular patterns in one. Median follow-up 60 months (range 12-96); recurrence in 2/5 (40%): Patient 3 (stage IA) recurred at 12 months as a 10 cm mass in the contralateral ovary with final histology gynandroblastoma, treated with surgery plus 3 cycles paclitaxel-carboplatin, no evidence of disease at 49 months; Patient 5 (stage IC2, had 6 cycles cisplatin-etoposide) recurred at 48 months, resected, no evidence of disease at 12 months. All patients were in remission at last follow-up and none died of disease. Four patients had mitotic index above 10/10 HPF and 3 of them did not recur, so the authors saw no correlation between mitotic index and relapse; the only vimentin-positive patient recurred. Authors conclude JGCT should be considered in a young patient with a unilateral adnexal mass with benign features and that recurrence is not uncommon even though stage IA prognosis is good.  Small institutional series showing 2/5 recurrences (12 and 48 months), including one recurrence of stage IA disease, with all patients alive in remission.

title: Immunohistochemical markers of prognosis in adult granulosa cell tumors of the ovary - a review.
author: Jung D
text: Systematic PubMed review (409 English full-text results 1965-2021; 54 articles in total) of immunohistochemical prognostic markers in ovarian granulosa cell tumors; the title and focus are adult-type (AGCT), and JGCT is covered only where the primary studies included it. Background statements: GCT are 1-2% of ovarian neoplasms; AGCT is 90-95% of GCT; JGCT mostly affects younger patients (commonly before age 30); AGCT tend to recur late, even more than 10 to 20 years after diagnosis, whereas JGCT generally recur within a few years. JGCT-containing studies cited: King 1996 (2 JGCT among 40 GCT), Sakr 2017 (12 JGCT among 125), Costa 1995 (7 JGCT among 56), Staibano (11 JGCT among 30, ER-beta); the review notes that many studies did not separate AGCT from JGCT. FOXL2: in JGCT, where FOXL2 mutation is rare, strong FOXL2 immunoreactivity correlated with decreased disease-free and overall survival (D'Angelo); in AGCT, the mutation (70% in that study) and FOXL2 mRNA correlated with reduced DFS, but FOXL2 IHC did not. p53: in Staibano, 12/30 GCT overexpressed p53, with correlation to progression predominantly in JGCT; other studies were inconsistent and older p53 IHC interpretation is considered outdated. Estrogen receptor-beta: in 30 GCT (19 AGCT, 11 JGCT) loss of ER-beta was significantly associated with worse prognosis (Staibano); other studies found no ER-prognosis association. Across all markers the review concludes that only CD56, GATA-4 and SMAD3 showed prognostic value for worse outcome; ER, AMH and inhibin IHC were not prognostic; mitotic rate, Ki-67, p53, beta-catenin and HER2 results were inconsistent. The authors call for large multicenter studies with a clear distinction between AGCT and JGCT, and for national and international tumor registries. FOXL2 TP53 (p53 IHC) Adult-type focused review; relevant to JGCT for a few subtype-specific IHC statements (FOXL2, p53, ER-beta) and for documenting that most prognostic marker studies pool or exclude JGCT.

title: Therapeutic Management and Prognostic Factors for Ovarian Malignant Tumours in Adolescents: A Comprehensive Review of Current Guidelines.
author: Margioula-Siarkou C
text: Narrative review (search September 2022) comparing five guidelines on malignant ovarian tumors in children and adolescents: Centres Experts TMRG 2022 (France), BritSPAG 2018, ESMO 2018, ESGO-SIOPE 2020, EXPeRT/PARTNER 2021; 96 items screened, 5 guidelines included. Cited epidemiology: about 2.6 cases per 100,000 girls per year; 10-30% of ovarian masses in girls up to 17 are malignant; about 85% of preadolescent malignant ovarian masses are germ cell tumors, 8% epithelial, 5% sex cord-stromal and steroid cell tumors; adolescents mostly have juvenile granulosa cell, Sertoli and Sertoli-Leydig tumors. Diagnostics: ultrasound first, serum markers (beta-hCG, AFP, LDH, CA125) in all suspicious masses, hormonal profile if hormone production or precocious puberty; AMH and inhibin B may indicate granulosa cell tumors; immunohistochemistry (inhibin A, calretinin, SF1, FOXL2, WT1, CD99 and others) and DICER1 testing in suspected sex cord-stromal tumors; EXPeRT/PARTNER recommends FOXL2 to distinguish adult from juvenile granulosa cell tumors. Prognosis per ESMO: sex cord-stromal tumors generally have a better prognosis, with 20% relapsing or dying of metastatic cancer; advanced FIGO stage, intraperitoneal rupture and tumor size above 5 cm are adverse factors; only ESMO and ESGO-SIOPE give prognostic factor detail. Staging by FIGO 2014 with complete surgical staging; systematic lymphadenectomy not recommended in early sex cord-stromal tumors; total hysterectomy only in stage II+ (Centres Experts TMRG); omentectomy only if adhesions (EXPeRT/PARTNER); open approach preferred to avoid rupture. JGCT-specific chemotherapy recommendations: stage IA-IC1 with complete resection may avoid chemotherapy and IC2-IC3 requires it (Centres Experts TMRG, ESGO-SIOPE; text says potentially IC1 per ESMO; ESMO table entry lists stage IC chemotherapy recommended); EXPeRT/PARTNER recommends 3-4 cycles in stage IC. For advanced stages debulking is recommended by ESMO and Centres Experts TMRG but EXPeRT/PARTNER states it has no role apart from palliation and advises biopsy and upfront chemotherapy followed by delayed resection; 4 cycles in stages II-IV with second-look surgery if incomplete resection. Fertility: ovarian stimulation allowed only for stage IA granulosa-type tumors after multidisciplinary discussion and contraindicated above IA (Centres Experts TMRG); hormone replacement generally avoided in sex cord-stromal tumors except stage IA-IB granulosa-type; estrogen-containing contraceptives contraindicated for these tumors. Authors conclude there is substantial agreement among the guidelines but call for an international consensus. DICER1 Compares adolescent ovarian cancer guidelines; gives the stage-based chemotherapy thresholds for JGCT and sex cord-stromal management, but contains no primary JGCT patient data.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor in an adult woman during pregnancy: A case report and review of the literature.
author: Cummings M
text: 33-year-old G3P1 had an 8 cm left adnexal mass found on 22-week anatomy ultrasound (not seen at 14 weeks); an 11 cm solid mass at 4 days later was presumed a degenerating fibroid; MRI showed a 14.8 x 9.8 x 14.0 cm left ovarian mass with ascites and omental, cul-de-sac and probable paracolic implants. At 24 weeks she presented with an acute abdomen; inhibin A 426 pg/mL and inhibin B 2,593.8 pg/mL were markedly elevated, AFP 74.5 ng/mL and CA-125 269.6 U/mL elevated, with normal LDH, CEA and CA 19-9. Laparotomy: ruptured 15 cm left ovarian mass adherent to small bowel and transverse colon with metastases; left salpingo-oophorectomy, omental biopsy and small bowel resection achieved R0; omental biopsy negative and ascites nonmalignant. Pathology: JGCT with capsular rupture and surface involvement, lacking Call-Exner bodies, hyperchromatic nuclei without grooves, numerous mitoses, focal inhibin positivity; outside review confirmed FIGO stage IIIB. Adjuvant BEP was delayed to after delivery because of fetal toxicity concerns, with monthly MRI surveillance; no progression during pregnancy; induction at 37 weeks and uncomplicated vaginal delivery; 3 cycles of BEP started 6 weeks postpartum. Inhibin A and B remained normal, menses resumed, and there was no recurrence at last contact over 5 years after initial presentation. Authors' literature statements: JGCT average age 13 years and 3% over 30; about 90% stage I; in Young et al. (125 cases) 94 stage IAI, 15 IAII, 2 IB, 10 IC, 2 IIB, 1 IIC with 6 of 7 deaths in stage IAII or higher and 0% one-year survival for IIB and IIC; two other pregnancy cases cited had no evidence of disease at 9 months to 7 years. Authors conclude shared decision making should guide chemotherapy timing in pregnancy and that large adnexal masses be removed in the second or third trimester.  Advanced-stage (IIIB) JGCT in an adult during pregnancy with long survival after surgery and delayed BEP; supports inhibin A/B as markers.

title: How social media can help to understand treatment experiences of survivors of rare cancers: Findings from the Granulosa Cell Tumor Survivor Sisters Facebook group member survey.
author: White VM
text: Self-report survey (43 items; 2014-2019) of members of the closed Granulosa Cell Tumor-Survivor Sisters Facebook group: 743 analyzed respondents (691 adult-type, 52 juvenile-type); 11 surveys were completed for a person aged 16 or younger, generally by a family member. Mean time since diagnosis 4.4 years (SD 5.9; median 2; range 0-38), with no significant difference between aGCT and jGCT. jGCT age at diagnosis (Table 1): 15.4% aged 0-12, 17.3% 13-19, 21.2% 20-29, 23.1% 30-39, 9.6% 40-49, 1.9% 50-59, 11.5% missing; authors note 50% diagnosed before 30 but a number diagnosed later. All jGCT respondents were premenopausal at diagnosis. jGCT stage at diagnosis (self-reported FIGO): IA 34.6%, IC 32.7%, IIA 1.9%, IIC 5.8%, III 9.6%, IV 0%, missing/unknown 15.3%. Tumors were larger in jGCT: 57.7% >=8.5 cm vs 19.2% <8.5 cm (p=.015 vs aGCT). jGCT treatment: 56% open surgery; less hysterectomy (13% vs 42%) and bilateral oophorectomy (8% vs 43%) than aGCT; 13 jGCT respondents had chemotherapy. Recurrence: 25% of jGCT (n=13) reported recurrent disease; 50% of recurrent jGCT recurred within 12 months of diagnosis versus 11% of recurrent aGCT (p<.01). The authors state there is little information on jGCT recurrence and that only about 50 jGCT respondents limit conclusions. In aGCT (not jGCT-specific), recurrence was higher with tumor rupture (p<.001) or cutting (p=.01) than with an encapsulated tumor, and with later stage; 30% of aGCT reported recurrence overall. Follow-up among non-recurrent respondents: inhibin A&B monitored in 60%, inhibin B 26%, CA-125 33%; scans 51%; few reported AMH monitoring. Authors conclude this is one of the largest treatment surveys of GCT and that treatment patterns are in line with clinical audits; they caution about self-report, selection and survival bias.  Patient self-report survey of aGCT and jGCT; 52 jGCT respondents give a patient-reported view of age, stage, tumor size, surgery and early recurrence in jGCT. Not verified against medical records.

title: ERβ in Granulosa Cell Tumors and Its Clinical Potential.
author: Birgersson M
text: Narrative review of ERbeta (ESR2) in granulosa cell tumors; GCT incidence 0.47 to 0.74 per 100,000 worldwide, under 5% of ovarian cancers; more than 90% are adult type, JGCT 3-10% of cases and mainly affects prepubertal girls and young women. Prognosis in GCT overall: 5-year survival about 95% at stage I, 55-75% at stage II and 22-50% at stage III (cited); stage is the best prognostic marker; recurrence rates 10-65% with mortality as high as 80% after relapse, but relapses 'appear specific to AGCTs' and JGCTs recur only in rare cases (cited). FOXL2 402C>G (C134W) is found in about 95% of adult GCTs and very rarely in JGCTs; reduced or absent wild-type FOXL2 expression has been associated with a more aggressive JGCT course, suggesting a tumor suppressor role for wild-type FOXL2. Genetic associations specifically with JGCT: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11), Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome (IDH1/2). TERT promoter C228T is more frequent in recurrent GCTs; KMT2D, TP53, WNK2, PIK3R1, CDK1 mutations in subsets (mainly adult). Testicular GCT is about 0.5% of male sex cord-stromal tumors; unlike the ovary, the juvenile subtype is more prevalent than the adult; most juvenile tumors are diagnosed below 6 months of age, often benign and rarely metastasizing. ERbeta is highly expressed in most GCTs (4 of 5, 80%, adult GCTs with a validated antibody in the authors' earlier work); the review notes that the fraction in JGCT versus AGCT is not established, that selective ERbeta antagonists have not been explored in GCT, and that estrogen ablation to prevent recurrence may not be relevant in JGCT given its rare recurrence. The authors state that juvenile and adult GCT may need to be treated as two entirely different cancers. FOXL2 STK11 IDH1/2 Review covering GCT biology; JGCT content includes epidemiology, wild-type FOXL2, syndrome associations, low recurrence and the testicular juvenile subtype, with ERbeta data mostly from adult tumors. No original patients.

title: Reclassification of two germline DICER1 splicing variants leads to DICER1 syndrome diagnosis.
author: Apellaniz-Ruiz M
text: Report of two unrelated teenage girls (13 and 15 years) with thyroid follicular nodular disease and ovarian tumors; both had DICER1 somatic RNase IIIb hotspot mutations and no coding germline DICER1 pathogenic variant, but germline intronic splice variants (c.5365-4A>G, c.5527+3A>G) that skip exon 25 on RNA assays and were classified likely pathogenic under ClinGen DICER1 rules. Case 2 had an emergency operation for ovarian torsion at age 5; the right ovarian mass was diagnosed as juvenile granulosa cell tumor (inhibin positive, calretinin negative) and treated with oophorectomy and two cycles of MAKEI-protocol chemotherapy. At age 15, expert gynecological pathology review of that tumor found lobulated architecture with slit-like spaces, bland epithelioid cells, focal inhibin positivity and no heterologous elements, and reclassified it as retiform Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor. The retiform SLCT carried the somatic DICER1 hotspot p.E1813D; the girl later developed intracerebral hemorrhages and a DICER1-mutant primary intracranial sarcoma (somatic NF1 and TP53 variants) and died at 16. Case 1 had a poorly differentiated SLCT (7.5 cm, hyperandrogenism, inhibin focally positive) treated with surgery and 4 cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin and remained in remission. Authors conclude that expert histopathological review is essential in atypical presentations and that DICER1 testing should follow rare DICER1-associated tumors, noting that overlapping sex cord-stromal morphology complicates diagnosis, as in case 2's initial JGCT diagnosis. DICER1 DICER1 Illustrates that a childhood ovarian tumor labelled JGCT (age 5, torsion) was reclassified as retiform SLCT in the context of DICER1 syndrome; relevant to differential diagnosis and to considering DICER1 testing. No confirmed JGCT.

title: Ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumors with Ollier's disease in children with IDH1 gene somatic mutation.
author: Zhang J
text: A 4-year-old girl with Ollier's disease (multiple lytic lesions of the right femur, tibia, fibula, left ulna, radius and phalanges; wide resection of a distal right femur lesion confirmed enchondroma) developed bilateral Tanner III breast development, labial hypertrophy and vulvar discharge about 9 months later. Estradiol was 1,211 pmol/L (reference <=115.6) and prolactin 43.99 ng/ml (3.3-24.1); ultrasound showed an 81 x 76 x 57 mm well-encapsulated multilocular-solid right ovarian tumor and CT showed a right ovarian solid mass; right salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. Histology showed juvenile granulosa cell tumor, FIGO stage IA; IHC: vimentin +, AE1/AE3 weak +, CD117 scattered +, PR +, CD99 +, alpha-inhibin single +, CD56 +, SMA +, Ki67 about 30%; negative for CK7, EMA, ER, CD30, PLAP, SALL4, OCT3/4, hCG, CK8, desmin and S-100. Whole-exome and Sanger sequencing found a somatic IDH1 c.394C>T (p.Arg132Cys) mutation in both the ovarian JGCT and the enchondroma but not in blood, skin, muscle, oral mucosa or the parents' blood. In HeLa cells, IDH1 R132C (3.77-fold overexpression) versus wild type (4.46-fold) reduced phosphorylation of S6 ribosomal protein, interpreted as an effect on the mTOR pathway; the regulatory mechanism was not defined. After surgery estradiol (70.83 pmol/L) and prolactin (20.54 ng/ml) normalized within 1 week, breasts regressed, no recurrence at 3 months, and hormones remained normal to 2 years of follow-up. The authors tabulated 10 prior published cases of JGCT with Ollier's disease (JGCT age 0.5 to 36 years; 8 salpingo-oophorectomies, 2 with postoperative chemotherapy; follow-up 6 months to 7 years without recurrence; 2 cases had chondrosarcoma transformation) and, with their case, 11 cases. The authors propose generalized mesodermal dysplasia with IDH1 somatic mutation as a contributor and recommend regular follow-up; they state this is the first report of gene testing among reported JGCT with Ollier's disease. IDH1 First reported IDH1 R132C somatic mutation shared by an ovarian JGCT and Ollier's enchondroma; links the two entities and provides a review table of 11 cases.

title: Ovarian Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor Case Report.
author: Lemmons J
text: A 5-month-old girl presented to the emergency department with 4 days of worsening abdominal distention and 1 day of postprandial projectile non-bloody non-bilious emesis; outside work-up showed anemia, leukocytosis and hyponatremia. Point-of-care FAST ultrasound showed extensive heterogeneous free fluid (Morison's pouch, subphrenic space, splenorenal recess) and a large heterogeneous pelvic mass. CT showed large-volume ascites with centralized bowel loops and a 6.4 x 6.8 x 10.9 cm midline pelvic mass. At laparotomy 500 mL of serosanguinous fluid was drained and a left salpingo-oophorectomy removed an actively bleeding tumor (described as arising from the left fallopian tube) with a ruptured tumor found; she was transfused and pathology showed juvenile granulosa cell tumor. No tumor markers, hormone levels, immunohistochemistry, stage, or post-discharge follow-up are reported. The discussion states JGCT presents as acute abdomen from rupture in about 6-10% of cases, there is no specific tumor marker though inhibin is elevated in adult and juvenile GCT, early-stage 5-year survival is 90-95%, adjuvant chemotherapy has not been found useful in early stages, and late recurrences require long-term follow-up (authors' literature statements).  Infant ovarian JGCT presenting as an acute abdomen with massive ascites and tumor rupture, recognized by bedside ultrasound; illustrates the rupture presentation.

title: Mixed sex cord-stromal tumor (gynandroblastoma) with malignant morphology involving both ovaries: a case report.
author: Maraqa B
text: A 15-year-old girl presented with left abdominal pain, prolonged menstrual bleeding and hirsutism; history of left nephrectomy at age 1 year for a reportedly benign mass; a first-degree relative had metastatic breast cancer at age 30. Ultrasound and CT showed a large left ovarian mass; left salpingo-oophorectomy removed an 18 x 14 x 7 cm tumor with nodular/diffuse growth, macro- and microfollicles with eosinophilic secretions; cells positive for SF-1 and inhibin, focally CK positive, SALL4 negative, membranous beta-catenin; diagnosed as juvenile granulosa cell tumor. One year later a 4.5 cm right ovarian mass was found on follow-up ultrasound; serum inhibin and AMH were negative; right salpingo-oophorectomy showed poorly differentiated spindle/polygonal Sertoli cells with fewer Leydig cells, focal tubules, cystic follicles, necrosis and mitotic rate of 20 per 10 HPF (positive SF-1, membranous beta-catenin, alpha-inhibin, calretinin; negative SALL4, CK7, EMA). Comparison with the first tumor showed areas with tubules and cords of Sertoli cells, so the authors concluded both tumors were related and most likely a gynandroblastoma (mixed sex cord-stromal tumor with juvenile GCT component and poorly differentiated Sertoli-Leydig component). The patient had oocyte cryopreservation and carboplatin/paclitaxel chemotherapy with no evidence of recurrence after 2 years; genetic testing found a pathogenic germline DICER1 variant (c.3094-2_3096del), and she developed multinodular goiter during follow-up; the childhood nephrectomy was thought probably DICER1-related. The authors state that juvenile GCT is about 5% of GCT but about 90% of GCT in prepubertal and under-30 patients, secretes estrogen causing precocious puberty in about 80%, and lacks FOXL2 mutation; they found no prior report of bilateral involvement by gynandroblastoma with a JGCT component and suggest the grade of the Sertoli-Leydig component may drive prognosis. DICER1 Documents JGCT morphology within a gynandroblastoma in a DICER1 germline carrier, with metachronous contralateral recurrence as poorly differentiated Sertoli-Leydig tumor, supporting DICER1 testing in JGCT-like tumors with mixed morphology.

title: Ovarian Masses in Children and Adolescents: A Review of the Literature with Emphasis on the Diagnostic Approach.
author: Birbas E
text: Review of paediatric ovarian masses; the JGCT section states that JGCT is a malignant pure sex cord tumour of primitive granulosa cells growing in solid and follicular patterns. JGCT accounts for 5% of granulosa cell tumours and 70% of all sex-cord stromal tumours in patients under 20 years; sex-cord stromal tumours are 10-20% of paediatric ovarian neoplasms; mean age at diagnosis is 13 years. Young et al. (cited) studied 125 JGCT patients: 44% occurred in the first and 34% in the second decade of life. JGCT is associated with Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome (enchondromatosis); listed in the review's table of cancer predisposition syndromes. JGCT typically secretes estrogens; granulosa cells produce inhibin, so serum inhibin is described as a useful tumour marker for diagnosis and follow-up (Table 2: inhibin - JGCT). Imaging is heterogeneous and nonspecific: typically large, mostly solid and cystic, may be entirely solid or cystic; hemorrhage, necrosis, fibrosis common; sponge-like T2 MRI appearance; T1-hyperintense hemorrhagic foci in cysts; endometrial thickening and uterine enlargement from estrogen. Review states prognosis is favorable, late recurrences are rare, most patients have stage-limited-to-ovary disease with survival over 90% with surgery alone; rare advanced cases have poorer prognosis and may require chemotherapy. General recommendation: management of paediatric ovarian masses should be curative, function-preserving and minimally invasive, in specialized centres; the review notes 46-54% of benign lesions undergo oophorectomy.  Broad review of paediatric ovarian masses; JGCT is covered in one subsection (3.3.1) and in the marker and predisposition tables. No new JGCT patient data.

title: Early-onset gynecological tumors in DNA repair-deficient xeroderma pigmentosum group C patients: a case series.
author: Yurchenko AA
text: Case series of 5 early-onset gynecological tumors in 4 patients with xeroderma pigmentosum group C (XP-C), aged 11 to 19 years: vaginal embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma in monozygotic twins (16 years), a JGCT plus a poorly differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (SLCT) in a 19-year-old, and a stage IC1 SLCT in an 11-year-old (aged 13 at reporting). JGCT patient (patient 3): 19-year-old with XP-C (homozygous XPC delTG, diagnosed at age 3, a few skin carcinomas) referred for ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome; an 11 cm rapidly growing left ovarian tumor, ruptured preoperatively; left adnexectomy; expert pathology: JGCT, partially ruptured, peritoneal cytology negative but tumor cells on the tubal serosa; stage reported as FIGO IC2. Adjuvant chemotherapy, theoretically indicated for IC2 JGCT, was declined because of the increased risk of adverse events in XP-C; restaging laparoscopy found no tumor on all biopsies, but hypercortisolism persisted 3 months after surgery. MRI then showed a 2.5 cm right ovarian mass and a micronodular left adrenal gland; right adnexectomy and left adrenalectomy showed a poorly differentiated stage IA SLCT of the right ovary (independent second ovarian tumor) and primary pigmented nodular adrenal dysplasia; Cushing's syndrome improved. At 9 months an MRI showed a bulky pelvic tumor; laparotomy with complete removal needing colorectal resection confirmed JGCT recurrence; treated with weekly paclitaxel x4 then paclitaxel 175 mg/m2 every 3 weeks x3 without serious adverse events; table lists progression after 4 cycles; alive, total follow-up 9 months. Whole-genome sequencing of the JGCT and the SLCT from patient 3: DICER1 oncogenic or likely oncogenic mutations in all four sequenced tumors of the series (biallelic in 2); TP53 mutated in the vaginal ERMS and in patient 3's SLCT; the JGCT and SLCT genomes were relatively stable without polyploidization. XP-C ovarian tumors (n=3) had 4.4-fold higher single-base-substitution density than sporadic ovarian granulosa cell tumors (n=45; P=0.00046) and 1.7-fold more indels (P=0.041), with SBS8 explaining 67-77% of mutations (vs 0-38% in sporadic tumors) and strong transcriptional strand bias. Authors' conclusion: XP-C status should be accounted for in prevention and treatment of gynecological tumors in young XP patients; regular gynecologic follow-up is suggested; a literature search found 11 earlier reports of gynecological tumors in XP patients (median age 18.5 years). DICER1 XPC Single JGCT case with whole-genome data in a DNA-repair-deficient host: reports a somatic DICER1 mutation in a JGCT and a recurrence managed without upfront chemotherapy. Not representative of sporadic JGCT.

title: Biallelic MAD2L1BP (p31comet) mutation is associated with mosaic aneuploidy and juvenile granulosa cell tumors.
author: Abdel-Salam GMH
text: Two siblings of consanguineous Egyptian parents carried a homozygous MAD2L1BP nonsense variant R253* (c.757C>T); the sister (patient 1a) had a left ovarian JGCT treated by surgery at 14 months and the brother (patient 1b) had a left testicular JGCT treated by radical orchiectomy at 11 months. Patient 1a received tamoxifen for 12 months after surgery and has been in complete remission since; she also had microcephaly, brain cysts, dysgyria/polymicrogyria, IQ 56 and generalized tonic-clonic seizures from age 5.5 years. Patient 1b had microcephaly with less pronounced brain abnormalities and normal psychomotor development. Testicular JGCT of patient 1b: macrofollicular pattern with cysts, progesterone receptor positive, diffuse S100, faint estrogen receptor, patchy inhibin. The ovarian JGCT of patient 1a showed macrofollicular architecture on H&E with reticulin and PAS staining typical for JGCT. Cultured lymphocytes and fibroblasts of both siblings showed high-grade mosaic variegated aneuploidy; parents and healthy sisters did not. A third patient (family 2, Saudi Arabia) with homozygous R227* had 10% aneuploid cells (200 metaphases reanalyzed), severe epileptic encephalopathy, elevated blood glucose and died at 23 months; he had no tumor. Tumor WES of both JGCTs (FFPE, variants filtered to allele frequency >=5%) showed low tumor mutational burden, microsatellite stability, no mutational signature indicating a DNA repair defect, and no oncogenic alteration in patient 1b; patient 1a had only a very-low-frequency NF1 splice-region variant. No MAD2L1BP mutations were found in 23 unrelated patients with sporadic JGCT (22 ovarian, 1 testicular; age at diagnosis 1 month to 22 years; no familial JGCT). Functionally, R253* leads to partial nonsense-mediated decay and a truncated p31comet with half-life of about 15 minutes (reduced by more than 80% in fibroblasts); truncated p31comet could not bind Trip13, was defective in Mad2 and Rev7 binding, could not support spindle assembly checkpoint silencing or homology-directed repair, and lost its interaction with tp53. Patient fibroblasts proliferated slower and were more resistant to paclitaxel and slightly to etoposide. In p31comet immunostaining, patient 1b's testicular JGCT showed faint nuclear expression in <5% of tumor cells versus about 50% in a reference testicular JGCT. The authors conclude that biallelic germline MAD2L1BP mutations predispose to the (usually sporadic) infantile JGCT in both sexes, probably through high-grade aneuploidy, possibly with the impaired p31comet-tp53 interaction; they note no tumor history in heterozygous carriers' families and no increased mutational rate. MAD2L1BP MAD2L1BP MAD2L1BP NF1 Describes the first germline genetic cause (biallelic MAD2L1BP loss of function with mosaic variegated aneuploidy) of familial JGCT affecting both ovary and testis; sporadic JGCT lacked MAD2L1BP mutations.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor in a transgender male with Ollier disease: A case report.
author: Ing BI
text: 34-year-old transgender man (G0) with Ollier disease (history of low-grade chondrosarcoma 2011, right below-knee amputation) on testosterone since February 2016 (200 mg IM every 2 weeks for ~5 years, then 160 mg subcutaneously) presented with 1 month of left lower quadrant pain, early satiety and bloating. Labs: CA-125 198 U/mL, LDH 426 U/L, inhibin A 473 pg/mL, inhibin B 23,419 pg/mL; hormone levels at presentation not obtained (last testosterone 567 ng/dL in 5/2022). CT: 15 cm cystic and solid right ovarian mass, 4.9 cm uterine fibroid, endometrial thickness 1.4 cm, omental stranding, trace right pleural effusion and 1.5 cm pleural nodule; ultrasound 20 cm right adnexal mass; Pap smear HPV 16 positive with atypical endometrial cells; endometrial biopsy non-atypical hyperplasia. Surgery: laparotomy, total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy with optimal cytoreduction; right ovarian mass 3340 g; pathology stage IA JGCT confined to right ovary, omentum negative; focal atypical endometrial hyperplasia in uterus. IHC on tumor: estrogen receptor 40% weak-moderate, progesterone receptor 90% moderate-strong, androgen receptor >90% strong. The pleural nodule regressed spontaneously before planned biopsy; no adjuvant therapy; surveillance by inhibin A and B every 3 months in year 1, every 4 months year 2, every 6 months year 3, then annually. Authors discuss association of Ollier disease with granulosa cell tumors (proposed generalized mesodermal dysplasia; IDH1 mutation reported in both enchondroma and JGCT in cited studies; not tested here) and ask whether testosterone therapy contributed to tumor growth; they recommended stopping testosterone for now and suggest pre-screening for hormonally responsive conditions in patients on hormone therapy.  Rare report of JGCT in an adult on long-term testosterone with Ollier disease, relevant to tumor hormone-receptor expression and to the link between enchondromatosis and granulosa cell tumors.

title: Relevance of Molecular Pathology for the Diagnosis of Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors of the Ovary: A Narrative Review.
author: Trecourt A
text: Narrative review (literature searched July-October 2023, PubMed Central and Google Scholar) of ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors organized by predominant cell morphology into five groups, with diagnostic algorithms; sex cord-stromal tumors are about 8% of ovarian tumors. JGCT is described as a very rare pure sex cord neoplasm, 5% of all ovarian granulosa cell tumors (adult type 95%); mean age 13 years, under 30 years in 97%, range newborn to 67 years. Clinical features: pelvic mass symptoms plus estrogenic manifestations (isosexual pseudoprecocity in 82% of prepubertal patients), rarely androgenic; rare associations with Ollier disease, Maffucci syndrome, DICER1 syndrome, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and tuberous sclerosis. Over 97% unilateral, mean size 12.5 cm (3-32 cm), solid and cystic or predominantly solid, necrosis/hemorrhage in 13%. Histology: diffuse, lobulated, follicle-like architecture in a myxoid/edematous/hyalinized background; abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm; nuclei usually lack grooves (grooves focally in about 50%); mitoses 1 to 32 per 10 HPF (mean 7), higher than adult GCT; necrosis in 40%; sclerosis in 95% of JGCT. Reticulin surrounds nests/cords, with monocellular network in thecomatous areas. Immunohistochemistry: SF1, inhibin, calretinin, WT1 and FOXL2 positive as in adult GCT; AE1/AE3 may be expressed; EMA typically negative. IHC cannot separate juvenile from adult GCT. Molecular: no FOXL2 variant; DICER1 variants in 6-23%, AKT1 activating variants in 29-60%, GNAS in 30%; recurrent KMT2C 52%, ARID1A 39%, KMT2D 35%, BRCA2 35%, ATM 26%, BRCA1 23%, POLE 23%, MLH1 19%, MSH6 10%, TERT variant 19% and rearrangement 13%, TP53 up to 16%; IDH1/2 in Ollier/Maffucci-associated cases. DICER1 and GNAS variants could worsen prognosis, but the authors state more data are needed. Differentials: luteinized JGCT versus steroid cell tumor, thecoma, sclerosing stromal tumor; FOXL2 variant favors luteinized adult GCT, DICER1 variant favors luteinized JGCT or Sertoli-Leydig tumor; small cell carcinoma of the ovary hypercalcemic type (young patients, brisk mitoses, pseudo-follicles) should be excluded with EMA and BRG1 (SMARCA4 surrogate). The authors suggest JGCT may be a distinct entity from adult GCT given different molecular alterations; DICER1 variant found in 6% of JGCT, 63-80% of Sertoli-Leydig tumors, 40% of gynandroblastomas (cited figures); DICER1 testing is not recommended to distinguish Sertoli-Leydig tumor from JGCT or gynandroblastoma. Gynandroblastoma shows no AKT1 variant in juvenile-type components. DICER1 AKT1 GNAS KMT2C/ARID1A/KMT2D BRCA2/ATM/BRCA1 POLE/MLH1/MSH6 TERT TP53 IDH1/IDH2 FOXL2 Pathology-oriented review with a dedicated JGCT section covering clinical, morphological, immunohistochemical and molecular features and the differential diagnosis against other ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors; reports no original patients.

title: Ovarian steroid cell tumors: what do we know so far?
author: Wei CH
text: Narrative review of ovarian steroid cell tumors (SCT), a rare sex cord-stromal tumor (fewer than a thousand cases reported); JGCT is not the subject. In the molecular section the authors contrast SCT, which lacks pathognomonic recurrent mutations, with other sex cord-stromal tumors: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors (DICER1 mutation in 60% in one series), SCTAT/Sertoli cell tumors (STK11 in Peutz-Jeghers), adult granulosa cell tumor (recurrent somatic FOXL2 mutation in over 95%). For JGCT the review states that it may occur in the setting of Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome, or somatic mosaic mutations in IDH1 and IDH2, and somatic copy number changes in AKT. Other JGCT-relevant mention: the review states sex cord-stromal tumors found during pregnancy include granulosa cell tumor (22%), but does not distinguish juvenile from adult type; paediatric SCT may present with isosexual precocious puberty and be misdiagnosed as congenital adrenal hyperplasia. IDH1/IDH2 AKT Peripheral: a steroid cell tumor review whose only JGCT-specific content is one sentence on genetic associations (Ollier/Maffucci, IDH1/IDH2 mosaicism, AKT copy number change).

title: A clinicopathological study about the epidemiology of granulosa cell tumors in Lebanon.
author: Yaacoub S
text: Retrospective single-center (National Institute of Pathology, Beirut) study of 65 consecutive ovarian granulosa cell tumors (GCT) referred from Lebanese hospitals January 2000 to January 2020; 6 (9.2%) juvenile and 59 (90.8%) adult type. Calculated GCT incidence 16.2 per million per year (authors describe this as upper end of international range). JGCT group (n=6): mean age 21 years (adult group 60); high tumor size >10 cm in 4/6 (66.7%) versus 20/59 (33.9%) adults; high mitotic index 1/6; grooved nuclei 1/6; Call-Exner bodies 1/6; microfollicular 3/6, macrofollicular 1/6, trabecular 1/6, insular 1/6. Authors report significant association of JGCT with young age and large size (p<0.05). Recurrence: 13/65 (20%) overall, 12 adult and 1 JGCT (1/6, 16.7%); recurrence not significantly related to type (p=0.09); recurrent cases were stage 3 (6) or 4 (6) except one stage 2, and had high mitotic index (10/13) and tumor size >10 cm (12/13). Stage was known for only 35 patients because of loss to follow-up; stage was not reported separately for JGCT. Immunohistochemistry (tests performed varied): inhibin positive 30/40 overall with 3 JGCT positive and 2 negative; calretinin 18/23 overall, JGCT 2 positive; cytokeratin 10/20, JGCT 1 positive and 1 negative; CD99 19/23, JGCT 2 positive; vimentin 18/18, JGCT 2 positive. FOXL2 testing was not performed because it is not covered by payers in Lebanon; authors suggest some tumors may be classified as GCT by default and possibly over-diagnosed. Authors conclude older age, high mitotic index, large size and advanced stage predict recurrence, and call for FOXL2 access and further Mediterranean epidemiology; JGCT conclusions rest on 6 patients.  Epidemiology and pathology series of ovarian granulosa cell tumors in Lebanon; JGCT is a 6-patient subgroup with age, size, histology and immunohistochemistry compared against adult-type tumors.

title: Vaginal bleeding imitated rape in a 6-year old girl, a case report about granulosa cell tumor as a reason of peripheral precocious puberty.
author: Amirkashani D
text: A 6-year-old girl admitted with 5 days of abdominal distension, lower abdominal pain, nausea and mild fever; blood stains in underwear prompted a forensic consultation for suspected abuse, but thelarche pointed to an endocrine cause. Ultrasound: multilocular-solid right-sided mass about 63 x 40 mm; CT: solid-cystic pelvic mass 122 x 106 mm. Hormones: estradiol 115 pg/mL (normal under 9), FSH under 0.55, LH under 0.10, androstenedione 5.8, AMH 1322 pmol/L (normal 0.1-38.6), inhibin A 291 pg/mL (normal under 4.7), inhibin B 956 pg/mL (normal under 111), AFP and beta-hCG normal. Right salpingo-oophorectomy; the opposite ovary and uterus were preserved. Specimen 11.5 x 8 x 2 cm multilocular cyst with thin septa and intact capsule; microscopy showed granulosa cells lining the cyst with microfollicles resembling Call-Exner bodies; inhibin and calretinin positive. All hormones returned to normal prepubertal levels two weeks after surgery; the authors suggest inhibin and hormone monitoring as tumor markers, with follow-up every 3 months in an endocrine clinic and pelvic ultrasound and labs at least every 6 months. The authors write that the microscopic characteristics were highly compatible with adult-type GCT and that assigning type by age range is not reliable; no association syndromes were present.  Prepubertal granulosa cell tumor with peripheral precocious puberty and markedly elevated AMH and inhibins that normalized after surgery; histologic subtype is ambiguous.

title: Clinicopathological features and surgical procedures of adnexal masses with abdominal pain in pediatric and adolescent patients.
author: Liu Q
text: Retrospective Peking Union Medical College Hospital cohort (2012-2019) of 212 pediatric and adolescent patients with an adnexal mass and abdominal pain; torsion in 78 (36.8%). Sex cord-stromal tumors were 7 of 212 (3.3%): 4 juvenile granulosa cell tumors, 1 malignant steroid cell tumor and 2 moderately differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors. The text states juvenile granulosa tumors and malignant steroid cell tumors received adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery; regimens, stages and outcomes are not given per tumor type. Among 14 complex lesions suspected malignant on ultrasound, 6 were malignant germ cell tumors and 3 were sex cord-stromal tumors. Table 4 lists one granulosa cell tumor in the torsion group managed by adnexectomy with omentum resection and biopsy. Malignant germ cell tumors (8/212) were treated with 3-6 cycles of PEB/PEV; tumor markers were elevated in 26 of 105 patients tested. Factors associated with torsion on multivariate analysis were mass over 5 cm (OR 4.134), acute onset pain (OR 15.911) and persistent or recurrent pain (OR 24.150).  Only a count of JGCT (4 of 212 patients with painful adnexal masses) and a statement of adjuvant chemotherapy; no JGCT outcomes. Useful as hospital-series frequency data for a Chinese pediatric gynecology center.

title: Granulosa cell tumor of the ovary: a series of 6 cases.
author: da Costa REAR
text: Retrospective chart review of 6 GCT patients (2011-2022) from a private oncology clinic in Teresina, Brazil: 5 adult-type and 1 juvenile; mean age 47 years; mean tumor size 11 cm; 5 stage Ia and 1 stage III. JGCT case (case 1): a 13-year-old (post-pubertal) with an 8 cm right ovarian mass, stage Ia; MRI showed an 8 cm right adnexal lesion with neoplastic appearance. JGCT immunohistochemistry: positive for cytokeratin, calretinin, Melan-A/Mart-1 and vimentin; negative for EMA, CD99, inhibin and WT-1 (the adult-type case 5 was FOXL2, calretinin, inhibin and WT1 positive). JGCT treatment: unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with contralateral ovarian biopsy and peritoneal lavage cytology; alive without disease at 58 months. Inhibin B was measured in 4 patients including case 1 and was not elevated in any; AMH was not measured. The one death was the stage III adult-type patient (suboptimal cytoreduction), who died of progression at 126 months; overall 5/6 (83%) alive and free of disease at mean follow-up of 62.7 months. Authors' discussion (literature, not series results): 80% of juvenile-type cases occur before age 20 and 45.5% before puberty; JGCT typically symptomatic, with precocious puberty from estrogen secretion; fertility-sparing surgery in JGCT is described as associated with higher recurrence odds if staging is inadequate.  A single post-pubertal JGCT case (13 years, stage Ia) with unusual IHC (inhibin negative) in a mostly adult GCT series.

title: Unusual radiologic imaging in juvenile granulosa cell tumor with precocious puberty: A unilocular cyst.
author: Afriliani N
text: 2-year-2-month-old girl with vaginal bleeding (first episode at 4 days, attributed to maternal hormones; recurrence 1 week before admission), breast enlargement from age 1 year and abdominal enlargement; weight 15 kg, height 86 cm; bone age (Greulich and Pyle) 3 years 6 months. Labs: prolactin 54.41 ng/mL, estradiol 120 pg/mL, LDH 328.5 U/L, CA-125 39.6 mIU/mL, low FSH 0.045 mIU/mL; LH, thyroid function, beta-hCG, AFP and CEA normal, indicating peripheral rather than central precocity. Ultrasound: single unilocular anechoic cyst, septa-free, with posterior enhancement and no visible solid component, about 10.1 x 4.76 x 9.8 cm extending from pelvis to abdomen. MRI: right ovarian cyst about 5.2 x 10.9 x 11.8 cm with an enhancing solid mural component up to about 1.01 cm, right hydroureter and mild pelviocaliceal ectasia, and enlarged uterus. Laparoscopic right ovariectomy after decompression; FIGO stage IA; no additional treatment. Pathology: sex cord-stromal tumor with high mitotic activity (20/10 HPF); IHC positive for inhibin, calretinin and WT-1, negative for CK and CD10, consistent with JGCT. Authors conclude imaging of JGCT is nonspecific, unilocular purely cystic presentation is rare, and histopathology with IHC remains mandatory for diagnosis. Authors cite from literature: JGCT about 5% of GCTs, average age 13 years, about 82% of prepubertal patients present with early puberty signs, JGCT cystic 14%, solid 37%, solid and cystic 45%, and about 90% 10-year survival with late recurrence possible 10-20 years later.  Rare unilocular cystic JGCT in a toddler, with peripheral precocious puberty and prolactin elevation; reviews imaging patterns.

title: The role of stathmin expression in the differential diagnosis, prognosis, and potential treatment of ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors.
author: Šafanda A
text: Tissue-microarray immunohistochemistry (clone EP247) in 390 ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors: 281 adult GCT, 5 JGCT, 33 Sertoli-Leydig tumors, 50 fibromas/thecomas, 11 Leydig/steroid cell tumors, 5 SCST-NOS, 3 Sertoli cell tumors, 2 sclerosing stromal tumors. All 5 JGCTs expressed stathmin diffusely and strongly (>50% of cells in 5/5; overall positivity 90-100%, mean 98 +/- 4; H-score median 280, mean 257.8 +/- 42), the same as adult GCT (281/281). JGCT patients: median age 26 years (range 21-43), mean 30 +/- 11.5; FIGO stage I in 2 cases and not available in 3; survival, disease status and recurrence data were not available for any of the 5 JGCTs. Negative cases (<5% positive) occurred only in fibroma/thecoma (12/50, 24%) and Leydig/steroid cell tumors (7/11, 64%); expression did not correlate with recurrence or FIGO stage and was not prognostic in adult GCT (the only group with enough clinical data). ROC analysis separated adult GCT from fibroma/thecoma (H-score cut-off 180, AUC 0.915, sensitivity 0.889, specificity 0.803), but the authors conclude stathmin has limited diagnostic value since morphology and molecular testing are more practical, and that it is not a prognostic marker; they speculate that lowering stathmin could increase taxane sensitivity (hypothesis, not tested). STMN1 (stathmin protein) Immunohistochemistry of 5 JGCTs within a large sex cord-stromal series: uniform strong stathmin expression, so no discriminatory value against adult GCT; no clinical outcomes for JGCT.

title: Update on Recommendations for Cancer Screening and Surveillance in Children with Genomic Instability Disorders.
author: Nakano Y
text: This is a review of the 2023 AACR Childhood Cancer Predisposition Workshop update on cancer screening and surveillance for children with recessive genomic instability disorders (ataxia telangiectasia, Nijmegen breakage syndrome, Bloom syndrome, Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, telomere biology disorders, Fanconi anemia, xeroderma pigmentosum, mosaic variegated aneuploidy); it is not specific to JGCT.
