The only JGCT-specific statement is in the mosaic variegated aneuploidy section: two siblings of consanguineous parents with biallelic mutations in MAD2L1B (as printed in the text) developed juvenile granulosa cell tumors of the ovary and testis, respectively, while a third unrelated affected individual did not develop cancer and other modifying genetic cancer risk factors in the siblings cannot be excluded. For MVA the review reports a convincing childhood cancer risk only for MVA1 (BUB1B; Wilms tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma, MDS/AML/ALL) and MVA3 (TRIP13; predominantly Wilms tumor); none of 15 individuals with MVA2 (CEP57) described in the literature developed cancer. The recommendation for MVA is awareness of tumor signs and renal ultrasound every 3 months from birth to age 7 (supporting SIOP-Europe Host Genome Working Group recommendations) with regular clinical review for rhabdomyosarcoma; no JGCT-specific surveillance is recommended. For xeroderma pigmentosum the review lists skin, oral, ocular, central nervous system and hematological malignancies (AML risk with XPC variants) and recommends dermatological exam every 3 months and ophthalmologic and oral exam at least twice yearly; it does not mention JGCT in the XP section. The review states that heterozygous carriers of recessive genomic-instability genes are not recommended for childhood surveillance. MAD2L1B (as printed; spindle assembly checkpoint gene) Points to biallelic MAD2L1B-related mosaic variegated aneuploidy as a possible rare predisposition associated with JGCT in two siblings (ovary and testis); evidence is a single sibling pair, and the review makes no JGCT-specific surveillance recommendation.

title: DICER1-Related Tumor Predisposition: Identification of At-risk Individuals and Recommended Surveillance Strategies.
author: Schultz KAP
text: Registry report (International PPB/DICER1 Registry, International OTST Registry, NCI DICER1 study) of 713 participants with germline DICER1 P/LP variant from 38 countries (574 registry plus 139 non-overlapping NCI participants); 61% (437/713) female, median enrollment age 9 years, median follow-up 35 months. JGCT is mentioned only marginally: Figure 2 legend lists 'juvenile granulosa cell tumor (n=2)' among other ovarian tumors in germline DICER1 carriers; the Discussion states that DICER1-related ovarian sarcoma and JGCT have been reported, with SLCT the most common ovarian tumor. Table 2 (testing indications) includes 'Ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumor (especially if anaplasia and/or high mitotic index)' as an indication to consider germline DICER1 testing. 103 participants had ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (SLCT) at median age 14 years (range 11 months-65 years); 13% diagnosed before age 8 and 4% before age 4; 11 had metachronous contralateral SLCT at median 45 months; 15% of all primary ovarian tumors occurred before age 8. Among 87 SLCT patients since the 2018 guidelines, surveillance-detected SLCT (10) were stage IA in 9/10 without chemotherapy, versus 42/77 stage IA and 34/77 chemotherapy among symptomatic cases (90% vs 55% stage IA, p=.032; chemotherapy 10% vs 44%, p=.038); median tumor size 6.6 cm vs 13.0 cm (p=.041). Registry now recommends starting pelvic ultrasound every 6 months at detection of a germline DICER1 variant (previously age 8-10), continuing at least to age 40 with shared decision-making thereafter. Authors note ultrasound is more sensitive than biochemical markers for gynecologic tumor surveillance and that rupture is associated with higher stage and worse prognosis (stated for SLCT). DICER1 Supports DICER1 germline testing in JGCT with anaplasia or high mitotic index and gives context on pelvic surveillance for DICER1 carriers; very few JGCT cases in the cohort (n=2).

title: Risk Factors and Clinical Outcomes of Recurrence in Adult Ovarian Granulosa Cell Tumors.
author: Golmohammadi Tavallaee M
text: Single-center retrospective cohort (Qhaem Hospital, Mashhad University of Medical Sciences, Iran; August 2012 to August 2023) of 92 granulosa cell tumor patients: 86 adult-type (AGCT) and 6 juvenile-type (JGCT). Mean age was 22.80 +/- 6.91 years in the 6 JGCT patients versus 44.89 +/- 13.72 years in the 86 AGCT patients (AGCT range 13 to 84). The authors state that because JGCT and AGCT have different etiologies, all further analyses were restricted to AGCT; no stage, treatment, recurrence or survival data are reported for the 6 JGCT patients. AGCT results (for context): 5-year overall survival 98.2% and 5-year progression-free survival 90.8% at median follow-up 72 months (0-180); recurrence in 19 of 86; stage IV was the only significant recurrence risk factor (HR 7.62, 95% CI 1.89-30.63, p=0.004). Authors' background statements: JGCT are considered borderline tumors prevalent in premenopausal individuals under 30 years; AKT1 activation is described as the primary oncogenic driver in JGCT in contrast to FOXL2 alterations in AGCT; unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is stated to suffice for pediatric and premenopausal patients.  Adult-type focused study; its only JGCT content is a count (6) and mean age (22.8 years) from a single Iranian center, plus background statements. Little JGCT-specific evidence.

title: Update on Cancer Screening in Children with Syndromes of Bone Lesions, Hereditary Leiomyomatosis and Renal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome, and Other Rare Syndromes.
author: Michaeli O
text: Consensus-based review from the 2023 AACR Childhood Cancer Predisposition Workshop on cancer surveillance in children with syndromes of bone lesions (Ollier disease, Maffucci syndrome, hereditary multiple osteochondromas and related), HLRCC, Schinzel-Giedion and Rubinstein-Taybi syndromes. For Ollier disease (OD) and Maffucci syndrome (MS), the paper states juvenile granulosa cell tumors were reported in at least twelve cases, some with molecular data showing the same IDH variant as in the enchondromas. Overall tumor risk in OD/MS is up to 50%; chondrosarcoma about 30% (median transformation age 30-52 years, rarely as young as 10); gliomas 1.2-16.3%; in MS 8.5% of vascular lesions become malignant. Somatic IDH1 (p.Arg132) or IDH2 (p.Arg172Ser) variants occur in about 80%. Surveillance recommended for OD/MS: baseline whole-body MRI (deferred to about 6-8 years to avoid general anesthesia), physical examination every 6-12 months until adulthood (12-24 months in adults), plain radiographs of known lesions every 2-3 years, yearly MRI for lesions >5-6 cm or in pelvis/scapula, WBMRI with dedicated brain MRI every 1-2 years from age 20. No JGCT-specific imaging or marker screening is proposed; the panel advises a high index of suspicion for other symptoms, specifically lower abdominal pain in women (juvenile granulosa cell tumor) and neurological symptoms (glioma). Table 1 groups vascular malignancies, gliomas and JGCT as a 1-16% risk category with 6-12 monthly physical examination. The panel acknowledges that higher malignancy risk in enchondromatoses may reflect ascertainment bias and that the key supporting study needs prospective validation. IDH1 / IDH2 Consensus surveillance recommendations that name JGCT as a tumor associated with Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome and give a symptom-based (lower abdominal pain) surveillance prompt; no JGCT patient series.

title: Ovarian Masses in Children: Surgical Experience and Outcomes.
author: Kapoor R
text: Single-center retrospective series of 30 children under 18 who had surgery for ovarian masses (2009-2023): 5 non-neoplastic, 10 benign, 3 borderline and 12 malignant neoplasms. Only 1 of 30 patients (3.3%) had juvenile granulosa cell tumor; Table 1 classifies it under borderline malignant tumors. The JGCT patient had normal preoperative tumor markers and received no postoperative chemotherapy; the authors note surgical resection alone with free margins was considered curative for such patients. At mean follow-up of 53.5 months (range 4-117) all 30 patients were alive and disease free, including the JGCT patient. Authors cite a meta-analysis in which sex cord-stromal tumors such as JGCT made up 14% of malignant pediatric ovarian masses and mixed germ cell tumors 30%. Cohort-level conclusions: tumor size, solid component and raised AFP/beta-hCG/LDH help distinguish malignant from benign masses; overall prognosis favorable.  Small pediatric ovarian-mass surgical series with a single JGCT case (surgery alone, disease free); little else JGCT-specific.

title: Complex immunohistochemical and molecular study on 5 cases of ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumors reveals a consistent alteration in the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway.
author: Šafanda A
text: Of 10 cases submitted as JGCT, central expert review reclassified 4 (2 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, 2 sex cord-stromal tumors NOS) and 1 was a duplicate (primary of a recurrent case), leaving 5 primary JGCTs and 1 recurrence; ages 6-43 years (mean 19, median 16), FIGO IC in 4 and IIIB in 1. Recurrence occurred in 3 patients (cases 1, 3, 4), all within the first year of diagnosis per the text; chemotherapy for recurrence was mostly platinum-based, with some paclitaxel; case 1 also received bevacizumab with limited response and died of disease at 21 months; case 3 was alive with disease at 79 months; case 4 had no evidence of disease at 44 months. Immunohistochemistry on tissue microarrays: SF1, inhibin A, calretinin, FOXL2, ER, PR, AR, CKAE1/3 and CD99 were positive in 5/5; WT1 in 1/5; GATA3, napsin A, SATB2, MUC4, CAIX, OCT3/4, SALL4, TTF1 and p16 negative; p53 wild type in all; BRG1, INI1, ARID1A, DPC4 and mismatch repair proteins retained; HER2 negative and PD-L1 negative (TPS <1%); Ki-67 median 30 (range 4-47). Targeted NGS (788-gene panel) found pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutations in 80% (4/5): AKT1 internal tandem duplication in 2/5 (40%), TERT promoter mutation in 1, EP400 in 1; none had the FOXL2 c.402C>G mutation or DICER1 mutations; tumor mutation burden was low (average 5 mutations/Mb); the case 3 recurrence had a mutational profile identical to its primary. PTEN protein expression was lost in 3/5 (60%) of tumors, all AKT1 wild type, without PTEN mutation, CNV deletion or promoter methylation, suggesting other mechanisms such as miRNA interference or post-translational modification. The two tumors with TERT and EP400 mutations both recurred; the AKT1-mutated tumors had lower Ki-67. The authors conclude that JGCT pathogenesis may be driven by PI3K/AKT/mTOR activation (AKT1 ITD or PTEN loss), that this needs a larger cohort, and note that PTEN/mTOR-targeted strategies are under investigation; they note Bessiere et al. found AKT1 ITD in 60% of 16 JGCTs restricted to patients under 15, and Onder et al. found DICER1 mutations in 2/8 (cited, not independently read). AKT1 TERT EP400 PTEN FOXL2 DICER1 Small but deeply characterized ovarian JGCT cohort showing AKT1 ITD in 2/5 and PTEN loss in the AKT1-wild-type tumors, consistent with PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activation; also gives a broad negative and positive IHC panel useful for pathology.

title: Histopathological spectrum of ovarian tumors in Jharkhand, India: A retrospective study.
author: Paswan MK
text: Single-center retrospective histopathology series (Rajendra Institute of Medical Sciences, Ranchi, India; March 2020-March 2024) of 190 ovarian tumors classified by WHO 2020; age range 8-72 years, mean 36 years. One juvenile granulosa cell tumor (0.5% of 190) was found; it was counted among the malignant tumors (JGCT 1 of 28 malignant) and among 3 pure sex cord tumors (2 adult GCT, 1 JGCT). Sex cord-stromal tumors were 11/190 (5.7%): 7 pure stromal (5 fibromas, 1 thecoma, 1 sclerosing stromal), 3 pure sex cord (2 AGCT, 1 JGCT) and 1 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor. No age, presentation, stage, marker, treatment or outcome data are given for the JGCT; diagnosis was by H&E morphology only, without immunohistochemistry or molecular testing (acknowledged by authors as a limitation). Overall: 154 benign (81.1%), 8 borderline (4.2%), 28 malignant (14.7%); surface epithelial tumors 73.2%, germ cell tumors 20%.  Minimal: reports a single H&E-diagnosed JGCT in a general hospital series of ovarian tumors in India; useful only as an epidemiologic count.

title: A Rare Case of Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor in a Premenarchal Female: Clinical Presentation, Diagnosis, and Management.
author: Kanna E
text: A 4.5-year-old girl had 2 weeks of pubic hair and breast development; estradiol was 294.70 pg/ml (reference <27), testosterone 1.330 ng/ml (<0.250), 17-OHP 5.23 ng/ml (<1.00), DHEA-S 0.467 ug/ml (normal), FSH <0.30 and LH <0.02 mIU/ml (gonadotropin-independent); AFP and beta-hCG normal. Ultrasound showed a pubertal-type uterus (387 cm3) and an 11.45 x 5.13 x 8.38 cm mixed cystic-solid left ovarian mass with blood flow; MRI confirmed a large multilocular mass from L3 to S1 without evidence of invasion. Left salpingo-oophorectomy en bloc was performed; peritoneal fluid and washings were cytologically negative; histology showed predominantly solid and follicular growth, hemorrhagic necrosis without capsular disruption, moderate nuclear atypia and a mitotic index of 0-4 per 40x field (6-15 per 10 HPF). Tumor cells were positive for calretinin, CD99, CD56, inhibin, SF1, SMA and AE1/AE3 and negative for EMA and synaptophysin; stage was pT1a (TNM/UICC). At 1 year there was no recurrence, precocious puberty features had resolved, estradiol and 17-OHP normalized, and LH/FSH remained prepubertal. The discussion states approximately 90% of JGCTs are FIGO stage I with 5-year disease-free survival 90-100%, contralateral involvement is rare (3%), BEP is the commonest adjuvant regimen for stage IC-IV, ESMO advises BEP for stage IC while ESGO suggests surgery alone may suffice for IC1 and chemotherapy for IC2/IC3; these are literature statements by the authors. The authors list recurrence risk factors from the literature as nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses >4/10 HPF, rupture, residual disease and FOXL2 mutation expression, and state no analogous genetic driver has been linked to JGCT (AGCT has FOXL2).  Prepubertal stage I ovarian JGCT with gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty and elevated testosterone and 17-OHP, cured by fertility-sparing surgery.

title: Giant Ovarian Tumors in Young Women: Diagnostic and Treatment Challenges-A Report of Two Cases and Narrative Review of the Recent Literature.
author: Melnyk M
text: Two own cases (17-year-old with cystadenofibroma, 25-year-old with intestinal-endocervical mucinous borderline tumor) are not JGCT; the paper reviews 39 publications (2019-2024) on giant ovarian tumors (over 10 cm) in patients aged 10-25 years. Among the 39 reviewed cases the authors list three granulosa cell tumors; the review table gives one as 'Granulosa cell tumor, juvenile type, FIGO IA' (age 12, 15.0 x 9.0 x 18.8 cm, laparotomy with left salpingo-oophorectomy, presenting with secondary amenorrhea, abdominal pain and galactorrhea with prolactin 70.5 ng/mL, no complications). The other two granulosa cell tumors in the table are not typed as juvenile: age 15, 22.3 cm, stage 1C, left salpingo-oophorectomy with omentectomy, recurrent ovarian cyst six weeks postoperatively; and age 14, 15 x 10 x 9 cm, hirsutism, amenorrhea, testosterone elevated, oophorectomy after detorsion. The text states that juvenile granulosa cell tumors, despite high mitotic activity, are typically confined to one ovary, and that patients with JGCT limited to one ovary generally have a favorable outcome after unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. The review also reports that, in a cited series of 63 patients with ovarian tumors over 20 cm, 66.67% were malignant, 26.98% benign and 6.35% borderline (not JGCT-specific).  Marginal. A general review of giant ovarian tumors in young women; JGCT is reflected by one tabulated case and one general statement on outcome, with no original JGCT data.

title: A Novel Pathogenic Variant of DICER1 Gene in a Young Greek Patient with 2 Different Sex-Cord Ovarian Tumors and Multinodular Goiter.
author: Roumpou A
text: Young Greek woman with germline DICER1 syndrome: multinodular goiter at 16 (7 nodules, benign FNA), irregular menses with testosterone 3.1 ng/mL and low FSH at 17, bilateral moderately differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors (SLCT) at 18 (20.6 cm left mass, 5.6 cm right mass, ascites; inhibin 443 pg/mL, CA125 359.7 U/mL; FIGO IB), and a JGCT at 21. JGCT: 13 x 9 x 7.5 cm multilocular cystic lesion in the right parametrial area found on follow-up MRI 3 years after SLCT surgery; no capsular tearing, 7 right pelvic lymph nodes tumor-free, FIGO stage IA; managed by excision and follow-up without adjuvant chemotherapy. JGCT immunohistochemistry: positive for CKAE1/AE3 (focal dot-like juxtanuclear), vimentin, inhibin, CD56, CD99, WT-1, PR and focally calretinin; histology showed a diffuse growth pattern with round hyperchromatic nuclei and rare grooves. WES found a novel heterozygous DICER1 frameshift variant in exon 16 (c.2685dupA, p.Phe896Ilefs*5), pathogenic by ACMG/AMP criteria; her mother carries it and is asymptomatic at 50; a maternal aunt had uterine rhabdomyosarcoma at 11 and goiter requiring thyroidectomy at 21. SLCT treatment: unilateral left oophorectomy and right tumor excision, 3 cycles of BEP; hormones and markers normalized within about 20 days of surgery; no recurrence at about 6 years. Literature statements: JGCT is a very rare DICER1-syndrome phenotype associated mainly with somatic DICER1 mutations; two probable germline-associated JGCT cases cited (age 16, and age 2 in a patient with a relative with pleuropulmonary blastoma); stage I JGCT survival about 97% as cited; about 5% (by age 10) and 19% (by age 50) of germline carriers develop a neoplasm. Authors conclude clinicians should consider germline DICER1 variants when multinodular goiter in young patients coexists with other neoplasms and that genetic testing and family screening are warranted. DICER1 Case of germline DICER1 syndrome with a stage IA JGCT arising 3 years after bilateral SLCT, with JGCT immunohistochemistry and a novel exon 16 DICER1 frameshift variant.

title: The Evaluation, Diagnosis, and Management of Ovarian Cysts, Masses, and Their Complications in Fetuses, Infants, Children, and Adolescents.
author: Bašković M
text: Narrative review of ovarian cysts and masses from fetus to adolescence; JGCT is mentioned only briefly in three places and no JGCT patient data are given. Sex cord-stromal tumors (thecomas, fibromas, juvenile granulosa cell tumor, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors) are stated to be rare in children and adolescents, approximately 5% of ovarian malignancies; unlike germ cell and epithelial tumors they often present with hormone production (hirsutism, virilization, menstrual change, precocious puberty). The review says a subset of sex cord-stromal tumors is associated with genetic aberrations and that an underlying cancer predisposition syndrome should always be considered. Markers: inhibin A and B are listed as the marker for juvenile granulosa cell tumors; estradiol and testosterone are measured for hormonally active tumors; the absence of elevated markers does not exclude malignancy. Imaging: masses with 50% or more solid component are considered malignant until histology shows otherwise, and solid ovarian masses in children can arise from sex cord-stromal tumors such as JGCT and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors. General management statements (not JGCT-specific): ovary-sparing minimally invasive surgery unless malignancy is strongly suspected; staging for suspected malignancy includes peritoneal lavage, biopsies and pelvic/periaortic lymph node sampling; follow-up every 3-6 months for 2-3 years then annually to 5 years or longer; treatment in specialized multidisciplinary centers.  General pediatric ovarian mass review with only passing JGCT statements (markers, solid mass imaging, hormone production); useful as context for diagnostic work-up.

title: Ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumor: A report from the International Ovarian and Testicular Stromal Tumor and International Pleuropulmonary Blastoma/DICER1 Registries.
author: Harris AK
text: 70 ovarian juvGCT patients enrolled in the International OTST and/or IPPB/DICER1 Registries, diagnosed 2001-2024; central pathology review for 80% (56/70); median age 10 years (range 1 day-38 years), 93% (65/70) younger than 20; median follow-up 31 months (range 0-271). Presentation: abdominal pain 35/65, distention 29/65, precocious puberty 17/65, secondary amenorrhea 7/34, virilization 8/65; median tumor size 12.0 cm (4.6-30.0); 36/69 right, 31/69 left, 2/69 bilateral. Inhibin B elevated in 38/42 (90%; median 3,759 pg/ml), inhibin A 22/34 (65%), CA125 20/42 (48%), total testosterone 9/21 (43%), AFP 2/46 (4%). Surgery: laparotomy 55/67 (82%), laparoscopy 12/67 (18%); salpingo-oophorectomy 48/69 (70%), oophorectomy 18/69, cystectomy 2/69; preoperative rupture (IC2) 15/66 (23%), intraoperative rupture (IC1) 25/66 (38%); second-look staging in 16/69. Peritoneal fluid collected in 58/70, malignant cells in 6/58, all with rupture and/or extra-ovarian tumor; no sampled lymph node involved. Only 14/70 (20%) had complete FIGO staging. 2014 FIGO stage: IA 25/70 (36%, three were IX), IC1 20/70 (29%), IC2 n=7 / IC3 n=2 / ICX n=3 (12/70, 17%), II-IV 10/70 (14%), not documented 3/70; 81% (57/70) were stage I. Mitotic index (MI) available in 60/70 (86%; median 26/10 HPF, range 1-104): low (<10) 9/60, intermediate (10-19) 14/60, high (>19) 37/60 (62%). High MI by stage: IA 11/21, IC1 11/17, IC2-IC3 7/12, II-IV 7/9. Adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy in 21/70 (30%), 17/21 with bleomycin-etoposide-platinum; in low-risk stages 1 stage IA and 3/20 stage IC1 received chemotherapy; no upfront radiation. Molecular (small subset): AKT1 in-frame duplications in 3 patients, GNAS p.R201C and TERT promoter in 2 each, TP53 in 4, one anaplastic tumor with somatic DICER1 RNase IIIb hotspot variant (patient died). Outcome: 14 recurrences (median 8.5 months, range 3-32; 13/14 within 2 years); 8 deaths, all from recurrent juvGCT (median 35 months from diagnosis, range 9-69). Of 6 surviving recurrent patients, 4 on treatment and 2 NED. Inhibin B was elevated at recurrence in 3/5 of those with elevated inhibin B at diagnosis who recurred. 3-year EFS / OS overall 73.2% (95% CI 61.9-86.5) / 91.7% (84.2-99.9). By stage 3-year EFS: IA 80.2% (62.4-100.0), IC1 87.4% (72.4-100.0), IC2-IC3 63.6% (40.7-99.5), II-IV 48.0% (24.6-93.8) (p=.05). Low-risk (IA/IX, IC1) vs high-risk (>=IC2 incl ICX) 3-year EFS 82.2% (68.8-98.2) vs 55.5% (37.4-82.4) (p=.02); 3-year OS 96.2% (89.0-100.0) vs 84.0% (68.8-100.0) (p=.13). 3-year OS by stage: IA/IX 100% (but two IA/IX patients died of recurrence at 64 and 69 months, both high MI and no chemotherapy), IC1 90.9% (75.4-100.0; 1 death, high MI, no chemotherapy), IC2/IC3/ICX 87.5% (67.3-100.0; 1 death, IC2, high MI, received chemotherapy), II-IV 77.8% (54.9-100.0; 4 deaths: 3 high MI with chemotherapy, 1 stage IIIC with unknown MI and no chemotherapy) (p=.01). High MI predicted worse outcome: 3-year EFS 55.5% (39.6-77.9) with high MI vs 100% with low/intermediate MI (p<.01); all 13 recurrences with known MI had high MI; relapse 13/37 high MI vs 0/23 low/intermediate; juvGCT death 7/37 vs 0/23. 3- and 5-year OS 85.5% / 79.3% (high MI) vs 100% (p=.03). Within low-risk stages with known MI, surgery-only: 16 patients with low MI none recurred; 18 with high MI had 5 recurrences, 3 deaths (3-year EFS 64.1%, 42.7-96.2, p=.12; 3-year OS 92.9%). Within high-risk stages: 14 high MI (12 chemo, 8 recurred) vs 7 low/intermediate (5 chemo, none recurred); 3-year EFS 37.1% vs no events (p=.02); 5-year OS 55.5% vs 100% (p=.08). Among low-risk surgery-only patients (n=41) larger tumor dimension (HR 1.13, 1.01-1.27) and MI as continuous variable (HR 1.15, 1.02-1.28) were associated with recurrence; >12 cm HR 4.48 (0.50-40.26), age and intraoperative rupture not significant. Authors strongly recommend MI assessment for all juvGCT, support chemotherapy beyond stage IC1, suggest considering chemotherapy individually for low-stage high-MI tumors, surveillance with imaging and markers up to 5 years, and tumor testing for targetable alterations (e.g. AKT-directed therapy). AKT1 GNAS TERT TP53 DICER1 Largest registry cohort of ovarian JGCT with central review; quantifies stage distribution, treatment and stage- and mitotic-index-specific survival, identifying high mitotic index as the main prognostic factor.

title: Testicular and ovarian Juvenile granulosa cell tumors in children and adolescents: Analysis of 113 patients registered to the German Registry for Rare Pediatric Tumors (STEP).
author: Schneider DT
text: Between 2001 and 2019, 119 patients with JGCT were prospectively registered in the German STEP/MAKEI registries (centers in Germany, Austria, Switzerland); after excluding those older than 18 years, 113 were analyzed: 24 testicular and 89 ovarian; reference pathology and central therapy recommendations were used. Testis (n=24): all neonates or infants, median age 16 days (day 1 to 12 months), 17 diagnosed in the first month and 7 at 6-12 months; 13 left, 10 right, 1 bilateral; painless scrotal swelling, no hormone signs, AFP and beta-hCG within age-related reference ranges; size 2-6 cm (median 2); all stage I; no relapse after median follow-up 95 months (1-155). One neonate with diffuse bilateral testicular JGCT was treated with buserelin (LH-RH blockage) and was histologically tumor free after 14 months; the authors suggest testicular JGCT may be a developmental tumor and recommend considering organ-sparing surgery, but not when AFP is above age-related levels or rising (to avoid missing yolk sac tumor). Ovary (n=89): median age 9.8 years (birth to 18), 7 in the first year, 44% under 8 years; median largest dimension 11 cm (2-30), smaller in prepubertal (7.8 cm) than pubertal (12.6 cm); AFP and beta-hCG not secreted; inhibin B measured in 11 patients (10-2284 ng/L), >1000 ng/L in 5 (3 with precocity) and normalizing after resection. Ovarian FIGO stage: IA 52 (58%), IC1 14, IC2 14, IC3 4, II 4, III 1 (II/III 5, 6%); no distant or lymph node metastases at diagnosis; mitotic rate low (<10/10 HPF) 38%, moderate (10-19) 26%, high (>19) 36%, median 14 (range 1-72). Treatment: laparotomy 86%, laparoscopy 14%; adnectomy 64%, ovariectomy 27%, organ-sparing resection 9%; R0 58%, R1 41%; adjuvant chemotherapy in 21 patients (24%): 2/52 stage IA, 1/14 IC1, 13/18 IC2/IC3, 5/5 II/III, mostly PEI (cisplatin 100 mg/m2, etoposide 300 mg/m2, ifosfamide 7500 mg/m2 per cycle), 3-6 cycles. Outcome (ovary): median follow-up 53 months (1-179); 4 relapses and 2 deaths; 5-year EFS 0.95 +/- 0.03 (85/89), OS 0.97 +/- 0.02 (87/89). Three relapses were stage IA (2 on watch-and-wait, 1 after 4 PEI) and one was stage IIB; all four tumors had high mitotic counts (20-67/10 HPF) or high Ki-67; three had organ-sparing surgery; no relapses in IC2/IC3 (which had unfavorable prognosis in the historical MAKEI cohort). Prognostic factor: EFS was 1.0 (61/61) for low or moderate mitotic rate (<20/10 HPF) versus 0.85 +/- 0.07 (24/28) for high (>19/10 HPF), log-rank p=.032; stage was not significantly correlated with outcome; the authors recommend considering mitotic rate and incomplete surgery in risk stratification and second-look surgery after organ-sparing resection with high mitotic activity. Comparison with the historical MAKEI cohort (45 patients, 27% chemotherapy, 6 relapses, 5 deaths; updated 5-year survival 50% for IC2 and 88% overall): current OS by stage IA 98%, IC1 100%, IC2/IC3 100%, II/III 80%, overall 97%; the authors conclude that restricting chemotherapy to IC2 and above and central reference review improved outcomes. The authors conclude testicular and ovarian JGCT are clinically distinct entities: testicular JGCT presents only in infancy with excellent prognosis, while ovarian JGCT can arise at any age and be aggressive. chromosome 10 Largest prospective pediatric JGCT cohort (113, testis and ovary): defines the stage-based chemotherapy stratification (chemotherapy for IC2 and higher), high mitotic rate as a risk factor, and testicular JGCT as benign with no relapses.

title: Role of adjuvant chemotherapy in stage IC ovarian granulosa cell tumors: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
author: Zhang T
text: PROSPERO CRD42024559478; PubMed, Embase and Cochrane searched to 1 December 2024; 703 records screened, 70 full texts assessed, 12 retrospective studies (695 stage IC GCT patients) included; 255 (36.7%) received adjuvant chemotherapy and 440 (63.3%) observation; follow-up 1-396 months. Overall recurrence 18.7% (50/268; 11 studies reporting) and mortality 7.6% (45/590). Recurrence 21/110 (19.1%) with chemotherapy vs 29/158 (18.4%) with observation (OR 1.32; 95% CI 0.67-2.58; p=0.424; I2=33%); mortality 15/221 (6.8%) vs 30/369 (8.1%) (OR 0.83; 0.44-1.57; p=0.560). Five-year DFS (OR 0.88; 95% CI 0.18-4.18; I2=54%) and 5-year OS (OR 1.28; 0.60-2.74; I2=0%) did not differ between adjuvant chemotherapy and observation; Egger test showed publication bias for recurrence (p=0.042) but trim-and-fill did not change results. Only 33 JGCT patients across 5 studies were included (Calaminus 1997, Ndhlovu 2021, Parikshaa 2021, Hamzaoglu Canbolat 2022, Marino 2024): 17 received adjuvant chemotherapy and 4 relapsed; none of the 16 observed relapsed. The pooled JGCT OR for recurrence was 4.20 (95% CI 0.51-34.28; p=0.180), not significant; the adult GCT subgroup (195 AGCT, 5 studies) OR was 1.72 (0.22-13.16). No significant recurrence difference by fertility-sparing surgery (FSS group OR 3.4, 95% CI 0.47-24.51; non-FSS OR 7.3, 0.71-75.35) or by regimen (BEP/EP 6/39 relapsed vs TC/TP 0/6; OR 1.53). BEP was used in 57/107 (53.3%) of patients with regimen details. The authors conclude that adjuvant chemotherapy did not add benefit for recurrence or mortality in stage IC GCT, in either adult or juvenile types, but caution that all studies were retrospective, JGCT numbers were very small, sicker patients probably received chemotherapy, and median follow-up was under 5 years. The authors cite that JGCT tends to recur early (median recurrence 4.5-12 months in cited studies) and that ESMO recommends adjuvant chemotherapy for stage IC JGCT while ESGO/SIOPE allows surgery alone for IC1 and chemotherapy for IC2/IC3 JGCT; clinicians tend to follow ESMO because of JGCT's aggressive early recurrence.  Most direct pooled evidence on whether adjuvant chemotherapy helps in stage IC granulosa cell tumors; the JGCT subgroup is only 33 patients and underpowered, and adult-type cases dominate.

title: Observer Variation in the Diagnosis of Testicular Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors by a Genitourinary Pathology Society and International Society of Urological Pathology Panel: Paving the Way for a New Classification.
author: Berney DM
text: TEsticular Sex cord-Stromal Tumor (TESST) group, cosponsored by ISUP and GUPS: 44 scanned H&E slides of testicular sex cord-stromal tumors reviewed online by 17 of 18 invited expert pathologists; consensus defined as 70% or more agreement. Consensus was reached in 26/44 cases (59%); a majority (over 50%) diagnosis was reached in 75% of cases. All 3 juvenile granulosa cell tumors reached consensus (100% for cases 35 and 36; 70%-79% for case 4); the authors conclude JGCT of the testis can be reliably identified on morphology with minimal workup. Only the single adult granulosa cell tumor case (with FOXL2 p.C134W, 14/17 = 82%) reached consensus; adult GCT was frequently diagnosed by some experts in other tumor types, suggesting overdiagnosis, and a cited analysis found FOXL2 pathogenic variant in only 1/13 testicular adult GCT. Table 2 states that because testicular JGCT is very different from its ovarian counterpart, a renaming emphasizing its benign nature is suggested. Consensus statements: WHO 2022 classification is not aligned with best evidence; terminology for gonadal stromal tumors, Sertoli, granulosa and mixed tumors needs standardization; referral to a specialist genitourinary pathologist is recommended; recommendations on diagnostic workup in pediatric sex cord-stromal tumors are needed. Other categories: Sertoli cell tumor consensus 8/12, sex cord-stromal NOS 2/8, Leydig cell tumor 6/6, large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor 2/4.  Testicular tumor pathology consensus exercise; JGCT is reported as 3 of 44 cases. Supports that testicular JGCT is reproducibly recognizable.

title: Assessment and classification of sex cord-stromal tumours of the testis: recommendations from the testicular sex cord-stromal tumour (TESST) group, an Expert Panel of the Genitourinary Pathology Society (GUPS) and International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP).
author: Acosta AM
text: Consensus statement of 20 genitourinary pathologists (modified Delphi, three questionnaires, live vote 3/23/2024 at Johns Hopkins) with 70% agreement threshold; testicular sex cord-stromal tumors are about 5% of testicular neoplasms, about 90% are indolent and about 10% aggressive. Recommendation: juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the testis should be renamed 'benign juvenile granulosa cell tumour' (consensus on need to rename 12/15, 80%; on the name 15/15, 100%), with a comment that it differs clinically and molecularly from ovarian JGCT, to avoid overtreatment. Panel states testicular JGCT is largely an infantile entity with more than 90% of cases in the first year of life, mostly hormonally inactive, a subset arising in dysgenetic gonads, and apparently without malignant potential; a genomic study of a limited number of cases showed they lack the alterations of ovarian JGCT. Panel states ovarian JGCT mostly affects children (median age about 8 years) with a subset in post-pubertal children and adults including during pregnancy, characteristically produces sex steroids, and about 10% behave aggressively with abdominal/pelvic recurrence or distant metastasis; ovarian tumors carry AKT1 pleckstrin-homology-domain internal tandem duplications and hotspot GNAS gain-of-function variants. Brisk mitotic activity predicts aggressive potential in Leydig and Sertoli cell tumors but not in juvenile granulosa cell tumor; JGCT, myoid gonadal stromal tumor, fibroma/thecoma are described as invariably indolent in published data. Testicular adult granulosa cell tumor should be diagnosed only sparingly (consensus 16/20, 80%); FOXL2 p.C134W (present in more than 90-95% of ovarian adult GCT) is found only in a small subset of testicular homonyms. Other recommendations: FH-deficient Leydig cell tumor (14/18, 78%), inflammatory and nested testicular sex cord tumor with EWSR1::ATF1 as a distinct entity (15/18, 83%), 'gonadal stromal tumour' umbrella for pure spindle cell tumors (16/20, 80%), testicular Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor as a rare distinct entity (15/15), do not use pTNM staging for these tumors (14/15, 93%), and classify post-pubertal tumors without metastasis as low or high risk (13/13). No consensus on whether myoid gonadal stromal tumor is a distinct entity (12/20, 60%), FH IHC in Leydig tumors without worrisome features (12/20), a mixed germ cell/sex cord-stromal category (13/20) or Ki-67 for risk (9/18). AKT1 / GNAS Guideline-level statement that testicular JGCT is benign and genetically distinct from ovarian JGCT, with a proposed rename; also summarizes ovarian JGCT features for contrast.

title: Imaging Evaluation of Ovarian Masses in a Pediatric Population: A Comprehensive Overview.
author: Bourgioti C
text: Narrative imaging review of pediatric (0-19 y) ovarian masses (PubMed search 1977 to April 2025, English only, non-systematic); JGCT is covered in one section plus a table; no JGCT patient series is reported. Pediatric ovarian tumor incidence is given as 2.6 per 100,000 girls; malignancy is found in 3-8% of children and adolescents with an adnexal mass; sex cord-stromal tumors (SCSTs) are about 10-20% of pediatric ovarian neoplasms. JGCT and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors are the commonest pediatric SCSTs, roughly 75% and 15% of SCSTs; JGCT is only 5% of all granulosa cell tumors; mean age at diagnosis 13 years; bilateral in 4-5%. JGCTs are often hormonally active, typically producing estradiol (usable as a diagnostic and follow-up marker); they can also secrete inhibin (particularly inhibin B) and Mullerian inhibiting substance, usable as tumor markers. Reports of JGCT in patients with Maffucci syndrome and Ollier disease exist, but a definitive link with enchondromatosis syndromes is not confirmed. Most JGCTs are diagnosed early with an excellent prognosis (survival over 90% after surgical resection); mitotic index correlates significantly with prognosis; long-term follow-up is needed because of rare late recurrence. Pathology: large solid masses with cystic spaces, average diameter 12.5 cm, primitive granulosa cells in solid and follicular patterns, with hemorrhage, necrosis and fibrosis. Imaging: nonspecific; US and CT show a large multicystic mass with solid, heterogeneous, highly vascular components and septations; MRI may show a sponge-like pattern of many small cysts among solid areas, with hemorrhage (high T1, fluid-fluid levels), plus endometrial thickening and uterine enlargement from estrogen. Pediatric ovarian SCSTs and epithelial tumors are staged by FIGO (germ cell tumors by COG); the authors state that ovarian-sparing, minimally invasive surgery with fertility preservation and referral to specialized centers is important, and that cancer predisposition (genetic testing, family history) should be considered in children with ovarian tumors. Authors note imaging risk scores (RMI, ROMA, IOTA, O-RADS) are poorly validated in children.  Radiology-oriented overview of all pediatric ovarian masses; useful for JGCT mainly for the summary of its epidemiology, hormone and marker profile, and imaging appearance relative to other pediatric ovarian tumors. No original JGCT data.

title: New histopathological and molecular findings in gynecological cancers.
author: McCluggage WG
text: Narrative pathology review of recent developments in gynecological tumor classification (2020 WHO 5th edition and later); no new data; 6th WHO edition expected 2026. Table 1 (molecular events in ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors): for juvenile granulosa cell tumor (JGCT) there are no recurrent molecular events useful in diagnosis; other molecular events that may be useful for prognostication are TERT, AKT1 (printed 'AKTC' in the table), GNAS and KMT2C; associated tumor syndromes are Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome. By contrast, adult granulosa cell tumors contain somatic FOXL2 (C134W missense) mutations in well over 90% of cases, and moderately/poorly differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors very commonly contain DICER1 mutations (somatic or germline); these are the molecular events the author highlights as diagnostically useful. The author notes immunohistochemistry confirms a sex cord-stromal tumor but is of minimal value in distinguishing between tumor types, and that rarity and morphologic overlap mean many cases benefit from specialist pathology referral, which also facilitates case-series accrual. The review otherwise covers endometrial TCGA classification, LVSI, mesonephric-like adenocarcinoma, uterine mesenchymal tumors, HPV-associated/independent cervical, vulvar and vaginal carcinomas and STK11 adnexal tumors, with no further JGCT content. TERT, AKT1 (printed 'AKTC'), GNAS, KMT2C Minimal but useful for molecular pathology: a 2025 expert review stating that JGCT lacks a recurrent diagnostic molecular event (unlike FOXL2 in adult granulosa cell tumor), with only candidate prognostic genes and Ollier/Maffucci association listed.

title: Survival outcomes in patients with recurrent mixed sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary.
author: Tahan E
text: Retrospective cohort from the MD Anderson Rare Gynecologic Malignancy Registry (2000-March 2025): 50 mixed ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors identified; 22 excluded (15 no follow-up, 7 diagnosed before 2000); 28 analyzed, 16 with documented recurrence and 12 without (recurrence rate 57%). Recurrent mixed tumors (n=16): 6 adult plus juvenile GCT, 4 juvenile GCT plus Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (SLCT), 6 adult GCT plus SLCT; 12 of 16 were FIGO stage I and 4 stage II at diagnosis; median time to first relapse 27.25 months. Comparators from the same registry with recurrent uniform histology: 97 adult GCT, 14 juvenile GCT, 11 SLCT. Median PFS-2 (from first recurrence) and OS (months): adult+juvenile GCT 8.7 and 83.8; pure JGCT 8.9 (95% CI 3.8-43.1) and 32.2 (20.3-NR); pure AGCT 21.2 and 181.9; juvenile GCT+SLCT 12.5 and 74.0. Adult+juvenile GCT vs pure AGCT: PFS-2 p=.03, OS p=.01 in the table and results text (the abstract states p=.001). Adult+juvenile GCT vs pure JGCT: PFS-2 p=.7, OS p=.8 (no difference). Juvenile GCT+SLCT vs pure JGCT: PFS-2 12.5 vs 8.9 months (p=1.00), OS 74.0 vs 32.2 months (p=.62); vs pure SLCT PFS-2 p=.55, OS p=.08. Molecular testing in 11/16 mixed tumors: FOXL2 c.C402G in 1/4, 1/4 and 1/3 of the three combinations; one adult GCT+SLCT had a DICER1 mutation; no AKT1 mutation in any tested tumor. Authors conclude recurrent adult+juvenile GCT may behave like JGCT (more aggressive than uniform AGCT) at recurrence, and caution that mixed tumors do not share the genetic identity of their components; sample too small for generalizable conclusions. Background (cited): recurrent JGCT behaves more aggressively than recurrent AGCT, with death 7 to 36 months after initial treatment in prior reports; 5-year survival 97% for stage I JGCT. FOXL2 DICER1 AKT1 Provides recurrence survival for 14 pure recurrent JGCT (registry comparator) and for 10 mixed tumors with a juvenile component, with molecular testing; JGCT recurrence after first relapse has short PFS-2 (median 8.9 months) and OS (32.2 months).

title: Prenatal diagnosis and postnatal management of perinatal thoracoabdominopelvic tumors: multicenter experience.
author: Khawand C
text: Retrospective multicenter study (Ile-de-France, January 2010-May 2021) of 153 perinatal thoracic, abdominal or pelvic solid tumors detected prenatally or within 3 months after birth; sacrococcygeal teratomas excluded. Two juvenile granulosa cell tumors were identified (1.3% of 153), both within the 'gonadal tumor' group of 6 (the others were 4 teratomas). Neither JGCT was detected on prenatal imaging; for both, the first sign or symptom occurred between 29 days and 3 months after birth. Imaging (Table 3): one ovarian JGCT was multicystic, maximum size 17.0 cm; one testicular JGCT was solid, 2.6 cm. Extent at postnatal diagnosis (Table 4): both JGCT had local extension only; no adjacent organ, nodal or distant spread. Gonadal tumors overall: 6/6 local only. Per-tumor treatment and outcome for the two JGCT are not reported; deaths in the cohort (6 prenatal, 11 postnatal) were attributed to other tumors (rhabdoid tumor 6/6, neuroblastoma 3/93, nephroblastoma 1/8, hemangioma-to-angiosarcoma 1). Overall 136 (89%) alive at median 5 years (range 0-14). Overall, only 35% (53/153) of perinatal thoracoabdominopelvic tumors were detected prenatally; authors conclude prognosis is largely favorable.  Small JGCT contribution: documents 2 congenital/early-infancy JGCT (one ovarian, one testicular) in a regional perinatal tumor series; useful for infantile onset and for the finding that they were not prenatally detected and were localized.

title: Rapid recurrence of ovarian mixed sex-cord-stromal tumor associated with DICER1 gene mutation: a case analysis and literature review.
author: Zhu F
text: 14-year-old girl with a large cystic-solid abdominopelvic mass on CT (suspected left adnexal), testosterone 457.00 ng/ml (reference 9.8-82.1), prolactin 40.6 ng/ml and AFP 41.0 ng/ml (reference 0-10); treated by exploratory laparotomy and excision. Gross tumor 17 x 14 x 4.5 cm. Histology: ovarian mixed sex-cord-stromal tumor with a juvenile granulosa cell tumor component (40%) and moderately differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (60%). Immunohistochemistry: CK +, WT-1 +, p53 + (60%), inhibin partial +, ER partial +, PR few +, synaptophysin few +, CD56 +, BRG1 +, SF-1 +, Ki-67 40%; PAX-8, NapsinA, CD99, S-100, CgA, CD117, PLAP, CD30 and calretinin negative. NGS found DICER1 exon 16 frameshift c.2517delT p.L840Yfs*6 (abundance 39.19%) and exon 25 missense c.5439G>T p.E1813D (42.47%), among 12 mutations in total; the authors state the E1813 hotspot supports the diagnosis. No standardized chemotherapy was given after the first surgery; markers and imaging were normal at 1 month, but CT at 6 months showed recurrence (19.8 x 19.1 x 11.0 cm) with pathology matching the original. After second surgery and 8 cycles of paclitaxel plus carboplatin there was no recurrence at 1 year. Literature statements cited by the authors: sequencing of 75 JGCT cases confirmed somatic DICER1 mutations in 6 (8%) with two possibly germline DICER1-syndrome JGCT; mixed sex-cord-stromal tumors have DICER1 mutations in 19-80%; only two prior recurrences of mixed tumors reported (this being the third); JGCT is about 5% of granulosa cell tumors and about 97% of JGCT patients are under 30. Authors recommend DICER1 testing (exon 16 and 24-25) for mixed tumors and consideration of adjuvant chemotherapy (BEP or paclitaxel/carboplatin) even after R0 resection when JGCT component exceeds 30% or DICER1 biallelic mutations are present; these are the authors' proposals from a single case, not evidence-graded guidance. Limitations stated: single case, 1-year follow-up, no exome or single-cell sequencing. DICER1 DICER1 Single case of an ovarian mixed sex-cord-stromal tumor containing a 40% juvenile granulosa cell tumor component with DICER1 variants and early recurrence; also cites DICER1 frequency in JGCT (6/75).

title: Tracing metastatic spread in pediatric solid tumors using copy number and targeted deep sequencing.
author: Andersson N
text: Swedish single-center study (diagnosed 2000-2020) of whole-genome copy number profiling (OncoScan SNP array) on 171 samples from 17 children with neuroblastoma (8), Wilms tumor (7) or gonadal tumors (2), with targeted deep sequencing (300-gene panel) of 64 samples from 8 patients; only one patient (GT1) had juvenile granulosa cell tumor. GT1: a JGCT with relapse and widespread metastasis despite the usually favorable prognosis; 19 samples from primary and metastatic sites (including liver and several peritoneal sites) were analysed. Targeted sequencing of GT1 found no truncal somatic point mutations; only RBM10 and AR mutations in two different metastases; copy number analysis showed a complex landscape with 135 unique CNAs. GT1 showed a segmental 14q gain including AKT1 in the stem, which the authors say confirms the reported AKT1 duplication/mutation in JGCT, plus a subclonal MYC amplification (8q24) and an amplified 2q31 region with no known oncogene. GT1 showed later, polyphyletic and polyclonal metastatic spread at several time points after local relapse and intermetastatic spread from liver metastases to two peritoneal sites; the authors say this is the first demonstration of intermetastatic spread in these tumors. Many small gains (<5 Mbp) were present in all GT1 samples and were enriched for serine-type endopeptidase inhibitor genes (18 genes) with 233 genes in lost segments linked to serine metabolism, which the authors suggest as a possible driver of aggressiveness. Across the cohort, 11 of 17 patients showed earlier metastatic spread, and intermetastatic spread occurred in 8 of 9 patients with metastases at two or more sites, including GT1; distant metastases had lower genomic diversity than primary tumors. AKT1 MYC RBM10 AR Single metastatic JGCT case with multiregional genomics (AKT1 gain, MYC amplification, intermetastatic spread); other tumors in the cohort are not JGCT.

title: Pediatric and young adult ovarian masses: clinical approach, diagnostic evaluation, and management.
author: Bayramoglu Z
text: Single-center retrospective cohort of 1,128 females under 30 who had surgery for ovarian masses (2003-2024); mean age 13.7 +/- 4.02 years; 760 (67.38%) non-neoplastic and 368 (32.62%) neoplastic. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor was recorded in 15 patients (1.33% of the cohort), listed third among malignant diagnoses after dysgerminoma (44) and immature teratoma (28). One JGCT patient also had Ollier syndrome, which the authors cite in support of genetic evaluation in pediatric ovarian tumors. Tumor markers for predicting malignancy across all tumors (not JGCT-specific): Inhibin B sensitivity 70%, specificity 85%, PPV 72%, NPV 84% (p = 0.03); AFP 92/88%; beta-hCG 85/90%; LDH 78/82%; CA-125 60/75% (p = 0.08). Malignant neoplasms were larger than benign (18.4 +/- 8.5 vs 6.3 +/- 5.7 cm); recurrence was reported for borderline tumors (31%), grade 2-3 immature teratomas (33%), grade 1 immature teratomas (5%) and malignant germ cell tumors (12%); no JGCT-specific recurrence, stage, treatment or survival data are given. Authors conclude that fertility-sparing surgery is feasible and should be prioritized and that structured long-term follow-up is needed; follow-up was not standardized.  Large pediatric/young-adult ovarian mass surgical series; JGCT contributes only a count (15), one Ollier syndrome association, and cohort-wide inhibin B marker performance.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor in an Adolescent With Xeroderma Pigmentosum: A Rare Case and Implications for Surveillance.
author: Erraoui I
text: A 14-year-old girl with xeroderma pigmentosum (multiple prior cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinoma surgeries and a toe myeloma) had an incidental ovarian mass on ultrasound; she had no endocrine manifestations and no palpable mass. Pelvic CT showed a 33 x 27 mm left latero-uterine mass; MRI showed a 31 x 21 mm lesion with restricted diffusion, central necrosis and O-RADS 4 classification. Serum markers were normal: inhibin B 80 pg/mL, AFP 5 ng/mL, beta-hCG 2 mIU/mL, CA-125 20 U/L, LDH 180 U/L. Laparoscopy found a well-circumscribed, predominantly solid 3.5 x 3.5 x 1 cm left ovarian mass without capsular invasion, normal contralateral ovary and uterus, no ascites or implants; left adnexectomy was performed. Histology showed solid nodules of monotonous oval to spindle cells with eosinophilic or luteinized vacuolated cytoplasm, occasional coffee-bean nuclear grooves, 2 mitoses per 10 HPF, fibrous stroma and no Call-Exner bodies; tumor cells were positive for inhibin, calretinin and reticulin (nodule outlines), negative for GATA3. The tumor was FIGO stage IA; a multidisciplinary team judged chemotherapy and radiotherapy unnecessary; follow-up showed no recurrence. The authors link JGCT to xeroderma pigmentosum (especially group C, defective nucleotide excision repair) and recommend proactive prolonged gynecological surveillance in adolescents with XP; no germline or tumor genetic testing was reported in this patient, so the XP group was not stated.  Case of ovarian JGCT in a patient with xeroderma pigmentosum; suggests but does not prove an association with DNA-repair deficiency.

title: A rare ovarian tumor in childhood: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor revealed by pelvic pain and ovarian torsion.
author: Haddar K
text: 5-year-old girl with one month of pelvic heaviness and 24 hours of acute pelvic pain, febrile, diffuse pelvic tenderness, no palpable mass. Ultrasound: large heterogeneous solid pelvic mass without cystic components or torsion signs; MRI: 41 x 57 x 48 mm solid mass, iso-intense T1, intermediate T2, restricted diffusion, heterogeneous enhancement with necrosis, abutting the recto-sigmoid junction suggesting possible infiltration; CT thorax-abdomen-pelvis showed no metastases. Markers: AFP and beta-hCG negative, LDH 269 U/L (normal 135-225), CA-125 20.4 U/mL, CA 15-3 7.2 U/mL; inhibin and AMH not measured (availability limited). Surgery: firm encapsulated 6 cm left ovarian mass, violaceous adnexa with 2 twists; detorsion and monobloc excision with partial oophorectomy; no bowel invasion; histopathology confirmed JGCT (no stage, IHC or mitotic details reported in the case section). Torsion was not recognized on preoperative imaging, which the authors attribute to the size and solid nature of the mass. Authors conclude JGCT should be considered in prepubertal girls with pelvic masses and that early surgical management has an excellent prognosis; discussion (literature-based) notes fertility-sparing surgery is preferred and that inhibin and AMH can be used to monitor recurrence.  Illustrates JGCT presenting as ovarian torsion in a 5-year-old with imaging mimicking malignancy and a fertility-sparing partial oophorectomy.

title: Surgical Management of Ovarian Masses in Children: A Comparative Analysis by Pediatric Surgeons and Gynecologists at Two Academic Hospitals in Johannesburg.
author: Mashaba NC
text: Retrospective 15-year review (2007-2022) of 288 children and adolescents (294 ovarian masses) surgically treated at two Johannesburg academic hospitals, 117 by paediatric surgery and 171 by gynecology; 51 (17.70%) were malignant. Granulosa cell tumours (adult and juvenile not separated) numbered 10 of the 51 malignant tumours and 10 of 18 malignant sex cord-stromal tumours; 4 were managed by paediatric surgery and 6 by gynecology. All 10 patients with precocious puberty in the series had sex cord-stromal tumours, specifically granulosa cell tumours. Tumour markers in granulosa cell tumours: AFP positive 0/6, beta-hCG 0/3 and CA125 3/5 (60%). Two gynecology patients (one juvenile, one adult granulosa cell tumour, FIGO IA) had minimally invasive surgery because they needed emergency exploration; all malignant tumours otherwise underwent oophorectomy, mostly open. Overall 5-year survival in the malignant cohort was 44/51 (86.28%); the 7 deaths were four yolk sac tumours, advanced dysgerminoma, stage 4 Sertoli-Leydig tumour and mesothelioma, none a granulosa cell tumour. Staging used COG in paediatric surgery (18 of 38 documented) and FIGO in gynecology (13/13); chemotherapy given to 21 of 38 paediatric surgery malignant patients was JEB or BEP, with no JGCT-specific regimen reported. The authors conclude that laparoscopic, ovary-sparing surgery should be preferred for benign lesions and call for standardised guidelines between paediatric surgeons and gynecologists.  Mixed paediatric ovarian-mass series from South Africa; JGCT-relevant content is limited to 10 granulosa cell tumours (adult and juvenile combined), all precocious puberty cases in the series, marker results and absence of deaths in this group.

title: Deciphering the Impact of AKT1 Pathogenic Variants in Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumors Using a Drosophila Model.
author: Veitia RA
text: Experimental (Drosophila) study, no patients; it models AKT1 variants previously found by the authors in human JGCTs (in-frame tandem duplications in the PH domain, >60% of JGCTs negative for GNAS variants; Q79K and W80R substitutions), cited as likely driver events. Transgenic flies expressed human WT AKT1, four duplication variants (T1, T5, T12, T15) and the Q79K-W80R double mutant under tissue-specific GAL4 drivers; all variants were expressed at similar levels and mutants showed strong Ser473 hyperphosphorylation versus WT. In follicle cells WT AKT1 was mainly cytoplasmic whereas mutants localized to the plasma membrane; mutant follicle cells were abnormally enlarged (most for Q79K-W80R), nuclei lay closer to the basal membrane (suggesting polarity defects), and mutants produced shorter or abnormal dorsal appendages, more at 25 C than 22 C. In wings, mutant AKT1 increased expressing-region surface area while reducing trichome density (larger cells rather than more cells) and raised trichome-angle dispersion; Q79K-W80R had the strongest effect. Proteomics of follicle cells: 255 differentially expressed proteins (202 up, 53 down) for all mutants vs WT (174 DEPs WT vs control, 171 with FC>=1.5), enriched for Rho GTPase signaling, autophagy, cytoskeleton and transport; WT AKT1 affected glycolysis, RNA degradation and lysosomal processes. 15 differentially phosphorylated peptides were identified (e.g. cup, LamC, Adk2, eIF4G1). RNA-Seq: 624 DEGs (353 up, 271 down) for mutants vs WT (296 for WT vs control); 79 DEGs were common to all mutants. Some genes upregulated by WT AKT1 were less activated by mutants (apparent loss of function) while another subset showed gain of function; T15 (smallest insertion) had fewest DEGs and Q79K-W80R the most. Only about 20% of differentially expressed proteins showed concordant mRNA change, interpreted as post-transcriptional (translation) regulation; AKT1 and calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase 1 were the PPI network hubs; glutathione S-transferase genes were upregulated, suggesting oxidative stress response. Authors conclude that expression of mutated AKT1 produces mutant phenotypes, supporting a probable causal role in JGCT, and that Drosophila is useful to study AKT1 pathogenic variants. AKT1 Provides in vivo functional evidence that JGCT-associated AKT1 duplications and Q79K-W80R are hyperactive and alter cell growth, polarity and proteome/transcriptome; background for AKT-targeted therapy rationale.

title: Adult granulosa cell tumours of the testis analogous to ovarian counterparts are exceptionally rare: analysis of a multicentric series and review of the literature.
author: Ricci C
text: Twenty testicular adult granulosa cell tumors (AGCT) from nine institutions (22-71 years, median 43.5) were sequenced; 12/20 yielded results, none with FOXL2 p.Cys134Trp. Three of 12 had pathogenic or likely pathogenic CTNNB1 alterations; 8/12 were wild-type for all panel genes (panel included DICER1). One CTNNB1 wild-type tumor showed areas of AGCT and foci with juvenile granulosa cell tumor-like morphology (follicles/cysts lined by small ovoid cells) with a cystic component; this is the only juvenile-like finding in the series. In the literature, only 2/29 bona fide testicular AGCTs carried FOXL2 p.Cys134Trp; the authors conclude most testicular tumors classified as AGCT are not analogous to ovarian AGCT and AGCT is a diagnosis of exclusion in the testis. Follow-up: one patient developed metastases, four others with follow-up had no recurrence (48 and 54 months for two). FOXL2 CTNNB1 KIT / MED12 Adult testicular granulosa-like tumors; included for the single tumor with JGCT-like morphology and the DICER1/CTNNB1 results. No JGCT patients (n_jgct_patients 0) and no pediatric data.

title: Management of ovarian granulosa cell tumor in childhood: a case report and recommendations for a multidisciplinary approach.
author: Arnaboldi SMC
text: Index case: a 10-month-old girl with bilateral breast enlargement (Tanner B3PH1A1), estrogenized genitalia, clitoromegaly and macrocephaly; estradiol 195 pg/mL, testosterone 1.64 ng/mL with FSH and LH <0.3 mIU/mL; elevated inhibin B; ultrasound 48 x 38 mm and MRI 56 x 34 x 46 mm solid pelvic mass; histology jGCT, capsule intact, pT1apNx, FIGO/WHO IA; no adjuvant chemotherapy; no recurrence at 15 months; overgrowth NGS panel and PTEN MLPA negative. The authors' PubMed review (search December 2024; 46 selected articles, 65 after reference screening) identified 94 pediatric jGCT cases (<18 years): mean age 7.2 years (range 0-17); 15 (15.9%) infants, 42 (44.7%) aged 1-8 years, 37 (39.4%) older than 8; 27 (28.7%) post-pubertal. Presentation in 57 patients aged <=8 years: isosexual precocious puberty 43 (75.4%), vaginal bleeding 18 (31.6%), heterosexual precocious puberty 20 (35.1%; pubarche 29.8%, clitoromegaly 8.8%); in 27 post-pubertal patients menstrual irregularities 11 (40.7%). Among all 94: abdominal mass 32 (34.0%), pain 17 (18.1%), distension 15 (15.9%), ascites 8 (8.5%), acute abdomen from rupture 5 (5.3%), Meigs syndrome 2 (2.1%). Inhibin A/B and AMH were reported as constantly elevated before surgery in previously published jGCT cases; estradiol and testosterone may serve as tumor markers when elevated preoperatively. Two ultrasound patterns are described: solid heterogeneous, and multilocular 'Swiss cheese'. Stage: 71.2% of 66 patients with stage specified were FIGO/WHO I; 95.7% of 47 FIGO I patients were alive at last follow-up; 78.9% of 19 stage II-IV patients received adjuvant chemotherapy; overall 92.7% of 69 patients with outcome data alive (mean follow-up 4.8 years, range 0.2-18); 81.2% of 16 advanced-stage patients alive (mean 4.4 years); 24.6% of 69 had follow-up <1.5 years. Three of five FIGO IC2 patients in the review received no adjuvant chemotherapy and were alive at 3-8 years follow-up, although EXPeRT/PARTNER recommends adjuvant chemotherapy for IC2 and IC3. Relapse occurred in 17.0% of 94 patients (mean time to relapse 1.4 years, range 0.12-8) and 43.7% of those relapsing died of disease; 4.3% developed a contralateral ovarian tumor (median 2.3 years, range 0.12-7); the authors state up to 10% may develop a contralateral metachronous tumor. Genetic or systemic conditions were found in 21 (22.3%) of 94: Ollier disease 14, Maffucci syndrome 1, ovotesticular DSD 1, DICER1 syndrome 1, Beckwith-Wiedemann 1, Li-Fraumeni plus PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome 1, NF1 1, tuberous sclerosis 1. Both the DICER1 and the LFS/PHTS patient died of tumor. Secondary malignancy occurred in 6 (6.4%), including 2 contralateral metachronous jGCT. Recommendations summarized (as authors' recommendations from EXPeRT/PARTNER and ESGO/SIOPE sources): fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for stage I with staging inspection, tumorectomy not generally recommended, no debulking in disseminated disease except palliative, PEB or PEI 4 cycles (6 if metastatic) for advanced disease, follow-up every 3 months for the first 3 years, and genetic counselling; authors propose multidisciplinary flowcharts for diagnosis and follow-up. (genetic testing) Pediatric-focused synthesis and 94-case literature review of juvenile granulosa cell tumor providing pooled presentation, stage, relapse and syndrome-association figures plus a multidisciplinary management flowchart.

title: Advances in non-germ cell tumours of the testis: focus on new molecular developments in sex cord-stromal tumours.
author: Lobo J
text: Narrative review of testicular sex cord-stromal tumours (TSCSTs, 4%-8% of testicular neoplasms; ~90%-95% benign, 5%-10% malignant and unresponsive to chemo- and radiotherapy), summarizing molecular findings and TESST group classification recommendations. Testicular juvenile granulosa cell tumour (JGCT) is described as an infantile disease that appears invariably benign, presenting largely in the first year of life (90% in infants 6 months or younger), mostly as a testicular mass; gynecomastia in rare patients; some associated with gonadal dysgenesis. Pathology: well-circumscribed multicystic or solid and cystic tumours with follicles containing eosinophilic or basophilic secretions, small round cells with scant eosinophilic cytoplasm, fibrous/myxoid stroma bands; solid areas may have spindle cells or reticular pattern mimicking yolk sac tumour. Mitotic activity may be prominent (>5-10 per 10 HPF) without aggressive behaviour; necrosis, lymphovascular invasion and rete testis involvement described in rare cases. Molecular: ovarian JGCT show AKT1 PH-domain internal tandem duplications and codon 201 GNAS mutations, which have not been identified in testicular JGCT; testicular JGCT shows monosomy 10 in ~60%. Immunohistochemistry: beta-catenin membranous (no nuclear), SF1, inhibin, calretinin, SOX9 and FOXL2 variably positive; classic sex cord markers are non-specific. TESST recommendation 8: testicular JGCT should be re-classified as 'benign juvenile-type granulosa cell tumour' to avoid confusion with ovarian JGCT, which has malignant potential (~10%), to prevent over-treatment and unnecessary work-ups; Table 4 lists JGCT as an example of invariably benign TSCST. Testicular adult-type granulosa cell tumour is a heterogeneous diagnostic category; FOXL2 p.C134W occurs only anecdotally in testicular cases (versus >90% of ovarian adult GCT). Therapeutic section is about malignant TSCSTs generally (CDK4, mTOR, PARP, Wnt and CD30-directed options experimental); none JGCT-specific. chromosome 10 AKT1 GNAS Contrasts testicular JGCT (benign infantile tumour, monosomy 10, no AKT1/GNAS) with ovarian JGCT and endorses re-labelling it as benign juvenile-type granulosa cell tumour.

title: Gynandroblastoma With a Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor Component Presenting as Ovarian Torsion in a 14-Year-Old Female Patient.
author: Su L
text: A 14-year-old girl presented with abdominal pain and a 16 x 12 x 10 cm predominantly solid left adnexal mass suspected to be torsed; menarche at 10 with irregular menses, no virilization or known syndrome. Preoperative markers: LDH 480 U/L, CA-125 93.2 U/mL, inhibin B 1,453.1 pg/mL (reference <362), AFP 35.3 ng/mL (upper limit of normal); CEA and CA 19-9 normal. Left salpingo-oophorectomy removed a 20.5 x 14.2 x 14.0 cm solid yellowish mass with intact capsule; the tumor was gynandroblastoma with a JGCT component (30-40% of volume) and a moderately differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor component (60-70%). Both components were positive for SF-1, calretinin and FOXL2, negative for SALL4, myogenin and MyoD1, with variable inhibin positivity. Stage FIGO I (2014); no adjuvant treatment; a pathogenic germline DICER1 mutation was found and the patient entered a DICER1 surveillance program. The authors cite that gynandroblastoma with a JGCT component has only 10 other English-language reports, mean age 28 years, and that the OTST Registry suggested DICER1-predisposed tumors present younger (16 vs 21 years) with better survival than tumor-limited mutations; poor prognostic factors cited are preoperative rupture and poorly differentiated SLCT. The authors conclude that ovarian torsion can be the first presentation, that rupture would upstage the disease, and that germline DICER1 testing is recommended for ovarian SLCT or gynandroblastoma per cited International DICER1 Symposium guidance. DICER1 Case of a mixed sex cord-stromal tumor with a JGCT component in an adolescent with a germline DICER1 mutation, relevant to the JGCT/DICER1 relationship and to differential diagnosis.

title: Improving diagnosis and management of pediatric ovarian masses: development of a risk stratification model incorporating sonographic and clinical features.
author: Chu L
text: Single-center retrospective study (Children's Hospital of Soochow University, China; 2018-2024) of 344 patients aged <=18 years (348 masses) who had ovarian surgery; aim was a sonographic/clinical malignancy prediction model. Histology: germ cell tumors 72.7% (253/348), epithelial 15.2% (53), sex-cord stromal 2.0% (7), follicular cysts 10.1% (35); malignant lesions 11.5% (40/348). Sex-cord stromal tumors (7) comprised juvenile granulosa cell tumor 4/7 (57.1%), Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor 2/7 and fibroma 1/7; by age, JGCT occurred in 3 children aged 1-8 years and 1 aged 9-16 years (none under 1). No JGCT-specific clinical, marker, imaging, stage, treatment or outcome data are reported; JGCT patients are not analyzed separately. Authors attribute the greater frequency of precocious puberty in malignant than benign masses (20.0% vs 8.6%, p=0.025) to hormone-secreting tumors such as juvenile granulosa cell tumors (an interpretation, not a JGCT-specific measurement). Model result: solid component proportion >80% strongest malignancy predictor (OR 576.5, 95% CI 74.0-4492.6); combined size plus solid proportion AUC 0.93, sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 83.2%.  Very limited: a general paediatric ovarian mass surgical series reporting 4 JGCT (of 348 masses) in an age table; no JGCT-specific outcomes.

title: Minimally invasive surgery guidelines in paediatric surgical oncology - role of MIS in fertility preservation.
author: Cornet M
text: Chapter on minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and fertility preservation in paediatric surgical oncology; JGCT is mentioned only once, as an example of rare malignancy that can occur even in cystic ovarian lesions. Authors do not recommend laparoscopic ovarian tumour resection in children; laparotomy via supra-pubic approach remains preferred because malignancy may be present even in cystic lesions (e.g. rare cases of juvenile granulosa cell tumours) and intraoperative rupture would worsen prognosis. In asymptomatic girls with an ovarian mass, work-up includes imaging and markers (alpha-fetoprotein, hCG, inhibin B, anti-Mullerian hormone, calcium); laparoscopic exploration is recommended as first step to assess the lesion and stage disease, followed by laparotomy for resection. Benign tumours are ~90% of childhood ovarian lesions; ovarian-sparing surgery should always be considered; in acute torsion or rupture, laparoscopic exploration with ascites sampling and detorsion is advised, with oophorectomy discussed only if malignant features are seen. Large tumours extending beyond the umbilicus are a contraindication to open-entry laparoscopy because of the rupture risk; laparotomy first. Other fertility-preservation topics (ovarian transposition for pelvic radiotherapy, uterine transposition, ovarian tissue cryopreservation) are covered generally, not specific to JGCT.  Surgical guidance relevant to JGCT management only by implication: favours open, rupture-avoiding ovarian-sparing surgery for paediatric ovarian masses where JGCT is possible.

title: Ultrasonic, Clinical, and Pathological Characteristics of Malignant Ovarian Tumors in Children.
author: Wei Y
text: Single-center retrospective study (Children's Hospital of Zhejiang University, 2020-2024) of 49 girls with malignant ovarian tumors: germ cell tumors 37 (75.5%), sex cord-stromal tumors 8 (16.3%), lymphoma 4 (8.2%). The authors state the sex cord-stromal tumors were mainly juvenile granulosa cell tumors; the exact JGCT count is not given. Sex cord-stromal tumors (n=8): mean maximum diameter 9.60 cm; 5/8 were 10 cm or smaller; solid or predominantly solid in 4/8; no calcification; O-RADS 4 in 4 and O-RADS 5 in 4; AFP median 1.11 ng/mL (IQR 0.71-1.62), far below germ cell tumors. A representative case: a 12-year-old girl with a 9.4 x 7.4 x 6.4 cm solid right adnexal mass, minimal flow, O-RADS 5, twisted 540 degrees at surgery, with juvenile granulosa cell tumor on pathology. Torsion occurred in 1/8 sex cord-stromal tumors; rupture in none. Authors attribute precocious puberty and menstrual irregularity to estrogen secretion; no treatment or outcome data were collected (authors note lack of long-term prognostic data).  Imaging and clinical features of pediatric sex cord-stromal tumors (mainly JGCT per the authors) at one center: solid, non-calcified, AFP-normal, estrogenic presentation in a minority; no JGCT-specific outcomes.

title: Management of andrological disorders from childhood and adolescence to transition age: guidelines from the Italian Society of Andrology and Sexual Medicine (SIAMS) in collaboration with the Italian Society for Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology (SIEDP) - part-2.
author: Bonomi M
text: Scope: this is a long Italian (SIAMS with SIEDP) GRADE-based guideline Part 2 on andrological disorders from childhood to transition age (minipuberty, cryptorchidism, disorders of sex development, micropenis, hypospadias, epididymitis/orchitis, testicular tumors, testicular torsion); it is not specific to JGCT and the testicular tumor chapter is the only relevant part. JGCT is mentioned once: in children and adolescents most testicular tumors are germ cell tumors, and sex cord-stromal tumors, including juvenile granulosa cell, Leydig and Sertoli cell tumors, are rare (10-13%) and usually benign in children, though malignancy is occasionally observed in adolescents and young adults. Pre-pubertal testicular tumors are described as very rare, generally benign and rarely metastatic, whereas post-pubertal tumors are malignant in 75% of cases and 20-30% present with distant metastases; prepubertal tumors are almost exclusively benign teratomas/dermoid cysts with yolk sac tumor the malignant exception. Diagnosis: scrotal ultrasound for any palpable testicular mass (R6.1, strong); serum tumor markers alpha-FP, beta-hCG and LDH before treatment, and in prepubertal patients alpha-FP alone is sufficient to discriminate malignant from benign tumors (R6.4); the guideline states that no male over 6 months of age with a testicular lesion and alpha-FP <100 ng/mL has a malignant tumor. Surgery: testis-sparing surgery with intraoperative frozen section is recommended in prepubertal tumors with negative markers (R6.9) and partial orchiectomy with frozen section is called standard practice because of the high rate of benign lesions; orchiectomy for very large lesions occupying the whole testicle or alpha-FP >100 ng/mL. Staging: not required for benign prepubertal tumors; prepubertal staging uses the COG system; the guideline recommends at least abdominal MRI in sex cord-stromal tumors because 10% are malignant with poor prognosis. No JGCT-specific recommendation, incidence, marker or outcome data, and no reference to JGCT's age at presentation or hormonal activity, are given.  General andrology guideline with one sentence classing testicular juvenile granulosa cell tumor among rare, usually benign sex cord-stromal tumors of childhood; its prepubertal testicular tumor recommendations (alpha-FP triage, testis-sparing surgery with frozen section) are the context in which testicular JGCT is managed.

title: Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Ovary in Pregnancy: A Case Report.
author: Khoiwal K
text: 28-year-old primigravida (conceived after ovulation induction) at 22+5 weeks presented with 1 month of dull abdominal pain; ultrasound showed a 15 x 11 cm predominantly solid right adnexal mass with mild ascites; MRI 14 x 11 x 13 cm solid-cystic right ovarian mass with omental thickening (O-RADS 5). Markers: CA-125 785 U/ml, AFP 51 ng/ml, beta-hCG 33547 mIU/ml (in pregnancy); inhibin B within normal limits (86.5 ng/ml) at 32 weeks and raised at 36 weeks (118 ng/ml). Surgery at 23+4 weeks: about 500 ml ascites, 15 x 10 cm solid right ovarian mass with intact capsule, omental nodularity; right salpingo-oophorectomy, infracolic omentectomy, left ovarian biopsy and bilateral paracolic gutter biopsies; ascites cytology, left ovary, omentum and peritoneal biopsies negative. Histology: sheets and nests of small cuboidal-polygonal cells with scant cytoplasm and grooved nuclei, necrosis and hemorrhage; IHC inhibin and calretinin positive; final diagnosis JGCT FIGO stage IA. Because of rising inhibin B, repeat MRI showed no recurrence; elective cesarean at 37 weeks with re-exploration and pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy (frozen and final histopathology negative); uterus and left ovary preserved; no adjuvant chemotherapy; disease-free at 24 months. Literature table of 12 published JGCT-in-pregnancy cases (since 1993): stages from IA to IIIB; stage IIIB and IC cases received chemotherapy (BEP, paclitaxel-carboplatin, or methotrexate/actinomycin D/chlorambucil) with disease-free follow-up of 30, 84 months in some; one IC3 case recurred at 3 months. Authors state that adjuvant chemotherapy is advised for mitotic index >20 per 10 HPF or stage IC or above; inhibin B (unlike inhibin A) is not affected by pregnancy and is a sensitive marker; conclusion that stage IA has excellent prognosis and fertility-preserving surgery has a role.  Adds a pregnancy-associated adult-onset JGCT case with surveillance by inhibin B and a tabulated review of published cases and management.

title: Folate receptor alpha (FRα) expression in tubo-ovarian and endometrial tumors: a study of 923 cases.
author: Töltési I
text: Tissue-microarray immunohistochemistry study of 923 tubo-ovarian and endometrial tumors (796 tubo-ovarian, 127 endometrial) with the VENTANA FOLR1 CDx assay; sex cord-stromal tumors numbered 338: 249 adult GCT, 4 JGCT, 35 Sertoli-Leydig tumors and 50 fibromas/thecomas. All 4 JGCTs were FRalpha negative (0/4; range and H-score 0). All other sex cord-stromal tumors were also negative (AGCT 0/249, SLT 0/35, F/T 0/50). FRalpha positivity was highest in serous tumors: HGSC 47/104 (45%), LGSC 22/87 (25%), endometrial serous carcinoma 3/27 (11%), serous borderline tumor 3/30 (10%); endometrioid 1/47 and clear cell 1/86 ovarian carcinomas positive; mucinous tumors negative. The authors state that sex cord-stromal tumors were analyzed for the first time in this series and that FRalpha-targeted therapy (mirvetuximab soravtansine, approved for platinum-resistant HGSC) has only been studied in HGSC; no role for it in JGCT is shown. FOLR1 (FRalpha protein) Minor: negative FRalpha immunohistochemistry in 4 JGCTs within a large series that is otherwise about epithelial tumors; no clinical data for the JGCT cases.

title: A novel classification of testicular sex cord-stromal tumours from the Testicular Sex Cord-Stromal Tumour (TESST) group: a collaboration of the Genitourinary Pathology Society (GUPS) and the International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP).
author: Acosta AM
text: Consensus classification of testicular sex cord-stromal tumours (TSCSTs) by the 30-member TESST group (GUPS and ISUP), developed through consensus activities in 2023-2025 including meetings in Baltimore (March 2024) and Boston (March 2025); hierarchical tiers: group, category, entity, histological pattern. 'Juvenile granulosa cell tumour' of the testis is renamed 'benign juvenile granulosa cell tumour' within the category granulosa cell tumours (defined as a benign, largely infantile testicular sex cord tumour closely resembling ovarian juvenile GCT). Rationale: testicular JGCT is largely infantile (>90% in the first year of life), hormonally inactive, not reported in adults; molecular alterations of ovarian JGCT have not been identified in testicular counterparts, which show monosomy 10 (~60%); testicular JGCT appears invariably indolent and cured by surgical resection. The descriptor 'benign' is meant to avoid overtreatment and excessive work-up because a subset of the more common ovarian JGCT shows malignant behaviour; authors state benign testicular JGCT does not require aggressive treatment or long-term follow-up after complete resection. Other changes: Sertoli cell tumour NOS becomes 'usual type'; inflammatory and nested testicular sex cord tumour (EWSR1::ATF1) is a new malignant entity; FH-deficient Leydig cell tumour and spindle cell gonadal stromal tumour are new entities; testicular Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour provisionally included (a DICER1 RNase IIIb hotspot mutation reported in one case). Limitations stated: relies on limited datasets, limited molecular validation for some entities, considerable interobserver variability, some entities provisional. chromosome 10 AKT1/GNAS Formal expert-consensus nomenclature that separates benign infantile testicular JGCT from ovarian JGCT, relevant to counselling and to avoiding overtreatment of testicular cases.

title: Ovarian Sex Cord Stromal Tumors in Children and Adolescents-The European Standard Clinical Practice Recommendations.
author: Schneider DT
text: European Standard Clinical Practice guideline from EXPeRT/ERN PaedCan for ovarian sex cord stromal tumors (OSCST) in children and adolescents, based on national and one European cohort analyses, a systematic literature review and expert consensus; evidence mostly level III (prospective cohorts) with grades A-E; no high-level (I-II) evidence exists.
