Diagnostic work-up: history (puberty, Ollier or Peutz-Jeghers, DICER1-spectrum family history), AFP, beta-hCG/total HCG to exclude germ cell tumor (note approximately 10% of SLCT show AFP up to 1000 ug/L), inhibin (Level III, Grade B), estrogen, DHEAS, LH, FSH, calcium (elevated calcium suggests small cell carcinoma, hypercalcemic type, the most important differential of JGCT), CA125; abdominal ultrasound and pelvic/abdominal MRI; chest imaging only if symptoms, abdominal metastases or DICER1 surveillance. JGCT characteristics per the guideline (Table 1): bimodal age (children versus adolescents/young adults), estrogen producing, signs of precocious puberty, abdominal distension or pain, favorable prognosis in stage IA-IC1; adult GCT is distinguished by FOXL2 mutation, occurs in adults and elderly and may recur very late (>10 years). Pathology: stage with the updated FIGO system for epithelial ovarian cancer, WHO classification, reference pathology required (Level III, Grade A); in JGCT the proliferation rate and mitotic index are prognostic (Level III, Grade B); SLCT should be checked for JGCT components and vice versa. Genetics: DICER1 testing advised in anaplastic JGCT (Level IV, Grade B) and in all SLCT; in multiple enchondromatosis (Ollier, Maffucci) with JGCT, germline testing is recommended and tumor tissue should be analysed for IDH1/IDH2; McCune-Albright (somatic GNAS) has also been described with JGCT. Surgery: open approach to avoid rupture (rupture is a major recurrence risk); laparoscopy only if rupture can be safely avoided; ascites or peritoneal lavage cytology, peritoneal biopsies of suspicious areas, lymph node biopsy only if suspicious; unilateral oophorectomy usually sufficient for encapsulated tumors; no contralateral biopsy, hysterectomy avoided, omentectomy not routine; after ovary-sparing excision with high mitotic count in JGCT, re-excision with oophorectomy is recommended (Level III, Grade B). Chemotherapy (Table 3): stage IA/IB surveillance; IC1 JGCT surveillance (consider chemotherapy if high mitotic count); IC2/IC3 JGCT 3(-4) or 4 cycles PEI/VIP or BEP; II-III at least 4(-6) cycles; extension to 5-6 cycles may be considered for JGCT with high mitotic index; carboplatin/paclitaxel proved as effective as cisplatin regimens in adults with OSCST in a study that included no JGCT. Radiotherapy not routinely recommended; GnRH blockade may be an add-on for relapsed tumors (Level V, Grade C), citing an infant with bilateral testicular JGCT who achieved complete remission with GnRH inhibitors as sole therapy. Follow-up: tumor markers (inhibin, estrogen/testosterone, CA125) if previously elevated; examination with abdominal and pelvic ultrasound every 3 months for the first 2 years after therapy, then longer intervals; MRI only if ultrasound unclear; no routine imaging above the diaphragm. Relapse: usually within 2 years (except adult GCT), most often peritoneal, prognosis poor with long-term survival approximately 20% or lower even in chemotherapy-naive patients; metachronous contralateral tumors (often with DICER1) usually appear after 2 years or more and have prognosis comparable to a first tumor. DICER1 IDH1/IDH2 GNAS FOXL2 Current European consensus standard for staging, surgery, risk-based adjuvant chemotherapy (cisplatin-based, from IC2), genetic testing and follow-up of pediatric ovarian JGCT.

title: Peripheral Precocious Puberty as the Initial Manifestation of Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor in Early Childhood.
author: Bouramdane S
text: A 2-year-9-month-old girl had 5 months of progressive breast development, persistent whitish discharge, vaginal bleeding for 15 days and a firm left pelvic mass of about 10 cm. LH <0.10 IU/L and FSH <0.30 IU/L (suppressed) with inhibin B >5000 pg/mL (reference <182); AMH 6.88 ng/mL, DHEAS, androstenedione, AFP 1.3 ng/mL and beta-hCG were normal; preoperative estradiol result was unavailable for review and bone age was not assessed. CT showed a 103 x 63 x 117 mm heterogeneous enhancing suprauterine mass with moderate ascites and endometrial thickening of 5 mm; MRI showed a 110 x 55 x 99 mm multilocular solid-cystic mass with hemorrhagic components, diffusion restriction and left pedicle twisting. Surgery found a well-encapsulated left ovarian tumor (10.5 x 8 x 6 cm); left oophorectomy preserved the ipsilateral tube, contralateral ovary and uterus. Ascitic cytology and omentum were negative; stage FIGO IA. Histology showed lobulated solid areas with cystic spaces, round cells with vesicular nuclei, necrosis foci and 8 mitoses per 10 HPF; IHC was calretinin and androgen receptor positive, focal inhibin positive, and CK19, AFP and CD117 negative. No adjuvant chemotherapy was given; at 12 months estrogenic signs had resolved, inhibin B, LH, FSH and estradiol were normal and there was no clinical, biochemical or radiological recurrence. The authors discuss (citing other studies) that mitotic index >19/10 HPF was associated with recurrences in an international cohort, that inhibin B was elevated in 90% of tested patients at diagnosis but only 3 of 5 evaluable relapsing patients re-elevated at relapse, and that AKT1 duplications rather than FOXL2 C134W characterize JGCT. The authors conclude that progressive estrogenic signs in a prepubertal girl should prompt pelvic imaging for an ovarian tumor and that complete resection of localized disease is generally curative.  Single well-documented case of FIGO IA JGCT in a toddler with peripheral precocious puberty, very high inhibin B and surgery-only management.

title: Rare Tumours in Children and Adolescents (STEP 2.0) registry (NCT05773651)
text: Observational, prospective, case-only patient registry (STEP 2.0) of rare solid tumors in children and adolescents; sponsor University Hospital Tuebingen; status RECRUITING (verified 2024-09); start 2023-01-11; estimated enrollment 10,000; target duration 50 years; primary completion estimated 2050-01. Aim: collect and evaluate experience and data on diagnosis and treatment of rare childhood tumors; includes biological and molecular genetic research and collaboration with the European EXPeRT group. Eligibility: diagnosis of a rare solid tumor from the neonatal period to 18 years; written consent; not recorded in another GPOH (German Society for Pediatric Oncology and Hematology) study or register; young adults may be registered or referred on request with consent. Primary outcome: event-free survival (time from study entry to failure of induction therapy, recurrence or death from any cause), time frame 5 years. Data collected include pathology (reference pathology) findings, name, birth date, gender and consent; pseudonymised data are to be shared with national and international rare-tumor databases. The registry record does not mention juvenile granulosa cell tumor or sex cord-stromal tumors by name and has no posted results.  German national registry for rare pediatric tumors; JGCT is not named in the registry entry, so its role as a JGCT data source is not stated by this record itself.

title: DICER1-Related Tumor Predisposition (GeneReviews, NBK196157)
author: Schultz KAP
text: GeneReviews chapter (initial posting 2014-04-24, last update 2026-03-25) on DICER1-related tumor predisposition; more than 1,500 individuals with a germline DICER1 pathogenic variant identified from literature and unpublished International PPB/DICER1 Registry and NIH Natural History Study data; population prevalence estimated at 1 in 6,099 to 8,416. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor (juvGCT) is listed among ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors that should prompt DICER1 consideration, 'especially if anaplasia and/or high mitotic index'; Table 2 states 'Juvenile granulosa cell tumor is rarely assoc w/DICER1', whereas about 10% of DICER1 carriers develop ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors and up to 60% of persons with SLCT or gynandroblastoma have DICER1. JuvGCT, especially anaplastic juvGCT, 'may be associated with DICER1' (Baillard 2021, Onder 2021, Boyraz 2026 cited). Presentation: abdominal pain, distention or mass; precocious puberty, secondary amenorrhea or virilization; markers variable (inhibin A, inhibin B, CA125, testosterone); inhibin B may be elevated at diagnosis and at recurrence. Prognosis of juvGCT: generally favorable at stage 1A or 1C1; high mitotic index, anaplastic features or higher stage are associated with worse prognosis; WHO classifies juvGCT as borderline malignant potential, but malignant behavior is described in older children, adolescents and those with higher-stage or higher mitotic index tumors. Treatment: surgical resection with staging per modified FIGO (NCCN); no formal lymph node dissection of normal-appearing nodes; fertility-sparing surgery recommended for most girls and young women; avoid tumor rupture (timing of rupture should be documented). Treatment regimens were mainly studied in granulosa cell tumors and are usually platinum-based; clinical trials are lacking. EXPeRT/PARTNER consensus (Schneider 2021) as summarized: adjuvant chemotherapy for all children and adolescents with juvGCT higher than stage IC1; high mitotic index (MI >=20 per 10 high-power fields) strongly predicts worse prognosis and recurrence in low-stage high-MI cases has been reported, so adjuvant chemotherapy for high MI but low stage may be considered individually. Preoperative work-up when an ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor is suspected: testosterone, AFP, inhibin A and B, estradiol to find a usable tumor marker; abdominopelvic CT or MRI; baseline chest CT reasonable. SLCT and rarely juvGCT may secrete AFP, leading to consideration of immature teratoma or yolk sac tumor; markers may or may not be elevated at recurrence. Gynandroblastoma usually has both SLCT and juvGCT components; gynandroblastoma with SLCT and follicular differentiation mimicking juvGCT is considered better classified as SLCT and is associated with DICER1. Surveillance for DICER1 carriers (female reproductive tract incl. juvGCT): symptom review every 6 months or at each visit and pelvic ultrasound every 6 months from diagnosis until at least age 40 years (95% of SLCT diagnosed before 40; shared decision after 40); pelvic ultrasound judged more sensitive than biochemical surveillance. Other schedules: chest radiograph, chest CT at 3 and 30 months, thyroid US every 3 years from age 8, abdominal US every 6 months to age 8 then annually to 12. Testing: DICER1 diagnosis requires a heterozygous germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant (sequence analysis detects >90%, deletion/duplication analysis <10%); tumor tissue testing for somatic DICER1 variants may suggest a germline variant but biallelic somatic variants have been found without germline variants; about 10% of de novo carriers are mosaic. Cascade testing of first-degree relatives recommended; newborns of at-risk families tested before 4 months. Penetrance is reduced and age dependent: in 102 non-proband carriers 5.3% had a neoplasm by age 10 years and 19.3% by age 50 (females 26.5%, males 10.2%). Ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors present most often in the reproductive years (95% before age 40). Contralateral metachronous SLCT reported in nearly 20% at ten years in DICER1-related SLCT. DICER1 FOXL2 Authoritative clinical-genetics chapter placing JGCT within the DICER1 spectrum as a rare and mainly anaplastic or high-mitotic-index association, and giving DICER1 testing, pelvic ultrasound surveillance and adjuvant chemotherapy thresholds relevant to JGCT.

title: Atypical presentations of dicer1 syndrome in adults with juvenile granulosa cell tumor
author: Hamai C
text: Two women (20 and 25 years old) had complex abdominal masses on imaging; final pathology after exploratory laparotomy with mass removal and staging was juvenile granulosa cell tumor (JGCT) in both. Both then had genetic testing showing heterozygous germline DICER1 pathogenic variants: patient 1 DICER1 c.556delT (all three of her male children were also found to carry it); patient 2 DICER1 c.2988-20_2988del, with malignant follicular thyroid carcinoma diagnosed at age 11. Family histories of both suggested undiagnosed DICER1 syndrome in multiple relatives. Authors conclude the association of JGCTs with DICER1 syndrome may be underrecognized and underreported; they describe JGCT as rarely seen with this syndrome. DICER1 DICER1 Two adult JGCT cases with germline DICER1 variants, supporting testing for DICER1 in JGCT.

title: Prepubertal Testicular Tumors in Children: Combined Ultrasound and Pathologic Study
author: Ma Y
text: Single-center retrospective study (Capital Center for Children's Health, Beijing; Nov 2016 to Jun 2024) of pathologically confirmed prepubertal testicular tumors aged 0-14 years: 125 identified, 8 excluded for incomplete US, 117 patients included (median age 27 months, IQR 8.5-83.5), 118 lesions. Histology: mature teratoma prepubertal type 62 (52.5%), yolk sac tumor 20 (16.9%), epidermoid cyst 12 (10.2%), immature teratoma 6 (5.1%), dermoid cyst 4 (3.4%), Leydig cell tumor 2, hemangioma 2, rhabdomyosarcoma 2, juvenile granulosa cell tumor 1 (0.8%), Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor 1, mixed teratoma and yolk sac tumor 1, seminoma 1, secondary tumors 4 (2 ALL, 1 Burkitt lymphoma, 1 neuroblastoma). The single JGCT patient was 2 months old with a 3.9 cm tumor; AFP was 244.19 ng/mL (all other non-yolk-sac, non-mixed tumors had normal AFP), and preoperative testosterone was elevated in this patient (also in 2 Leydig cell tumors and 6 teratomas); beta-hCG normal in all. US of the JGCT was predominantly cystic ('Swiss cheese' multilocular pattern, hypoechoic or isoechoic solid components with increased vascularity); the authors describe JGCT as showing pathognomonic 'swiss-cheese' morphology and classify it among benign tumors with cystic or cystic-dominant pattern. Cystic or cystic-dominant US pattern: PPV 96.1% (95% CI 85.4-99.3) for benignity, NPV 47.8%; solid or solid-dominant: NPV 91.5% for malignancy, PPV 49.2%; solid pattern plus AFP >300 ng/mL for yolk sac tumors: PPV 94.7% (95% CI 71.9-99.7), NPV 97.0% (95% CI 90.8-99.2). Discussion (authors, citing literature): testicular JGCT is the most common congenital testicular tumor, typically within the first 6 months of life, benign and hormonally inactive, rarely recurring after testis-sparing surgery; normal or mildly elevated AFP differentiates it from yolk sac tumor. Authors conclude combined US and pathology offers a diagnostic framework for risk stratification and testis-sparing decisions. No treatment or outcome data are reported for the JGCT patient.  Contributes one testicular JGCT in a 2-month-old with the characteristic multicystic ultrasound pattern and mildly raised AFP in a 118-lesion pediatric testicular tumor series.

title: Childhood Ovarian Cancer Treatment (PDQ) - Health Professional Version: Childhood Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumors section
text: NCI PDQ summary (updated 03/03/2025, editorial changes only) on childhood ovarian cancer; most ovarian masses in children are not malignant; malignant types in order are germ cell, epithelial, stromal, other; most malignant ovarian tumors occur in girls aged 15 to 19 years. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor (JGCT) is the most common sex cord-stromal tumor subtype in girls younger than 18 years (median age 7.6 years; range birth to 17.5 years); about 5% of ovarian tumors in children and adolescents; distinct from adult granulosa cell tumors. Risk factors: JGCT has been reported in children with Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome (cited case reports). Presentation: precocious puberty (most common, from estrogen secretion), abdominal pain, abdominal mass, ascites. Metastatic spread of sex cord-stromal tumors is rare, usually confined to the peritoneal cavity, and distant metastases mostly occur at relapse. As many as 90% of children with JGCT have FIGO stage I disease and are usually curable with unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy alone; in one series 15 of 17 had fertility-sparing surgery and only 2 got adjuvant chemotherapy, with no recurrences. Patients with spontaneous rupture or malignant ascites (FIGO IC2, IC3), advanced disease (stages II-IV) or high mitotic activity have poorer prognosis and require chemotherapy; cisplatin-based regimens have been used with some success in adjuvant and recurrent settings. Prognostic factors in pediatric sex cord-stromal tumors (German MAKEI, 54 patients, 48 stage I, 6 peritoneal metastases): stage IC, preoperative rupture, stages II-III and high mitotic count identify patients at risk. French TGM-95 registry (38 girls): of 15 with rupture and/or ascites, 11 received chemotherapy without recurrence while all 4 who did not receive chemotherapy recurred and 2 died. DICER1: the PDQ links Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, not JGCT, to germline DICER1 variants (191 SLCT patients in registries; 58% of 156 tested had a germline P/LP variant; RNase IIIb hotspot variants in 97% (88/91) of intermediate/poorly differentiated tumors; 3-year RFS 93.6% stage IA vs 67.1% IC vs 60.6% stage II-IV). Registries and consensus: US International Ovarian and Testicular Stromal Tumor Registry; European national rare tumor groups; EXPeRT/PARTNER consensus recommendations on diagnosis and therapy; work-up, staging and therapy harmonized between registries. Table of FIGO staging for ovarian carcinoma provided (IA to IVB).  Authoritative NCI summary of JGCT epidemiology, presentation, stage distribution and the stage and mitotic-rate-based indication for cisplatin-based chemotherapy.

title: International Ovarian & Testicular Stromal Tumor Registry (NCT01970696)
text: International OTST Registry (Children's Hospitals and Clinics of Minnesota; PI Kris Ann Schultz) collects clinical and biologic data on ovarian and testicular stromal tumors; status RECRUITING (verified 2026-10); start 2011-12-08; estimated enrollment 500; primary completion estimated 2030-12-31. Arms: ovarian stromal tumors, testicular stromal tumors, ovarian small cell carcinoma; keywords include juvenile granulosa cell tumor, Sertoli, Leydig, gynandroblastoma. Eligibility: all patients with a suspected gonadal stromal tumor or similar tumor, any age, most expected under 20. Rationale stated: ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors have been associated with pleuropulmonary blastoma/DICER1; DICER1 mutations are seen in some patients with ovarian tumors; ovarian stromal tumors are highly curable when found at early stage but later-stage forms are aggressive and often fatal. Six registry goals: understand risk factors (age, subtype, histology, invasiveness, differentiation, metastasis); collect personal and family history incl. germline DICER1 status; relate gene expression/DNA alterations to predisposition, behavior and outcome; determine optimal screening; refine treatment algorithms; bank annotated tumor and germline specimens. Enrollment is by local diagnosis with central pathology review offered; requested materials are blood for DNA and lymphoblastoid cell lines, slides/blocks/snap-frozen/fresh tumor; cases come from clinician or pathologist referral, family self-referral, and requests to authors of published cases. Primary outcome: DICER1 mutations in ovarian and testicular stromal tumors (germline and tumor sequencing, mRNA/miRNA expression correlated with outcome), 3 years; secondary: clinical factors associated with outcome (10 years) and pathologic/genetic correlations (5 years). No results posted.  The registry that underlies several JGCT-relevant reports (including the OTST conference abstracts); it explicitly lists juvenile granulosa cell tumor among its tumor types and enrolls patients, families and biospecimens.

title: cBioPortal public instance: samples with OncoTree GRCT / 'Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor' across public studies (queried 2026-10-30)
text: Re-run this session of a scan of all 551 public cBioPortal studies (attributes ONCOTREE_CODE, CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED, CANCER_TYPE) found the label 'Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor' on exactly one sample: P-0013654-N01 in msk_ch_ped_2021 (a normal/blood sample from a clonal hematopoiesis study; patient AGE 6.611909866, female, White; CHEMO_TX, CISPLATIN_TX, PLATINUM_TX, TOPO_II_TX all Yes; no mutations listed). The same patient's tumor sample P-0013654-T01-IM5 in msk_impact_50k_2026 is labeled only 'Granulosa Cell Tumor' (GRCT): AGE_AT_DX 6, primary site ovary, IMPACT410 panel, MUTATION_COUNT 0, FRACTION_GENOME_ALTERED 0.0956, OS_STATUS 0:LIVING, OS_MONTHS 50.597. msk_impact_50k_2026 holds 58 GRCT samples from 56 patients (ages 1 to 77 years); FOXL2 C134W is present in 47 samples. OncoTree has no juvenile subtype code under GRCT, so juvenile and adult cases share the GRCT label. Young GRCT samples in msk_impact_50k_2026 (all labeled GRCT, not juvenile): P-0039024-T01-IM6 age 7, ovary, AKT1 R76_C77insLKTERPRPNTFIIR plus TP53 X293_splice, living at 26.466 months; P-0064771-T01-IM7 age 1, ovary, no mutations called, 2.992 months; P-0061283-T01-IM7 age 16, ovary, no mutations called, 1.973 months; P-0022880-T01-IM6 age 7, primary site Skin, PTPRD T1450R, 21.567 months; all living at last follow-up. Two samples of patient P-0021806 (age 22, ovary primary, metastases) carry BMPR1A G298D (and AXIN1 R723* in one). Other studies with GRCT-labeled samples: msk_ch_2023 (73 samples/patients, all blood normal samples with no mutations listed, FOXL2 not detected), msk_impact_2017 (14 samples, 13 patients; FOXL2 C134W in 12), pan_origimed_2020 (4 samples labeled 'Ovarian Granulosa Cell Tumor', ages 45 to 55, FOXL2 C134W in 3), pog570_bcgsc_2020 (2 samples, ages 52 and 55, both FOXL2 C134W, both deceased), ccle_broad_2019 (2), ccle_broad_2025 (1), ccle_genentech_2014 (1). AACR GENIE cBioPortal requires login (HTTP 401 in the earlier session) and was not queried. AKT1 FOXL2 Public genomic database view of granulosa cell tumors: only one patient is explicitly labeled JGCT (no mutations called in the tumor); FOXL2 C134W dominates adult-type samples and the FOXL2-wild-type, AKT1-insertion GRCT in a 7-year-old is consistent with a JGCT profile but is not labeled juvenile by the database.

title: Randomized Phase II Trial of Paclitaxel and Carboplatin vs. BEP for Advanced Stage and Recurrent Chemonaive Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors of the Ovary (NCT01042522, GOG)
text: GOG-0264 (GOG Foundation/NRG Oncology; PI Jubilee Brown), randomized phase II of paclitaxel/carboplatin vs BEP in newly diagnosed stage IIA-IV or recurrent chemonaive ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors; start 2010-02-08; 63 patients enrolled (31 vs 32) of 128 planned; all female, age 20 or older (mean 47.33 years, SD 13.53). Cell types enrolled: granulosa cell tumor 55 (28 vs 27), Sertoli-Leydig 3, unclassified SCST 4, lipid cell 1. Measurable disease in 23 (11 vs 12), none in 40. Primary outcome, median PFS (RECIST 1.1, ITT): paclitaxel/carboplatin 27.7 months (95% CI 11.2-41.0) vs BEP 19.7 months (95% CI 10.4-52.7); median follow-up 48 months. Secondary: response rate in patients with a target lesion 0.43 (95% CI 0.21-0.67; n=14) vs 0.54 (95% CI 0.29-0.77; n=13); deaths 5/31 vs 8/32; serious adverse events 6/31 vs 11/32; completed protocol cycles 23/31 vs 26/32. Limitations posted: study closed at the interim analysis (planned after 20 PFS events; futility threshold HR >1.10 for paclitaxel/carboplatin relative to BEP) and because of poor accrual, with 63 of 128 patients enrolled. Inhibin A and B changes were a pre-specified other outcome but results are not posted. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor is not a listed condition; participants were adults.  Randomized comparison of TC vs BEP in ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors, predominantly adult-type granulosa cell tumor in adults; informs chemotherapy choices for advanced SCST but contains no pediatric or JGCT-specific data.

title: A rare congenital benign testis tumour in a newborn (ESPR 2013 abstract 076)
author: Czerwinska K
text: Full-term newborn admitted for a left scrotal mass present from birth; testicular ultrasound on day 2 showed a well-defined, large, complex cystic mass with significant septal blood flow on Doppler. Serum tumour markers and karyotype were examined; tumour markers were not elevated and the karyotype was normal. After surgical resection, histology showed juvenile granulosa cell tumour (JGCT). The authors state that testicular JGCT is a benign, rarely diagnosed subset of testicular sex-stromal tumours, most cases occurring in the first 6 months of life, typically as a painless unilateral scrotal mass, hormonally inactive without raised serum markers, and associated with chromosome X abnormalities (not found in this case). The child stays under oncological observation; authors conclude JGCT of the testis should be considered in the differential of scrotal masses in newborns and note that 75% of prepubertal testis tumours are benign.  Neonatal testicular JGCT case with imaging features (complex cystic mass with septal flow), normal markers and normal karyotype.

title: Precocious Puberty Secondary to Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor - A Case Report (APPES 2016 abstract P2-6-24)
author: Malabuyoc MLC
text: 4-year-old girl with prolonged vaginal bleeding, breast budding and abdominal enlargement; elevated estradiol and a left adnexal mass. Surgical excision of the tumor led to cessation of vaginal bleeding and normalization of estradiol; pathology reported a juvenile granulosa tumor of the ovary. The abstract notes that in girls with peripheral precocious puberty a common etiology is an ovarian tumor; no estradiol values, stage, or follow-up duration are given.  Short case of peripheral precocious puberty from ovarian JGCT cured by surgery.

title: Orphanet ORPHA:99915 Malignant granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
text: Orphanet API (definition endpoint, entry dated 2026-07-02) defines ORPHA:99915 as a rare malignant sex cord stromal tumor of the ovary arising from granulosa cells, occurring in peri- and post-menopausal women. Stated presentation: abnormal vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain and distension; the tumor is frequently unilateral and estrogen secreting. Stated natural history: slow, with a tendency to relapse long after the initial diagnosis. The definition describes the adult-type granulosa cell tumor; juvenile granulosa cell tumor is not mentioned in this entry.  Describes the adult-type malignant ovarian granulosa cell tumor (peri/post-menopausal women); it is not a JGCT definition and serves only as a contrast to JGCT.

title: Phase II Study of Paclitaxel for Ovarian Stromal Tumors as Second-Line Therapy (NCT00006227)
text: GOG-0187, single-arm phase II (Gynecologic Oncology Group/NRG Oncology; PI Linda Van Le), start 2000-11-20, completed 2016-07-16; 31 women enrolled and evaluated; conditions listed include adult-type ovarian granulosa cell tumor, gynandroblastoma, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, SCTAT, steroid cell tumor. Population: recurrent ovarian stromal tumor with measurable disease (GOG RECIST) after no more than one prior chemotherapy regimen; ages <40 (n=7), 40-49 (n=8), 50-59 (n=9), 60 or more (n=7); 20 White, 7 Black, 4 Asian. Primary outcome, probability of complete clinical response: 3.2% (80% CI 0.74-15.30); one patient had an indeterminate response. Secondary: median progression-free survival 10.0 months (80% CI 6.0-19.6); median overall survival 73.6 months (80% CI 63.7-112.9); 16 of 31 patients died. Adverse events (CTC 2.0/CTCAE 4.0): serious events in 1 patient each for neutrophil count decrease, WBC decrease, lower limb muscle weakness, hyperglycemia, injection site reaction and febrile neutropenia; common non-serious events included neutropenia 21/31, leukopenia 19/31, anemia 20/31, dermatologic 22/31, pain 22/31, neurologic 21/31. Secondary aim of evaluating inhibin for predicting response is stated in the protocol; no inhibin results are posted. The record does not name JGCT; eligible patients were adults.  Second-line paclitaxel data for recurrent ovarian stromal tumors (mostly adult-type); shows low objective response in an adult-dominated population and is not JGCT-specific.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor
author: Tuteja G
text: Poster abstract (RGCON 2016, MMIMSR Ambala, India) reporting a rare cause of isosexual precocious puberty, ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumour, with a brief literature review. A one-year-old girl presented with abdominal mass, vaginal discharge and rapid onset of pubertal development; she underwent exploratory laparotomy with tumour resection and pathology reported juvenile granulosa cell tumour of the ovary. Authors state that early-stage granulosa cell tumor treated surgically has a good prognosis and adjuvant chemotherapy is not indicated in this setting. The abstract gives no hormone values, stage or follow-up.  Infant JGCT with isosexual precocious puberty; surgery alone, as the authors recommend for early stage.

title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour or adult granulosa cell tumour - a diagnostic dilemma (ECP 2019 abstract E-PS-09-021)
author: Kirigin M
text: 16-year-old girl with irregular cycles; ultrasound showed a 12 cm right ovarian cyst, extirpated with ovary sparing, then salpingo-oophorectomy. First specimen: firm fibrous 0.5 cm wall with cords and trabeculae of small uniform cells and some larger clear-cytoplasm cells, up to 8 mitoses/10 HPF; IHC negative for epithelial, muscle, germ cell, lymphocytic and neuroendocrine markers, strongly positive for vimentin, CD99 and CD56; inhibin and calretinin positive only in larger cells; reticulin fibers around cell groups; read as luteinized granulosa cell tumour. Salpingo-oophorectomy specimen: macrofollicular and solid pattern, same IHC; some solid areas had 40 mitoses/10 HPF with proliferative activity up to 50%; a small area showed classic adult granulosa cell tumour (AGCT) morphology. Authors conclude JGCT and AGCT share morphologic features and diagnostic difficulty arises when JGCT contains AGCT elements, as in this patient. Stage, treatment beyond surgery and outcome are not reported.  Pathology case showing overlap between juvenile and adult granulosa cell tumour morphology in an adolescent.

title: DICER1 Mutations and miRNA in Ovarian and Testicular Sex Cord Stromal Tumors of Childhood (NCT01572467)
text: Children's Oncology Group study ARAR12B2 (sponsor COG; collaborator NCI; PI Dana A. Hill), observational, retrospective, case-only; status COMPLETED (primary completion 2016-07; start 2012-04); estimated enrollment 50. Objective: assess the role of DICER1 mutations and miRNA pathways in the etiology and progression of ovarian or testicular sex cord-stromal tumors. Method: archived fixed and frozen tumor tissue is analyzed for DICER1 mutation and mRNA expression by RT-PCR and laser microdissection, then correlated with age, diagnosis, pathology report, presenting symptoms, family history, treatment, outcome and follow-up. Eligible tissue: from the COG ATBR01 B1 tissue bank and the International Pleuropulmonary Blastoma Registry, Children's Hospital of Boston and Massachusetts General Hospital; ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, juvenile granulosa cell tumor, adult granulosa cell tumor, gynandroblastoma, SCTAT, undifferentiated SCST, Sertoli and Leydig tumors; testicular granulosa cell, Sertoli, Leydig, Sertoli-Leydig and undifferentiated stromal tumors. Primary outcome: correlation between DICER1 mutations and miRNA pathways with outcomes using descriptive analysis. No results are posted on the registry record.  Registered study of DICER1 in pediatric ovarian and testicular sex cord-stromal tumors including JGCT; the record reports design only and no results.

title: Precocious Pseudo-Puberty Presenting with Bilateral Ovarian Involvement and Progressing to Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor in a 2-Year-Old Girl
author: Barakizou H
text: Girl aged 2 years 2 months with premature sexual development (Tanner B3P2A1, bone age 5 years, height +2.6 SD vs midparental -0.4 SD) and a single 3 cm cafe au lait patch; no bony lesion. LHRH test: basal/peak LH 0.43/0.18 mIU/ml, FSH <0.1 mIU/ml; ultrasound showed enlarged cystic ovaries on both sides (left 63 mm, right 66 mm, largest cysts 38 mm). McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS) was considered likely and tamoxifen 20 mg daily started; after 7 weeks there was rapid growth, breast development to B3-4, menorrhagia and bone age 6.5 years; repeat ultrasound showed a left-sided 10x8x6 cm vascular solid/cystic ovarian tumour with a normal right ovary. The tumour torted within a week and was removed: 850 g, juvenile granulosa cell tumour, FIGO stage IA; GNAS mutational analysis negative; AKT1 testing planned. Authors conclude the aetiology remains unclear, with MAS unproven and evolution towards JGCT, highlighting uncertainty about the relationship between MAS and JGCT. GNAS Case in which bilateral ovarian cysts with precocious puberty (MAS presumed) preceded a unilateral JGCT; GNAS negative in tumour.

title: TC or BEP in Treating Patients With Ovarian Malignant Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors (NCT02429700)
text: Multicenter, prospective, randomized phase 3 trial (SCST-01; sponsor/PI Beihua Kong, Shandong University; Qilu Hospital, Jinan, China) comparing paclitaxel plus carboplatin (TC/PT) with BEP in newly diagnosed ovarian malignant sex cord-stromal tumors after surgery; start 2015-04; status RECRUITING (verified 2023-04); estimated enrollment 132. Primary objective: progression-free survival of paclitaxel/carboplatin relative to BEP; secondary: toxicity, overall survival, response rate in measurable disease. Follow-up every 3 months for 2 years, every 6 months for 3 years, then yearly. Eligibility: Chinese women aged 14-65 years (listing says age 65 or younger; minimum age 14), stage IIA-IVB, histologically confirmed granulosa cell, granulosa-theca, Sertoli-Leydig, steroid cell, gynandroblastoma, unclassified SCST or SCTAT; surgery within 8 weeks; Karnofsky score 60 or more. Arms: PT (paclitaxel 175 mg/m2 + carboplatin AUC 5-6, 4-6 courses) vs BEP (bleomycin 30000 IU IM days 1-3, etoposide 100 mg/m2 and cisplatin 20 mg/m2 days 1-5, 3 courses good risk or 4 poor risk). Juvenile granulosa cell tumor is not named; the trial population is mainly adult-type ovarian stromal tumors, with a minimum age of 14. No results posted.  Trial of first-line chemotherapy for malignant ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors; JGCT is not named as an eligible subtype and the minimum age of 14 means it could include only adolescent patients.

title: Ovarian Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor in 9-Month-Old female Infant presented with Isosexual Pseudo Puberty: Case Report
author: Ahmed S
text: 9-month-old girl with a day of bloody vaginal secretions, bilateral breast enlargement for 2 months (Tanner 2) and fine pubic hair; bone age 1.8 years (+4.3 SDS). Labs: estradiol 1091 pmol/l (ref 0-132), FSH and LH <0.3 IU/l, AMH >1714.0 pmol/l (ref 0.1-38.6), inhibin A 385 pg/ml (<4.7), inhibin B 3805 pg/ml (<111), androstenedione 6.8 nmol/l, testosterone 2.2 nmol/l, beta-hCG 0.9 IU/l, AFP 6 kIU/l (normal). Ultrasound: round heterogeneous hypoechoic lesion 5.4x4.12x5.39 cm (62.8 ml), no calcifications; MRI: large solid pelvic lesion related to the left ovary with enhancement and minimal central necrosis; chest CT normal. Open total left salpingo-oophorectomy: encapsulated ovoid 75 g mass, 100x50x40 mm, solid yellow nodular cut surface, capsule intact; histopathology juvenile-type granulosa cell tumor pT1a, inhibin A positive; no chemotherapy or radiation. At 1 month estradiol was 62 pmol/l and AMH 9 pmol/l; authors conclude surgical removal was curative with all hormones regressing to prepubertal levels.  Infant JGCT with very high AMH and inhibin A/B at diagnosis and normalisation of estradiol and AMH after surgery alone.

title: Testicular juvenile granulosa cell tumour: a case report in a newborn (ECP 2019 abstract PS-16-002)
author: Barona Garcia L
text: Neonate aged 10 days with an enlarged descended right testis, smooth and firm; alpha-fetoprotein slightly increased; scrotal ultrasound showed a multicystic mass with internal vascular flow replacing the testis. Right radical inguinal orchiectomy without complications. Gross: 2.2 x 1.5 x 1.0 cm gray-white ovoid mass with multiple cysts of light yellow glistening fluid. Histology: follicles of varying size lined by bland oval to round cells in single and multiple layers with basophilic luminal fluid; fibrous stroma with actin-positive spindle cells around follicles. IHC: tumour cells positive for inhibin, WT1 and calretinin; negative for panCK, AFP, CD30, CD117, PLAP, D2-40 and OCT3/4; diagnosis juvenile granulosa cell tumour. Authors state JGCT is the most common testicular tumour in infants younger than 6 months, with few reported cases; its importance lies in the differential with yolk sac tumour and other sex cord-stromal tumours.  Neonatal testicular JGCT with a slightly raised AFP and a full IHC panel (inhibin, WT1, calretinin positive; AFP, OCT3/4 negative).

title: Precocious puberty and ovarian tumors - 2 case reports
text: Two-case abstract of peripheral precocious puberty from ovarian tumors; only case 1 was a juvenile granulosa cell tumor (JGCT). Case 1: 3-year-old girl, breast enlargement over 1 year, irregular vaginal bleeding for 10 months, pubic hair for 2 months, Tanner B3P3, firm mobile pelvic mass in right lower abdomen; bone age 8 years 10 months vs chronological age 3 years. Case 1 hormones: LH <0.1 and FSH <0.1 mIU/ml, testosterone 0.334 ng/ml, DHEAS 17.97 ug/dl, estradiol >1000 pg/ml; CT showed a heterogeneously enhancing abdomino-pelvic mass without separately visualised ovaries; resected right tubo-ovarian mass was juvenile granulosa cell tumor; estradiol fell to 17 pg/ml; no vaginal bleeding at 1 year. Case 2: 6-year-old girl, breast enlargement over 7 months, cyclical vaginal bleeding for 4 months, Tanner B3P3, bone age 7.8 years, estradiol 162.8 pg/ml (text also gives 162.9), CT showed a bulky 5.4 cm left ovary; laparoscopic resection of the 'right' tubo-ovarian mass showed a mixed germ cell sex cord stromal tumor; estradiol 14.37 pg/ml afterwards; no bleeding at 6 months. Authors conclude the cases illustrate heterogeneity in presentation, biochemistry and histopathology; both had successful outcomes without recurrence (12 and 6 months follow-up as stated).  Peripheral precocious puberty from JGCT with estradiol above 1000 pg/ml and normalisation after oophorectomy; contrasted with a mixed sex cord-stromal tumor.

title: International Pleuropulmonary Blastoma/DICER1 Registry (NCT03382158)
text: International PPB/DICER1 Registry (Children's Hospitals and Clinics of Minnesota; PI Kris Ann Schultz), observational cohort patient registry; status RECRUITING (verified 2026-10); start 2016-12-06; estimated enrollment 3,400; primary completion estimated 2031-12-06. Inclusion: known or suspected PPB or related thoracic tumor; known or suspected sex cord-stromal tumor including Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor and gynandroblastoma (males or females); other DICER1-related conditions; and individuals with known or suspected DICER1 pathogenic variants regardless of disease. Listed DICER1-associated conditions include Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, gynandroblastoma, ovarian sarcoma, PPB, lung and renal cysts, cystic nephroma, Wilms tumor, CNS sarcoma, pineoblastoma, pituitary blastoma, multinodular goiter, thyroid carcinoma, nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma, ciliary body medulloepithelioma, intestinal polyps and embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor is not named in the summary or eligibility text. The registry estimates 30-50 cases of Type I and Ir PPB and 40-60 cases of Type II and III PPB diagnosed annually worldwide. Treatment described is the treating institution's choice: Type I PPB surgery with optional 22-week VAC/VA chemotherapy; Type II/III PPB surgery, chemotherapy (often 36-week IVADo) and sometimes radiation. Primary outcome: event-free survival (7 years); secondary: response, overall survival, quality of life, cardiac and pulmonary outcomes, and incidence of neoplasms in individuals with germline DICER1 variants. Tumor tissue, blood, urine and CSF may be banked. No results posted.  Registry of DICER1-related tumors and carriers; it enrolls sex cord-stromal tumors (Sertoli-Leydig, gynandroblastoma) but does not name JGCT, so relevance to JGCT is indirect (DICER1 context).
